atoms.title: Official API documentation: numpy.quantile (numpy 2.5.3)
atoms.text:
Docstring of the installed package, unchanged.

```text
numpy.quantile(a, q, axis=None, out=None, overwrite_input=False, method='linear', keepdims=False, *, weights=None)

Compute the q-th quantile of the data along the specified axis.

Parameters
----------
a : array_like of real numbers
    Input array or object that can be converted to an array.
q : array_like of float
    Probability or sequence of probabilities of the quantiles to compute.
    Values must be between 0 and 1 inclusive.
axis : {int, tuple of int, None}, optional
    Axis or axes along which the quantiles are computed. The default is
    to compute the quantile(s) along a flattened version of the array.
out : ndarray, optional
    Alternative output array in which to place the result. It must have
    the same shape and buffer length as the expected output, but the
    type (of the output) will be cast if necessary.
overwrite_input : bool, optional
    If True, then allow the input array `a` to be modified by
    intermediate calculations, to save memory. In this case, the
    contents of the input `a` after this function completes is
    undefined.
method : str, optional
    This parameter specifies the method to use for estimating the
    quantile.  There are many different methods, some unique to NumPy.
    The recommended options, numbered as they appear in [1]_, are:

    1. 'inverted_cdf'
    2. 'averaged_inverted_cdf'
    3. 'closest_observation'
    4. 'interpolated_inverted_cdf'
    5. 'hazen'
    6. 'weibull'
    7. 'linear'  (default)
    8. 'median_unbiased'
    9. 'normal_unbiased'

    The first three methods are discontinuous. For backward compatibility
    with previous versions of NumPy, the following discontinuous variations
    of the default 'linear' (7.) option are available:

    * 'lower'
    * 'higher',
    * 'midpoint'
    * 'nearest'

    See Notes for details.

    .. versionchanged:: 1.22.0
        This argument was previously called "interpolation" and only
        offered the "linear" default and last four options.

keepdims : bool, optional
    If this is set to True, the axes which are reduced are left in
    the result as dimensions with size one. With this option, the
    result will broadcast correctly against the original array `a`.

weights : array_like, optional
    An array of weights associated with the values in `a`. Each value in
    `a` contributes to the quantile according to its associated weight.
    The weights array can either be 1-D (in which case its length must be
    the size of `a` along the given axis) or of the same shape as `a`.
    If `weights=None`, then all data in `a` are assumed to have a
    weight equal to one.
    Only `method="inverted_cdf"` supports weights.
    See the notes for more details.

    .. versionadded:: 2.0.0

Returns
-------
quantile : scalar or ndarray
    If `q` is a single probability and `axis=None`, then the result
    is a scalar. If multiple probability levels are given, first axis
    of the result corresponds to the quantiles. The other axes are
    the axes that remain after the reduction of `a`. If the input
    contains integers or floats smaller than ``float64``, the output
    data-type is ``float64``. Otherwise, the output data-type is the
    same as that of the input. If `out` is specified, that array is
    returned instead.

See Also
--------
mean
percentile : equivalent to quantile, but with q in the range [0, 100].
median : equivalent to ``quantile(..., 0.5)``
nanquantile

Notes
-----
Given a sample `a` from an underlying distribution, `quantile` provides a
nonparametric estimate of the inverse cumulative distribution function.

By default, this is done by interpolating between adjacent elements in
``y``, a sorted copy of `a`::

    (1-g)*y[j] + g*y[j+1]

where the index ``j`` and coefficient ``g`` are the integral and
fractional components of ``q * (n-1)``, and ``n`` is the number of
elements in the sample.

This is a special case of Equation 1 of H&F [1]_. More generally,

- ``j = (q*n + m - 1) // 1``, and
- ``g = (q*n + m - 1) % 1``,

where ``m`` may be defined according to several different conventions.
The preferred convention may be selected using the ``method`` parameter:

=============================== =============== ===============
``method``                      number in H&F   ``m``
=============================== =============== ===============
``interpolated_inverted_cdf``   4               ``0``
``hazen``                       5               ``1/2``
``weibull``                     6               ``q``
``linear`` (default)            7               ``1 - q``
``median_unbiased``             8               ``q/3 + 1/3``
``normal_unbiased``             9               ``q/4 + 3/8``
=============================== =============== ===============

Note that indices ``j`` and ``j + 1`` are clipped to the range ``0`` to
``n - 1`` when the results of the formula would be outside the allowed
range of non-negative indices. The ``- 1`` in the formulas for ``j`` and
``g`` accounts for Python's 0-based indexing.

The table above includes only the estimators from H&F that are continuous
functions of probability `q` (estimators 4-9). NumPy also provides the
three discontinuous estimators from H&F (estimators 1-3), where ``j`` is
defined as above, ``m`` is defined as follows, and ``g`` is a function
of the real-valued ``index = q*n + m - 1`` and ``j``.

1. ``inverted_cdf``: ``m = 0`` and ``g = int(index - j > 0)``
2. ``averaged_inverted_cdf``: ``m = 0`` and
   ``g = (1 + int(index - j > 0)) / 2``
3. ``closest_observation``: ``m = -1/2`` and
   ``g = 1 - int((index == j) & (j%2 == 1))``

For backward compatibility with previous versions of NumPy, `quantile`
provides four additional discontinuous estimators. Like
``method='linear'``, all have ``m = 1 - q`` so that ``j = q*(n-1) // 1``,
but ``g`` is defined as follows.

- ``lower``: ``g = 0``
- ``midpoint``: ``g = 0.5``
- ``higher``: ``g = 1``
- ``nearest``: ``g = (q*(n-1) % 1) > 0.5``

**Weighted quantiles:**
More formally, the quantile at probability level :math:`q` of a cumulative
distribution function :math:`F(y)=P(Y \leq y)` with probability measure
:math:`P` is defined as any number :math:`x` that fulfills the
*coverage conditions*

.. math:: P(Y < x) \leq q \quad\text{and}\quad P(Y \leq x) \geq q

with random variable :math:`Y\sim P`.
Sample quantiles, the result of `quantile`, provide nonparametric
estimation of the underlying population counterparts, represented by the
unknown :math:`F`, given a data vector `a` of length ``n``.

Some of the estimators above arise when one considers :math:`F` as the
empirical distribution function of the data, i.e.
:math:`F(y) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i 1_{a_i \leq y}`.
Then, different methods correspond to different choices of :math:`x` that
fulfill the above coverage conditions. Methods that follow this approach
are ``inverted_cdf`` and ``averaged_inverted_cdf``.

For weighted quantiles, the coverage conditions still hold. The
empirical cumulative distribution is simply replaced by its weighted
version, i.e.
:math:`P(Y \leq t) = \frac{1}{\sum_i w_i} \sum_i w_i 1_{x_i \leq t}`.
Only ``method="inverted_cdf"`` supports weights.

Examples
--------
>>> import numpy as np
>>> a = np.array([[10, 7, 4], [3, 2, 1]])
>>> a
array([[10,  7,  4],
       [ 3,  2,  1]])
>>> np.quantile(a, 0.5)
3.5
>>> np.quantile(a, 0.5, axis=0)
array([6.5, 4.5, 2.5])
>>> np.quantile(a, 0.5, axis=1)
array([7.,  2.])
>>> np.quantile(a, 0.5, axis=1, keepdims=True)
array([[7.],
       [2.]])
>>> m = np.quantile(a, 0.5, axis=0)
>>> out = np.zeros_like(m)
>>> np.quantile(a, 0.5, axis=0, out=out)
array([6.5, 4.5, 2.5])
>>> m
array([6.5, 4.5, 2.5])
>>> b = a.copy()
>>> np.quantile(b, 0.5, axis=1, overwrite_input=True)
array([7.,  2.])
>>> assert not np.all(a == b)

See also `numpy.percentile` for a visualization of most methods.

References
----------
.. [1] R. J. Hyndman and Y. Fan,
   "Sample quantiles in statistical packages,"
   The American Statistician, 50(4), pp. 361-365, 1996
```

atoms.title: Official API documentation: scipy.stats.chi2 (scipy 1.18.1)
atoms.text:
Docstring of the installed package, unchanged.

```text
scipy.stats.chi2(*args, **kwds)

A chi-squared continuous random variable.

For the noncentral chi-square distribution, see `ncx2`.

As an instance of the `rv_continuous` class, `chi2` object inherits from it
a collection of generic methods (see below for the full list),
and completes them with details specific for this particular distribution.

Methods
-------
rvs(df, loc=0, scale=1, size=1, random_state=None)
    Random variates.
pdf(x, df, loc=0, scale=1)
    Probability density function.
logpdf(x, df, loc=0, scale=1)
    Log of the probability density function.
cdf(x, df, loc=0, scale=1)
    Cumulative distribution function.
logcdf(x, df, loc=0, scale=1)
    Log of the cumulative distribution function.
sf(x, df, loc=0, scale=1)
    Survival function  (also defined as ``1 - cdf``, but `sf` is sometimes more accurate).
logsf(x, df, loc=0, scale=1)
    Log of the survival function.
ppf(q, df, loc=0, scale=1)
    Percent point function (inverse of ``cdf`` --- percentiles).
isf(q, df, loc=0, scale=1)
    Inverse survival function (inverse of ``sf``).
moment(order, df, loc=0, scale=1)
    Non-central moment of the specified order.
stats(df, loc=0, scale=1, moments='mv')
    Mean('m'), variance('v'), skew('s'), and/or kurtosis('k').
entropy(df, loc=0, scale=1)
    (Differential) entropy of the RV.
fit(data)
    Parameter estimates for generic data.
    See `scipy.stats.rv_continuous.fit <https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.rv_continuous.fit.html#scipy.stats.rv_continuous.fit>`__ for detailed documentation of the
    keyword arguments.
expect(func, args=(df,), loc=0, scale=1, lb=None, ub=None, conditional=False, **kwds)
    Expected value of a function (of one argument) with respect to the distribution.
median(df, loc=0, scale=1)
    Median of the distribution.
mean(df, loc=0, scale=1)
    Mean of the distribution.
var(df, loc=0, scale=1)
    Variance of the distribution.
std(df, loc=0, scale=1)
    Standard deviation of the distribution.
interval(confidence, df, loc=0, scale=1)
    Confidence interval with equal areas around the median.

See Also
--------
ncx2

Notes
-----
The probability density function for `chi2` is:

.. math::

    f(x, k) = \frac{1}{2^{k/2} \Gamma \left( k/2 \right)}
               x^{k/2-1} \exp \left( -x/2 \right)

for :math:`x > 0`  and :math:`k > 0` (degrees of freedom, denoted ``df``
in the implementation).

`chi2` takes ``df`` as a shape parameter.

The chi-squared distribution is a special case of the gamma
distribution, with gamma parameters ``a = df/2``, ``loc = 0`` and
``scale = 2``.

The probability density above is defined in the "standardized" form. To shift
and/or scale the distribution use the ``loc`` and ``scale`` parameters.
Specifically, ``chi2.pdf(x, df, loc, scale)`` is identically
equivalent to ``chi2.pdf(y, df) / scale`` with
``y = (x - loc) / scale``. Note that shifting the location of a distribution
does not make it a "noncentral" distribution; noncentral generalizations of
some distributions are available in separate classes.

Examples
--------
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from scipy.stats import chi2
>>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
>>> fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1)

Get the support:

>>> df = 55
>>> lb, ub = chi2.support(df)

Calculate the first four moments:

>>> mean, var, skew, kurt = chi2.stats(df, moments='mvsk')

Display the probability density function (``pdf``):

>>> x = np.linspace(chi2.ppf(0.01, df),
...                 chi2.ppf(0.99, df), 100)
>>> ax.plot(x, chi2.pdf(x, df),
...        'r-', lw=5, alpha=0.6, label='chi2 pdf')

Alternatively, the distribution object can be called (as a function)
to fix the shape, location and scale parameters. This returns a "frozen"
RV object holding the given parameters fixed.

Freeze the distribution and display the frozen ``pdf``:

>>> rv = chi2(df)
>>> ax.plot(x, rv.pdf(x), 'k-', lw=2, label='frozen pdf')

Check accuracy of ``cdf`` and ``ppf``:

>>> vals = chi2.ppf([0.001, 0.5, 0.999], df)
>>> np.allclose([0.001, 0.5, 0.999], chi2.cdf(vals, df))
True

Generate random numbers:

>>> r = chi2.rvs(df, size=1000)

And compare the histogram:

>>> ax.hist(r, density=True, bins='auto', histtype='stepfilled', alpha=0.2)
>>> ax.set_xlim([x[0], x[-1]])
>>> ax.legend(loc='best', frameon=False)
>>> plt.show()
```

A generalized Pareto continuous random variable.

As an instance of the `rv_continuous` class, `genpareto` object inherits from it
a collection of generic methods (see below for the full list),
and completes them with details specific for this particular distribution.

Methods
-------
rvs(c, loc=0, scale=1, size=1, random_state=None)
    Random variates.

sf(x, c, loc=0, scale=1)
    Survival function  (also defined as ``1 - cdf``, but `sf` is sometimes more accurate).
logsf(x, c, loc=0, scale=1)
    Log of the survival function.
ppf(q, c, loc=0, scale=1)
    Percent point function (inverse of ``cdf`` --- percentiles).

    Inverse survival function (inverse of ``sf``).
moment(order, c, loc=0, scale=1)
    Non-central moment of the specified order.

    Mean('m'), variance('v'), skew('s'), and/or kurtosis('k').
entropy(c, loc=0, scale=1)
    (Differential) entropy of the RV.
fit(data)
    Parameter estimates for generic data.
    See `scipy.stats.rv_continuous.fit <https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.rv_continuous.fit.html#scipy.stats.rv_continuous.fit>`__ for detailed documentation of the
    keyword arguments.
expect(func, args=(c,), loc=0, scale=1, lb=None, ub=None, conditional=False, **kwds)
    Expected value of a function (of one argument) with respect to the distribution.
median(c, loc=0, scale=1)
    Median of the distribution.
mean(c, loc=0, scale=1)
    Mean of the distribution.
var(c, loc=0, scale=1)
    Variance of the distribution.
std(c, loc=0, scale=1)
    Standard deviation of the distribution.
interval(confidence, c, loc=0, scale=1)
    Confidence interval with equal areas around the median.

Notes
-----
The probability density function for `genpareto` is:

.. math::

    f(x, c) = (1 + c x)^{-1 - 1/c}

defined for :math:`x \ge 0` if :math:`c \ge 0`, and for
:math:`0 \le x \le -1/c` if :math:`c < 0`.

`genpareto` takes ``c`` as a shape parameter for :math:`c`.

For :math:`c=0`, `genpareto` reduces to the exponential
distribution, `expon`:

.. math::

    f(x, 0) = \exp(-x)

For :math:`c=-1`, `genpareto` is uniform on ``[0, 1]``:

.. math::

    f(x, -1) = 1

The probability density above is defined in the "standardized" form. To shift
and/or scale the distribution use the ``loc`` and ``scale`` parameters.
Specifically, ``genpareto.pdf(x, c, loc, scale)`` is identically
equivalent to ``genpareto.pdf(y, c) / scale`` with
``y = (x - loc) / scale``. Note that shifting the location of a distribution
does not make it a "noncentral" distribution; noncentral generalizations of
some distributions are available in separate classes.

Examples
--------
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from scipy.stats import genpareto
>>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
>>> fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1)

Get the support:

>>> c = 0.1
>>> lb, ub = genpareto.support(c)

Calculate the first four moments:

>>> mean, var, skew, kurt = genpareto.stats(c, moments='mvsk')

Display the probability density function (``pdf``):

>>> x = np.linspace(genpareto.ppf(0.01, c),
...                 genpareto.ppf(0.99, c), 100)
>>> ax.plot(x, genpareto.pdf(x, c),
...        'r-', lw=5, alpha=0.6, label='genpareto pdf')

Alternatively, the distribution object can be called (as a function)
to fix the shape, location and scale parameters. This returns a "frozen"
RV object holding the given parameters fixed.

Freeze the distribution and display the frozen ``pdf``:

>>> rv = genpareto(c)
>>> ax.plot(x, rv.pdf(x), 'k-', lw=2, label='frozen pdf')

Check accuracy of ``cdf`` and ``ppf``:

>>> vals = genpareto.ppf([0.001, 0.5, 0.999], c)
>>> np.allclose([0.001, 0.5, 0.999], genpareto.cdf(vals, c))
True

Generate random numbers:

>>> r = genpareto.rvs(c, size=1000)

And compare the histogram:

>>> ax.hist(r, density=True, bins='auto', histtype='stepfilled', alpha=0.2)
>>> ax.set_xlim([x[0], x[-1]])
>>> ax.legend(loc='best', frameon=False)
>>> plt.show()
```

atoms.title: Official API documentation: scipy.stats.rv_continuous.fit (scipy 1.18.1)
atoms.text:
Docstring of the installed package, unchanged.

```text
scipy.stats.rv_continuous.fit(self, data, *args, **kwds)

Return estimates of shape (if applicable), location, and scale
parameters from data. The default estimation method is Maximum
Likelihood Estimation (MLE), but Method of Moments (MM)
is also available.

Starting estimates for the fit are given by input arguments;
for any arguments not provided with starting estimates,
``self._fitstart(data)`` is called to generate such.

One can hold some parameters fixed to specific values by passing in
keyword arguments ``f0``, ``f1``, ..., ``fn`` (for shape parameters)
and ``floc`` and ``fscale`` (for location and scale parameters,
respectively).

Parameters
----------
data : array_like or `CensoredData` instance
    Data to use in estimating the distribution parameters.
arg1, arg2, arg3,... : floats, optional
    Starting value(s) for any shape-characterizing arguments (those not
    provided will be determined by a call to ``_fitstart(data)``).
    No default value.
**kwds : floats, optional
    - `loc`: initial guess of the distribution's location parameter.
    - `scale`: initial guess of the distribution's scale parameter.

    Special keyword arguments are recognized as holding certain
    parameters fixed:

    - f0, ..., fn : hold respective shape parameters fixed.
      Alternatively, shape parameters to fix can be specified by name.
      For example, if ``self.shapes == "a, b"``, ``fa`` and ``fix_a``
      are equivalent to ``f0``, and ``fb`` and ``fix_b`` are
      equivalent to ``f1``.

    - floc : hold location parameter fixed to specified value.

    - fscale : hold scale parameter fixed to specified value.

    - optimizer : The optimizer to use.  The optimizer must take
      ``func`` and starting position as the first two arguments,
      plus ``args`` (for extra arguments to pass to the
      function to be optimized) and ``disp``.
      The ``fit`` method calls the optimizer with ``disp=0`` to suppress output.
      The optimizer must return the estimated parameters.

    - method : The method to use. The default is "MLE" (Maximum
      Likelihood Estimate); "MM" (Method of Moments)
      is also available.

Raises
------
TypeError, ValueError
    If an input is invalid
`~scipy.stats.FitError`
    If fitting fails or the fit produced would be invalid

Returns
-------
parameter_tuple : tuple of floats
    Estimates for any shape parameters (if applicable), followed by
    those for location and scale. For most random variables, shape
    statistics will be returned, but there are exceptions (e.g.
    ``norm``).

Notes
-----
With ``method="MLE"`` (default), the fit is computed by minimizing
the negative log-likelihood function. A large, finite penalty
(rather than infinite negative log-likelihood) is applied for
observations beyond the support of the distribution.

With ``method="MM"``, the fit is computed by minimizing the L2 norm
of the relative errors between the first *k* raw (about zero) data
moments and the corresponding distribution moments, where *k* is the
number of non-fixed parameters.
More precisely, the objective function is::

    (((data_moments - dist_moments)
      / np.maximum(np.abs(data_moments), 1e-8))**2).sum()

where the constant ``1e-8`` avoids division by zero in case of
vanishing data moments. Typically, this error norm can be reduced to
zero.
Note that the standard method of moments can produce parameters for
which some data are outside the support of the fitted distribution;
this implementation does nothing to prevent this.

For either method,
the returned answer is not guaranteed to be globally optimal; it
may only be locally optimal, or the optimization may fail altogether.
If the data contain any of ``np.nan``, ``np.inf``, or ``-np.inf``,
the `fit` method will raise a ``RuntimeError``.

When passing a ``CensoredData`` instance to ``data``, the log-likelihood
function is defined as:

.. math::

    l(\pmb{\theta}; k) & = \sum
                            \log(f(k_u; \pmb{\theta}))
                        + \sum
                            \log(F(k_l; \pmb{\theta})) \\
                        & + \sum
                            \log(1 - F(k_r; \pmb{\theta})) \\
                        & + \sum
                            \log(F(k_{\text{high}, i}; \pmb{\theta})
                            - F(k_{\text{low}, i}; \pmb{\theta}))

where :math:`f` and :math:`F` are the pdf and cdf, respectively, of the
function being fitted, :math:`\pmb{\theta}` is the parameter vector,
:math:`u` are the indices of uncensored observations,
:math:`l` are the indices of left-censored observations,
:math:`r` are the indices of right-censored observations,
subscripts "low"/"high" denote endpoints of interval-censored observations, and
:math:`i` are the indices of interval-censored observations.

Examples
--------

Generate some data to fit: draw random variates from the `beta`
distribution

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from scipy.stats import beta
>>> a, b = 1., 2.
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(172786373191770012695001057628748821561)
>>> x = beta.rvs(a, b, size=1000, random_state=rng)

Now we can fit all four parameters (``a``, ``b``, ``loc`` and
``scale``):

>>> a1, b1, loc1, scale1 = beta.fit(x)
>>> a1, b1, loc1, scale1
(1.0198945204435628, 1.9484708982737828, 4.372241314917588e-05, 0.9979078845964814)

The fit can be done also using a custom optimizer:

>>> from scipy.optimize import minimize
>>> def custom_optimizer(func, x0, args=(), disp=0):
...     res = minimize(func, x0, args, method="slsqp", options={"disp": disp})
...     if res.success:
...         return res.x
...     raise RuntimeError('optimization routine failed')
>>> a1, b1, loc1, scale1 = beta.fit(x, method="MLE", optimizer=custom_optimizer)
>>> a1, b1, loc1, scale1
(1.0198821087258905, 1.948484145914738, 4.3705304486881485e-05, 0.9979104663953395)

We can also use some prior knowledge about the dataset: let's keep
``loc`` and ``scale`` fixed:

>>> a1, b1, loc1, scale1 = beta.fit(x, floc=0, fscale=1)
>>> loc1, scale1
(0, 1)

We can also keep shape parameters fixed by using ``f``-keywords. To
keep the zero-th shape parameter ``a`` equal 1, use ``f0=1`` or,
equivalently, ``fa=1``:

>>> a1, b1, loc1, scale1 = beta.fit(x, fa=1, floc=0, fscale=1)
>>> a1
1

Not all distributions return estimates for the shape parameters.
``norm`` for example just returns estimates for location and scale:

>>> from scipy.stats import norm
>>> x = norm.rvs(a, b, size=1000, random_state=123)
>>> loc1, scale1 = norm.fit(x)
>>> loc1, scale1
(0.92087172783841631, 2.0015750750324668)
```

atoms.title: Glossary as code: defaults for terms a task may state without a formula / units after a fit on 100 * r (every reported GARCH output)
atoms.text:
## units after a fit on 100 * r (every reported GARCH output)

```python
omega = res.params["omega"] / 100**2                      # decimal daily variance units
alpha, beta = res.params["alpha[1]"], res.params["beta[1]"]  # unchanged by the scaling
cond_vol = res.conditional_volatility / 100                 # decimal daily volatility
assert omega < 1e-3 and float(cond_vol.mean()) < 0.1, "still in percent units"
```

atoms.title: Glossary as code: defaults for terms a task may state without a formula / long-run (unconditional) variance and volatility of GARCH(1,1)
atoms.text:
## long-run (unconditional) variance and volatility of GARCH(1,1)

```python
assert alpha + beta < 1
long_run_var = omega / (1 - alpha - beta)                   # decimal daily variance
long_run_vol_ann = np.sqrt(B * long_run_var)                # "unconditional vol (annualised, decimal)"
assert 0.03 < long_run_vol_ann < 1.5, long_run_vol_ann
```

atoms.title: Glossary as code: defaults for terms a task may state without a formula / annualised (any volatility, variance or mean return)
atoms.text:
## annualised (any volatility, variance or mean return)

```python
vol_ann = vol_daily * np.sqrt(B)                            # also for composite, portfolio and long-run volatilities
var_ann = var_daily * B
mean_ann = mean_daily_log_return * B
assert 0.03 < float(np.nanmean(vol_ann)) < 1.5              # an annual volatility, not a daily one
```

## standardised residuals

```python
z = res.std_resid                                           # residual / conditional volatility, no units
assert abs(float(z.std()) - 1) < 0.2
```

## return type kept throughout

```python
port_ret = r @ w                                            # the same return series (log or simple) the task defined first
```
Do not rebuild returns from prices with the other definition at a later step (backtests included).

atoms.title: Glossary as code: defaults for terms a task may state without a formula / VaR and ES as positive losses
atoms.text:
## VaR and ES as positive losses

```python
p = 0.01                                                    # tail probability: a "1% VaR" and a "99% VaR" both mean p = 0.01
z_q = norm.ppf(p)                                           # -2.326
var_p = -(mu + sigma * z_q)                                 # keep mu unless the task states a zero mean
es_p = -mu + sigma * norm.pdf(z_q) / p                      # divide by the tail probability p, not by 1 - p
assert es_p > var_p > 0 and 1.1 < (es_p + mu) / (var_p + mu) < 1.3
```

atoms.title: Glossary as code: defaults for terms a task may state without a formula / warm-up: indicators that do not exist yet
atoms.text:
## warm-up: indicators that do not exist yet

```python
valid = fast.notna() & slow.notna()
signal = pd.DataFrame(np.where(fast > slow, 1.0, -1.0), index=fast.index, columns=fast.columns).where(valid)
```
`np.where` on NaN returns the "else" value (a full short position) unless the rows are masked first.

Sources: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (scaling with trading days); Bollerslev (1986) and Engle (2001,
J. Econ. Perspectives) for GARCH variance; McNeil, Frey and Embrechts, Quantitative Risk Management (VaR, ES,
standardised residuals); arch 8.0.0 API reference.

atoms.title: arch 8.0.0: which call and which output for a task
atoms.text:
Use the installed arch functions; their official descriptions are attached separately. This entry only adds what those
descriptions leave open.

Which output:
- volatility of in-sample period t as forecast the day before (the label arch uses): `res.conditional_volatility[t]`.
- volatility known once day t has closed (end-of-day signals, sizing, regimes): `res.forecast(horizon=1, start=0, align="origin")` row t, which equals `conditional_volatility[t+1]`.
- volatility for the day after the sample (pricing, current VaR): `res.forecast(horizon=1)` last row, not
  `conditional_volatility[-1]`; annualize with sqrt(252) when an annual volatility is reported.
- standardized residuals for EVT or filtered simulation: `res.std_resid`.

Units after a fit on `100 * r` (r in decimal): mu and every volatility / 100; omega and every variance / 100**2; alpha,
beta and nu unchanged. Long-run variance = omega / (1 - alpha - beta) with omega already divided by 100**2.

Fit checks: `convergence_flag == 0` does not prove the optimizer moved; compare `res.params` with the starting values.

Resampling: `StationaryBootstrap` draws random numbers in its own order. When the task prescribes the draws (a named
generator with explicit uniform and geometric draws), write those draws directly.

atoms.title: Asian Options under Black–Scholes / 1. Shared Foundations
atoms.text:
## 1. Shared Foundations

Map quantities by meaning and units, not by letter; revisit the mapping when inputs or contract conventions change.

| Symbol | Definition |
|---|---|
| $S$ | Current underlying price, strictly positive |
| $r, q$ | Constant annual continuous risk-free rate and dividend yield |
| $\sigma$ | Annual volatility in decimal units |
| $t_{i}$ | Time in years from valuation to fixing i |
| $w_{i}$ | Nonnegative fixing weight, with $\sum  w_{i} = 1$ |
| $T$ | Final fixing time (end of the averaging window), in years |
| $T_{p}$ | Time in years to payment, $T_{p} \ge  T$ |
| $K$ | Fixed strike, positive unless handled separately |
| $A, G$ | Arithmetic and geometric averages |
| $\Phi , \phi$ | Standard normal CDF and density |

Notation: $\sum_i$ sums over fixing indices; $\cdot$ denotes multiplication. $\operatorname{Normal}(  \mu , v )$ uses variance v, not standard deviation. Displayed formulas are mathematical notation, not executable Python.

All expectations below are risk-neutral. Under constant-parameter GBM,
**Risk-neutral stock dynamics**

$$
\mathrm{d}S_{t} / S_{t} = (r - q) \cdot  \mathrm{d}t + \sigma  \cdot  \mathrm{d}W_{t}
$$

**Log-price solution**

$$
\ln (S_{t}) = \ln (S) + (r - q - \sigma ^{2} / 2) \cdot  t + \sigma  \cdot  W_{t}
$$

Write $\nu  = r - q - \sigma ^{2} / 2$. A supplied log drift already includes the Itô correction. For FX, q is the foreign rate; historical mean returns do not replace the risk-neutral drift.

For future fixings, let $X_{i} = \ln (S(t_{i}))$; these log prices are jointly normal.

**Mean of the log price at fixing date $t_{i}$**

$\mu _{i}$ is the risk-neutral expectation of $X_{i}$.

$$
\mu _{i} = \ln (S) + \nu  \cdot  t_{i}
$$

**Covariance between log fixings**

$$
\Sigma _{ij} = \sigma ^{2} \cdot  \min (t_{i}, t_{j})
$$

Set $\mathrm{disc} = \exp (-r \cdot  T_{p})$. Discount a terminal payoff once: $V = \mathrm{disc} \cdot  \operatorname{E}[\;\text{payoff}\;]$. For zero volatility or fully known fixings, evaluate the deterministic payoff instead of dividing by a zero variance.

atoms.title: Asian Options under Black–Scholes / 2. Contract and Fixing Schedule
atoms.text:
## 2. Contract and Fixing Schedule

**Discrete arithmetic average**

$$
A = \sum _{i}(w_{i} \cdot  S(t_{i}))
$$

**Discrete geometric average**

$$
G = \exp (\sum _{i}(w_{i} \cdot  \ln (S(t_{i}))))
$$

| Contract | Call payoff | Put payoff |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed-strike arithmetic | $\max ( A-K, 0 )$ | $\max ( K-A, 0 )$ |
| Fixed-strike geometric | $\max ( G-K, 0 )$ | $\max ( K-G, 0 )$ |
| Floating-strike arithmetic | $\max (  S_{T} -A, 0 )$ | $\max ( A- S_{T} , 0 )$ |

Here $\max ( x, 0 )$ denotes the positive part. Floating-strike terminology can differ: the specified payoff controls.

Build the actual fixing vector, not a generic time grid. Equal spacing with n future fixings and no initial fixing means $t_{i} = i \cdot  T / n$, $i=1,\ldots ,n$, and $w_{i}=1/n$. Including today's price changes both weights and moments. Payment may occur after averaging ends. Historical observations already fixed are constants, not resimulated prices.

Continuous averaging is a different contract. For a fresh uniform window [0,T],
**Continuous arithmetic average**

$$
A = (1 / T) \cdot  \int_{0}^{T}(S_{t}) \mathrm{d}t
$$

**Continuous geometric average**

$$
\ln (G) = (1 / T) \cdot  \int_{0}^{T}(\ln (S_{t})) \mathrm{d}t
$$

Discrete formulas approximate these integrals only as an explicitly chosen numerical approximation.

atoms.title: Asian Options under Black–Scholes / 3. Geometric Average: Exact Pricing
atoms.text:
## 3. Geometric Average: Exact Pricing

Use [Shared Foundations](#1-shared-foundations) and the fixing schedule in Section 2.

Because a linear combination of jointly normal variables is normal,
**Normal distribution of the log geometric average**

$$
\begin{gathered}
Y = \ln (G) \sim \operatorname{Normal}(\mu _{G}, v_{G}) \\
\mu _{G} = \sum _{i}(w_{i} \cdot  \mu _{i}) \\
v_{G} = \sum _{i} \sum _{j}(w_{i} \cdot  w_{j} \cdot  \Sigma _{ij})
\end{gathered}
$$

Define $F_{G} = \exp (\mu _{G} + v_{G} / 2)$,
**Standardized geometric-option thresholds**

$$
\begin{gathered}
d_{2} = (\mu _{G} - \ln (K)) / \sqrt{v_{G}} \\
d_{1} = d_{2} + \sqrt{v_{G}}
\end{gathered}
$$

Integrating the normal density over $Y > \ln  K$ gives
**Exact geometric-average call price**

$$
C_{G} = \mathrm{disc} \cdot  (F_{G} \cdot  \Phi (d_{1}) - K \cdot  \Phi (d_{2}))
$$

**Exact geometric-average put price**

$$
\operatorname{P}_{G} = \mathrm{disc} \cdot  (K \cdot  \Phi (-d_{2}) - F_{G} \cdot  \Phi (-d_{1}))
$$

These are exact for the specified geometric average under GBM. The total log variance is $v_{G}$, not an annual volatility to multiply by T again.

For n equally weighted future fixings at iT/n,
**Log-geometric moments for equally spaced fixings**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mu _{G} = \ln (S) + \nu  \cdot  T \cdot  (n + 1) / (2 \cdot  n) \\
v_{G} = \sigma ^{2} \cdot  T \cdot  (n + 1) \cdot  (2 \cdot  n + 1) / (6 \cdot  n^{2})
\end{gathered}
$$

For continuous averaging over [0,T], the covariance integral gives
**Log-geometric moments for continuous averaging**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mu _{G} = \ln (S) + \nu  \cdot  T / 2 \\
v_{G} = \sigma ^{2} \cdot  T / 3
\end{gathered}
$$

Use the general sums for irregular dates or unequal weights.

atoms.title: Asian Options under Black–Scholes / 4. Arithmetic Average: Moments and Levy Approximation
atoms.text:
## 4. Arithmetic Average: Moments and Levy Approximation

Section 3 supplies the lognormal payoff integral.

A sum of correlated lognormal variables is generally not lognormal. Its first two moments are nevertheless exact:
**First moment of the arithmetic average**

$$
M_{1} = \operatorname{E}[A] = \sum _{i}(w_{i} \cdot  S \cdot  \exp ((r - q) \cdot  t_{i}))
$$

**Second moment of the arithmetic average**

$$
\begin{gathered}
M_{2} = \operatorname{E}[A^{2}] = \sum _{i} \sum _{j}(w_{i} \cdot  w_{j} \cdot  S^{2} \\
\cdot  \exp ((r - q) \cdot  (t_{i} + t_{j}) + \sigma ^{2} \cdot  \min (t_{i}, t_{j})))
\end{gathered}
$$

The second formula follows by taking the expectation of $\exp (X_{i}+X_{j})$. It includes the covariance between observations.

The two-moment lognormal approximation replaces A with $\exp (Z)$, choosing
**Moment-matched lognormal parameters**

$$
\begin{gathered}
v_{A} = \ln (M_{2} / M_{1}^{2}) \\
\mu _{A} = \ln (M_{1}) - v_{A} / 2
\end{gathered}
$$

**Standardized moment-matching thresholds**

$$
\begin{gathered}
h_{2} = (\mu _{A} - \ln (K)) / \sqrt{v_{A}} \\
h_{1} = h_{2} + \sqrt{v_{A}}
\end{gathered}
$$

**Moment-matched arithmetic call price**

$$
C_{\mathrm{MM}} = \mathrm{disc} \cdot  (M_{1} \cdot  \Phi (h_{1}) - K \cdot  \Phi (h_{2}))
$$

**Moment-matched arithmetic put price**

$$
\operatorname{P}_{\mathrm{MM}} = \mathrm{disc} \cdot  (K \cdot  \Phi (-h_{2}) - M_{1} \cdot  \Phi (-h_{1}))
$$

This is the Levy-style moment-matching construction for the chosen schedule. Distinguish this discrete implementation from a specified continuous-average Levy formula. Matching moments does not make the option price exact.

For continuous uniform averaging, replace the sums by
**Continuous-average first moment**

$$
M_{1} = (S / T) \cdot  \int_{0}^{T}(\exp ((r - q) \cdot  t)) \mathrm{d}t
$$

**Continuous-average second moment**

$$
M_2=\frac{S^2}{T^2}\int_0^T\int_0^T\exp\big((r-q)(s+t)+\sigma^2\min(s,t)\big)\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}s
$$

Evaluate limiting cases or stable quadrature rather than divide by a nearly zero carry rate. Compute $v_{A}$ as $\operatorname{log1p}(\operatorname{Var}(A)/M_1^2)$ when useful; materially negative variance indicates an error.

atoms.title: Asian Options under Black–Scholes / 5. Curran Geometric-Conditioning Approximation (1)
atoms.text:
## 5. Curran Geometric-Conditioning Approximation

Use [Shared Foundations](#1-shared-foundations) and Section 3's Y, $\mu _{G}$ and $v_{G}$.

Conditioning is different from substituting geometric variance into an arithmetic pricing formula. For $v_{G} > 0$, define
**Gaussian conditioning coefficients and residual covariance**

$$
\begin{gathered}
c_{i} = \operatorname{Cov}(X_{i}, Y) = \sum _{j}(\Sigma _{ij} \cdot  w_{j}) \\
b_{i} = c_{i} / v_{G} \\
R_{ij} = \Sigma _{ij} - c_{i} \cdot  c_{j} / v_{G}
\end{gathered}
$$

Conditional normality gives
**Conditional mean of a log fixing**

$$
a_{i}(y) = \mu _{i} + b_{i} \cdot  (y - \mu _{G})
$$

**Conditional mean of the arithmetic average**

$$
m(y) = \operatorname{E}[A \vert  Y=y] = \sum _{i}(w_{i} \cdot  \exp (a_{i}(y) + R_{ii} / 2))
$$

**Conditional second moment of the arithmetic average**

$$
\begin{gathered}
m_{2}(y) = \operatorname{E}[A^{2} \vert  Y=y] \\
= \sum _{i} \sum _{j}(w_{i} \cdot  w_{j} \\
\cdot  \exp (a_{i}(y) + a_{j}(y) + (R_{ii} + R_{jj} + 2 \cdot  R_{ij}) / 2))
\end{gathered}
$$

The exact identity is $C_{A} = \mathrm{disc} \cdot  \operatorname{E}[\operatorname{E}[\max (A - K, 0) \vert  Y]]$. Taking a positive part after a conditional mean loses conditional uncertainty:
**Conditional-expectation lower bound for the arithmetic call**

$$
C_{\mathrm{LB}} = \mathrm{disc} \cdot  \operatorname{E}[\max (m(Y) - K, 0)] \le  C_{A}
$$

**Selected method: Curran (1994), Section 2.3, naive approximation.** This is the version used for the Asian results in the paper's Section 3. It is a lower-bound approximation, not an exact arithmetic price. The implementation below evaluates its exercise threshold numerically; it does not substitute an approximate strike threshold.

First apply Section 6 to remove past fixings and any known initial fixing. For positive remaining weights at strictly positive times and $\sigma  > 0, m(y)$ is strictly increasing from zero to infinity, so there is exactly one root $m(y_{\mathrm{star}})=K$ for $K > 0$. Weighted AM–GM implies $m(\ln  K) \ge  K$, giving an upper bracket. Expand the lower bracket until $m(y_{\mathrm{low}}) < K$, then solve with a bracketed root finder. Use log-sum-exp for $\log  m(y)$ to avoid overflow. Do not interpret an arbitrary finite lower bracket as minus infinity. With $F_{i} = \exp (\mu _{i} + \Sigma _{ii} / 2)$,
**Curran naive call value at the solved threshold**

$$
\begin{gathered}
C_{\mathrm{LB}} = \mathrm{disc} \cdot  (\sum _{i}(w_{i} \cdot  F_{i} \cdot  \Phi ((\mu _{G} + c_{i} - y_{\mathrm{star}}) / \sqrt{v_{G}})) \\
- K \cdot  \Phi ((\mu _{G} - y_{\mathrm{star}}) / \sqrt{v_{G}}))
\end{gathered}
$$

**Truncated asset moment used in the conditional lower bound**

$$
\operatorname{E}[\exp (X_{i}) \cdot  \operatorname{indicator}(Y > h)] = F_{i} \cdot  \Phi ((\mu _{G} + c_{i} - h) / \sqrt{v_{G}})
$$

explains the price formula: integrate the conditional payoff only where $m(y)>K$. No extra time factor belongs in $\sqrt{v_{G}}$.

**Conditional-pricing calculation:** construct dates and weights; compute $\mu _{i}$, $\Sigma$, $\mu _{G}$, $v_{G}$ and $c_{i}$; solve $\log  m(y_{\mathrm{star}})=\log  K$; evaluate the truncated expectations; discount once. Record the root residual. Obtain the corresponding approximate put from parity with the exact arithmetic mean M1. The parity identity is exact, but the resulting put retains the call's approximation error.

**Boundary handling:** if all prices are known or $\sigma =0$, evaluate the deterministic average directly. If the effective strike after seasoned-contract reduction is nonpositive, the call payoff is linear and the put is zero. This exact statement concerns the contractual effective strike. An approximate geometric threshold such as $\hat{K}=2K-m(\ln  K)$ is a different object: $\hat{K}\le 0$ does not prove that the actual payoff is always positive. Fall back to the root calculation, not an asserted exact linear price.

atoms.title: Asian Options under Black–Scholes / 5. Curran Geometric-Conditioning Approximation (2)
atoms.text:
The original paper also presents a refined residual-moment variant. This reference implements only the selected naive variant; it does not supply the refined algorithm.

Use the selected naive variant unless a different conditioning variant is specified. State which variant was implemented; do not substitute Levy or geometric pricing under the Curran name.

atoms.title: Asian Options under Black–Scholes / 6. Seasoned and Floating-Strike Contracts
atoms.text:
## 6. Seasoned and Floating-Strike Contracts

Use [Shared Foundations](#1-shared-foundations); retain Section 2's original weights.

For arithmetic averaging with past fixings, write
**Known-past and future-average decomposition**

$$
\begin{gathered}
A = a_{\mathrm{past}} + W_{f} \cdot  A_{f} \\
a_{\mathrm{past}} = \sum _{\mathrm{past}}(w_{i} \cdot  S_{i}) \\
W_{f} = \sum _{\mathrm{future}}(w_{i}) \\
A_{f} = \sum _{\mathrm{future}}((w_{i} / W_{f}) \cdot  S_{i})
\end{gathered}
$$

For $W_{f} > 0$, set $K_{f}=(K-a_{\mathrm{past}})/W_{f}$. A fixed-strike call is $W_{f}$ times a call on $A_{f}$ with strike $K_{f}$, discounted to the original payment date. If $K_{f} \le  0$, its payoff is linear: $\mathrm{price}=\mathrm{disc}(a_{\mathrm{past}}+W_f\operatorname{E}[A_f]-K)$, and the put is zero. If $W_{f}=0$, all payoffs are known.

For geometric averaging, add past contributions to $\mu _{G}$ as $\sum _{\mathrm{past}} w_{i} \ln  S_{i}$; only future fixings contribute covariance. This preserves the original averaging weights.

For a floating-strike arithmetic payoff, simulate the joint pair ($S_{T}$,A); replacing the random strike by E[A] changes the contract. The geometric floating-strike call has an exact joint-lognormal benchmark. Let $X=\ln  S_{T}, Y=\ln  G$, means $\mu _{X}$,$\mu _{Y}$, variances $v_{X}$,$v_{Y}$, covariance $c_{\mathrm{XY}}$, and $v_{\mathrm{diff}}=v_{X}+v_{Y}-2\cdot c_{\mathrm{XY}}$. For $v_{\mathrm{diff}}>0$,
**Expected positive difference of two jointly lognormal variables**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{E}[\max (\exp (X) - \exp (Y), 0)] \\
= \exp (\mu _{X} + v_{X} / 2) \cdot  \Phi ((\mu _{X} - \mu _{Y} + v_{X} - c_{\mathrm{XY}}) / \sqrt{v_{\mathrm{diff}}}) \\
- \exp (\mu _{Y} + v_{Y} / 2) \cdot  \Phi ((\mu _{X} - \mu _{Y} + c_{\mathrm{XY}} - v_{Y}) / \sqrt{v_{\mathrm{diff}}})
\end{gathered}
$$

Multiply by disc; obtain the put from the corresponding expectation difference. Compute $c_{\mathrm{XY}}$ from the actual fixing schedule, including any past constants. Handle $v_{\mathrm{diff}}=0$ as a deterministic log ratio.

atoms.title: Asian Options under Black–Scholes / 7. Monte Carlo and Control Variates
atoms.text:
## 7. Monte Carlo and Control Variates

Use [Shared Foundations](#1-shared-foundations) and the contractual dates in Section 2.

At successive future fixings, use exact GBM transitions:
**Exact GBM stepping between fixing dates**

$$
\ln (S(t_{i})) = \ln (S(t_{i-1})) + \nu  \cdot  \mathrm{d}t_{i} + \sigma  \cdot  \sqrt{\mathrm{d}t_{i}} \cdot  Z_{i}
$$

$$
\mathrm{d}t_{i} = t_{i} - t_{i-1}
$$

The $Z_{i}$ are independent standard normal draws.
Compute the contractual average on each path, then the payoff, then discount. Averaging option payoffs over dates is a different operation. Process paths in batches when storing the entire path matrix is unnecessary.

For discounted arithmetic payoff $U_{A}$ and matching discounted geometric payoff $U_{G}$ with exact mean $V_{G}$, use
**Geometric control-variate estimator and coefficient**

$$
\begin{gathered}
U_{\mathrm{CV}} = U_{A} - \beta  \cdot  (U_{G} - V_{G}) \\
\beta  = \operatorname{Cov}(U_{A}, U_{G}) / \operatorname{Var}(U_{G})
\end{gathered}
$$

Estimate $\beta$ on a separate pilot sample, then hold it fixed on independent pricing paths. If $\operatorname{Var}(U_{G})=0$, omit that control. Dates, weights, historical fixings, strike and payment date of the control must match its analytic benchmark.

Report $\operatorname{mean}(U_{\mathrm{CV}})$ and $\mathrm{sample\_std}(U_{\mathrm{CV}})/\sqrt{M}$ for M independent observations. For antithetic paths, average each pair first and compute standard error across independent pairs. A price approximation can differ from MC by more than sampling error because it has approximation bias; an exact geometric benchmark should agree within sampling uncertainty and implementation accuracy.

atoms.title: Asian Options under Black–Scholes / 8. Checks and Scope
atoms.text:
## 8. Checks and Scope

Use [Shared Foundations](#1-shared-foundations); compare identical contracts and payment dates.

For a nonnegative average A and positive K,
**Bounds for the arithmetic-average call**

$$
\mathrm{disc} \cdot  \max (\operatorname{E}[A] - K, 0) \le  C_{A} \le  \mathrm{disc} \cdot  \operatorname{E}[A]
$$

**Arithmetic-average put-call parity**

$$
C_{A} - \operatorname{P}_{A} = \mathrm{disc} \cdot  (\operatorname{E}[A] - K)
$$

For identical nonnegative weights, $A\ge G$ pathwise, so $C_{A}\ge C_{G}$ and $\operatorname{P}_{A}\le \operatorname{P}_{G}$. A one-fixing contract reduces to an ordinary option on that fixing; discount to the specified payment date. These are checks of the true prices: approximations and finite MC estimates need suitable error allowances.

Check dates and moments before comparing prices. Test the zero-volatility limit, single fixing, irregular dates and known past fixings. Use exact geometric pricing to validate the path simulation; use a separate MC implementation to assess arithmetic approximations. Parity or bounds alone do not establish method identity or price accuracy.

The displayed analytic formulas assume European payoffs, constant-parameter GBM and deterministic nonnegative weights. Continuous arithmetic averages need integration or a converged discretization; early exercise, stochastic volatility, jumps and negative weights require appropriate extensions. Do not silently reuse these approximations outside their assumptions.

atoms.title: Asian Options under Black–Scholes / 9. References
atoms.text:
## 9. References

- Curran (1994), [Valuing Asian and Portfolio Options by Conditioning on the Geometric Mean Price](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.40.12.1705): Sections 2.2–2.3, pp. 1706–1709; Section 3 uses the naive variant for Asians.
- Levy (1992), *Pricing European average rate currency options*, Journal of International Money and Finance 11(5), 474–491: lognormal moment-matching approximation.
- [QuantLib discrete geometric Asian implementation](https://github.com/lballabio/QuantLib/blob/master/ql/pricingengines/asian/analytic_discr_geom_av_price.cpp): a separately implemented geometric benchmark.
- Kyriakou (2010), [Efficient valuation of exotic derivatives with path-dependence and early exercise features](https://openaccess.city.ac.uk/id/eprint/23459/), Section 4.6.2: distinction between strike-frozen and pointwise conditional-moment approximations. The pointwise variant is not implemented in this reference.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions
atoms.text: Use this reference for positions driven by historical signals, cash-funded trades and portfolio performance measurement. It explains financial accounting and information availability, not a strategy's choice of indicator or trading threshold.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions / Map the conventions
atoms.text:
## Map the conventions

Identify the observation time, decision time, fill time and valuation time separately. A signal using a period's final price is not available earlier in that period. A rule that fills at a later opening price does not earn the intervening return on newly purchased shares. Explicit task conventions determine corporate-action adjustments, price units, fees, financing, rounding and final liquidation.

An adjusted-price series may incorporate splits or distributions; its adjustment definition matters. Applying distributions again to a total-return-adjusted valuation can double count them. Adjusted fractional holdings describe a synthetic accounting convention and need not equal exchange-traded share counts through a corporate action.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions / Cash and holdings at a trade
atoms.text:
## Cash and holdings at a trade

Let q be signed shares traded, positive for buying; p the execution price; h the shares before execution; B cash; and F the nonnegative transaction charge. The following identity assumes immediate settlement and no external cash movement at that instant.

**Cash and shares after execution**

$$
\begin{gathered}
B_{\mathrm{new}} = B-q\cdot p-F \\
h_{\mathrm{new}} = h+q
\end{gathered}
$$

**Value at the execution price**

$$
B_{\mathrm{new}}+h_{\mathrm{new}}\cdot p = B+h\cdot p-F
$$

Buying does not itself create a loss equal to the purchase notional: cash becomes an asset. Selling converts an asset to cash. Fees reduce equity. Between trades, financing accrues according to the stated lending/borrowing convention and holdings are marked to the chosen valuation price.

For a long purchase with flat charge f, proportional rate c and available cash B, assuming these are charged only when a positive trade occurs:

**Cash-feasible whole-share limit**

$$
q_{\mathrm{max}} = \max (0, \operatorname{floor}((B-f)/(p\cdot (1+c))))
$$

A risk budget divided by a stop distance is a sizing heuristic, not a loss guarantee: a gap can make the realized exit worse than the stop level. A trailing-stop decision depends on when its reference peak is observed; it does not imply execution at that peak or stop price.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions / Returns from marked equity
atoms.text:
## Returns from marked equity

For positive consecutive portfolio values $V_{\mathrm{prev}}$ and V, with no external flows between them:

**Single-period simple return**

$$
r = V/V_{\mathrm{prev}}-1
$$

When deposits or withdrawals occur, a raw value ratio mixes capital flows with performance. Time-weighted returns split the measurement at external flows and link the resulting subperiod returns. Purchases and sales within the portfolio are internal transfers, not external contributions.

**Geometrically linked wealth index**

$$
W_{t} = \prod _{j=1}^{t} (1+r_{j})
$$

A signal may deliberately sum historical returns or compound them; these are different ranking rules. Changing one to the other is not a harmless numerical improvement.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions / Annualization and risk measures
atoms.text:
## Annualization and risk measures

Let A be observations per year, n the number of measured periods, and $s_{r}$ the standard deviation under the prescribed divisor. Arithmetic annual return and geometric annual growth answer different questions.

**Arithmetic annual mean**

$$
\mu _{\mathrm{annual}} = A\cdot \operatorname{mean}(r)
$$

**Compound annual growth for positive terminal wealth**

$$
\mathrm{growth}_{\mathrm{annual}} = W_{n}^{A/n}-1
$$

**Conventional volatility scaling**

$$
\mathrm{vol}_{\mathrm{annual}} = \sqrt{A}\cdot s_{r}
$$

The last expression assumes an appropriate uncorrelated-return approximation; serial covariance changes multi-period variance. Sharpe's numerator ordinarily uses excess returns and arithmetic mean. A specified alternative such as growth divided by volatility must be labeled as that convention, not silently replaced. Zero volatility makes the usual ratio undefined.

**Drawdown with positive high-water mark $H_{t}$**

$$
\begin{gathered}
H_{t} = \max (W_{\mathrm{initial}},W_{1},\ldots ,W_{t}) \\
\mathrm{drawdown}_{t} = 1-W_{t}/H_{t}
\end{gathered}
$$

Maximum drawdown is the maximum of this positive loss fraction. Whether the initial capital point belongs to the observed curve must be explicit; omitting it can hide a loss in the first period. Position-price drawdown and portfolio-equity drawdown differ when cash, leverage or fees are present.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions / Accounting checks
atoms.text:
## Accounting checks

At a trade, the change in equity at its fill price equals negative fees. With all positions closed and no flows or financing, terminal cash minus initial cash equals the sum of net completed-trade profits. If positions remain open, unrealized profit also belongs in total equity. The product of value-based returns reproduces the terminal-to-initial equity ratio on the same interval.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources

[CFA Institute, GIPS Standards for Asset Owners (2020)](https://www.cfainstitute.org/-/media/documents/code/gips/2020-gips-standards-asset-owners.pdf), calculation methodology, for external-flow treatment and linked returns. Cash conservation, annualization distinctions and gross/net exposure above are direct accounting or algebraic identities. This note does not assert GIPS compliance of a backtest.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions / Long-short and repeated estimation (1)
atoms.text:
## Long-short and repeated estimation

Net exposure is the sum of signed weights; gross exposure is the sum of their absolute values. A short book can be written two ways: signed weights, where each short weight is negative (with gross g split equally across n shorts, $-g/n$) and P&L is the sum of weight times return; or positive short sizes, where P&L is the long leg minus the short leg. Use one of them, not both, since applying a negative weight and then subtracting the short leg cancels the short side. Derive each sign from its long or short label, and check that the short leg's P&L has the opposite sign to its names' returns. A unit long leg minus a unit short leg has gross exposure two before any financing convention, so its reported return needs a stated capital denominator. Equity weights, return-spread indices and invested dollars are not interchangeable.

Forecasts, fitted transformations and rankings use information available by the decision time. When a position is the product of a signal and a volatility-based size, align the whole position with the return interval it earns: the holding applied to the return of day t is built only from data through day t−1, both its signal and its volatility size. Lagging only the signal while the size uses a volatility that already includes the same day's squared return is look-ahead; lagging a series that is already aligned shifts it twice. A rule that defines a position at every date has no flat state; a warm-up period without enough history is dropped or handled as the task states, not set to zero exposure silently. The evaluated return series starts at the stated first trading date; days before it belong to the warm-up and enter no performance statistic unless the task says so. When the task states an evaluation or trading start after a signal or risk warm-up → every statistic and regression (mean, volatility, Sharpe, drawdown, hit rate, factor regression) uses the returns from that start onward, flat or cash days inside the evaluation period included → check that the number of return observations equals the length of the stated evaluation period. A task that asks for full-history statistics keeps the full history.

```python
eval_ret = port_ret.loc[eval_start:]                     # the stated first trading or evaluation date
assert len(eval_ret) == (dates >= eval_start).sum()
hit_rate = (eval_ret > 0).mean()                          # every statistic and regression from eval_ret, not port_ret
``` A single lag is enough when the weights are built from data through t−1 and applied to the return of t; building from t−1 data and then shifting again uses information two days old. Once a sample already contains its rolling warm-up, do not trim it again. Walk-forward evaluation separates historical estimation from subsequent realizations. Selecting a model using a later full sample is a retrospective comparison, not proof of live predictive performance.

When a strategy holds constant target weights from one rebalance date to the next → start the weight frame as NaN, set the rebalance rows, then forward-fill (and fill the rows before the first rebalance with 0):

```text
weights = pd.DataFrame(np.nan, index=dates, columns=assets)
weights.loc[rebalance_dates] = targets              # a complete row per rebalance: every asset, 0 for those exited
weights = weights.ffill().fillna(0.0)
```

Check that every non-rebalance day carries the most recent target, an all-zero target included; a frame started with zeros stays zero between rebalances after `ffill`, so positions exist only on rebalance days. When the strategy holds share counts whose weights drift with prices, carry the shares instead and recompute the weights each day.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions / Long-short and repeated estimation (2)
atoms.text:
When a cross-sectional long-short book is rebalanced on the first trading day of every month from a daily signal → use the tested engine in the Python session rather than your own holdings loop: hand-written loops for this book keep slipping on the rebalance dates, the signal lag, exits and the first position. Write your own only where the task's rules differ from the contract in the comments below:

```python
from backtest_tools import monthly_long_short, factor_regression, arithmetic_metrics
res = monthly_long_short(returns, signal, first_trade_row, n_long, n_short, w_long, w_short, cost_bps)
# returns: daily simple returns, one column per asset, on the trading-day index (missing values handled as the task says)
# signal: same index and columns; row t uses data through row t; do not shift it (the engine ranks on row i-1 for row i)
# first_trade_row: the stated trading start as a row position; the book opens there, then rebalances each later month start
# each rebalance writes the whole book (exits at 0); costs are cost_bps per unit of turnover, on the first row it earns
# limits: pass max_position= only for a cap the task states; a stated per-name weight that breaks a stated cap is a conflict to report
r = res["returns"]                                                # daily returns from first_trade_row on
assert res["n_rebalances"] == 1 + sum(d > returns.index[first_trade_row] for d in returns.index.to_series().groupby(returns.index.to_period("M")).min())
```

When a long-short strategy rebalances monthly from a daily signal and trading starts on a stated row → the book opens on the trading start row (even mid-month) and is rebalanced on the first trading day of each later month; each rebalance ranks on the previous row's signal, known at that close. Here `signal` row t uses data up to row t with no shift of its own, and it shares the returns' date index (a signal built on an integer index and reindexed to dates is all NaN). Adapt the signal and sizes to the task:

```python
dates = returns.index                                            # trading days
first_of_month = dates.to_series().groupby(dates.to_period("M")).min()
start = dates[trade_start_row]                                   # the stated trading start
rebal = [start] + [d for d in first_of_month if d > start]       # open at the start, then each later month start
assert signal.index.equals(dates)
w = pd.DataFrame(np.nan, index=dates, columns=returns.columns)
for d in rebal:
    s = signal.iloc[dates.get_loc(d) - 1].dropna()               # previous row: known at the prior close
    assert len(s) >= n_long + n_short and s.std() > 0             # a valid, varying cross-section
    target = pd.Series(0.0, index=returns.columns)
    target[s.nlargest(n_long).index] = w_long
    target[s.nsmallest(n_short).index] = -w_short
    w.loc[d] = target                                             # the complete row, exits at 0
w = w.ffill().fillna(0.0)                                         # flat before the start
cost = (w - w.shift(1).fillna(0.0)).abs().sum(axis=1) * cost_rate
port = (w * returns).sum(axis=1) - cost                          # the rebalance row's weights earn from that row
eval_ret = port.loc[start:]
assert len(rebal) == 1 + sum(d > start for d in first_of_month)
```

atoms.title: Principal-protected note with a down-and-out call: workflow
atoms.text:
Work in this order; every later step uses the values named in the earlier ones.

1. GARCH(1,1), zero mean, on percent log returns; convert back.
```python
res = arch_model(100 * r, vol="GARCH", mean="Zero", rescale=False).fit(disp="off")
omega, alpha, beta = res.params["omega"] / 100**2, res.params["alpha[1]"], res.params["beta[1]"]
persistence = alpha + beta; long_run_variance = omega / (1 - persistence)
garch_vol = np.asarray(res.conditional_volatility)[-1] / 100 * np.sqrt(252)   # annualized; report and price with this
```
2. Bond and option count: `bond_pv = N * exp(-r*T)`, `n_options = N * participation / S0`.
3. Down-and-out call (barrier B below strike K, no dividend), closed form: vanilla call minus down-and-in call.
```python
def doc(S, sig):
    if S <= B: return 0.0
    st = sig * np.sqrt(T); d1 = (np.log(S / K) + (r + sig**2 / 2) * T) / st; d2 = d1 - st
    call = S * norm.cdf(d1) - K * np.exp(-r * T) * norm.cdf(d2)
    lam = (r + sig**2 / 2) / sig**2; y = np.log(B**2 / (S * K)) / st + lam * st
    cdi = S * (B / S)**(2 * lam) * norm.cdf(y) - K * np.exp(-r * T) * (B / S)**(2 * lam - 2) * norm.cdf(y - st)
    return max(call - cdi, 0.0)
```
4. `option_unit_price = doc(S0, garch_vol)`, `option_value = n_options * option_unit_price`, `fair_value = bond_pv + option_value`.
5. The note is sold at par (issue price N): `markup_pct = (N - fair_value) / fair_value * 100`; `breakeven_vol` solves `bond_pv + n_options * doc(S0, s) = N` (`brentq` on [0.01, 3]).
6. Delta by a central 1% spot bump: `dS = 0.01 * S0`, `option_delta = (doc(S0+dS, garch_vol) - doc(S0-dS, garch_vol)) / (2*dS)`, `note_delta = n_options * option_delta`.
7. One-day delta-normal risk at confidence c: `z = norm.ppf(c)`, `note_var = z * abs(note_delta) * S0 * garch_vol / np.sqrt(252)`; the note report scales ES from VaR: `note_es = note_var * norm.pdf(z) / (1 - c)` (z times the textbook normal ES).

atoms.title: American options: Barone-Adesi & Whaley (1987) quadratic approximation
atoms.text: **If the task text defines the formula, inputs or conventions differently, the task text wins.**

atoms.title: American options: Barone-Adesi & Whaley (1987) quadratic approximation / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| $S$ | spot (or futures price F when $b = 0$) | price |
| $X$ | strike | price |
| $T$ | time to expiry (years, day count from the task) | years |
| $r$ | continuously compounded risk-free rate; 5% is `0.05` | $1/\mathrm{year}$ |
| $b$ | cost of carry, continuous: stock with dividend yield q: $b = r - q$; non-dividend stock: $b = r$; futures: $b = 0; \mathrm{FX}$: $b = r_{\mathrm{dom}} - r_{\mathrm{for}}$ | $1/\mathrm{year}$ |
| $\sigma$ | annual lognormal vol; 20% is `0.20` | $1/\sqrt{\mathrm{year}}$ |

atoms.title: American options: Barone-Adesi & Whaley (1987) quadratic approximation / European pieces (generalized Black-Scholes)
atoms.text:
## European pieces (generalized Black-Scholes)

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{d1}(S) = [\ln (S/X) + (b + \sigma ^{2}/2) T] / (\sigma  \sqrt{T}),   \mathrm{d2} = \mathrm{d1} - \sigma  \sqrt{T} \\
c(S) = S e^{(b-r)T} N(\mathrm{d1}) - X e^{-rT} N(\mathrm{d2}) \\
p(S) = X e^{-rT} N(-\mathrm{d2}) - S e^{(b-r)T} N(-\mathrm{d1})
\end{gathered}
$$

N = standard normal CDF, n = standard normal density.

atoms.title: American options: Barone-Adesi & Whaley (1987) quadratic approximation / Coefficients
atoms.text:
## Coefficients

$$
\begin{gathered}
M = 2r / \sigma ^{2},   \mathrm{Nb} = 2b / \sigma ^{2},   K = 1 - e^{-rT} \\
\mathrm{q1} = [-(\mathrm{Nb} - 1) - \sqrt{(\mathrm{Nb} - 1)^{2} + 4M/K}] / 2\quad (\mathrm{q1} < 0, \;\text{put}\;) \\
\mathrm{q2} = [-(\mathrm{Nb} - 1) + \sqrt{(\mathrm{Nb} - 1)^{2} + 4M/K}] / 2\quad (\mathrm{q2} > 0, \;\text{call}\;)
\end{gathered}
$$

(The paper calls Nb just "N"; it is not the normal CDF.)

atoms.title: American options: Barone-Adesi & Whaley (1987) quadratic approximation / Put
atoms.text:
## Put
- Critical price $S^{**} < X$ solves  $X - S^{**} = p(S^{**}) - [1 - e^{(b-r)T} N(-\mathrm{d1}(S^{**}))] S^{**}/\mathrm{q1}$

$$
\mathrm{A1} = -(S^{**}/\mathrm{q1}) [1 - e^{(b-r)T} N(-\mathrm{d1}(S^{**}))]\quad (> 0 \mathrm{because} \mathrm{q1} < 0)
$$

When $S > S^{**}$:

$$
\operatorname{P} = p(S) + \mathrm{A1} (S/S^{**})^{\mathrm{q1}}
$$

When $S \le  S^{**}$:

$$
\operatorname{P} = X - S
$$

Early-exercise premium:

$$
\mathrm{A1} (S/S^{**})^{\mathrm{q1}}
$$

atoms.title: American options: Barone-Adesi & Whaley (1987) quadratic approximation / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources
G. Barone-Adesi and R. E. Whaley (1987), "Efficient Analytic Approximation of American Option Values",
Journal of Finance 42(2), 301-320 (eqs. 13, 19-20, 24-25, 26-33). L. W. MacMillan (1986), "Analytic Approximation for the
American Put Option", Advances in Futures and Options Research 1, 119-139 (as cited by BAW).

atoms.title: American options: Barone-Adesi & Whaley (1987) quadratic approximation / Model and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Model and assumptions
- Underlying S follows GBM under the risk-neutral measure with constant vol $\sigma$, constant rate r and constant
  cost of carry b. Option can be exercised at any time up to T. No cash dividends, no smile.
- Idea: the early-exercise premium $e(S,T) = \;\text{American}\; - \;\text{European}\;$ obeys the Black-Scholes PDE. BAW write it as
  K(T) f(S), with $K(T) = 1 - e^{-rT}$, then drop one term. That leaves an ODE with power solutions S^q.
  The result is an **approximation**, not an exact price.

atoms.title: American options: Barone-Adesi & Whaley (1987) quadratic approximation / Call
atoms.text:
## Call
- **If $b \ge  r$: the American call is never exercised early; price = European call c(S). Stop.**
- Otherwise, critical price $S^{*} > X$ solves  $S^{*} - X = c(S^{*}) + [1 - e^{(b-r)T} N(\mathrm{d1}(S^{*}))] S^{*}/\mathrm{q2}$

$$
\mathrm{A2} = (S^{*}/\mathrm{q2}) [1 - e^{(b-r)T} N(\mathrm{d1}(S^{*}))]\quad (> 0)
$$

When $S < S^{*}$:

$$
C = c(S) + \mathrm{A2} (S/S^{*})^{\mathrm{q2}}
$$

When $S \ge  S^{*}$:

$$
C = S - X
$$

Early-exercise premium:

$$
\mathrm{A2} (S/S^{*})^{\mathrm{q2}}
$$

atoms.title: American options: Barone-Adesi & Whaley (1987) quadratic approximation / Newton iteration for the critical price (BAW Section II)
atoms.text:
## Newton iteration for the critical price (BAW Section II)
Call, $i = 1, 2$, ...: $\mathrm{RHS}(\mathrm{Si}) = c(\mathrm{Si}) + [1 - e^{(b-r)T} N(\mathrm{d1}(\mathrm{Si}))] \mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{q2}$

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{slope} \mathrm{bi} = e^{(b-r)T} N(\mathrm{d1}(\mathrm{Si})) (1 - 1/\mathrm{q2}) + [1 - e^{(b-r)T} n(\mathrm{d1}(\mathrm{Si})) / (\sigma  \sqrt{T})] / \mathrm{q2} \\
S_{i+1} = [X + \mathrm{RHS}(\mathrm{Si}) - \mathrm{bi} \mathrm{Si}] / (1 - \mathrm{bi})
\end{gathered}
$$

Put: $\mathrm{RHS}(\mathrm{Si}) = p(\mathrm{Si}) - [1 - e^{(b-r)T} N(-\mathrm{d1}(\mathrm{Si}))] \mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{q1}$

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{slope} \mathrm{bi} = -e^{(b-r)T} N(-\mathrm{d1}(\mathrm{Si})) (1 - 1/\mathrm{q1}) - [1 + e^{(b-r)T} n(\mathrm{d1}(\mathrm{Si})) / (\sigma  \sqrt{T})] / \mathrm{q1} \\
S_{i+1} = [X - \mathrm{RHS}(\mathrm{Si}) + \mathrm{bi} \mathrm{Si}] / (1 + \mathrm{bi})
\end{gathered}
$$

Stop when $\vert \mathrm{LHS}(\mathrm{Si}) - \mathrm{RHS}(\mathrm{Si})\vert  / X < \mathrm{tol}$(paper: 1e-5; a tighter tol such as 1e-8 costs nothing). $\mathrm{LHS} = \mathrm{Si} - X$(call), X - Si (put).
Seeds (or simply $\mathrm{Si} = X$): with q2inf, q1inf = the q2, q1 formulas with 4M in place of 4M/K,

$$
\begin{gathered}
\;\text{call}\;: \mathrm{Sinf} = X / (1 - 1/\mathrm{q2inf}),  \mathrm{h2} = -(bT + 2 \sigma  \sqrt{T}) X / (\mathrm{Sinf} - X),  \mathrm{S1} = X + (\mathrm{Sinf} - X)(1 - e^{\mathrm{h2}}) \\
\;\text{put}\;:  \mathrm{Sinf} = X / (1 - 1/\mathrm{q1inf}),  \mathrm{h1} = (bT - 2 \sigma  \sqrt{T}) X / (X - \mathrm{Sinf}),  \mathrm{S1} = \mathrm{Sinf} + (X - \mathrm{Sinf}) e^{\mathrm{h1}}
\end{gathered}
$$

$S^{*}$ scales with X: $S^{*}(\mathrm{X2}) = S^{*}(\mathrm{X1}) \mathrm{X2}/\mathrm{X1}$.

atoms.title: American options: Barone-Adesi & Whaley (1987) quadratic approximation / Variants and common mistakes
atoms.text:
## Variants and common mistakes
- Futures options (Black-76 world): use F for S and $b = 0$. Non-dividend stock: $b = r$(call = European; put = MacMillan 1986).
  Stock index / dividend yield q: $b = r - q$. FX: $b = r_{d} - r_{f}$. Do not put q where b belongs.
- The q1, q2 used in the price and the iteration must use **$4M/K$ with $K=1-e^{-rT}$**; the 4M-without-K versions
  belong to the seed only (a bad seed only costs iterations; the wrong q changes the price).
- d1 inside A1, A2 and the iteration is evaluated at the critical price, not at spot.
- Below $S^{**}$ (put) / above $S^{*}$ (call) return intrinsic value; do not add the premium there.
- $r = 0$: $M/K$ tends to $2/(\sigma^2T)$; the put then has no early exercise (American put = European).
- BAW does not satisfy the American put-call symmetry $C(S,X,r,b) = \operatorname{P}(X,S,r-b,-b)$ exactly
  (differences of a few cents in our tests): if the task asks for BAW put, apply the put formulas, not symmetry.
- Other American approximations (e.g. Bjerksund-Stensland) are different formulas; use them only if the task names them.

atoms.title: American options: Barone-Adesi & Whaley (1987) quadratic approximation / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- Sanity: result >= $\max ( \;\text{European}\;, \mathrm{intrinsic} )$. Value matching and smooth pasting hold at $S^{*}$ by construction.
- Accuracy (our checks vs a 4001-step Leisen-Reimer tree): within about 0.1 absolute (about 1% of price for prices above 1)
  for $T \le  0.25$; error grows with T, $\sigma$ and r. At $T = 3$ years, $\sigma  = 0.4$ it overprices by up to 0.65 (call) / 0.87 (put),
  i.e. up to several times the true early-exercise premium. Errors are mostly positive (BAW above the tree) for long T.
  For long-dated options, a task asking for the "exact" American price wants a tree / PDE, not BAW.
- The critical price itself is approximate (about 1-2% from the tree boundary in our tests).
- Cash dividends, time-varying $r$ or $\sigma$, barriers or Bermudan exercise are outside the model.

atoms.title: Binomial valuation and exercise opportunities
atoms.text: Use this reference for a CRR stock-price tree and European, Bermudan or American exercise under constant rates, continuous dividend yield and volatility. It supplies numerical pricing mathematics, not a replacement for a specifically requested PDE or analytical approximation.

atoms.title: Binomial valuation and exercise opportunities / Conventions and notation
atoms.text:
## Conventions and notation

Explicit task definitions take precedence. S0 is current stock price, K is strike, r is the continuously compounded rate, q is continuous dividend yield, $\sigma  > 0$ is annualized volatility, $T > 0$ is remaining maturity, and n is the number of equal time intervals. Rates and volatility are decimal quantities. Node (i,j) means time i*dt and j upward moves, with $0 \le  j \le  i$. Cash dividends require separate event treatment and are not equivalent to a constant q.

atoms.title: Binomial valuation and exercise opportunities / Transition model
atoms.text:
## Transition model

Time interval:

$$
\mathrm{d}t = T/n
$$

CRR upward and downward stock multipliers:

$$
\begin{gathered}
u = \exp (\sigma \cdot \sqrt{\mathrm{d}t}) \\
d = 1/u
\end{gathered}
$$

Stock price at a recombining node:

$$
S_{i,j} = \mathrm{S0} \cdot  u^{j} \cdot  d^{i-j}
$$

The pricing probability matches the stock's risk-neutral growth after continuous dividend yield:

$$
p = (\exp ((r-q)\cdot \mathrm{d}t)-d)/(u-d)
$$

An arbitrage-free nondegenerate step requires $d < \exp ((r-q)\cdot \mathrm{d}t) < u$. A probability outside [0,1] indicates an invalid discretization; clipping changes the model. This probability is unrelated to an estimated historical upward-return frequency.

atoms.title: Binomial valuation and exercise opportunities / Payoffs and stopping
atoms.text:
## Payoffs and stopping

Call exercise payoff:

$$
g_{\mathrm{call}}(S) = \max (S-K,0)
$$

Put exercise payoff:

$$
g_{\mathrm{put}}(S) = \max (K-S,0)
$$

Terminal value for the selected payoff g:

$$
V_{n,j} = g(S_{n,j})
$$

Continuation value H at an earlier node:

$$
H_{i,j} = \exp (-r\cdot \mathrm{d}t) \cdot  [p\cdot V_{i+1,j+1} + (1-p)\cdot V_{i+1,j}]
$$

Value when exercise is permitted at that node:

$$
V_{i,j} = \max (g(S_{i,j}),H_{i,j})
$$

Value when exercise is not permitted:

$$
V_{i,j} = H_{i,j}
$$

European exercise is only at expiry; Bermudan exercise uses specified dates; American tree exercise is available at every time node. The latter approximates continuous exercise as the time spacing shrinks. An exercise boundary represents positive exercise payoff that dominates continuation; zero-payoff ties are not evidence of economic early exercise.

atoms.title: Binomial valuation and exercise opportunities / Checks and limits
atoms.text:
## Checks and limits

On the same tree and contract, adding exercise opportunities cannot lower value. A non-dividend-paying call with nonnegative interest rates equals its European counterpart. European call-put parity holds on the tree. Convergence to a diffusion price can oscillate as strike alignment changes; more time steps need not improve every individual error monotonically.

At $\sigma =0$ the stock path is deterministic and the probability formula is singular: value follows from discounted contractual cash flows and allowed exercise times. At expiry the value is the payoff. The plain stock-only state does not retain running extrema or averages, so it is insufficient for path-dependent payoffs without additional state.

atoms.title: Binomial valuation and exercise opportunities / Source and derivation
atoms.text:
## Source and derivation

[Cox, Ross and Rubinstein (1979), Option Pricing: A Simplified Approach](https://bpb-us-w2.wpmucdn.com/u.osu.edu/dist/7/36891/files/2017/07/CRR79-1yy8av8.pdf), sections 3, 5 and 6: recombining valuation, diffusion limit and early exercise. The continuous-yield probability here follows directly from $p\cdot u+(1-p)\cdot d=\exp ((r-q)\cdot \mathrm{d}t)$; notation uses continuous annual rates rather than the paper's one-period gross return.

atoms.title: Black-Litterman (1992) posterior returns, He-Litterman (1999) Omega and Idzorek confidence views / Model and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Model and assumptions
- N assets, returns $r\sim N(\mu,\Sigma)$ with $\Sigma$ known. The unknown mean $\mu$ has a prior centred on the market equilibrium:
  $\mu  \sim N(\pi , \tau  \Sigma )$ ($\tau$ $\Sigma$ is the uncertainty of the MEAN, not of returns).
- K views: $P\mu+\mathrm{eps}=Q$, $\mathrm{eps} \sim N(0, \Omega )$, independent of the prior. Posterior = Gaussian (Bayes / Theil mixed estimation).
- All returns are EXCESS returns over the risk-free rate unless the task says otherwise; add $r_{f}$ back only if total returns are asked for.

atoms.title: Black-Litterman (1992) posterior returns, He-Litterman (1999) Omega and Idzorek confidence views / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | shape / units |
|---|---|---|
| $\Sigma$ | covariance of asset returns over the chosen period (annual or monthly, as given) | N x N, return^2 per period |
| $w_{\mathrm{mkt}}$ | market-cap weights, summing to 1 | $N$ |
| $\delta$ | risk-aversion coefficient; implied by the market: $\delta  = (\operatorname{E}[r_{m}] - r_{f}) / \sigma _{m}^{2}$ ($\mathrm{Sharpe}_{m}$ / $\sigma _{m}$) | none if premium and variance use the same period |
| $\pi$ | implied equilibrium excess returns | N, decimal (5% is 0.05) |
| $\tau$ | scalar shrinking $\Sigma$ to the uncertainty of the mean; given by the task | none |
| $\operatorname{P}$ | view-pick matrix; row k = one view | K x N |
| $Q$ | view returns, same period and units as $\pi$ | $K$ |
| $\Omega$ | covariance of view errors, usually diagonal | K x K, return^2 per period |

atoms.title: Black-Litterman (1992) posterior returns, He-Litterman (1999) Omega and Idzorek confidence views / Formulas
atoms.text:
## Formulas
Reverse optimization:

$$
\pi  = \delta  \Sigma  w_{\mathrm{mkt}}
$$

Master form:

$$
\mu _{\mathrm{BL}} = [ (\tau  \Sigma )^{-1} + \operatorname{P}' \Omega ^{-1} \operatorname{P} ]^{-1} [ (\tau  \Sigma )^{-1} \pi  + \operatorname{P}' \Omega ^{-1} Q ]
$$

Update form; with zero view noise, the displayed inverse requires full row rank of the view matrix and positive-definite prior covariance:

$$
\mu _{\mathrm{BL}} = \pi  + \tau  \Sigma  \operatorname{P}' (\operatorname{P} \tau  \Sigma  \operatorname{P}' + \Omega )^{-1} (Q - \operatorname{P} \pi )
$$

$$
M = [ (\tau  \Sigma )^{-1} + \operatorname{P}' \Omega ^{-1} \operatorname{P} ]^{-1} = \tau  \Sigma  - \tau  \Sigma  \operatorname{P}' (\operatorname{P} \tau  \Sigma  \operatorname{P}' + \Omega )^{-1} \operatorname{P} \tau  \Sigma
$$

The precision expression for $M$ requires invertible $\Omega$. With zero or singular view noise, use the covariance-update expression under its stated rank/compatibility conditions, rather than inverting $\Omega$.

Covariance of next-period returns (He–Litterman):

$$
\Sigma _{\mathrm{BL}} = \Sigma  + M
$$

Unconstrained mean-variance weights:

$$
w^{*} = (\delta  \Sigma _{\mathrm{BL}})^{-1} \mu _{\mathrm{BL}}
$$

- Check M: it is no larger than $\tau\Sigma$, so every diagonal entry of M is positive and at most the matching entry of $\tau\Sigma$. A sign error in the update ($+$ instead of $-$ in the second form above) gives entries larger than $\tau\Sigma$.
- M is the posterior covariance of the MEAN; $\Sigma _{\mathrm{BL}}$ is the predictive covariance of RETURNS. Say which one the task asks for.
- He-Litterman decomposition: with $\Sigma _{\mathrm{BL}}$ in the optimizer, $w^{*} = w_{\mathrm{mkt}}/(1+\tau ) + \operatorname{P}' \Lambda$ for some K-vector $\Lambda$;
  with no views $w^{*} = w_{\mathrm{mkt}}/(1+\tau )$. If the optimizer uses $\Sigma$ instead of $\Sigma _{\mathrm{BL}}$, no views give exactly $w_{\mathrm{mkt}}$.
- For certain views and positive-definite prior covariance, full-row-rank $P$ makes $P(\tau\Sigma)P'$ invertible and gives $P\mu_{\mathrm{BL}}=Q$. Redundant exact views require consistency: $Q-P\pi$ must lie in the range of $P(\tau\Sigma)P'$. For compatible redundancy, its Moore-Penrose inverse gives the Gaussian conditional mean and covariance. Contradictory exact views do not define a posterior; a generalized inverse cannot make them mutually true.
- Weights not summing to 1 is normal in the unconstrained solution; normalize or add constraints only if the task says so.

atoms.title: Black-Litterman (1992) posterior returns, He-Litterman (1999) Omega and Idzorek confidence views / Choosing Omega
atoms.text:
## Choosing Omega
- He-Litterman (1999): $\Omega  = \operatorname{diag}( \operatorname{P} (\tau  \Sigma ) \operatorname{P}' )$, i.e. $\omega _{k} = \tau  p_{k} \Sigma  p_{k}'$. Then the ratio $\Omega/\tau$ is fixed
  and $\mu _{\mathrm{BL}}$ does NOT depend on $\tau$ (M and $\Sigma _{\mathrm{BL}}$ still do). Off-diagonal terms are dropped (independent views).
- Idzorek (2007) confidence $C_{k}$ in (0, 1]: choose $\omega _{k}$ so that the single-view tilt of the weights equals $C_{k}$ times the
  100%-confidence tilt: $w_{k} = w_{\mathrm{mkt}} + C_{k} (w_{100,k} - w_{\mathrm{mkt}})$, with weights $(\delta  \Sigma )^{-1} \mu$. Idzorek solves $\omega _{k}$ numerically
  (minimize squared weight distance). For an unconstrained optimizer this equals the closed form (Walters):
