Reprice vanillas across expiries and strikes. Separate sampling uncertainty from time/space discretization and calibration error; refine the grid where needed. Diagnose unresolved discrepancies before relying on exotic prices. For antithetic simulation, estimate uncertainty from independent pair averages, not by treating both members as independent observations.

**Closeness of a simulated vanilla to the surface price.** The criterion depends on how local volatility was built; use the situation table in the option-numerics conventions, section 7 (sampling part, structural allowance from sensitivity runs, and the checks for a gap of tens of percent).

Option premiums quoted in units of the underlying coin convert to quote currency at that expiry's forward: the quote-currency premium is the coin premium times F. With zero discounting, parity C − P = F − K reads c − p = 1 − K/F in coin units, so a call-put pair gives F = K/(1 − (c − p)); a pair near the money pins it best, and that one forward converts every premium of the expiry. Neither the spot nor a per-row underlying price is that forward, and converting the strike to coin at spot is an inconsistent identity that shows up as a jump where put-based synthetic calls hand over to direct calls. Order the expiry axis by time to maturity (or by the parsed expiry date), never by an expiry label string: labels such as day-month-year codes sort alphabetically out of time order, and a finite difference in T over a mis-ordered axis gives wrong derivatives without any error. Pivoting or grouping by a label also re-sorts by the text, so reorder the matrix rows by numeric time to maturity and assert that the time coordinates strictly increase before differentiating. Sort output rows by maturity, then strike, using the numeric columns. A surface restricted to a target expiry and strike grid has exactly (number of target expiries) × (number of target strikes) nodes; count those, not the larger set of nodes it was built from. Map every contractual observation timestamp to the path time grid. If column zero stores the initial state, the end of step j is column j, not j-1. Include required terminal observations and keep intraday simulation steps distinct from barrier observation times. A constant-volatility Brownian-bridge correction applied with a frozen local coefficient is an approximation for state-dependent local volatility; it also changes the monitoring interpretation and must not replace explicitly discrete monitoring.

atoms.title: Dupire local volatility: from call prices or implied total variance, and pricing under local vol / Grid semantics, interpolation and simulation checks / Simulation checks (2)
atoms.text:
For a rectangular price grid, preserve labels as identifiers and explicitly order numeric coordinates before differentiating. Column names below are illustrative: map input names without renaming required output fields. First select the requested rows; reject missing cells rather than filling them with zero.

```python
# "label": the expiry identifier exactly as the input writes it (written to output label columns);
# "time": years to maturity computed from the exact timestamp (used only for ordering and derivatives)
axis = frame[["label", "time"]].drop_duplicates().sort_values("time")
assert axis["label"].is_unique
assert np.all(np.diff(axis["time"]) > 0)
strikes = np.sort(frame["strike"].unique())
assert not frame.duplicated(["label", "strike"]).any()
prices = frame.pivot(index="label", columns="strike", values="price")
prices = prices.reindex(index=axis["label"], columns=strikes)
assert np.isfinite(prices.to_numpy()).all()
# every output table: sort by the numeric time column, then strike; never by the label text
out = out.merge(axis, on="label").sort_values(["time", "strike"])
```

When a target strike lies outside the strikes quoted for an expiry, evaluate the interpolant the task names there too (`PchipInterpolator` extrapolates unless `extrapolate=False`), then floor at intrinsic value, `C = np.maximum(interp(K), np.maximum(F - K, 0))`. Holding the boundary price flat beyond the last quote breaks the decrease and convexity in strike that the local-vol formula relies on.

Use this exact matrix order and its matching coordinates for the specified derivative method, then map each result back to its original label. For a rectangular target grid, rows per expiry equal its target strike count; total nodes equal target expiries times target strikes, not the source paired-quote count.

atoms.title: European option finite-difference PDE
atoms.text:
Use this reference to assemble and check a finite-difference solver for European vanilla prices and Greeks, including specified cash-dividend events.

Map task quantities to these definitions by meaning and units, not by letter, before the first calculation; recheck when inputs or conventions change.

Explicit task definitions and contract conventions take precedence. If they conflict or are incomplete, identify the ambiguity and state the convention used.

atoms.title: European option finite-difference PDE / 1. Shared foundations
atoms.text:
## 1. Shared foundations
Symbols are local. Use S for spot, K for strike, $\sigma$ for annualized decimal volatility, r for the rate, q for continuous yield, and $\tau =T_{\mathrm{expiry}}-t$ for remaining time in years. European payoff is $g(S); V(S,0)=g(S)$. This entry assumes constant coefficients and payment at expiry. For closed-form comparisons use Black-Scholes under identical inputs. For American exercise, impose the early-exercise constraint using an LCP solver or another justified American method; a plain European linear solve alone is insufficient. Require $K>0$ and $\sigma \ge 0$; the grid formulas describe the diffusion case $\sigma >0$. Zero volatility is a first-order transport limit and needs suitable deterministic or monotone handling.

atoms.title: European option finite-difference PDE / 2. Space operator and time stepping
atoms.text:
## 2. Space operator and time stepping
In remaining time:
**European pricing PDE in remaining time**

$$
V_{\tau} = L V = \sigma ^{2}\cdot S^{2}\cdot V_{\mathrm{SS}}/2 + (r-q)\cdot S\cdot V_{S} - r\cdot V.
$$

On a uniform spot grid $S_{i}=i\cdot h$, interior row i has
**Lower-diagonal operator coefficient**

$$
\mathrm{lower}_{i} = \sigma ^{2}\cdot S_{i}^{2}/(2\cdot h^{2}) - (r-q)\cdot S_{i}/(2\cdot h)
$$

**Main-diagonal operator coefficient**

$$
\operatorname{diag}_{i} = -\sigma ^{2}\cdot S_{i}^{2}/h^{2}-r
$$

**Upper-diagonal operator coefficient**

$$
\mathrm{upper}_{i} = \sigma ^{2}\cdot S_{i}^{2}/(2\cdot h^{2}) + (r-q)\cdot S_{i}/(2\cdot h).
$$

**Apply the assembled spatial operator**

Thus $(LV)_i=\mathrm{lower}_i V_{i-1}+\operatorname{diag}_i V_i+\mathrm{upper}_i V_{i+1}$. The coefficient belongs to row i, not to the neighboring value's index.

For a step dtau and theta-method weight $\eta$:
**One theta-method time step with boundary contributions**

$$
(I-\eta \cdot \mathrm{dtau}\cdot L_{\mathrm{II}})\cdot V_{\mathrm{new}} = (I+(1-\eta )\cdot \mathrm{dtau}\cdot L_{\mathrm{II}})\cdot V_{\mathrm{old}} + \mathrm{dtau}\cdot ((1-\eta )\cdot b_{\mathrm{old}}+\eta \cdot b_{\mathrm{new}}).
$$

$L_{\mathrm{II}}$ contains interior-to-interior coefficients. The first component of b is $\mathrm{lower}_1V_0$ and the last is $\mathrm{upper}_{M-1}V_M$; other components are zero (add both terms if only one interior node exists). Weight old and new boundary contributions by $(1-\eta)$ and $\eta$ respectively; for backward Euler the old contribution is zero. $\eta =1$ gives backward Euler; $\eta =1/2$ gives Crank-Nicolson. Solve the tridiagonal system rather than explicitly inverting it. Nonsmooth payoffs can cause CN oscillations: two backward-Euler half steps for the first full step are a common Rannacher startup; document the schedule. Central differencing can lose monotonicity when drift dominates diffusion; refine or use a justified monotone discretization.

atoms.title: European option finite-difference PDE / 3. Boundaries and Greeks
atoms.text:
## 3. Boundaries and Greeks
Boundaries use remaining time $\tau$.
**Call boundary values**

$$
\;\text{Call}\;: V(0,\tau )=0; V(S_{\mathrm{max}},\tau ) \approx  S_{\mathrm{max}}\cdot \exp (-q\cdot \tau )-K\cdot \exp (-r\cdot \tau ).
$$

**Put boundary values**

$$
\;\text{Put}\;: V(0,\tau )=K\cdot \exp (-r\cdot \tau ); V(S_{\mathrm{max}},\tau ) \approx  0.
$$

The large-spot approximations require a sufficiently distant boundary; enlarge $S_{\mathrm{max}}$ to test truncation error. Negative rates are allowed and can make the put's left boundary exceed K.

**$\Delta$ and $\Gamma$ on the stock grid**

At interior nodes $\Delta\approx(V_{i+1}-V_{i-1})/(2h)$, $\Gamma\approx(V_{i+1}-2V_i+V_{i-1})/h^2$. Calendar $\Theta =-V_{\tau}$, and may be computed from the PDE operator or a time difference with the correct sign. Using the same operator for Theta and the PDE residual makes that residual a consistency check, not independent validation.

Vega/Rho from bumped PDE solves require identical domains, grids and interpolation conventions. If reporting values off-grid, state the interpolation; differentiating a piecewise-linear interpolant twice does not give a useful Gamma.

atoms.title: European option finite-difference PDE / 4. Events and convergence
atoms.text:
## 4. Events and convergence
Between discrete dividend events use the PDE above; do not also include those same dividends in q. For a deterministic cash dividend $D_{\mathrm{cash}}$, assumed ex-dividend and paid at calendar time $t_{d}$, the backward event map is $V_{\mathrm{before}}(S)=V_{\mathrm{after}}(\max (S-D_{\mathrm{cash}},0))$ under this specified stock-jump convention. Interpolate from the post-event grid; do not reverse the sign. This convention needs explicit treatment near zero and is not the continuous-yield model. Align time steps with events; do not smooth a discrete dividend across time.

Refine space and time separately and enlarge the domain. Compare prices AND Greeks with an independent closed form when applicable. Test puts, calls, nonzero q, non-ATM inputs, and expiry kinks. A residual near zero alone does not establish accuracy. Calendar t and remaining $\tau$ are different coordinates; their relation is $\tau =T_{\mathrm{expiry}}-t$.

atoms.title: European option finite-difference PDE / Efficient linear time stepping
atoms.text:
## Efficient linear time stepping

A one-dimensional nearest-neighbor spatial stencil gives a tridiagonal interior system. Store three diagonals and form the right-hand side using adjacent vector slices, including the appropriate boundary terms. Dense construction and dense factorization discard this structure.

For row coefficients $a_i,d_i,c_i$, SciPy's three-row band storage places the upper entry $c_i$ in column $i+1$, the diagonal $d_i$ in column $i$, and the lower entry $a_i$ in column $i-1$. The two unused corners are zero. A small-system comparison to a dense solve tests this packing.

When the operator, grid, step length and scheme weight are unchanged, the left matrix can be factored once and used for multiple right-hand sides. A new coefficient regime or a different step length may require new factors. Repeated calls to `solve_banded` do not promise cached factors. Thomas elimination needs safe pivots; it does not justify ignoring a near-zero pivot. These are linear European solves, not an obstacle solver.

Source: [SciPy solve_banded](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.linalg.solve_banded.html).

## 5. References
Crank and Nicolson (1947), A practical method for numerical evaluation of solutions of partial differential equations of the heat-conduction type. Black and Scholes (1973). The operator above follows directly by central differencing the stated PDE.

atoms.title: Event-study test statistics: market model, Patell, BMP, Kolari-Pynnonen, Corrado rank test / Setting and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Setting and assumptions
- N events (firms) i = 1..N. Event time: day 0 = event date, counted in trading days of the data (not calendar days).
  Estimation window $\operatorname{E}_{i}$: L1 days before the event window ($t = \mathrm{T0}+1\ldots \mathrm{T1}$). Event window: L2 days ($t = \mathrm{T1}+1\ldots \mathrm{T2}$), contains day 0.
  The test window [tau1, tau2] lies inside the event window; $L = \mathrm{tau2} - \mathrm{tau1} + 1$ counts both ends.
- Null H0: mean abnormal return is zero on the tested day, or mean CAR over [tau1, tau2] is zero.
- Market model $R_{it} = \alpha _{i} + \beta _{i} R_{mt} + e_{it}$, fitted by OLS on $\operatorname{E}_{i}$ only. The exact small-sample results below need
  iid normal $e_{it}$ and no event effect on the estimation window; the Z statistics are asymptotic (N large).

atoms.title: Event-study test statistics: market model, Patell, BMP, Kolari-Pynnonen, Corrado rank test / Inputs and units
atoms.text:
## Inputs and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| $R_{it}, R_{mt}$ | firm and market returns (simple or log, as the task says; 2% is `0.02`) | per day |
| L1, L2, L | estimation, event and test-window lengths in trading days | days |
| $N$ | number of events with valid data ($N_{t}$ on day t if some are missing) | count |

atoms.title: Event-study test statistics: market model, Patell, BMP, Kolari-Pynnonen, Corrado rank test / Market model and abnormal returns (means and sums over the estimation window E_i)
atoms.text:
## Market model and abnormal returns (means and sums over the estimation window E_i)

$$
\begin{gathered}
S_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sum _{\operatorname{E}} (R_{mt} - \bar{R}_{m})^{2},  \beta _{i} = \sum _{\operatorname{E}} (R_{mt} - \bar{R}_{m})(R_{it} - \bar{R}_{i}) / S_{\mathrm{xx}},  \alpha _{i} = \bar{R}_{i} - \beta _{i} \bar{R}_{m} \\
e_{it} = R_{it} - \alpha _{i} - \beta _{i} R_{mt} (t \in  \operatorname{E}),   s_{i}^{2} = \sum _{\operatorname{E}} e_{it}^{2} / (\mathrm{L1} - 2) \\
\mathrm{AR}_{it} = R_{it} - \alpha _{i} - \beta _{i} R_{mt} (\mathrm{event} \;\text{window}\;),   \mathrm{CAR}_{i} = \sum _{t=\mathrm{tau1}}^{\mathrm{tau2}} \mathrm{AR}_{it} \\
\mathrm{AAR}_{t} = (1/N) \sum _{i} \mathrm{AR}_{it},   \mathrm{CAAR} = (1/N) \sum _{i} \mathrm{CAR}_{i}
\end{gathered}
$$

Forecast-error (prediction-error) correction, since $\alpha _{i}$, $\beta _{i}$ are estimates:

$$
C_{it} = 1 + 1/\mathrm{L1} + (R_{mt} - \bar{R}_{m})^{2} / S_{\mathrm{xx}}
$$

$$
\mathrm{SAR}_{it} = \mathrm{AR}_{it} / (s_{i} \sqrt{C_{it}})
$$

Exact $t(\mathrm{L1}-2)$, with variance $(\mathrm{L1}-2)/(\mathrm{L1}-4)$.

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{CAR}_{i}) = s_{i}^{2} [ L + L^{2}/\mathrm{L1} + ( \sum _{t=\mathrm{tau1}}^{\mathrm{tau2}} (R_{mt} - \bar{R}_{m}) )^{2} / S_{\mathrm{xx}} ]
$$

$$
\mathrm{SCAR}_{i} = \mathrm{CAR}_{i} / \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{CAR}_{i})}
$$

Exact $t(\mathrm{L1}-2)$. The equivalent matrix expression is $\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{CAR}_i)=s_i^2 1'(I+X^{*}(X'X)^{-1}(X^{*})')1$, with $X$ and $X^{*}$ the $[1,R_m]$ regressor matrices of E and of the window.

atoms.title: Event-study test statistics: market model, Patell, BMP, Kolari-Pynnonen, Corrado rank test / Patell (1976) Z
Event-study test statistics: market model, Patell, BMP, Kolari-Pynnonen, Corrado rank test / Boehmer-Musumeci-Poulsen (1991) standardized cross-sectional test
atoms.text:
## Boehmer-Musumeci-Poulsen (1991) standardized cross-sectional test

$$
t_{\mathrm{BMP}} = \sqrt{N} \cdot  \mathrm{Xbar} / S_{X},   \mathrm{Xbar} = (1/N) \sum _{i} X_{i},   S_{X} = \sqrt{\sum _{i} (X_{i} - \mathrm{Xbar})^{2} / (N - 1)}
$$

$X_{i} = \mathrm{SAR}_{\mathrm{i0}}$(single day) or $\mathrm{SCAR}_{i}$ (window). Reference t(N-1) (N(0,1) for large N). Robust to event-induced variance.

atoms.title: Event-study test statistics: market model, Patell, BMP, Kolari-Pynnonen, Corrado rank test / Kolari-Pynnonen (2010) adjustment for cross-sectional correlation (clustered event dates)
atoms.text:
## Kolari-Pynnonen (2010) adjustment for cross-sectional correlation (clustered event dates)
$\bar{r}$ is the average over the $N(N-1)/2$ pairs $i < j$ of $\mathrm{corr}(e_{i}., e_{j}.)$, the Pearson correlation of the two firms' estimation-window residuals over their common calendar dates (diagonal 1's excluded).
Same reference as BMP:

$$
t_{\mathrm{KP}} = t_{\mathrm{BMP}} \cdot  \sqrt{(1 - \bar{r}) / (1 + (N - 1) \bar{r})}
$$

Adjusted Patell: software implementations multiply $Z_{\operatorname{P}}$ by the same factor; the variance of $Z_{\operatorname{P}}$ under equicorrelation
gives $Z_{\operatorname{P}}$ / $\sqrt{1 + (N - 1) \bar{r}}$. They differ by $\sqrt{1 - \bar{r}}$; use the one the task names.

atoms.title: Event-study test statistics: market model, Patell, BMP, Kolari-Pynnonen, Corrado rank test / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- Our null simulation (validation.md): all tests are near nominal size with iid normal residuals. Fat-tailed residuals
  make Patell over-reject (about 7% at nominal 5%); BMP and Corrado stay near nominal.
- Event-induced variance (higher variance in the event window): Patell and Corrado over-reject strongly; BMP does not.
- Same event date for all firms with correlated residuals: Patell and BMP over-reject badly even for small rbar;
  KP-adjusted BMP and the variance-algebra adjusted Patell restore the size; Corrado stays close to nominal.
- KP adjustment without clustering adds noise from rbar and slightly over-rejects; compute rbar on overlapping
  calendar dates and adjust only when event windows overlap in calendar time.
- Patell version b over-rejects for long windows (daily SARs share the estimation error); version a is exact.
- The multi-day Corrado statistic under-rejects as L grows (ranks within a firm are dependent).

atoms.text:
## Sources
Patell (1976) J. Accounting Research 14(2):246-276; Boehmer, Musumeci & Poulsen (1991) J. Financial Economics
30(2):253-272; Kolari & Pynnonen (2010) Review of Financial Studies 23(11):3996-4025; Corrado (1989) J. Financial
Economics 23(2):385-395; Corrado & Zivney (1992) J. Financial and Quantitative Analysis 27(3):465-478; Cowan (1992)
Review of Quantitative Finance and Accounting 2:343-358; Campbell & Wasley (1993) J. Financial Economics 33(1):73-92;

atoms.title: Event-study test statistics: market model, Patell, BMP, Kolari-Pynnonen, Corrado rank test / Corrado (1989) rank test
atoms.text:
## Corrado (1989) rank test
The S_K formulas below are one of two standardizations of the same ranks (Reading A); Reading B is at the end of this section. The order of presentation is not a default.
- Per firm, pool its L1 estimation residuals $e_{it}$ and L2 event-window $\mathrm{AR}_{it}$: $T = \mathrm{L1} + \mathrm{L2}$ values in time order.
  $K_{it} = \operatorname{rank}$ of $\mathrm{AR}_{it}$ among these T values (1 = smallest). Ties: average (mid) ranks. Expected rank (T + 1)/2.
Average over firms with data on day $t$:

$$
D_{t} = (1/N_{t}) \sum _{i} (K_{it} - (T + 1)/2)
$$

Sum over all $T$ pooled days $t$, including estimation AND event days; divisor $T$:

$$
S_{K} = \sqrt{(1/T) \sum _{t} D_{t}^{2}}
$$

Single day, reference $N(0,1)$:

$$
T_{C} = D_{0} / S_{K}
$$

Window (Cowan 1992; Campbell–Wasley 1993):

$$
T_{C} = \sum _{t=\mathrm{tau1}}^{\mathrm{tau2}} D_{t} / ( \sqrt{L} S_{K} )
$$

- Unequal or missing data (Corrado-Zivney 1992): $U_{it} = K_{it} / (T_{i} + 1)$ with $T_{i}$ the firm's count of valid returns,
  and use $U_{it}$ - 1/2 in place of $K_{it}$ - (T + 1)/2 (with equal $T_{i}$ the statistic is unchanged).

Two standardizations of the same ranks share the numerator and give different numbers.
They differ in the order of two steps, averaging across events and dividing by a standard deviation.
With d_it = U_it - 1/2 on every pooled day of event i (T_i pooled days, L window days, N events):
Reading A (Corrado 1989, the S_K formulas above): average across events first, then standardize.
  D_t = mean_i d_it on pooled day t;  S = sqrt( mean over all T pooled days of D_t^2 )
  day statistic D_t / S;  window sum_t D_t / (sqrt(L) S)
  S is the time-series sd of the cross-event average, so it absorbs cross-event correlation; it needs one pooled-day grid.
Reading B (per-event standardization, then aggregation across events as independent draws): standardize first, then average.
  sd_i = sqrt( (1/T_i) * sum over event i's pooled days of d_it^2 );  theta_it = d_it / sd_i
  day statistic Z_t = sqrt(N_t) * mean_i theta_it;  window sum_t Z_t / sqrt(L)
  With no ties sd_i^2 = (T_i - 1) / (12 (T_i + 1)).
Match the reading to the steps the task describes: what is averaged across events, and whose standard deviation divides it. If the wording fits both, compute both, print both, and state which one the output uses.
```python
d = [rankdata(np.r_[E[i], AR[i]]) / (len(E[i]) + L + 1) - 0.5 for i in range(N)]
D = np.mean(d, axis=0); S = np.sqrt(np.mean(D**2))
zA_day, zA_win = D[-L:] / S, D[-L:].sum() / (np.sqrt(L) * S)
theta = np.array([di / np.sqrt(np.mean(di**2)) for di in d])
zB_day = np.sqrt(N) * theta[:, -L:].mean(axis=0); zB_win = zB_day.sum() / np.sqrt(L)
```

atoms.title: Event-study test statistics: market model, Patell, BMP, Kolari-Pynnonen, Corrado rank test / Common variants and mistakes
atoms.text:
## Common variants and mistakes
- Randomization p-values (sign-flip, permutation, bootstrap) count draws whose statistic is at least as extreme as the observed one.

hit = np.abs(stat_star) >= np.abs(stat_obs) * (1 - 1e-12)
assert hit[identity_draw].all()   # the draw that reproduces the data must count
 The draw that reproduces the observed sample (all signs +1, the identity permutation) gives the observed statistic only up to floating-point round-off, so an exact comparison such as `abs(t_star) >= abs(t_obs)` can drop it or keep it by chance. Compare with a relative tolerance, for example `abs(t_star) >= abs(t_obs) * (1 - 1e-12)`, and check that the reproducing draw is counted.
- $s_{i}^{2}$ divisor: L1 - 2 (market model), L1 - 1 (constant-mean model, where $C_{it} = 1 + 1/\mathrm{L1}$ and
  $\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{CAR})=s^2(L+L^2/\mathrm{L1})$), L1 (MLE). Market-adjusted model ($\mathrm{AR} = R - R_{m}$): no estimation, $C_{it} = 1$.
- Forecast-error correction omitted ($C_{it} = 1, \operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{CAR}) = L s_{i}^{2}$) is a common simpler variant; it changes the number.
- Patell window version a vs b, and BMP on SCAR vs on CSAR, give different numbers; follow the task's wording.
- BMP compared with t(N-1) vs N(0,1); one-sided vs two-sided p-values; p = 2 * (1 - F(|stat|)) for two-sided.
- Corrado: rank over the pooled estimation + event window, not the event window alone; $S_{K}$ uses every pooled day;
  ranking SAR instead of AR, or re-standardizing day-0 SARs by their cross-sectional sd before ranking
  (Corrado-Zivney), are different tests.
- Off-by-one windows: (-1, +1) is three days; the estimation window must end before the event window starts.
- Lagged regressors: compute the change series once and shift it by exactly one row; re-deriving lagged differences with nested index offsets shifts twice and can leave the earliest windows empty.
- A lagged fit inside a window (y_t on y_{t-1}, as in an AR(1) of daily changes): take the positions `js` of the window's responses in the full series and pair each with its own previous value, `y = series[js]`, `x = series[js - 1]`, then fit once and reuse the coefficients for the forecast. Cutting the window out first and offsetting it (`w[1:]` against `w[:-1]`) drops the window's first response, whose previous value lies just before the window. If the task requires both values of a pair to lie inside the window, follow the task.
- When a window is stated as the n valid observations before an event → keep the rows where every field the window needs is valid, then take the last n of them before the event (`valid = frame.dropna(subset=needed_fields); window = valid[valid.index < event_date].iloc[-n:]`); n positions of the raw index span invalid rows and give a different window. Check the window length and its first and last dates.

atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| $n$ | number of loss observations | count |
| $u, N_{u}$ | threshold, number of $x_{i} > u; y_{i} = x_{i} - u$ for those i | loss units, count |
| $\xi$ | shape (tail index $1/\xi$ when $\xi>0$); $\xi>0$ heavy tail, $\xi  = 0$ exponential, $\xi  < 0$ bounded tail | none |
| $\beta$ | $\mathrm{GPD} \mathrm{scale}, \beta  > 0$ | loss units |
| $p$ | VaR/ES confidence level (99% is 0.99); tail probability is 1 - p | none |

atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / GPD (exceedance y >= 0)
atoms.text:
## GPD (exceedance y >= 0)
When $\xi  \ne  0$:

$$
G(y) = 1 - (1 + \xi  y / \beta )^{-1/\xi}
$$

$$
g(y) = (1/\beta ) (1 + \xi  y / \beta )^{-1/\xi  - 1}
$$

When $\xi  = 0$:

$$
G(y) = 1 - \exp (-y / \beta )
$$

$$
g(y) = (1/\beta ) \exp (-y / \beta )
$$

Support: $y \ge  0$ if $\xi  \ge  0$; $0 \le  y \le  -\beta /\xi$ if $\xi  < 0$.Log-likelihood of the $N_{u}$ exceedances:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\xi  \ne  0:  l(\xi , \beta ) = -N_{u} \ln (\beta ) - (1 + 1/\xi ) \cdot  \sum _{i} \ln (1 + \xi  y_{i} / \beta ) \\
\xi   = 0:  l(\beta )     = -N_{u} \ln (\beta ) - \sum _{i} y_{i} / \beta
\end{gathered}
$$

MLE constraints: $\beta  > 0$ and $1 + \xi  y_{i} / \beta  > 0$ for every i (return -inf otherwise; this matters for $\xi  < 0$).
Maximize numerically (e.g. Nelder-Mead on -l from a method-of-moments start $\mathrm{xi0} = (1 - m^{2}/s^{2})/2$, $\mathrm{beta0} = m (1 + m^{2}/s^{2})/2$, $m, s^{2} = \operatorname{mean}$, variance of y).
Use the $\xi  = 0$ branch (or |$\xi$| tiny) to avoid dividing by zero. MLE is regular for $\xi  > -1/2$; for $\xi  \le  -1$ the likelihood is unbounded (Smith 1985).
Library check: `scipy.stats.genpareto` uses the same sign of $\xi$ ($c = \xi$), fit with $\mathrm{floc}=0$ on the $y_{i}$.

atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / Tail estimator, VaR and ES (McNeil & Frey 2000)
atoms.text:
## Tail estimator, VaR and ES (McNeil & Frey 2000)
For $x > u$: $\hat{F}(x) = 1 - (N_{u} / n) (1 + \xi  (x - u) / \beta )^{-1/\xi}$. Inverting at level p:

When $\xi  \ne  0$:

$$
\operatorname{VaR}_{p} = u + (\beta  / \xi ) \cdot  ( ((n / N_{u}) (1 - p))^{-\xi} - 1 )
$$

When $\xi  = 0$:

$$
\operatorname{VaR}_{p} = u - \beta  \cdot  \ln ( (n / N_{u}) (1 - p) )
$$

Valid only for $\xi  < 1$ (ES is infinite for $\xi  \ge  1$):

$$
\operatorname{ES}_{p} = \operatorname{VaR}_{p} / (1 - \xi ) + (\beta  - \xi  u) / (1 - \xi )
$$

Valid only when $1 - p < N_{u} / n$ ($\operatorname{VaR}_{p}$ above u); otherwise use the empirical quantile. Mean excess over $v \ge  u$: $(\beta  + \xi  (v - u)) / (1 - \xi )$.

atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- GPD needs enough exceedances and a high enough u; too low u biases $\xi$ (e.g. a Student-t tail fitted at a moderate quantile gives $\xi$ below $1/\nu$), too high u inflates variance.
- ES formula requires $\xi  < 1$; second moments need $\xi  < 1/2$. Clustered (non-i.i.d.) losses: filter first (GARCH) or decluster.

atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / Sources
Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / Setting and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Setting and assumptions
- Work with LOSSES, large = bad: $x_{t} = -r_{t}$ (or `-(P&L)`). Fit the right tail of x. A task that keeps returns must flip the sign; VaR/ES are then reported as positive loss numbers.
- Pickands-Balkema-de Haan: above a high threshold u, the excess $Y = X - u \vert  X > u$ is approximately generalized Pareto (GPD).
  Data are treated as i.i.d. (or as GARCH-standardized residuals, McNeil & Frey 2000; then scale back with the forecast mean and $\sigma$).
- Threshold u: given by the task, or an empirical quantile, or "the k largest losses" (then u = the (k+1)-th largest loss and $N_{u} = k$).
  Diagnostics: mean-excess plot $e(v) = \operatorname{mean}(x_{i} - v \vert  x_{i} > v)$ approximately linear for $v\ge u$ (slope $\xi/(1-\xi)$); fitted $\xi$ stable when u is moved.
  Exceedances use strict $x_{i} > u$; ties at u are not exceedances.

atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / Variant: Hill estimator (xi > 0, positive losses only)
atoms.text:
## Variant: Hill estimator (xi > 0, positive losses only)
Sort descending $X_{1} \ge  \ldots  \ge  X_{n}$; with k upper order statistics (all $X_{i} > 0$):

$$
\xi _{H} = (1/k) \cdot  \sum _{i=1}^{k} \ln  X_{i} - \ln  X_{k+1}
$$

Tail index:

$$
\alpha _{H} = 1 / \xi _{H}
$$

Weissman quantile:

$$
\operatorname{VaR}_{p} = X_{k+1} \cdot  ( (n / k) (1 - p) )^{-\xi _{H}}
$$

For $\xi _{H} < 1$:

$$
\operatorname{ES}_{p} = \operatorname{VaR}_{p} / (1 - \xi _{H})
$$

Some texts use $X_{(k)}$ as the threshold with divisor k - 1 or k; these are different estimators. Hill assumes a Pareto-type tail and is biased when the tail is not exactly Pareto.

atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / VaR backtests (hit sequence $I_t=1$ if $\mathrm{loss}_t>\operatorname{VaR}_t$, else 0; $t=1,\ldots,T$)
atoms.text:
## VaR backtests (hit sequence $I_t=1$ if $\mathrm{loss}_t>\operatorname{VaR}_t$, else 0; $t=1,\ldots,T$)
p0 = expected violation probability = 1 - (VaR confidence). $x = \sum  I_{t}, \hat{\pi} = x / T$. Convention: $0 \cdot  \ln (0) = 0$.

Kupiec POF:

$$
\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{POF}} = -2 [ (T - x) \ln (1 - \mathrm{p0}) + x \ln (\mathrm{p0}) ] + 2 [ (T - x) \ln (1 - \hat{\pi}) + x \ln (\hat{\pi}) ] \sim \mathrm{chi2}(1)
$$

For $x = 0$:

$$
\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{POF}} = -2 T \ln (1 - \mathrm{p0})
$$

For $x = T$:

$$
\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{POF}} = -2 T \ln (\mathrm{p0})
$$

Christoffersen independence: count transitions over $t = 2\ldots T$, $n_{ij}$ = #$\{I_{t-1} = i, I_{t} = j\}$:

$$
\pi _{01} = \mathrm{n01} / (\mathrm{n00} + \mathrm{n01})
$$

$$
\pi _{11} = \mathrm{n11} / (\mathrm{n10} + \mathrm{n11})
$$

$$
\pi  = (\mathrm{n01} + \mathrm{n11}) / (\mathrm{n00} + \mathrm{n01} + \mathrm{n10} + \mathrm{n11})
$$

Null: no clustering.

$$
\ln  \mathrm{L0} = (\mathrm{n00} + \mathrm{n10}) \ln (1 - \pi ) + (\mathrm{n01} + \mathrm{n11}) \ln (\pi )
$$

Alternative: first-order Markov.

$$
\ln  \mathrm{L1} = \mathrm{n00} \ln (1 - \pi _{01}) + \mathrm{n01} \ln (\pi _{01}) + \mathrm{n10} \ln (1 - \pi _{11}) + \mathrm{n11} \ln (\pi _{11})
$$

$$
\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{ind}} = -2 (\ln  \mathrm{L0} - \ln  \mathrm{L1}) \sim \mathrm{chi2}(1)
$$

$$
\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{cc}} = \mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{POF}} + \mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{ind}} \sim \mathrm{chi2}(2)
$$

Edge cases: no hits $\to  \mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{ind}} = 0; \mathrm{n10} + \mathrm{n11} = 0$(only hit is the last observation) -> $\pi _{11}$ terms drop out; n11 = 0 -> $\mathrm{n11} \ln (\pi _{11}) = 0$ and $\mathrm{n10} \ln (1) = 0$.
p-value = $1 - \mathrm{chi2}.\operatorname{cdf}(\mathrm{LR}, \mathrm{df})$; reject at level a if p-value < a. $\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{ind}}$ equals the G-test of independence on the 2x2 table [[n00, n01], [n10, n11]].
$\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{cc}}$ variants: (a) $\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{POF}}$ on all T plus $\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{ind}}$ (common), (b) $-2 (\ln  L(\mathrm{p0}) - \ln  \mathrm{L1})$ on the T-1 transitions, which equals $\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{POF}}$ on $I_2,\ldots,I_T$ plus $\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{ind}}$ exactly. Results differ slightly.

atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / Common variants and mistakes
atoms.text:
## Common variants and mistakes
- Several models in one session: the GPD scale $\beta$, a normal or GARCH volatility $\sigma$ and a t scale are different parameters. Keep each under its own name (for example `gpd_beta`, `normal_sigma`), pass the intended one to each formula, and when a fitted parameter changes, recompute every VaR, ES and derived result that uses it before writing outputs.
- Level labels built from a confidence level p: take the digits after the decimal point (0.99 → "99", 0.995 → "995", 0.999 → "999"), for example `format(p, "g").split(".")[1]` or the string the task lists. A fixed multiplier fails for one of them: `int(p * 100)` turns 0.995 into "99", `int(p * 1000)` turns 0.99 into "990", and floating point can make `int(0.29 * 100)` 28.
- Sign: fitting the GPD to returns (left tail as negative numbers) or forgetting $y = x - u$ (fitting x itself) gives nonsense $\beta$.
- $N_{u}$ / n vs (1 - threshold quantile): use the actual count $N_{u}$ when u is an empirical quantile.
- Violation as $\ge$ vs $>$, and `return < -VaR` vs $\mathrm{loss} > \operatorname{VaR}$: same thing if VaR is positive.
- Basel traffic light (BCBS 1996): with T daily 99% VaR hits, yellow zone starts at the smallest x with $\mathrm{BinomCDF}(x; T, 0.01) \ge  0.95$, red at $\ge  0.9999$.
- Kupiec has low power in small samples, and its exact size differs from nominal because x is discrete; $\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{ind}}$ is oversized when few hits are expected.

atoms.title: Tail VaR/ES four ways with a rolling backtest: workflow
atoms.text:
Read the task's formula file first; the code below follows the usual definitions. When result keys drop the leading "0." of a level, build them from the text of the number, `str(p)[2:]` (0.99 -> "99", 0.995 -> "995", 0.999 -> "999"), not from `int(p * 1000)`, which turns 0.99 into "990"; print the keys before writing. Method names inside keys are written in full exactly as the output section lists them (for example `historical`, `normal`, `evt`, `garch_evt`), never abbreviated. Losses L = -r (log returns r).
Every quantile uses `method="lower"`; every sample std uses `ddof=1`.

1. Helpers.
```python
q = lambda x, a: np.quantile(x, a, method="lower")
def pot(x, uq):                                   # threshold, GPD fit on excesses (location fixed at 0)
    u = q(x, uq); ex = x[x > u] - u
    xi, _, s = genpareto.fit(ex, floc=0)
    return u, xi, s, len(ex), len(x), ex
def pot_var_es(u, xi, s, nu, n, p):
    v = u + s / xi * ((n / nu * (1 - p)) ** (-xi) - 1)
    return v, v / (1 - xi) + (s - xi * u) / (1 - xi)
def hist(x, p):   v = q(x, p); return v, x[x >= v].mean()
def normal(x, p): m, sd = x.mean(), x.std(ddof=1); z = norm.ppf(p); return m + sd * z, m + sd * norm.pdf(z) / (1 - p)
def garch(rr):
    res = arch_model(100 * rr, p=1, q=1, mean="Zero", vol="GARCH", dist="Normal").fit(disp="off")
    return res, np.asarray(res.conditional_volatility) / 100          # omega: res.params["omega"] / 1e4
```
Every GPD fit uses excesses, `x[x > u] - u`, never the exceedances themselves; this holds for the full-sample losses, the standardized losses of GARCH-EVT and each backtest window, so call the same `pot()` helper everywhere. In `pot_var_es` the ratio is `n / nu`, all observations over exceedances (greater than 1); writing `nu / n` inflates VaR several-fold. Check before writing: for each level, the full-sample POT VaR should be within about 25% of the historical VaR at that level (GARCH-EVT VaR scales with the current volatility and need not be). For GARCH-EVT check the standardized VaR before scaling: at 99% it is usually between 2 and 4 (the standard normal value is 2.33); a value above 6 means the ratio was written as `nu / n`.

2. Full sample, for every confidence level p: `hist(L, p)`, `normal(L, p)` (keeps the mean), `pot_var_es(*pot(L, uq)[:5], p)`.
   GARCH-EVT: `res, sig = garch(r)`; standardized losses `zl = -np.asarray(res.std_resid)`; POT on `zl` with its own threshold quantile;
   VaR and ES are `sig[-1]` times the standardized values. Hill: sort L descending, `k = floor(sqrt(N))`,
   `mean(log(L_(1..k))) - log(L_(k+1))`.
3. Rolling backtest at the backtest level only (not the last level of an earlier loop): for each `i` in `range(W, N)` use the
   window `L[i-W:i]` (and `r[i-W:i]`), forecast VaR four ways, and compare with `L[i]` (violation: strictly greater).
   For GARCH-EVT refit on the window and scale by the one-step forecast
   `sqrt(res.forecast(horizon=1, reindex=False).variance.iloc[-1, 0]) / 100`, not by the last fitted value.
4. Coverage tests with `xlx(c, p) = 0 if c == 0 else c * log(p)`, alpha = 1 - level, T forecast days, x violations, pi = x/T:
   `LR_uc = -2 * (xlx(x, alpha) + xlx(T-x, 1-alpha) - xlx(x, pi) - xlx(T-x, 1-pi))`, p-value `chi2.sf(LR_uc, 1)`.
   Transition counts n00, n01, n10, n11 over consecutive indicators; `p01 = n01/(n00+n01)`, `p11 = n11/(n10+n11)`,
   `pa = (n01+n11)/(all)`; `LR_ind = -2 * (l(pa) - l(p01, p11))` with Bernoulli log-likelihoods built from xlx,
   p-value `chi2.sf(LR_ind, 1)`; `LR_cc = LR_uc + LR_ind`, p-value `chi2.sf(LR_cc, 2)`.

atoms.title: EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition
atoms.text: Use this document to estimate exponentially weighted return covariance and attribute a linear portfolio's volatility or normal VaR to its assets. It distinguishes conditional EWMA forecasts from centered weighted sample covariance, and marginal risk from component risk. It does not cover nonlinear portfolio revaluation or risk-parity optimization.
