atoms.title: EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition / 2. EWMA Covariance and Estimation Conventions / Conditional covariance forecast
atoms.text:
### Conditional covariance forecast

Use this branch for a RiskMetrics-style conditional forecast. Under the zero-conditional-mean approximation, $e_{t} = r_{t}$. If a nonzero conditional mean model is specified, use its innovations. Subtracting the full sample mean instead defines a different estimator and can introduce future information into historical forecasts.

The innovation outer product supplies one variance or covariance update for each asset pair; it is an n-by-n matrix, not the scalar sum of squared innovations.

The $(i,j)$ entry of $e_{t} e_{t}^{T}$ is $e_{t,i} \cdot  e_{t,j}$.

The covariance forecast weights the previous forecast and the latest outer product.

$$
C_{t} = \lambda \cdot C_{t-1} + (1-\lambda )\cdot e_{t} e_{t}^{T}
$$

Given an initial forecast $C_{0}$ before the m observations being incorporated, expanding the recursion gives its finite-history form.

$$
C_{m} = \lambda ^{m}\cdot C_{0} + (1-\lambda )\cdot \sum _{j=1}^{m}[\lambda ^{m-j}\cdot e_{j} e_{j}^{T}]
$$

The initial condition remains with weight $\lambda^{m}$. A zero matrix, a first-observation outer product and an initial sample covariance are distinct seeds; EWMA alone does not choose between them. A first-observation seed already incorporates that observation, so the next update incorporates the next observation. A sample-covariance seed also requires its own sample interval, centering and divisor conventions.

**Estimation window and initialization window are different.** A trailing estimation window selects which recent observations enter an estimate at a particular date. An initialization window supplies a starting matrix, after which subsequent observations update it. An expanding recursive history retains older information through the previous matrix. Neither a window length nor a decay factor specifies all three choices. Preserve the stated sample interval, seed and normalization together.

atoms.title: EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition / 2. EWMA Covariance and Estimation Conventions / Normalized finite-window moments
atoms.text:
### Normalized finite-window moments

Use this branch only when the specification explicitly requests exponentially weighted moments whose weights sum to one. A window length for a recursive EWMA does not by itself request this branch. Let k be the age of an observation ($k=0$ is newest), and L the window length.

The normalized observation weight is:

$$
p_k=\frac{\lambda^k}{\sum_{a=0}^{L-1}\lambda^a},\qquad k=0,\ldots,L-1
$$

For a zero-mean model, the finite-window second moment is:

$$
C_{\mathrm{zero}} = \sum _{k=0}^{L-1}[p_{k}\cdot r_{t-k} r_{t-k}^{T}]
$$

If instead a centered weighted sample covariance is requested, first define the weighted sample mean.

$$
\bar{r} = \sum _{k=0}^{L-1}[p_{k}\cdot r_{t-k}]
$$

The centered population-form weighted covariance is:

$$
C_{\mathrm{centered}} = \sum _{k=0}^{L-1}[p_{k}\cdot (r_{t-k}-\bar{r})\cdot (r_{t-k}-\bar{r})^{T}]
$$

For fixed deterministic weights and independent observations with a common mean and covariance, the usual unbiased correction divides $C_{\mathrm{centered}}$ by $1-\sum (p_{k}^{2})$, when positive. That correction is not part of the conditional EWMA recursion. The normalization and centering choices in a statistical covariance routine cannot be assumed to match a requested forecast.

With zero initialization, uncentered recursion over L observations equals $(1-\lambda^L)C_{\mathrm{zero}}$. Dividing a recursion with a nonzero seed by this factor does not remove the seed and is not the same finite-window estimator.

atoms.title: EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition / 4. Euler Risk Decomposition
atoms.text:
## 4. Euler Risk Decomposition

Use this block for attribution of volatility with C fixed and $\sigma _{p} > 0$. Derivatives vary one weight while holding other weights fixed; renormalizing weights during differentiation measures a different sensitivity.

The covariance exposure vector has one element per asset.

$$
b = C\cdot w
$$

Marginal risk is the derivative of portfolio volatility with respect to an asset weight.

$$
\mathrm{MRC}_{i} = \partial (\sigma _{p})/\partial (w_{i}) = b_{i}/\sigma _{p}
$$

Component risk multiplies that derivative by the position's weight.

$$
\mathrm{RC}_{i} = w_{i}\cdot \mathrm{MRC}_{i}
$$

Fractional contribution divides component risk by total volatility; multiply by 100 only when reporting percent rather than a fraction.

$$
\mathrm{PRC}_{i} = \mathrm{RC}_{i}/\sigma _{p} = w_{i}\cdot b_{i}/v_{p}
$$

Euler's identity for the degree-one volatility function gives full allocation.

$$
\sum _{i} \mathrm{RC}_{i} = \sigma _{p};  \sum _{i} \mathrm{PRC}_{i} = 1
$$

Negative contributions can represent hedging and need not be clipped. Weights need not all be positive or sum to one for the algebraic identity to hold. Replacing them by absolute values changes the portfolio.

If the requested risk measure is variance, an additive variance allocation has different units.

$$
\mathrm{VC}_{i} = w_{i}\cdot b_{i};  \sum _{i} \mathrm{VC}_{i} = v_{p}
$$

Variance is homogeneous of degree two, so its literal Euler derivative contributions sum to twice the variance; they are not the volatility components above.

$$
\partial (v_{p})/\partial (w_{i}) = 2\cdot b_{i}
$$

For normal VaR with fixed C and $\mu$, the component allocation also includes the mean term.

$$
\mathrm{RC}_{\mathrm{VaR}},i = w_{i}\cdot (z_{\alpha}\cdot \mathrm{MRC}_{i} - \mu _{i})
$$

These components sum to $\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}$. With zero mean they are $z_{\alpha}$ times the volatility components. Multiplication by a positive portfolio value converts them to currency; it does not change fractional contributions when the total is nonzero. A zero total VaR has no defined percentage allocation.

atoms.title: EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition / 5. Checks and Scope
atoms.text:
## 5. Checks and Scope

A common $\lambda$ and a positive-semidefinite seed preserve symmetry and positive semidefiniteness in exact arithmetic. Applying unrelated decay factors separately to matrix entries need not do so. Materially negative eigenvalues or variance indicate a problem; small roundoff negatives require a scale-aware tolerance rather than arbitrary changes to the estimate.

The expanded-history formula checks the recursion, including the seed and observation order. With $\lambda =0$ the next forecast is the latest outer product; with $\lambda =1$ it remains the seed. Finite-window normalization and the unbiased correction have separate edge cases; one observation has no unbiased centered covariance estimate.

The Euler sum identities check allocation algebra **but cannot establish that the covariance estimator, window, asset ordering or horizon is correct**. Independent checks include a diagonal covariance case, consistent asset permutations, the expanded-history result, and volatility derivatives with C held fixed. A scalar rank-one update cannot reproduce differing asset variances and cross-covariances.

If $\sigma _{p}=0$, the displayed MRC and PRC ratios are undefined; adding an arbitrary positive denominator changes their meaning. A singular covariance can still produce positive portfolio volatility, in which case these formulas remain valid.

EWMA responds to squared innovations; it does not by itself establish normal tails, remove serial dependence, or describe a nonlinear payoff. Quantile risk and volatility attribution are distinct from identifying equal-risk portfolio weights.

atoms.title: EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition / 6. References
atoms.text:
## 6. References

J.P. Morgan / Reuters, *RiskMetrics — Technical Document*, fourth edition (1996), §5.2.1 and §5.2.1.1: exponential variance and covariance forecasts. The matrix expansion and estimator distinctions above follow by algebra under the explicitly stated seed and mean conventions. [Publisher PDF](https://www.msci.com/documents/10199/5915b101-4206-4ba0-aee2-3449d5c7e95a).

Dirk Tasche, *Capital Allocation to Business Units and Sub-Portfolios: the Euler Principle*, arXiv:0708.2542, revised 2008, §2 and §3.1: homogeneous risk allocation and standard-deviation contributions. The weight-coordinate and normal-quantile forms above follow by differentiation. [Author paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.2542).

atoms.title: EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition / 1. Shared Foundations
atoms.text:
## 1. Shared Foundations

Map the task's notation, definitions and units to the quantities here. Explicit task conventions take precedence; if they conflict or leave an estimator unspecified, identify the ambiguity and state the interpretation. A parameter's name alone does not define its statistical role.

| Symbol | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| n; i, j | Number of assets; asset indices |
| $t$ | Observation index, increasing from oldest to newest |
| $r_{t}$ | Column vector of simultaneous one-period returns, in decimals |
| $m_{t}$ | Conditional mean of $r_{t}$, specified using information available before t |
| $e_{t}$ | Return innovation $r_{t}$ - $m_{t}$ |
| $C_{t}$ | Covariance forecast after incorporating observation t, for the next period |
| $\lambda$ | Decay factor, normally $0 < \lambda  < 1$ |
| $w$ | Asset weights, in exactly the same order as $C_{t}$'s rows and columns |
| $C; \mu$ | Covariance matrix and mean-return vector for the risk horizon being measured |
| $\sigma _{p}$ | Portfolio volatility in return units |
| $\alpha$; $\Phi$ | Confidence probability in (0,1); standard normal cumulative distribution |
| $A$ | Number of observation periods per year |

For simple returns and beginning-of-period weights, the portfolio return is the weighted asset return. A weighted sum of log returns is generally only an approximation to a portfolio's log return.

$$
r_{p,t} = w^{T} r_{t}
$$

Here superscript T means transpose. Changes from decimal returns to percentage-point returns multiply covariance by $100^2$ and volatility by 100. Asset order, units and observation dates must agree before combining covariance with weights. Missing observations require a specified policy; they are not zero returns.

## 2. EWMA Covariance and Estimation Conventions

atoms.title: EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition / 2. EWMA Covariance and Estimation Conventions / Recursive EWMA over an estimation window
atoms.text:
### Recursive EWMA over an estimation window

This block is the first-observation-seeded convention, as in `ewm(adjust=False)`, applied to the most recent $L$ observations. Use it only when that initialization is selected; a window length and decay factor alone do not choose the seed. A zero-seed finite-history alternative is $C=(1-\lambda)\sum_{k=0}^{L-1}\lambda^k e_{t-k}e_{t-k}^T$, which is not renormalized and gives a different oldest-observation weight.

Window from oldest to newest: $e_{t-L+1}, \ldots , e_{t}$.

$$
C = e_{t-L+1} e_{t-L+1}^{T}
$$

For $s = t-L+2, \ldots , t$:

$$
C = \lambda \cdot C + (1-\lambda )\cdot e_{s} e_{s}^{T}
$$

The result is the forecast after the newest observation. It is not centered, renormalized or divided by $(1-\lambda^L)$. A window length given in the configuration applies even when existing code ignores it; observations older than the window do not enter.

atoms.title: EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition / 3. Portfolio Volatility and Normal VaR
atoms.text:
## 3. Portfolio Volatility and Normal VaR

For a linear portfolio, variance is the covariance quadratic form.

$$
v_{p} = w^{T} C w
$$

Portfolio volatility is its nonnegative square root.

$$
\sigma _{p} = \sqrt{v_{p}}
$$

The normal quantile is determined by the confidence probability, not by a fixed rounded constant.

$$
z_{\alpha} = \Phi ^{-1}(\alpha )
$$

When loss is minus return, the normal loss quantile includes the portfolio mean. A zero-mean specification sets $\mu$ to zero. Here $\mu$ is the conditional mean forecast that goes with $C$. The RiskMetrics EWMA method takes the conditional mean of daily returns as zero, consistent with its uncentered recursion, so with an EWMA covariance a full-sample average return is not $\mu$ unless the task says to use one.

$$
\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha} = z_{\alpha}\cdot \sigma _{p} - w^{T} \mu
$$

This is a return-unit quantile; for a positive portfolio value P, currency VaR is $P\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha$. A convention that floors VaR at zero is an additional convention, not part of this formula.

Under the conventional unchanged per-period covariance and uncorrelated additive-return assumptions, annualized volatility is:

$$
\sigma _{\mathrm{annual}} = \sqrt{A}\cdot \sigma _{p}
$$

The corresponding annualized covariance is A*C. These are horizon-scaling assumptions, not exact laws for compounded returns or serially correlated returns. An already annualized covariance must not be annualized again.

atoms.title: Execution benchmarks, participation and volume profiles
atoms.text: Use this reference to interpret execution costs, signed spread measures and quantity allocations. An execution schedule is a target; a fill record is a realized or explicitly modeled outcome. A volume cap alone is not a model of queue priority, available liquidity or market impact.

atoms.title: Execution benchmarks, participation and volume profiles / Reference prices and time
atoms.text:
## Reference prices and time

Map the trade side, quantity units, reference clock and quote-selection rule first. Transaction time, exchange publication time and local receipt time can differ. A quote known just before a decision and a quote first observed after it answer different questions. A retrospective specification can prescribe either; only information already available can drive a live decision.

For positive quantities $q_{i}$ and fill prices $p_{i}$, execution weighting uses quantities, not the count of fills.

**Average execution price**

$$
\bar{p}=\frac{\sum_i q_i p_i}{\sum_i q_i}
$$

Market VWAP uses the same weighted-price operation on its specified eligible market trades, which may differ from the order's fills. Both averages are undefined when the denominator is zero.

atoms.title: Execution benchmarks, participation and volume profiles / Signed cost and spreads
atoms.text:
## Signed cost and spreads

Let $s=+1$ for a buy and $s=-1$ for a sell, $m_{0}$ a positive benchmark midpoint and $m_{H}$ a later midpoint. Positive cost denotes a worse price for the investor. The following expressions use one fixed reference denominator; definitions using different denominators must not be mixed.

**Executed-price slippage in basis points**

$$
\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{bps}} = 10000\cdot s\cdot (\bar{p}-m_{0})/m_{0}
$$

**Two-sided effective spread**

$$
\mathrm{effective}_{\mathrm{bps}} = 20000\cdot s\cdot (\bar{p}-m_{0})/m_{0}
$$

**Two-sided realized spread at the specified later benchmark**

$$
\mathrm{realized}_{\mathrm{bps}} = 20000\cdot s\cdot (\bar{p}-m_{H})/m_{0}
$$

**Signed reference-price movement**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{movement}_{\mathrm{bps}} = 10000\cdot s\cdot (m_{H}-m_{0})/m_{0} \\
\mathrm{effective}_{\mathrm{bps}} = \mathrm{realized}_{\mathrm{bps}}+2\cdot \mathrm{movement}_{\mathrm{bps}}
\end{gathered}
$$

The identity is arithmetic, not evidence of causal impact. Arrival-reference order averages differ from measures using each fill's own reference midpoint. Averaging individual percentages is generally not equal to a percentage formed from aggregated prices when denominators vary. Fixing a later horizon does not establish permanent versus temporary impact economically.

Executed-price slippage excludes fees and nonexecution opportunity cost unless explicitly added. Full implementation shortfall can include both, relative to a stated decision portfolio. A report containing only the fills does not measure the cost of the unfilled balance.

atoms.title: Execution benchmarks, participation and volume profiles / Participation and residual quantity
atoms.text:
## Participation and residual quantity

If a rule limits a child order by remaining quantity R, participation fraction p times eligible market volume v, and size cap M, its allowable quantity is the minimum of those nonnegative quantities. A filled amount can be smaller under a separate fill model. Distinguish target quantity, permitted order quantity and actual quantity. No-volume intervals do not imply zero price; they imply no observed volume for that interval.

Volume known only at the end of an interval cannot be used as a forecast at its beginning. Ex-post participation reconstructions are valid descriptive calculations but are not automatically implementable trading strategies.

atoms.title: Execution benchmarks, participation and volume profiles / Checks and scope
atoms.text:
## Checks and scope

Quantity reconciliation connects executed and residual quantities to the target. Conditional shares sum to one only on their declared eligible set. Out-of-sample profile R-squared can be negative; it is not bounded below by zero, and a flat realized profile needs a specified zero-denominator convention. Similar-looking timestamp or volume columns are different economic objects when their availability or aggregation differs.

atoms.title: Execution benchmarks, participation and volume profiles / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources

[SEC staff FAQ on Rule 605, execution-quality statistics](https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/staff-guidance/trading-markets-frequently-asked-questions/frequently-asked-questions-rule-605-regulation-nms), for benchmark-time and quantity-weighting distinctions. The formulas here state generic conventions, not a claim that every market or contract follows US equity reporting rules. Spread reconciliation and conditional allocation follow directly from the definitions above.

atoms.title: Execution benchmarks, participation and volume profiles / Intraday share estimates
atoms.text:
## Intraday share estimates

For historical session d and bucket b, let $v_{d,b}$ be volume and $V_{d}$ its full-session total, assumed positive.

**A session's volume fractions**

$$
s_{d,b} = v_{d,b}/V_{d}
$$

Averages of s give each session equal influence. Dividing pooled bucket volumes by pooled session volume instead weights high-volume sessions more heavily. Coordinatewise medians or winsorized means need not sum to one.

For historical lag l and positive half-life H, exponential weighting has:

**Decay weight by age**

$$
a_{l} = \exp (-\ln (2)\cdot l/H)
$$

A finite weighted average divides by the sum of the included weights. This is not automatically the same as a recursive infinite-history estimator with a particular initialization.

Given nonnegative predicted bucket scores $u_{b}$ and eligible set E with positive total mass:

**Conditional allocation over the remaining opportunities**

$$
w_b=\frac{u_b}{\sum_{j\in E}u_j},\qquad b\in E
$$

If E is empty or its total mass is zero, no proportional schedule is defined by these scores. A fallback requires an explicit convention. A bar timestamp can label its beginning or its end; that convention determines whether the bar is eligible at a decision time.

For integer total Q, allocations $Qw_b$ can be rounded down, then the remaining units assigned in descending fractional-remainder order with a specified tie rule. This preserves nonnegativity and the total; it does not guarantee participation constraints. Conflicting constraints require a different allocation problem.

atoms.title: Factor regressions and covariance attribution
atoms.text: Use this reference to interpret linear factor exposures and additive variance contributions. It distinguishes fitted return components from risk contributions and robust inference from changing the fitted model. It does not identify causal risk premia from correlated proxies.

atoms.title: Factor regressions and covariance attribution / Definitions and conventions
atoms.text:
## Definitions and conventions

Map return frequency, units, information dates and the intercept convention to the task. A stock excess return subtracts its matching-period risk-free return; an already excess or zero-investment factor is not reduced by that rate again. Percentage-point spreads and decimal returns are different units. Explicit definitions govern annualization, missing observations and covariance divisors.

Let y contain T observations, F contain K factor columns, X include the intercept and F, b contain regression coefficients, and e denote residuals. A prime denotes transpose. These identities concern an unweighted, unpenalized OLS fit with an intercept, full column rank and a common sample.

**Fitted regression and residual**

$$
\begin{gathered}
b = (X'X)^{-1}\cdot X'\cdot y \\
\hat{y} = X\cdot b \\
e = y-\hat{y}
\end{gathered}
$$

The inverse expresses the mathematical solution; near collinearity makes coefficients unstable. Singular designs do not identify unique individual exposures. Robust standard errors cannot remedy identification failure.

atoms.title: Factor regressions and covariance attribution / Components of a fitted observation
Factor regressions and covariance attribution / Covariance allocation of variance
atoms.text:
## Covariance allocation of variance

Use sample covariances over exactly the fitted observations and one shared divisor. Assume $\operatorname{Var}(y)>0$. Covariance allocation shares correlated contributions; it is not a decomposition into independent factor variances.

**Fraction of total variance assigned to a fitted component**

$$
a_{j} = \operatorname{Cov}(c_{j},y)/\operatorname{Var}(y)
$$

OLS orthogonality makes the residual contribution equal to its variance fraction on that same sample.

**Residual variance share and coefficient of determination**

$$
\begin{gathered}a_e=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(e)}{\operatorname{Var}(y)}\\ R_{\mathrm{squared}}=1-\frac{\sum_t e_t^2}{\sum_t(y_t-\operatorname{mean}(y))^2}\\ a_e=1-R_{\mathrm{squared}}\end{gathered}
$$

**Exhaustiveness of the allocation**

$$
\sum _{j} a_{j} + a_{e} = 1
$$

To see why, center the level identity, take covariance with y, and use $X'e=0$. Shares can be negative or exceed one; replacing them with absolute values or clipping changes this allocation. With no intercept, shrinkage, out-of-sample residuals or unequal covariance samples, the identity need not hold. A zero total variance gives an undefined fraction.

atoms.title: Factor regressions and covariance attribution / Inference versus estimation
atoms.text:
## Inference versus estimation

HAC inference retains the OLS coefficients but estimates their sampling covariance allowing serial dependence and heteroskedasticity. It does not whiten the data or eliminate serial dependence. Lag bandwidth, finite-sample correction and t versus asymptotic-normal reference distributions are distinct choices. Fixed observation spacing is the usual HAC assumption; deleting an internal month and treating the neighboring rows as adjacent changes the meaning of a lag. It is not necessary for trading-day observations to be adjacent calendar days.

Multiplying y by a positive constant multiplies coefficients and their standard errors by that constant; t-statistics and R-squared remain unchanged. Rescaling a factor instead rescales its coefficient inversely, leaving fitted components unchanged. An annualized $\alpha$ based on arithmetic scaling is not a compounded investment return.

For overlapping windows the estimates share observations; consecutive estimates are not independent. A low rolling R-squared is a descriptive signal, not by itself a statistical test of structural change. Carrying a discontinued proxy forward is an explicit imputation convention, not new information about the underlying risk.

atoms.title: Factor regressions and covariance attribution / Checks and scope
atoms.text:
## Checks and scope

Check reconstruction including the intercept, residual orthogonality, allocation totals before rounding, and invariance to consistent unit changes. Risk contribution does not establish causality or tradability of a proxy. This reference supplements rather than replaces the HAC and GRS definitions; their distributional assumptions differ.

atoms.title: Factor regressions and covariance attribution / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources

Newey and West (1987), [A Simple, Positive Semi-Definite, Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent Covariance Matrix](https://www.nber.org/papers/t0055), for robust covariance estimation. [Statsmodels HAC documentation](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.stats.sandwich_covariance.cov_hac.html), for the single-series, ordered-observation assumption. The reconstruction, covariance allocation and unit-invariance identities above follow directly from the OLS normal equations; they are algebraic derivations, not empirical error guarantees.

atoms.title: Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions (with Newey-West, Shanken, z-scored characteristics, residual momentum) / Setting and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Setting and assumptions
- Panel of assets i over periods $t = 1\ldots T$. Each period, regress a cross-section of outcomes (usually next-period or
  future returns) on regressors known at the forecast date: firm characteristics, or betas estimated in a first pass.
- The per-period slopes are treated as a time series; their average is the estimate and their time-series variability gives
  the standard error. This handles cross-sectional correlation of returns automatically; it assumes the slopes are
  uncorrelated over time (otherwise use the Newey-West version).

atoms.title: Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions (with Newey-West, Shanken, z-scored characteristics, residual momentum) / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning |
|---|---|
| $y_{it}$ | dependent variable of asset i for period t (e.g. return from t to t+1; align dates exactly as the task says) |
| $x_{it}$ | K regressors of asset i observed at t (characteristics, or estimated betas $\hat{\beta}_{i}$) |
| $N_{t}$ | number of assets with complete data at t (must exceed K + 1) |
| $T$ | number of periods with a valid cross-sectional regression (NOT the number of stock-month observations) |
| $\lambda _{t}$ | (K+1)-vector of per-period coefficients (intercept first) |
| $L, h$ | Newey-West lag; return horizon in periods when returns overlap |

atoms.title: Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions (with Newey-West, Shanken, z-scored characteristics, residual momentum) / Formulas
atoms.text:
## Formulas
Pass 1, only if regressors are betas: for each asset, over the beta window,

$$
R_{it} = a_{i} + b_{i}' f_{t} + e_{it}
$$

This gives $\hat{\beta}_{i}$.
Pass 2, each $t$:

$$
X_{t} = [1, x_{.t}]
$$

The shape is $N_{t}$ by $K+1$.

$$
\hat{\lambda}_{t} = (X_{t}' X_{t})^{-1} X_{t}' y_{t}
$$

Estimate:

$$
\bar{\lambda} = (1/T) \sum _{t} \hat{\lambda}_{t}
$$

FM standard error:

$$
\mathrm{se}_{j} = s_{j} / \sqrt{T}
$$

$$
s_{j}^{2} = (1/(T-1)) \sum _{t} (\hat{\lambda}_{jt} - \bar{\lambda}_{j})^{2}
$$

The t-statistic (p-value from $t(T-1)$ or normal, as the task says):

$$
t_{j} = \bar{\lambda}_{j} / \mathrm{se}_{j}
$$

Covariance:

$$
V_{\mathrm{FM}} = (1/(T(T-1))) \sum _{t} (\hat{\lambda}_{t} - \bar{\lambda})(\hat{\lambda}_{t} - \bar{\lambda})'
$$

The standard error is NOT the per-period OLS standard error, not an average of per-period standard errors, and not
the standard error of one pooled regression. If asked for an average R^2, average the per-period R^2 values.

atoms.title: Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions (with Newey-West, Shanken, z-scored characteristics, residual momentum) / Newey-West version (overlapping or persistent slopes)
Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions (with Newey-West, Shanken, z-scored characteristics, residual momentum) / Shanken (1992) correction (variant; only when regressors are ESTIMATED betas)
atoms.text:
## Shanken (1992) correction (variant; only when regressors are ESTIMATED betas)

$$
\Gamma  = (\gamma _{0}, \gamma _{a}')'
$$

$\gamma _{a}$ denotes the $K$ factor premia (per period, same frequency as returns).

$$
c = \gamma _{a}' \Sigma _{f}^{-1} \gamma _{a}
$$

$\Sigma _{f}$ is the $K$ by $K$ covariance of the factors $f_{t}$ over the pass-1 sample. $\mathrm{Sf}_{\mathrm{star}}$ is block-diagonal: 0 for the intercept, $\Sigma _{f}$ for the factors.
Practical form on top of $V_{\mathrm{FM}}$:

$$
V_{\mathrm{Shanken}} = (1 + c) \cdot  (V_{\mathrm{FM}} - \mathrm{Sf}_{\mathrm{star}} / T) + \mathrm{Sf}_{\mathrm{star}} / T
$$

Asymptotic form it comes from: $\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\Gamma}) = (1/T) [(1 + c) A \Sigma  A' + \mathrm{Sf}_{\mathrm{star}}]$, $A = (X'X)^{-1} X'$, $X = [1, \hat{\beta}]$,
$\Sigma$ = pass-1 residual covariance. Both forms agree asymptotically, not exactly. No intercept in pass 2: drop its row/column.
Not used for observed characteristics (they are not estimated). c is not annualized when the data are monthly.

atoms.title: Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions (with Newey-West, Shanken, z-scored characteristics, residual momentum) / Cross-sectional standardization of characteristics
atoms.text:
## Cross-sectional standardization of characteristics

$$
z_{it} = (x_{it} - \operatorname{mean}_{t}(x)) / \operatorname{sd}_{t}(x)
$$

Mean and standard deviation are over the $N_{t}$ assets present at date $t$.

- Population sd divides by $N_{t}$, sample sd by $N_t-1$. numpy `std` defaults to $\mathrm{ddof}=0$, pandas `.std()` to $\mathrm{ddof}=1$: set ddof
  explicitly to match the task ("population" -> 0, "sample" -> 1). The z-scores differ by the factor $\sqrt{N_{t}/(N_{t}-1)}$.
- Standardize within each date (groupby date), never over the pooled panel (look-ahead). Drop or fill missing values and
  winsorize first if the task says so, then standardize over exactly the assets used in that date's regression.
- Rank variant: replace x by its cross-sectional rank (often scaled to [0,1] or demeaned) before regressing.

atoms.title: Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions (with Newey-West, Shanken, z-scored characteristics, residual momentum) / Residual momentum (variant; Blitz, Huij and Martens 2011, standardization as in Gutierrez and Prinsky 2007)
atoms.text:
## Residual momentum (variant; Blitz, Huij and Martens 2011, standardization as in Gutierrez and Prinsky 2007)
For each stock i and formation date t (ranking for the holding period that starts at t):
1. Over the W months t-W..t-1 regress excess returns on the factor model (BHM: Fama-French three factors) with an intercept:
   $r_{is} = \alpha _{i} + \beta _{i}' f_{s} + \mathrm{eps}_{is}$; keep only stocks with a complete window.
2. Residuals exclude $\alpha$: $\hat{\mathrm{eps}}_{is} = r_{is} - \hat{\alpha}_{i} - \hat{\beta}_{i}' f_{s}$ (do not add $\alpha$ back).
3. Formation months: $s = t-J\ldots t-1-S$(S = skip months; BHM use the past year and skip the most recent month).
4. Score: $\sum  \hat{\mathrm{eps}}_{is} / \operatorname{sd}(\hat{\mathrm{eps}}_{is})$ over the formation months (sd over the SAME months; ddof per task).
   mean/sd ranks identically when every stock has the same number of formation months.
5. Sort stocks on the score each date (e.g. deciles), long the top, short the bottom, weighting as the task says.
Mistakes: regressing without an intercept; including month t-1; using factor betas estimated with data after t-1;
scaling by total-return volatility or by the whole W-month residual sd (only if the task defines it that way).

atoms.title: Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions (with Newey-West, Shanken, z-scored characteristics, residual momentum) / Sources
Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions (with Newey-West, Shanken, z-scored characteristics, residual momentum) / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- FM se is robust to cross-sectional correlation but not to serial correlation of $\lambda _{t}$ (persistent characteristics,
  overlapping returns); then use Newey-West. With estimated betas the slopes have errors-in-variables bias in finite T and
  the non-factor variance component receives the Shanken multiplier $1+c$; the corresponding standard-error multiplier is $\sqrt{1+c}$, not $1+c$. The full covariance also contains the separate factor component shown above.
- Unbalanced panels are fine; T counts only periods actually regressed. Small $N_{t}$ makes per-period slopes noisy.
- That T is for averaging slopes and their standard errors. A start or window rule stated in calendar periods (forecasts begin after the n-th calendar month, say) counts calendar periods of the sample, including periods that produced no regression; it is not the n-th estimated period. An expanding average of slopes at a forecast date uses every slope estimated before that date. The forecast is the averaged intercept plus the averaged slopes times every regressor of the fitted model, controls included, standardized as in the fit; leaving the controls out ranks the assets on a different model.

atoms.title: Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions (with Newey-West, Shanken, z-scored characteristics, residual momentum) / Before coding: three rules that change every number
Filtered historical simulation with a stationary bootstrap
atoms.text:
Draw one set of B row indices into the standardized-residual matrix Z (T rows) and reuse it for every day. Use exactly this
loop, so that a given seed gives the same rows: the start is drawn before the loop and again on the first row, and on later
rows a uniform draw decides between a new block start and continuing the current block (wrapping at T).

```python
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
idx = np.empty(B, dtype=int)
pos = int(rng.integers(0, T))
for i in range(B):
    if i == 0 or rng.random() < p:      # p = 1 / expected block length
        pos = int(rng.integers(0, T))
    else:
        pos = (pos + 1) % T
    idx[i] = pos
```

On every day, multiply the resampled rows by that day's conditional volatilities of the assets and aggregate with the
portfolio weights; VaR is the negative empirical percentile, ES the mean of the simulated returns at or below it:

```python
for t in range(T):
    sim = (Z[idx] * sigma[t]) @ w                  # sigma[t]: sqrt of the diagonal of H[t], one value per asset
    cut = np.percentile(sim, 100 * level)          # level = 0.01 for 1%
    var_fhs[t] = -cut
    es_fhs[t] = -sim[sim <= cut].mean()
```

atoms.title: First-passage time of drifted Brownian motion and GBM; running maximum / minimum with the terminal value / Model and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Model and assumptions
- Arithmetic Brownian motion $X_{t} = \mathrm{x0} + \mu  t + \sigma  W_{t}$, constant $\mu , \sigma  > 0$. Level b (upper if $b > \mathrm{x0}$, lower if $b < \mathrm{x0}$).
  $\tau  = \inf \{t \ge  0 : X_{t} = b\}$; for continuous paths "reaches", "touches" and "crosses" are the same event. If x0 is at or beyond $b, \tau  = 0$.
- GBM $S_{t} = \mathrm{S0} \exp (\nu  t + \sigma  W_{t})$ with $\nu  = m - \sigma ^{2}/2$, where m is the drift of dS/S (risk-neutral: $m = r - q$; real-world: expected return).
  Then $X = \ln  S$ is the model above with $\mathrm{x0} = \ln  \mathrm{S0}$, $\mu  = \nu$, $b = \ln  H$.
- One level, continuous monitoring, constant coefficients. Exit from a corridor (two levels) is NOT covered by these formulas.

atoms.title: First-passage time of drifted Brownian motion and GBM; running maximum / minimum with the terminal value / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| x0, b | start value and level of X (for GBM: $\ln  \mathrm{S0}, \ln  H$) | units of X |
| $\mu$, $\sigma$ | drift and volatility of X; $\sigma$ of 30% is `0.30` | per year, per $\sqrt{\mathrm{year}}$ |
| $a$ | distance to the level, $a = \mathrm{abs}(b - \mathrm{x0}) > 0$ | units of X |
| $\theta$ | drift TOWARDS the level: $\theta  = \mu$ if b > x0, $\theta  = -\mu$ if b < x0 | per year |
| $t, T$ | horizon in years (same time unit as $\mu$ and $\sigma^{2}$) | years |

atoms.title: First-passage time of drifted Brownian motion and GBM; running maximum / minimum with the terminal value / First-passage law (N = standard normal cdf)
atoms.text:
## First-passage law (N = standard normal cdf)
For $t > 0$:

$$
\operatorname{P}(\tau  \le  t) = N((\theta  t - a) / (\sigma  \sqrt{t})) + \exp (2 \theta  a / \sigma ^{2}) \cdot  N((-\theta  t - a) / (\sigma  \sqrt{t}))
$$

Density of $\tau$ on $t > 0$:

$$
f(t) = a / (\sigma  \sqrt{2 \pi  t^{3}}) \cdot  \exp (-(a - \theta  t)^{2} / (2 \sigma ^{2} t))
$$

For $\theta  \ge  0$, $\operatorname{P}(\tau  < \infty ) = 1$. For $\theta  < 0$:

$$
\operatorname{P}(\tau  < \infty ) = \exp (-2 \mathrm{abs}(\theta ) a / \sigma ^{2})
$$

- f integrates to $\operatorname{P}(\tau  < \infty )$, so it is a defective density when $\theta  < 0$. Evaluate the second CDF term as
  $\exp (2 \theta  a / \sigma ^{2} + \log  N(\ldots ))$ to avoid overflow when $\theta a/\sigma^2$ is large.
- $\theta  > 0$: $\tau$ is inverse Gaussian with mean $a / \theta$ and shape $a^{2} / \sigma ^{2}$; $\operatorname{Var}(\tau ) = a \sigma ^{2} / \theta ^{3}$.
  $\theta  < 0$: conditional on $\tau  < \infty , \tau$ has the same law with $\mathrm{abs}(  \theta  )$. $\theta  = 0$: $\operatorname{P}(\tau  \le  t) = 2 N(-a / (\sigma  \sqrt  t))$,
  $\tau  < \infty$ almost surely but E[$\tau$] is infinite.
- GBM: $a = \mathrm{abs}(\ln (H / \mathrm{S0}))$, $\theta  = \nu$ for $H > \mathrm{S0}$ and -$\nu$ for $H < \mathrm{S0}$. Ever hitting H: $\operatorname{P} = \min (1, (H / \mathrm{S0})^{2 \nu  / \sigma ^{2}})$.

atoms.title: First-passage time of drifted Brownian motion and GBM; running maximum / minimum with the terminal value / Conditional hitting given the endpoints (Brownian bridge)
atoms.text:
## Conditional hitting given the endpoints (Brownian bridge)
Given $X_{u} = x_{u}$ and $X_{v} = x_{v}$ ($v > u$), both strictly on the starting side of b:

$$
\operatorname{P}(\mathrm{path} \mathrm{touches} b \mathrm{on} [u, v] \vert  x_{u}, x_{v}) = \exp (-2 (b - x_{u})(b - x_{v}) / (\sigma ^{2} (v - u)))
$$

It does not depend on $\mu$; it is 1 if either endpoint is at or beyond b. The same expression holds for a lower level. For GBM use logs and log-vol.

atoms.title: First-passage time of drifted Brownian motion and GBM; running maximum / minimum with the terminal value / Monte Carlo, never-hit paths and empirical CDFs
atoms.text:
## Monte Carlo, never-hit paths and empirical CDFs
- Simulate X exactly on a grid of step dt (GBM in logs). For each step compute the bridge probability $p_{k}$. Either draw $U < p_{k}$ to flag a
  hit in that step ($\tau$ is then known only to within dt), or carry the survival weight $\prod _{k} (1 - p_{k})$: its mean estimates
  $\operatorname{P}(\tau  > t_{k})$ and $\operatorname{E}[1\{X_{T} \le  x\} \prod  (1 - p_{k})]$ estimates $\operatorname{P}(M_{T} \le  b, X_{T} \le  x)$, both without discretization bias at grid times.
- A plain check "a grid point is beyond b" misses crossings between grid points and underestimates hitting by order $\sigma  \sqrt{\mathrm{d}t}$.
- Paths that do not hit by the horizon have $\tau  = +\infty$(censored at T). Empirical CDF: $F(t) = \#\{i : \tau _{i} \le  t\} / N_{\mathrm{all}}$, with $N_{\mathrm{all}}$
  counting EVERY path. Do not drop never-hit paths (that gives $\operatorname{P}(\tau  \le  t \vert  \tau  \le  T)$, which reaches 1 at T); do not set them to T
  (a false atom at T); do not average $\tau$ over a sample containing inf, or with nanmean.
- E[$\tau$] is finite only for $\theta  > 0 (= a / \theta )$. Otherwise report what the task defines: $\operatorname{P}(\tau  \le  T)$,
  $\operatorname{E}[\tau  \vert  \tau  \le  T] = (\int _{0}^{T} t f(t) \mathrm{d}t) / \operatorname{P}(\tau  \le  T)$, or $\operatorname{E}[\min (\tau , T)] = \int _{0}^{T} \operatorname{P}(\tau  > t) \mathrm{d}t$.
  A quantile q of $\tau$ exists only for $q < \operatorname{P}(\tau  < \infty )$(within the horizon: $q \le  \operatorname{P}(\tau  \le  T)$).

atoms.title: First-passage time of drifted Brownian motion and GBM; running maximum / minimum with the terminal value / Discrete monitoring
atoms.text:
## Discrete monitoring
- If the level is checked only at dates spaced dt (e.g. daily closes), the discrete probability is the target: simulate on those dates
  without bridge correction, or use the continuous formula with the level moved AWAY from the start (Broadie-Glasserman-Kou):
  $b' = b + \beta  \sigma  \sqrt{\mathrm{d}t}$ for an upper level, $b - \beta  \sigma  \sqrt{\mathrm{d}t}$ for a lower level (GBM: $H \exp (\pm \beta  \sigma  \sqrt{\mathrm{d}t})$),
  $\beta  = -\zeta (1/2) / \sqrt{2 \pi} \approx 0.5826$. Never compare a discretely monitored simulation with the continuous formula directly.
- The shift is an asymptotic correction: it is less accurate with few monitoring dates or when the start is within a few $\sigma  \sqrt{\mathrm{d}t}$ of the level.

atoms.title: First-passage time of drifted Brownian motion and GBM; running maximum / minimum with the terminal value / Variants and common mistakes
atoms.text:
## Variants and common mistakes
- GBM: using m instead of $\nu  = m - \sigma ^{2}/2$, or the price distance H - S0 instead of $\ln (H/\mathrm{S0})$.
- Wrong sign of $\theta$ for a lower level; time units of t inconsistent with annualized $\mu$, $\sigma$.
- Terminal probability $\operatorname{P}(X_{T} \ge  b)$ is not the hitting probability (for $\mu  = 0$ hitting is twice the terminal probability: reflection principle).

## Applicability and known limits
- Exact for constant drift and volatility with continuous monitoring. Jumps, stochastic or time-varying volatility, mean reversion
  (OU) and two-sided barriers need other formulas or simulation; the bridge probability assumes Brownian motion within each step.

atoms.title: First-passage time of drifted Brownian motion and GBM; running maximum / minimum with the terminal value / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources
Shreve (2004) Stochastic Calculus for Finance II, Springer (Sec. 7.2, maximum of Brownian motion with drift); Borodin & Salminen (2002)
Handbook of Brownian Motion: Facts and Formulae, 2nd ed., Birkhauser; Chhikara & Folks (1978) J. R. Statist. Soc. B 40:263-289 (inverse Gaussian);
Beaglehole, Dybvig & Zhou (1997) Financial Analysts Journal 53(1):62-68 and Glasserman (2004) Monte Carlo Methods in Financial Engineering,
Springer (Brownian-bridge correction); Broadie, Glasserman & Kou (1997) Mathematical Finance 7(4):325-349 (continuity correction).

atoms.title: First-passage time of drifted Brownian motion and GBM; running maximum / minimum with the terminal value / Running maximum / minimum with the terminal value
atoms.text:
## Running maximum / minimum with the terminal value
Let $M_{T} = \max _{0\le s\le T} X_{s}$, $L_{T} = \min _{0\le s\le T} X_{s}$, and shift to the start: $m' = m - \mathrm{x0}$, $l' = l - \mathrm{x0}$, $y = x - \mathrm{x0}$, $s = \sigma  \sqrt  T$.
For $m' \ge  0, y \le  m'$:

$$
\operatorname{P}(M_{T} \ge  m, X_{T} \le  x) = \exp (2 \mu  m' / \sigma ^{2}) N((y - 2 m' - \mu  T) / s)
$$

$$
\operatorname{P}(M_{T} \le  m, X_{T} \le  x) = N((y - \mu  T) / s) - \exp (2 \mu  m' / \sigma ^{2}) N((y - 2 m' - \mu  T) / s)
$$

$$
\operatorname{P}(M_{T} \le  m) = N((m' - \mu  T) / s) - \exp (2 \mu  m' / \sigma ^{2}) N((-m' - \mu  T) / s) = 1 - \operatorname{P}(\tau _{m} \le  T)
$$

For $l' \le  0, y \ge  l'$:

$$
\operatorname{P}(L_{T} \ge  l, X_{T} \ge  x) = N((\mu  T - y) / s) - \exp (2 \mu  l' / \sigma ^{2}) N((2 l' - y + \mu  T) / s)
$$

Joint density of $(M_{T}, X_{T})$ at $(m', y)$, where $m' \ge  \max (0, y)$:

$$
2 (2 m' - y) / (\sigma ^{3} \sqrt{2 \pi  T^{3}}) \cdot  \exp (-(2 m' - y)^{2} / (2 \sigma ^{2} T) + \mu  y / \sigma ^{2} - \mu ^{2} T / (2 \sigma ^{2}))
$$

- For $\operatorname{P}(M_T\le m,X_T\le x)$ only: when $y>m'$, replace $y$ by $m'$; when $m'<0$, this probability is zero.
- For $\operatorname{P}(M_T\ge m,X_T\le x)$, the two shortcuts differ. If $m'\le0$, the maximum condition is automatic and the probability is $N((y-\mu T)/s)$. If $m'>0$ and $y>m'$, use:

$$
\operatorname{P}(M_T\ge m,X_T\le x)
=e^{2\mu m'/\sigma^2}N((-m'-\mu T)/s)
+N((y-\mu T)/s)-N((m'-\mu T)/s).
$$

  The added CDF difference counts endpoints above the barrier, which necessarily crossed it. Minimum formulas follow by applying the corresponding maximum event to $-X$ with drift $-\mu$. For GBM map every price level into logs and use log drift $\nu$.
- Dependence on the level and the horizon (any drift): if $\mathrm{l1} < \mathrm{l2}$, the event "running minimum <= l1" implies "running minimum
  <= l2", so $\operatorname{P}(L_{T} \le  l)$ does not decrease as l rises; a lower level is harder to reach. Likewise $\operatorname{P}(M_{T} \ge  m)$ does not
  increase as m rises, and both hitting probabilities do not decrease as T grows (a longer window contains the shorter one).
  To check, state the event first, sort the levels (or horizons) in increasing numeric order, hold every other input fixed
  and compare the probabilities in that order.

atoms.title: First-passage time of drifted Brownian motion and GBM; running maximum / minimum with the terminal value / Drift and probability checks before interpretation
atoms.text:
## Drift and probability checks before interpretation

For GBM, distinguish the return drift $m$ in $\mathrm{d}S/S=m\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma\,\mathrm{d}W$ from log drift $\nu=m-\sigma^2/2$. If the supplied drift is already $\nu$, the exact log increment is $\Delta\log S=\nu\Delta t+\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}Z$; subtracting another $\sigma^2/2$ changes the model. Keep these two inputs separately named.

First check probabilities lie in $[0,1]$, a CDF is nondecreasing in time, and time-zero hits match the starting side. Under the same process and barrier, discrete-date hitting is a subset of continuous hitting. A Monte Carlo excess over the continuous probability needs assessment against its sampling standard error; a material excess calls for checking drift, event direction, endpoints and monitoring before attributing the gap to noise. Lower touches use $S_t\le H$; upper touches use $S_t\ge H$.

atoms.title: Forward returns in rolling (walk-forward) prediction: one time label per array
atoms.text: Use this when a model predicts the return over the next step from information available at time $t$, and the predictions are scored against realized returns (information coefficient, hit rate, regression fit).

atoms.title: Forward returns in rolling (walk-forward) prediction: one time label per array / Definitions
atoms.text:
## Definitions

| symbol | meaning |
|---|---|
| $m_t$ | price or midpoint observed at time $t$ |
| $r^{\mathrm{fwd}}_{t}$ | one-step forward log return, labelled at the START of its interval |
| $\hat r_{t}$ | prediction made at time $t$ with information up to $t$ |

$$
r^{\mathrm{fwd}}_{t} = \ln (m_{t+1} / m_{t})
$$

In pandas, `r_fwd = np.log(m.shift(-1) / m)` produces exactly this array: row $t$ holds the return from $t$ to $t+1$, and the last row is undefined.

atoms.title: Forward returns in rolling (walk-forward) prediction: one time label per array / Check before writing outputs
atoms.text:
## Check before writing outputs

Print a few rows with $t$, $m_{t}$, $m_{t+1}$, `r_fwd[t]` and recompute one value by hand, for example `np.isclose(r_fwd[i], np.log(m[i+1] / m[i]))`. For the scored pairs, assert that each prediction and its realized return carry the same label $t$. A second shift shows up as `r_fwd[i]` matching $\ln(m_{i+2}/m_{i+1})$ instead.

atoms.title: Forward returns in rolling (walk-forward) prediction: one time label per array / Alignment rules
atoms.text:
## Alignment rules

- A prediction made at time $t$ targets $r^{\mathrm{fwd}}_{t}$. Pair $\hat r_{t}$ with `r_fwd[t]`, not with `r_fwd[t+1]`: the shift is already inside the array, and indexing it at $t+1$ shifts a second time and scores the prediction against the return one step later.
- A training pair $(x_{s}, r^{\mathrm{fwd}}_{s})$ is usable at prediction time $t$ only if its target is already observed, that is $s + 1 \le t$. Follow the task's own window definition for which rows enter the window; this rule only says that no target from the future enters the fit.

- Slice the window by position. "The previous W rows" before row t is df.iloc[t - W:t] (end excluded). df.loc[t - W:t] on an integer index is a label slice that INCLUDES row t, so the window has W + 1 rows and the target of row t leaks into the fit.
    tr = df.iloc[t - W:t]
    assert len(tr) == W and tr.index.max() < df.index[t]
- Fit every transform (scaler, PCA, sign choice) on tr only, then apply the same fitted objects and the same sign to row t. Decide a component's sign once (s = +1 or -1) and multiply both the training scores and the new score by s; negating components_ and then also negating the transformed score cancels the flip.

- Reporting "the forward return at index $i$" means `r_fwd[i]` $= \ln(m_{i+1}/m_{i})$.
- Correlations between predictions and realized returns (Spearman or Pearson IC) use the same set of time labels on both sides: every $t$ that has both $\hat r_{t}$ and $r^{\mathrm{fwd}}_{t}$.

atoms.title: Forward-start and cliquet pricing under deterministic-coefficient GBM
atoms.text:
Map task quantities to these definitions by meaning and units, not by letter, before the first calculation; recheck when inputs or conventions change.

Use this document for future-reset strikes and cliquet coupons: Black–Scholes building blocks, local cap/floor decomposition, and additive versus globally constrained contracts. Choose payoff units and payment dates first. It is not a stochastic-volatility or cash-dividend cliquet pricing formula.

Explicit task definitions, contract conventions and required input handling take precedence. Map them to the assumptions here; if they differ, these formulas may not apply unchanged. Identify unresolved ambiguity rather than silently mixing conventions.

atoms.text:
## Contents

1. [Definitions and method selection](#1-definitions-and-method-selection)
2. [Normalized option block](#2-normalized-option-block)
3. [Future reset: price and return coupons](#3-future-reset-price-and-return-coupons)
4. [Local and global constraints](#4-local-and-global-constraints)

atoms.title: Forward-start and cliquet pricing under deterministic-coefficient GBM / 1. Definitions and method selection
atoms.text:
## 1. Definitions and method selection

Time zero is the valuation date. Spot S0 is positive. Constant r and q are continuously compounded domestic rate and dividend/carry yield; $\sigma  \ge  0$ is annualized volatility. Rates and volatility are decimals, times are years. Ncdf denotes the standard normal CDF. Q is a fixed cash notional, not a probability measure. Let $0 \le  s \le  e \le  p$ be reset, final fixing, and payment times. The strike multiplier $\alpha$ is dimensionless. Let $\tau  = e-s$.

| Observable contract feature | Calculation |
|---|---|
| Pays $\max (  S_{e} - \alpha \cdot S_{s} , 0 )$, with s in the future | Price-unit block in §3 |
| Pays $Q\max(S_e/S_s-\alpha,0)$ | Return-unit block in §3 |
| Sum of individually capped/floored returns | Decompose each coupon using §4, then add present values |
| Cap/floor applied to the whole sum | Path-level calculation in §4; do not cap a sum of expected values |
| $S_{s}$ has already been observed | Fixed-strike block in §5 |

An ATM reset uses $\alpha =1$. A strike k on a simple return uses $\alpha =1+k$. A ratchet whose strike only moves upward, depends on an average, or remembers a running maximum requires additional state; it is not the plain reset contract above. Follow explicit contract definitions rather than the product label alone.

atoms.title: Forward-start and cliquet pricing under deterministic-coefficient GBM / 2. Normalized option block
atoms.text:
## 2. Normalized option block

Use this block for one period of length $\tau$. c and u are respectively call and put values at the period start on unit spot, with payoff fixed and paid at the period end. For $\alpha >0$ and $\sigma \cdot \sqrt{\tau}>0$:

**Total volatility and normalized pricing thresholds**

$$
\begin{gathered}
x = \sigma \cdot \sqrt{\tau} \\
\mathrm{d1} = (-\log (\alpha ) + (r-q)\cdot \tau  + x\cdot x/2)/x \\
\mathrm{d2} = \mathrm{d1}-x
\end{gathered}
$$

**Normalized call price**

$$
c(\alpha ,\tau ) = \exp (-q\cdot \tau )\cdot \mathrm{Ncdf}(\mathrm{d1}) - \alpha \cdot \exp (-r\cdot \tau )\cdot \mathrm{Ncdf}(\mathrm{d2})
$$

**Normalized put price**

$$
u(\alpha ,\tau ) = \alpha \cdot \exp (-r\cdot \tau )\cdot \mathrm{Ncdf}(-\mathrm{d2}) - \exp (-q\cdot \tau )\cdot \mathrm{Ncdf}(-\mathrm{d1})
$$

At zero variance, evaluate the deterministic payoff instead of dividing by x. This also handles $\tau =0$. Nonpositive $\alpha$ is handled by linearity, not $\log (\alpha )$.

**Deterministic growth factor**

$$
f = \exp ((r-q)\cdot \tau )
$$

**Zero-variance call price**

$$
\mathrm{zero}_{\mathrm{variance},\mathrm{call}} = \exp (-r\cdot \tau )\cdot \max (f-\alpha ,0)
$$

**Zero-variance put price**

$$
\mathrm{zero}_{\mathrm{variance},\mathrm{put}}  = \exp (-r\cdot \tau )\cdot \max (\alpha -f,0)
$$

**Nonpositive-strike branch**

If $\alpha  \le  0$:

$$
c = \exp (-q\cdot \tau )-\alpha \cdot \exp (-r\cdot \tau )
$$

$$
u = 0
$$

A negative volatility or negative period length is invalid input, not a zero-variance case.

atoms.title: Forward-start and cliquet pricing under deterministic-coefficient GBM / 3. Future reset: price and return coupons
atoms.text:
## 3. Future reset: price and return coupons

Use the price-unit block when the payoff contains $S_e-\alpha S_s$. Homogeneity makes its value at s equal to $S_sc$. Under GBM the discounted expected $S_{s}$ contributes the pre-reset dividend factor.

**Price-unit forward-start call value**

$$
\mathrm{price}_{\mathrm{call},0} = \exp (-r\cdot (p-e))\cdot \mathrm{S0}\cdot \exp (-q\cdot s)\cdot c(\alpha ,\tau )
$$

**Price-unit forward-start put value**

$$
\mathrm{price}_{\mathrm{put},0}  = \exp (-r\cdot (p-e))\cdot \mathrm{S0}\cdot \exp (-q\cdot s)\cdot u(\alpha ,\tau )
$$

**Price-unit put-call parity**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{price}_{\mathrm{call},0}-\mathrm{price}_{\mathrm{put},0} = \exp (-r\cdot (p-e))\cdot \mathrm{S0}\cdot \exp (-q\cdot s) \\
\cdot  (\exp (-q\cdot \tau )-\alpha \cdot \exp (-r\cdot \tau ))
\end{gathered}
$$

Use the return-unit block when the payoff contains $S_e/S_s-\alpha$. Independent GBM increments remove $S_{s}$ from that ratio. Q is fixed, not equal to the random reset spot.

**Return-unit forward-start call value**

$$
\mathrm{return}_{\mathrm{call},0} = Q\cdot \exp (-r\cdot (p-e))\cdot \exp (-r\cdot s)\cdot c(\alpha ,\tau )
$$

**Return-unit forward-start put value**

$$
\mathrm{return}_{\mathrm{put},0}  = Q\cdot \exp (-r\cdot (p-e))\cdot \exp (-r\cdot s)\cdot u(\alpha ,\tau )
$$

The normalized block already discounts the period. Do not use $\exp (-r\cdot s)$ for a price-unit coupon; do not multiply a return-unit coupon by S0 unless its notional is explicitly S0. Delayed payment contributes only $\exp (-r\cdot (p-e))$, since the cash amount is fixed at e and assumed not to accrue before payment.

For a plain additive cliquet with reset dates $t_{0}=0 < \ldots  < t_{n}$, apply the correct block to each ($s=t_{i-1}, e=t_{i}, p=p_{i}$) and sum its time-zero values. The first price-unit period is an ordinary option with strike $\alpha S_0$. Equal interval lengths do not imply equal price-unit present values when q is nonzero. Payment at each fixing and common payment at final maturity are distinct contracts.

atoms.title: Forward-start and cliquet pricing under deterministic-coefficient GBM / 4. Local and global constraints
atoms.text:
## 4. Local and global constraints

For a local return $R=S_{e}/S_{s}-1$ with floor L and cap $U, L\le U$, use the following pathwise identities. The normalized block also supports L or $U \le  -1$ via its nonpositive-strike branch.

**Local cap-and-floor payoff decomposition**

$$
\mathrm{clipped}_{\mathrm{return}} = L + \max (R-L,0) - \max (R-U,0)
$$

**Floor-only payoff decomposition**

$$
\operatorname{floor}_{\mathrm{only}} = L + \max (R-L,0)
$$

**Cap-only payoff decomposition**

$$
\mathrm{cap}_{\mathrm{only}} = R - \max (R-U,0)
$$

**Present value of the locally clipped return**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{PV}_{\mathrm{clipped}} = Q\cdot \exp (-r\cdot p)\cdot L \\
+ Q\cdot \exp (-r\cdot (p-e))\cdot \exp (-r\cdot s)\cdot (c(1+L,\tau )-c(1+U,\tau ))
\end{gathered}
$$

**Present value of the uncapped return**

$$
\mathrm{PV}_{\mathrm{plain},\mathrm{return}} = Q\cdot \exp (-r\cdot p)\cdot (\exp ((r-q)\cdot \tau )-1)
$$

**Present value of a cap-only return**

$$
\mathrm{PV}_{\mathrm{cap},\mathrm{only}} = \mathrm{PV}_{\mathrm{plain},\mathrm{return}}-Q\cdot \exp (-r\cdot (p-e))\cdot \exp (-r\cdot s)\cdot c(1+U,\tau )
$$

If a global constraint acts on the aggregate, simulate the joint fixing schedule, compute each realized coupon, aggregate on each path, apply the global function, then discount to its payment date. Independent period increments do not justify moving a nonlinear cap/floor outside expectation. For a reverse cliquet, translate its coupon-minus-losses rule and any aggregate floor literally; do not assume that every reverse contract has the same payoff.

**Simulate one log-return increment**

$$
\log (S_{ti}/S_{\mathrm{tprev}}) = (r-q-\sigma \cdot \sigma /2)\cdot \mathrm{d}t_{i} + \sigma \cdot \sqrt{\mathrm{d}t_{i}}\cdot Z_{i}
$$

**Convert to a simple return**

$$
R_{i} = \exp (\log (S_{ti}/S_{\mathrm{tprev}}))-1
$$

**Apply local coupon limits**

$$
\mathrm{local}_{i} = \min (U_{i},\max (L_{i},R_{i}))
$$

**Apply the global payoff and discount**

$$
Y = Q\cdot \exp (-r\cdot p)\cdot \min (U_{\mathrm{global}},\max (L_{\mathrm{global}},\sum _{i} \mathrm{local}_{i}))
$$

**Monte Carlo price estimate**

$$
\mathrm{price} = \operatorname{mean}(Y)
$$

**Standard error across independent paths**

$$
\mathrm{SE} = \;\text{sample}\;_{\mathrm{sd}}(Y)/\sqrt{\mathrm{number}_{\mathrm{of},\mathrm{independent},\mathrm{paths}}}
$$

Use independent standard normals across intervals. For antithetic sampling, average each pair first and estimate SE across independent pairs. The displayed global example is a capped/floored sum paid once; different global rules require their own payoff function.

atoms.title: Forward-start and cliquet pricing under deterministic-coefficient GBM / 5. A reset already observed
atoms.text:
## 5. A reset already observed

If the reset price H is known today and the end fixing is still in the future, the strike is fixed. With remaining end time e and payment time p, use today's S0 and $K=\alpha \cdot H$, not a fresh future-reset formula. $\mathrm{BS}_{\mathrm{call}}$(S,K,T) and $\mathrm{BS}_{\mathrm{put}}$(S,K,T) denote ordinary European Black–Scholes values payable at expiry, using the same r, q and $\sigma$. They are mathematical price functions, not a required software API. For $H>0$:

**Price-unit call after its reset is known**

$$
\mathrm{price}_{\mathrm{coupon},0} = \exp (-r\cdot (p-e))\cdot \mathrm{BS}_{\mathrm{call}}(\mathrm{S0},\alpha \cdot H,e)
$$

**Return-unit call after its reset is known**

$$
\mathrm{return}_{\mathrm{coupon},0} = (Q/H)\cdot \exp (-r\cdot (p-e))\cdot \mathrm{BS}_{\mathrm{call}}(\mathrm{S0},\alpha \cdot H,e)
$$

Use $\mathrm{BS}_{\mathrm{put}}$ for puts. A coupon whose end fixing has already occurred is known cash: discount that amount to its unpaid payment date. Paid coupons are excluded. If a global constraint remains, keep the known accumulated coupons as state inside the final payoff instead of valuing them independently.

atoms.title: Forward-start and cliquet pricing under deterministic-coefficient GBM / 6. Calculation and checks
atoms.text:
## 6. Calculation and checks

Historical volatility estimation and risk-neutral pricing use different quantities: a historical return mean does not replace the pricing drift r-q.

For additive period payoffs, present values sum over periods with their own reset, fixing and payment dates. A fixed-strike European option and a reset-strike contract are different payoffs; changing reset frequency has no universal monotonic effect on value.

Check reset-at-zero against ordinary BS, put-call parity, scaling in S0 for price coupons and in Q for return coupons, and independence from S0 for future return coupons with fixed Q. Check zero volatility and zero period length. Local capped returns lie between L and U pathwise, so their PV lies between $Q\cdot \exp (-r\cdot p)\cdot L$ and $Q\cdot \exp (-r\cdot p)\cdot U$ for positive Q. Validate a synthetic period against direct lognormal integration or simulation, including nonzero q and $p>e$.

atoms.title: Forward-start and cliquet pricing under deterministic-coefficient GBM / 7. Scope and references
atoms.text:
## 7. Scope and references

For deterministic time-varying parameters replace $r\tau$, $q\tau$ and $\sigma^2\tau$ by the corresponding period integrals, the pre-reset yield factor by $\exp (-\int _{0}^{s} q)$, and all bond factors by their interval rate integrals. These replacements rely on independent Gaussian increments and deterministic discounting.

Discrete cash dividends break multiplicative GBM. If no cash dividend lies inside the reset period, homogeneity conditional on $S_{s}$ can still be useful, but the pre-reset factor becomes $\exp (-r\cdot s)\cdot \operatorname{E}[S_{s}]$, evaluated under the actual dividend model. It is not generally S0 minus dividend PV when q is nonzero or cash jumps are capped at zero. Cash dividends inside the period require another pricing method. Stochastic volatility, smile dynamics, jumps, and stochastic rates are outside these exact blocks.

Before a future reset the price-unit formula is linear in S0, giving zero spot $\gamma$ under these assumptions. Once the strike is known, ordinary fixed-strike Greeks apply. Do not infer that every Greek must jump at every reset.

The single-period blocks follow directly from Black–Scholes homogeneity and independent lognormal increments; the derivation is stated above. Rubinstein (1991), “Pay Now, Choose Later,” is historical attribution, not a newly verified original source here. For local/global cliquet definitions and model sensitivity, see Windcliff, Forsyth and Vetzal (2006), §4.1–4.2, [Numerical Methods and Volatility Models for Valuing Cliquet Options](https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/~paforsyt/cliquet.pdf). The formulas above do not implement that paper's full PIDE method.

atoms.title: Financial reports: fact context, scale and comparable fundamentals
atoms.text: Use this note when reading annual reports, inline XBRL and financial-statement tables. A requested business quantity must match concept, entity, segment, period and unit. Explicit definitions determine the requested comparison; an ambiguous label does not justify selecting a convenient nearby number.

atoms.title: Financial reports: fact context, scale and comparable fundamentals / Fact identity and period
atoms.text:
## Fact identity and period

A financial fact combines its concept with an entity, a period, optional dimensions and a unit. An instant fact describes a balance at a date; a duration fact describes a flow or average over an interval. Fiscal year, calendar year, filing date and the date of a cover-page disclosure can differ. A comparative column in a newer filing can restate an earlier year; distinguish as-reported from latest-restated comparisons.

Context identifiers are local labels, not globally meaningful dates. Dimension members can identify a security class, segment or geography. Removing dimensions can turn a specific-class fact into an unrelated consolidated one. Equal values under different contexts do not make the contexts interchangeable. Missing, nil, an explicit zero and a textual dash need not mean the same thing.

atoms.title: Financial reports: fact context, scale and comparable fundamentals / Numeric scale and precision
atoms.text:
## Numeric scale and precision

For a non-fraction inline numeric fact, let $a$ be the magnitude after applying the specified locale transformation, $s$ its decimal scale and $\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}$ its explicit sign. Its normalized instance value is:

$$
v=\epsilon a\,10^s
$$

This does not treat display parentheses, visible percentage marks or comma punctuation as universal parsing rules: the transformation determines the lexical number. An extracted XBRL instance may already contain normalized $v$; applying table scale a second time would double-scale it. The decimals attribute expresses rounding accuracy, not a multiplier. A percent displayed in prose and a dimensionless ratio in a tagged fact can differ by a factor of $100$.

Units matter independently of scale. Currency, shares, currency per share, area and counts cannot be combined as one numeric type. A table-level unit heading can apply only to particular columns or exclude per-share figures. A sign in a calculation relationship defines an aggregation weight; it does not by itself negate the stored fact.

atoms.title: Financial reports: fact context, scale and comparable fundamentals / Statements and denominator choice
atoms.text:
## Statements and denominator choice

For compatible revenue $R$, cost of sales $C$ and operating expense $E$, define gross profit $G$ and operating profit $O$:

$$
G=R-C,\qquad O=G-E
$$

Additional operating gains or losses require the corresponding statement lines; net income also reflects non-operating items and taxes. Gross margin on revenue differs from profit relative to cost:

$$
m_R=\frac GR,\qquad m_C=\frac GC
$$

For nonzero denominators their relationship is $m_C=m_R/(1-m_R)$. A phrase referring to cost must not silently be replaced by the more usual revenue denominator. Likewise a sales amount, a profit amount and a margin percentage are distinct, even if a field label loosely uses margin.

Operating cashflow is not operating income. Investing cashflow can include acquisitions and asset disposals beyond capital expenditure. A line describing cash used can be a positive outflow magnitude, while its contribution to net cash movement is negative. Statement arithmetic and the requested sign convention determine the sign; subtracting two outflow magnitudes differs from subtracting signed cashflows.

atoms.title: Financial reports: fact context, scale and comparable fundamentals / Aggregation and comparisons
atoms.text:
## Aggregation and comparisons

Let $q_j$ be amounts purchased or issued and $p_j$ their per-unit prices, all on a consistent basis. For a positive total quantity, weighted average price is:

$$
\bar p=\frac{\sum_jq_jp_j}{\sum_jq_j}
$$

Displayed average prices may be rounded, so their product with displayed counts need not reproduce reported total consideration exactly. Repurchases, equity awards, weighted-average diluted shares and period-end shares describe different populations. Share counts can change through splits without an equivalent economic cashflow.

If an inclusive total $A$ and an exclusive amount $B$ share scope and period, the excluded component is $A-B$. Segment totals cannot be summed without checking overlaps and consolidation eliminations. An average area per location is total area divided by the matching location count, not an unweighted average across differently sized location groups.

For comparable amounts $x_A,x_B$, an absolute difference, a relative change and a percentage-point difference use different units:

$$
\Delta x=x_B-x_A,\qquad
 g=\frac{x_B-x_A}{x_A}
$$

The relative change requires $x_A\ne0$ and may be economically awkward for a negative base. For ratios represented as decimals, the percentage-point change is $100(x_B-x_A)$; it is not the relative percentage change. Rate averages require the stated exposure or time weights.

atoms.title: Financial reports: fact context, scale and comparable fundamentals / Structured extraction from filing bundles (1)
atoms.text:
## Structured extraction from filing bundles

Use this extraction workflow directly; a separate written plan is unnecessary. Choose the field groups from the request. Steps may share a cell; they do not each require a reply.

1. Locate and parse the reporting documents once. Continue only after checking that fact contexts and numeric units resolve.
2. Build reusable fact and table indexes. Match requested quantities to their period, scope and unit; use narrative/table evidence when tagged facts are absent.
3. Process a coherent group of requested quantities across the reports. Verify the source evidence, update the results dictionary, and save it before moving to the next group. Preserve earlier verified values; track unresolved requests separately and follow explicit missing-value requirements without inventing entries.
4. Compute comparisons from compatible normalized values. Check required fields, JSON types and unresolved items, then save again. After a correction, refresh dependent comparisons and outputs.

Reuse existing indexes and verified results. If a structural check fails, repair that step rather than continue with guesses.

Step 1 when the first message says `read_filing` is installed: call it instead of writing a parser.

```python
from filing_io import read_filing
doc = read_filing(zip_path)           # the bundle's inline-XBRL document; facts, tables and visible text
print(doc.check)                      # fact counts, context and unit resolution, conversion statuses
results = autosave_json("<required JSON output path>")   # a dict whose file is rewritten after every assignment
```

Put each value into `results` as soon as it is verified (`results["<key>"] = value`); the file on disk is then always current, and no separate save step is needed.

Continue only when both fact counts are positive and both resolved shares are 1.0. Each item of `doc.facts` keeps its concept, context, period, members, unit and conversion status; `doc.tables` keeps rows with column positions; `doc.text` leaves out the header block, scripts and hidden content. Use `doc.find_facts`, `doc.find_rows` and `doc.search_text` rather than new parsing code.

Step 2 with `read_filing`: find the tables for a whole group of requested items, both reports in one cell, and print each table compactly. Table indices differ between reports, so look them up in each. Facts and table cells are plain dicts and lists (`f["concept"]`, `t["rows"]`).

```python
for name, doc in (("A", doc_a), ("B", doc_b)):
    for words in ["<row label words of one requested item>", "<another>"]:   # all items of a group at once
        for t_index, rows in doc.find_tables(words):
            print(name, words, "->", doc.show_table(t_index))              # unit notes, then "row: cell | cell"
```

`show_table` drops empty cells, so a row reads label, then values in header order; read the year order from the header rows above. Apply the stated unit note to every amount taken from that table, and `t["values"]` gives the full value of a tagged cell. Put each value into `results` as soon as it is read, then continue with the next group.

Step 2 continued: copy this pattern for each verified field. Fill the evidence from the request, table headers and referenced footnotes before assigning a result. These are local helpers, not additional `filing_io` methods. Search routes are hints; follow cross-references and inspect the matching disclosure.

```python
from decimal import Decimal

search_routes = {
    "operating footprint": ("Business", "Properties"),
    "monthly repurchases": ("Issuer Purchases of Equity Securities",),
    "segment profit": ("Segment", "Management's Discussion"),
    "capital spending": ("Liquidity and Capital Resources", "Segment"),
    "consolidated cash flow": ("Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows",),
    "rate-specific debt": ("Market Risk", "Borrowings", "Debt"),
    "equity awards": ("Share-based Compensation", "Stock-based Compensation"),
}

# Construct both dictionaries from evidence, not from the first keyword hit.
# metric distinguishes quantity / expense / fair value / area / principal / rate.
# basis distinguishes GAAP / adjusted / period-end / period-average, as applicable.
# row distinguishes ending nonvested / granted / vested / forfeited, as requested.
def verify_selection(request, evidence):
    for dimension in ("metric", "scope", "period", "basis", "row", "unit"):
        assert request[dimension] is not None, ("unresolved request", dimension)
        assert evidence[dimension] == request[dimension], ("mismatch", dimension)
    assert evidence["source"]       # record document, heading, row and column
    assert evidence["notes_read"]   # includes every applicable header footnote

# Call only after verifying the cell's unit and scale. Never infer area scale
# from currency headings. For normalized tagged values use multiplier=1;
# do not apply their display sign or scale again.
def normalize_cell(value, *, normalized, multiplier, unsigned=False):
    assert multiplier is not None, "read the unit note first"
    if normalized:
        assert multiplier == 1, "tagged value is already normalized"
        amount = Decimal(str(value))
    else:
        text = str(value).strip().replace(",", "").replace("−", "-")
        negative = text.startswith("(") and text.endswith(")")
        text = text[1:-1].strip() if negative else text
        amount = Decimal(text)      # select numeric text without currency symbols
        assert not negative or amount >= 0
        amount = (-amount if negative else amount) * Decimal(str(multiplier))
    return abs(amount) if unsigned else amount  # unsigned only if explicitly requested

# First prefer a directly disclosed component or average with the same definition.
# Derive only when the request permits it and the evidence establishes compatibility.
def derive_component(including, excluding, *, same_basis_and_only_difference):
    assert same_basis_and_only_difference
    return including - excluding

def derive_average(total, count, *, same_population_and_date):
    assert same_population_and_date and count > 0
    return total / count

# After selecting and reading a field, use these calls with evidence-filled variables:
# verify_selection(request, evidence)
# value = normalize_cell(cell, normalized=is_normalized, multiplier=unit_multiplier,
#                        unsigned=request_explicitly_requires_unsigned)
# results[required_key] = float(value)  # use the JSON type required by the schema
```

atoms.title: Financial reports: fact context, scale and comparable fundamentals / Structured extraction from filing bundles (2)
atoms.text:
For matching consolidated measures, use the financial statement and supporting notes before a summary; a requested segment or adjusted measure uses its matching disclosure. An award category alone identifies neither a quantity nor an ending balance: resolve the requested measure and activity row first. Pair rate-specific debt principal with the rate for the same category, date and column; distinguish maturity totals, fair values and period-average balances, and read the rate assumptions. Do not average displayed rates without their weights. Keep unresolved fields separate from verified `results`; never fill the template with guessed metadata merely to satisfy an assertion.

Disclosure bases: Form 10-K Items 1, 2, 5, 7, 7A and 8; Regulation S-K Items 102, 303 and 305; ASC 230-10-45-10 and 45-24; ASC 280-10-50-22, 50-25, 50-29 and 50-30; ASC 718-10-50-2. The selection checks and helper functions are extraction strategies, not prescribed accounting procedures.

Step 1 in code, only when `read_filing` is not available:

```python
import zipfile
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

def load_ixbrl(zip_path):
    with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_path) as z:   # read members directly; no shell unzip is needed
        name = next(n for n in z.namelist() if n.lower().endswith((".htm", ".html")) and b"ix:header" in z.read(n))
        raw = z.read(name)                 # the main document; exhibits have no ix:header
    soup = BeautifulSoup(raw, "xml")       # XML mode keeps names as written: nonFraction, contextRef, unitRef
    contexts = {c["id"]: c for c in soup.find_all("context")}
    units = {u["id"] for u in soup.find_all("unit")}
    facts = [dict(kind=t.name, concept=t.get("name"), context=t.get("contextRef"), unit=t.get("unitRef"),
                  scale=t.get("scale"), fmt=t.get("format"), sign=t.get("sign"), text=t.get_text(" ", strip=True))
             for t in soup.find_all(["nonFraction", "nonNumeric"])]      # a list: repeated facts are all kept
    num = [f for f in facts if f["kind"] == "nonFraction"]
    check = dict(numeric=len(num), non_numeric=len(facts) - len(num),
                 contexts_resolved=sum(f["context"] in contexts for f in facts) / max(1, len(facts)),
                 units_resolved=sum(f["unit"] in units for f in num) / max(1, len(num)))
    return name, soup, contexts, facts, check
```

Print `check` and continue only when both fact counts are positive and both resolved shares are 1.0; otherwise fix the parse first. An HTML parser lowercases these names (`nonfraction`, `contextref`), so a query written with the original case silently finds nothing. Keep `facts` as a list of records; a dict keyed by concept name drops contexts and repeated facts. A context's members are `contexts[id].find_all("explicitMember")`, and its period is in `startDate`/`endDate` or `instant`.

atoms.title: Financial reports: fact context, scale and comparable fundamentals / Structured extraction from filing bundles (3)
atoms.text: Facts can be nested (an `ix:nonNumeric` may contain other facts), which is why a parser is used and not a regular expression. Key each fact by concept name plus `contextRef`, and use `members` to tell apart facts that share a concept but differ by context, such as one per class of security or per period. Apply each fact's `format` transform and `scale` before using the number. Many requested items are not tagged at all (officer names and ages, square footage, figures in narrative tables). If a concept search finds nothing, do not try more concept names: read the item from the HTML text or table rows around its heading, using the table's stated unit. A job title, officer age, security description or policy statement can come from prose rather than a numeric tag. Interpret the text at its stated date and scope. A named officer's age is not automatically the age of the role's current holder at another date. Inline continuation chains can join text separated in the HTML; excluded text is not part of the tagged fact. Presentation position or taxonomy label alone does not establish that the company reported a value. Taxonomy definitions explain concepts; they are not a substitute for the issuer's facts.

atoms.title: Financial reports: fact context, scale and comparable fundamentals / Structured extraction from filing bundles / Extraction details
atoms.text:
### Extraction details

The structural check includes inspecting a small sample of instant/duration periods and dimensional members. A large fact count with missing contexts is an extraction failure, not a usable index.

Keep concept, context, unit, raw text, transformation, scale, sign and nil status. Preserve repeated observations instead of silently overwriting a dictionary entry; resolve duplicates by meaning and consistency. Decode the declared transformation and continuation/exclusion rules before normalizing values.
