Connect related disclosures through compatible contexts and dimensions; never substitute a year embedded in a label for an instrument's identity.

Use tagged facts and narrative/table evidence as complementary sources. If a concept query fails, inspect nearby document headings and labelled rows rather than repeatedly guessing taxonomy names. For prose searches, extract normalized text from the relevant document section, not CSS or raw markup. A plain `get_text` call is not a visibility filter: remove scripts, styles and hidden presentation content from a separate narrative view while retaining hidden inline facts in the fact index.

The table index retains table identity, row labels, headers, cell positions, spans and surrounding unit notes. Preserve percent marks and negative parentheses until interpretation; dropping blank cells or currency symbols must not destroy column alignment. Report layouts can change between filings, so match by meaning rather than reuse a column number. When the request is for an average the report discloses, use the disclosed value; when it asks for an average to be computed, compute it by the stated definition. The two can differ by rounding without contradiction.

Keep provenance for verified observations. Schema checks concern representation as well as value: an integral-valued float must remain a float when required.

atoms.title: Financial reports: fact context, scale and comparable fundamentals / References
atoms.text:
## References

[XBRL International: iXBRL Tagging Features](https://www.xbrl.org/guidance/ixbrl-tagging-features/), transformed values and scale versus accuracy. [Inline XBRL 1.1 specification index](https://specifications.xbrl.org/work-product-index-inline-xbrl-inline-xbrl-1.1.html), typed facts and continuation semantics. [SEC EDGAR APIs](https://www.sec.gov/search-filings/edgar-application-programming-interfaces), fact contexts, units and submissions. [SEC Guide to Financial Statements](https://www.sec.gov/about/reports-publications/beginners-guide-financial-statements), statement distinctions. Ratio, weighting and comparison formulas above follow from their explicit accounting definitions.

atoms.title: FX quote direction, funded forwards and forward value
atoms.text: Use this note for currency quote inversion, covered forwards and carry cashflows. Specify base currency, reporting currency, settlement dates and executable bid/ask sides. Follow explicit day-count, collateral and contractual conventions; do not infer them from a currency name.

atoms.title: FX quote direction, funded forwards and forward value / Existing forward value
atoms.text:
## Existing forward value

For a positive foreign notional $N_f$ bought at contractual delivery rate $K$, and current forward $F(t,T)$, domestic value is:

$$
V_d=N_fD_d(t,T)\{F(t,T)-K\}
$$

The short position has the opposite sign. Current contract value, settlement P&L and quote return are distinct. With spot defined at the valuation instant and matched curves, the same value is $N_f\{S D_f(t,T)-K D_d(t,T)\}$. Initial zero value does not mean zero future exposure.

atoms.title: FX quote direction, funded forwards and forward value / Carry and perspective
atoms.text:
## Carry and perspective

A foreign asset with simple local return $r_f^{\mathrm{asset}}$, converted through domestic-per-foreign FX, earns the domestic gross return:

$$
1+R_d=(1+r_f^{\mathrm{asset}})\frac{S_1}{S_0}
$$

Funding cost and transaction costs are additional cashflows. Reversing the quote changes the FX ratio, not the investor's economic position. A forward hedge's payoff depends on its locked notional and maturity; a current asset basket does not retroactively change an existing hedge book.

atoms.title: FX quote direction, funded forwards and forward value / Quote consistency checks
atoms.text:
## Quote consistency checks

Write the quote as terms currency per base unit before calculating. Under compatible deterministic curves, $F=S D_{\mathrm{base}}/D_{\mathrm{terms}}$; the growth-factor ratio is the reciprocal of this discount-factor ratio. Inverting a bid/ask quote gives bid $1/\mathrm{ask}$ and ask $1/\mathrm{bid}$. Check each forward's direction against the relative accrual factors, its spot-date origin, and each currency's own day count. Convert outright differences to pips only with the pair's point multiplier. A cashflow's payment currency and present-value conversion must remain explicit; a pair name alone does not set a position's sign.

atoms.title: FX quote direction, funded forwards and forward value / References
atoms.text:
## References

[Reiswich and Wystup, FX Volatility Smile Construction](https://www.econstor.eu/bitstream/10419/40186/1/613825101.pdf), quotation and forward notation. The forward, implied-rate, mark-to-market and return expressions above follow by equating the two stated funded currency legs and converting terminal cashflows.

atoms.title: FX quote direction, funded forwards and forward value / Forward points, exposures and signs
atoms.text:
## Forward points, exposures and signs

- Forward points are quoted in pips: points $= (F - S)\times m$ with the pair's point multiplier m (for example $10^{4}$ for most pairs, $10^{2}$ when the terms currency is JPY, or the multiplier the inputs give). The outright is $F = S + \mathrm{points}/m$. A reported "forward points" figure of about $10^{-3}$ for a major pair is the unmultiplied difference.
- A forward or spot position in base/terms creates two currency exposures: $+N$ units of the base currency and $-N\cdot K$ units of the terms currency for a long base position (signs reversed for a short one). Net exposure per currency sums these legs over all trades, including currencies that appear only as the terms side of a cross, and then converts each currency's net amount to the reporting currency.
- Profit attribution signs follow the position direction: a long base position gains when the base/terms rate rises, a short one loses. Keep the trade's direction as a signed notional and apply it once.

atoms.title: FX quote direction, funded forwards and forward value / Executable quote direction
atoms.text:
## Executable quote direction

For positive dealer quotes in domestic units per foreign unit, reversing the pair reverses bid and ask as well as taking reciprocals:

$$
S_{\mathrm{bid}}^{\mathrm{inverse}}=1/S_{\mathrm{ask}},\qquad
S_{\mathrm{ask}}^{\mathrm{inverse}}=1/S_{\mathrm{bid}}
$$

For compatible pairs quoted as units of $B$ per $A$ and units of $C$ per $B$, synthetic $A/C$ bid and ask multiply corresponding executable sides. If a leg is divided rather than multiplied, its side reverses through reciprocal quotation. A cross of midpoints need not equal the midpoint of crossed bid/ask quotes.


Each tenor's forward uses the deposit rates quoted for that tenor in each currency (the mid of a bid/offer snapshot when one is given); interpolate between quoted tenors only for a broken date. A single-tenor rate series, such as a monthly 3M history used for carry signals, is not the rate for every forward tenor.

atoms.title: FX quote direction, funded forwards and forward value / Covered forward
atoms.text:
## Covered forward

Parity formulas name currencies by their place in the quote, not by the investor's home: the terms currency (the one the price is counted in) plays the domestic role and the base currency the foreign role, so for a USD-base pair the USD rate sits in the denominator even for a USD investor. Write the outright as $F=S(1+r_{\mathrm{terms}}\tau_{\mathrm{terms}})/(1+r_{\mathrm{base}}\tau_{\mathrm{base}})$, each year fraction on that currency's own day-count basis from the spot date. An unknown rate comes from the same identity: $r_{\mathrm{terms}}=((F/S)(1+r_{\mathrm{base}}\tau_{\mathrm{base}})-1)/\tau_{\mathrm{terms}}$. Check before writing: the outright lies above spot exactly when the terms rate exceeds the base rate, and an implied rate far outside the quoted deposit range means the identity was inverted.

Let $S$ be domestic-per-foreign FX for spot value date $v$, with forward delivery $T$. With deterministic collateral-compatible discount curves, the outright forward is:

$$
F(v,T)=S\frac{D_f(v,T)}{D_d(v,T)}
$$

For simple deposit rates with currency-specific year fractions, the no-basis funded expression is:

$$
F=S\frac{1+r_d\tau_d}{1+r_f\tau_f}
$$

Discount factors over $[v,T]$ are ratios $D_c(t,T)/D_c(t,v)$. Forward points are increments to spot, divided by the quoted point multiplier when converting to an outright. Interpolation of outright FX, forward points, log forwards and implied yields defines different broken-date curves. A traded non-deliverable forward can carry basis relative to deliverable covered parity.

For the same mid-market convention, implied simple foreign funding solves the forward identity:

$$
r_f=\frac{S(1+r_d\tau_d)/F-1}{\tau_f}
$$

Here $f$ is the base currency of the quote and $d$ the terms currency, whichever of them is the investor's home currency: in a EURUSD quote the implied foreign rate is the EUR rate, in a USDJPY quote it is the USD rate. In code:

```python
def implied_base_rate(spot, forward, r_terms, tau_terms, tau_base):
    return (spot * (1 + r_terms * tau_terms) / forward - 1) / tau_base
```

A higher forward implies a lower base rate: the offer forward gives the lower implied rate, which is the rate bid, and the bid forward gives the rate offer. Check that the bid rate is below the offer rate before writing.

Executable bid/ask implied rates require the stated borrowing/lending and FX sides; a mid identity alone does not determine them. When the inputs give spot bid and ask but a single deposit rate per currency, apply the same accrual factor to each side: $F_{\mathrm{bid}}=S_{\mathrm{bid}}\,D_{\mathrm{base}}/D_{\mathrm{terms}}$ and $F_{\mathrm{ask}}=S_{\mathrm{ask}}\,D_{\mathrm{base}}/D_{\mathrm{terms}}$, with points on each side $F_{\mathrm{side}}-S_{\mathrm{side}}$ in pips; the mid is computed from the mid inputs or the average of the sides, as the task states. A two-sided quote with bid equal to ask is not an executable quote; it means the sides were dropped. Check bid < ask for every outright and cross before writing. In a P&L decomposition of a forward position (spot move, carry, residual), apply the position sign (+1 long the base currency, −1 short) to every component, not only to the total. When the residual is defined as total minus the other components, the components sum to the total whatever error they contain; check instead that the residual is small next to the spot and carry terms and that the spot term has the sign the spot move implies for that position.

atoms.title: GARCH volatility in an end-of-day strategy
atoms.text:
Two index conventions. An end-of-day strategy has every price through the day-t close, so its day-t quantities
include r[t] (an EWMA variance at t uses `r[t]**2`). The arch library labels by target period instead:
`res.conditional_volatility[t]` is the forecast for the return of period t, built from returns through t-1, without r[t].
The GARCH volatility known once day t has closed, with r[t] in, is therefore `conditional_volatility[t+1]`; after the
last return it is the one-step forecast from the full fit. Both conventions use the same information; only the date
label differs. arch exposes both: `res.forecast(horizon=1, start=0, align='origin')` puts the forecast made with r[t] on
row t (the end-of-day label), and `align='target'` puts the same number on row t+1, the label of `conditional_volatility`. Where a strategy writes the day-t GARCH volatility as
sigma[t] or conditional_volatility[t] next to day-t signals, read it in the end-of-day convention and take it from arch
as below.

Use this one series as the GARCH volatility of every asset on day t. Build the composite from it in the units the
task defines; when the composite is annualized, the percentile thresholds and the regime labels use that annualized
composite, never the daily one. Size day t next to the price signal and EWMA volatility of day t; then lag the whole
weight row once, so day t multiplies return t+1.

```python
res = arch_model(100 * r, vol="GARCH", mean="Zero", rescale=False).fit(disp="off")   # r: daily decimal returns (Series)
omega, alpha, beta = res.params["omega"] / 100**2, res.params["alpha[1]"], res.params["beta[1]"]   # omega and every variance: / 100**2
sigma_close = np.sqrt(res.forecast(horizon=1, start=0, align="origin", reindex=False).variance["h.1"]) / 100  # known at the close of t; the only division by 100
```

Per asset, `long_run_variance = omega / (1 - alpha - beta)` with omega already divided by `100**2` (decimal daily units); average these across assets. Keep the return dates as the index of every table (do not reset it to 0..n-1).

Put every day-t input on the return row of the same date by label, e.g. `signal.loc[returns.index]`; do not cut a
price-dated table by position and relabel it, which moves it by one day.

An SMA-seeded EMA with pandas `ewm`: put the SMA of the first `span` prices at position span-1, blank the earlier rows,
and let `ewm(adjust=False, span=span)` (alpha = 2 / (span + 1)) run the recursion from that seed:

```python
def sma_seeded_ema(s, span):                    # s: one price column (Series on the price dates)
    seeded = s.astype(float).copy()
    seeded.iloc[:span - 1] = np.nan
    seeded.iloc[span - 1] = s.iloc[:span].mean()
    return seeded.ewm(adjust=False, span=span).mean()
fast = prices[cols].apply(sma_seeded_ema, span=fast_span)
```

Signals exist only once both indicators exist; mask the rest before sizing:

```python
valid = fast.notna() & slow.notna()
signal = pd.DataFrame(np.where(fast > slow, 1.0, -1.0), index=fast.index, columns=fast.columns).where(valid)
```

Divide an annualized volatility target only by an annualized volatility: `ewma_vol = np.sqrt(252 * ewma_var)`.

atoms.title: GARCH fitting: numerical scale, optimizer termination and reported units / Python arch scaling choices
atoms.text:
## Python arch scaling choices

In `arch_model`, `rescale=None` warns about poor scale without applying a change; `rescale=True` permits automatic power-of-ten scaling and the fitted result exposes `scale`; `rescale=False` disables that automatic adjustment/check. If scaling manually, track that factor and any automatic factor so conversion is applied once. Prefer one explicit scaling mechanism. An output-unit conversion does not retroactively change the units used for estimation.

atoms.title: GARCH fitting: numerical scale, optimizer termination and reported units / Diagnose an apparent fit
atoms.text:
## Diagnose an apparent fit

Do not silence warnings before a fit: arch's DataScaleWarning and convergence warnings are the first sign of a poorly scaled or failed optimization. A result object does not establish convergence. Inspect `convergence_flag`, `optimization_result`, finite objective value, admissible parameters and positive filtered variances. Compare the returned objective with its value at the actual starting vector. Repeated estimates at a library's starting grid, zero iterations or an almost unchanged vector are leads to inspect the stopping condition and scaling, not proof that the estimate is wrong. Initial grids are version-dependent; inspect the installed implementation instead of treating a remembered grid as a model identity.

When permitted, compare alternative feasible starts or scaled fits in common likelihood units. Do not select an infeasible point because its reported objective looks better, clip a result without refitting, substitute unconditional variance for a requested forecast, or change the prescribed estimator silently. A convergence flag alone does not prove a global optimum.

After fitting, keep filtered variance, the next-observation forecast and long-run variance separate. Their definitions and multi-step recursion are in the conditional-volatility entry. Validate all output units together, especially the intercept and long-run variance after a percent-scale fit.

atoms.title: GARCH fitting: numerical scale, optimizer termination and reported units / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources

[arch model settings](https://arch.readthedocs.io/en/stable/univariate/introduction.html) and [result API](https://arch.readthedocs.io/en/stable/univariate/generated/arch.univariate.base.ARCHModelResult.html), scaling and optimizer diagnostics. The dimensional and likelihood identities follow directly by substituting $y=cr$ in the Gaussian conditional density. This is numerical implementation guidance, not a new volatility estimator.

atoms.title: GARCH fitting: numerical scale, optimizer termination and reported units
atoms.text: Use this implementation note with the conditional-volatility formulas. Preserve the specified return series, mean model, initialization, likelihood sample and parameter domain. Numerical scaling is optional only when the specification permits it; a native-unit fit requirement takes precedence.

atoms.title: GARCH fitting: numerical scale, optimizer termination and reported units / Inputs and units
atoms.text:
## Inputs and units

Before fitting, verify finite observations, date alignment, sample length and nonzero variation. Do not confuse raw portfolio returns, excess returns and model innovations. If a zero conditional mean is specified, fitting a constant mean is a different model.

When allowed, fitting small decimal returns on a percent scale can improve numerical conditioning. For a positive scale $c$ and $y_t=cr_t$, use the same transformed initialization:

$$
\mu_y=c\mu_r,\qquad \omega_y=c^2\omega_r,\qquad
h_{y,t}=c^2h_{r,t},\qquad \sigma_{y,t}=c\sigma_{r,t}.
$$

The dimensionless coefficients $\alpha,\beta$ stay unchanged. A percent-return fit has $c=100$; convert the intercept and variances back by $100^2$, and means/standard deviations by $100$. Report the factor actually applied, not a factor inferred from a parameter's size. Scaling data changes neither the return definition nor its observation clock.

For the same $n$ Gaussian likelihood observations, the reported log likelihood obeys:

$$
\ell_r=\ell_y+n\ln c.
$$

This comparison requires the same mean specification, transformed variance seed, innovation distribution, sample and likelihood normalization. Numerical optimizers need not return exactly equivalent parameter estimates after a scale change.

atoms.title: GARCH fitting: numerical scale, optimizer termination and reported units / Fitting daily returns with arch
atoms.text:
## Fitting daily returns with arch

Daily decimal returns (of order 0.01) are badly scaled for arch's optimizer: it warns with a DataScaleWarning and can stop at or near its starting values (for example alpha 0.01, beta 0.97 exactly). Where the task leaves the estimation units open, one remedy is to fit on percentage returns, `arch_model(100 * r, ..., rescale=False)`, then convert back to the data's units before reporting or using the results: omega and every variance divided by $100^2$, volatilities divided by 100; alpha and beta are unit-free. Where the task fixes the units (for example native returns, no rescaling), keep them: pass `rescale=False`, try several feasible starting vectors through `fit(starting_values=...)`, tighten the optimizer tolerance if needed, and keep the start whose fit has the highest log-likelihood in those native units. A higher likelihood shows that an earlier fit was worse; it does not prove a global maximum. Estimates equal to round starting values are a lead to compare against other starts, not proof by themselves that the fit failed. In native daily units arch's optimizer can stay at every starting vector it is given, because omega is many orders of magnitude smaller than alpha and beta. Then reparameterize instead of rescaling the data: keep the returns in native units, write $\omega=\hat v\,e^{\theta}$ with $\hat v$ the sample variance, and maximize the Gaussian GARCH log-likelihood $-\tfrac12\sum_t(\ln 2\pi h_t+r_t^2/h_t)$ over $(\theta,\alpha,\beta)$ with scipy (for example Nelder–Mead from two or three starts), rejecting $\alpha<0$, $\beta<0$ or $\alpha+\beta\ge1$. Initialize $h_0$ as the task states; arch's default is a backcast, so a different $h_0$ moves the estimates slightly. Report $\omega$ in native units and confirm the log-likelihood is at least that of the arch result. Check that the reported omega/(1 - alpha - beta) equals the reported long-run variance in the same units.

atoms.title: GARCH fitting: numerical scale, optimizer termination and reported units / Recipe first (arch, daily returns)
atoms.text:
## Recipe first (arch, daily returns)

Set `MEAN` to the mean model the task states (`"Zero"` or `"Constant"`). Do not silence warnings before the fit.

```python
# A. the task leaves the estimation units open: fit percent returns, convert back
res = arch_model(100 * r, vol="GARCH", mean=MEAN, rescale=False).fit(disp="off")  # GARCH(1,1) by default
omega, alpha, beta = res.params["omega"] / 100**2, res.params["alpha[1]"], res.params["beta[1]"]
variance_daily_next = float(res.forecast(horizon=1, reindex=False).variance.iloc[-1, 0]) / 100**2
sigma_daily_path = np.asarray(res.conditional_volatility) / 100
# Apply the requested annualization only after returning to decimal daily units.

# B. the task fixes native units: keep r as given, reparameterize omega = v * exp(theta)
v = float(np.var(r))
def nll(p):
    om, a, b = v * np.exp(p[0]), p[1], p[2]
    if a < 0 or b < 0 or a + b >= 1:
        return 1e10
    h = np.empty(len(r)); h[0] = v
    for t in range(1, len(r)):
        h[t] = om + a * r[t - 1] ** 2 + b * h[t - 1]
    return 0.5 * np.sum(np.log(2 * np.pi * h) + r ** 2 / h)
best = min((minimize(nll, [np.log(1 - a0 - b0), a0, b0], method="Nelder-Mead",
                     options={"xatol": 1e-10, "fatol": 1e-10, "maxiter": 20000})
            for a0, b0 in [(0.05, 0.90), (0.10, 0.80)]), key=lambda o: o.fun)
omega, alpha, beta = v * np.exp(best.x[0]), best.x[1], best.x[2]
```

After either: check that alpha and beta moved away from round starting values (such as 0.10 / 0.88 or 0.01 / 0.97), that `omega / (1 - alpha - beta)` is near the sample variance in the same units, and that persistence is below one. For many rolling-window refits, start each window from the previous window's estimate.

atoms.title: Gaussian mixtures and kernel-density tail risk
atoms.text: Use this document for VaR and expected shortfall of Gaussian mixtures or a univariate Gaussian kernel-density estimate (KDE). It complements normal/Student-t risk formulas; it does not define a portfolio strategy or a simulation design.

atoms.title: Gaussian mixtures and kernel-density tail risk / Conventions
atoms.text:
## Conventions

Map the task's loss sign, confidence level, bandwidth and estimation conventions before applying these identities. Explicit task definitions take precedence. Here L is loss, c in (0,1) is confidence, $q_{c}$ is loss VaR, and $\operatorname{ES}_{c}$ is upper-tail expected loss. $\Phi$ and $\phi$ denote the standard-normal CDF and density. Each Gaussian component j has probability $p_{j} \ge  0, \operatorname{mean} \mu _{j}$ and standard deviation $s_{j} > 0$; probabilities sum to one. A component's variance is $s_{j}^{2}$, not $s_{j}$.

atoms.title: Gaussian mixtures and kernel-density tail risk / Mixture distribution
atoms.text:
## Mixture distribution

Standardized distance from a component mean to a loss threshold x:

$$
z_{j}(x) = (x - \mu _{j})/s_{j}
$$

Mixture cumulative probability, with a weighted sum of probabilities rather than quantiles:

$$
F_{L}(x) = \sum _{j} p_{j} \cdot  \Phi (z_{j}(x))
$$

Loss quantile defined by the mixture CDF:

$$
F_{L}(q_{c}) = c
$$

Mixture VaR is generally not the probability-weighted average of component VaRs. Positive component scales make the CDF continuous and strictly increasing.

The unnormalized upper-tail first moment of one component follows by substituting a standard normal and integrating $z\phi(z)$:

$$
M_{j}(q) = \mu _{j} \cdot  (1 - \Phi (z_{j}(q))) + s_{j} \cdot  \phi (z_{j}(q))
$$

Continuous-mixture expected shortfall, using the same quantile for every component:

$$
\operatorname{ES}_{c} = \sum _{j} p_{j} \cdot  M_{j}(q_{c}) / (1-c)
$$

This identity is an analytic check on tail quadrature, not a substitute when a task explicitly requires a particular numerical estimator. Integrating only to a finite upper bound omits tail mass and its first moment. With degenerate components or other atoms, conditional tail means and quantile-integrated ES can differ; the continuous formula above assumes all $s_{j} > 0$.

atoms.title: Gaussian mixtures and kernel-density tail risk / Gaussian KDE as a mixture
atoms.text:
## Gaussian KDE as a mixture

For observations $x_{i}$ with nonnegative normalized weights $w_{i}$, and a common positive bandwidth h in loss units, each kernel is a Gaussian component with mean $x_{i}$ and standard deviation h.

KDE density:

$$
f_{h}(x) = \sum _{i} w_{i} \cdot  \phi ((x-x_{i})/h) / h
$$

KDE CDF:

$$
F_{h}(x) = \sum _{i} w_{i} \cdot  \Phi ((x-x_{i})/h)
$$

KDE upper-tail first moment:

$$
M_{h}(q) = \sum _{i} w_{i} \cdot  [x_{i}\cdot (1-\Phi ((q-x_{i})/h)) + h\cdot \phi ((q-x_{i})/h)]
$$

KDE expected shortfall at its own continuous quantile:

$$
\begin{gathered}
F_{h}(q_{c}) = c \\
\operatorname{ES}_{c} = M_{h}(q_{c})/(1-c)
\end{gathered}
$$

A smoothed distribution is distinct from the empirical sample. Averaging only observations above the KDE quantile is not the KDE tail expectation.

A bandwidth factor is dimensionless; h is not. For an unweighted, one-dimensional Gaussian KDE using the covariance-scaling convention, let $s_{\mathrm{sample}}$ be the sample standard deviation (divisor n-1) and b the selected factor.

Kernel standard deviation in the same units as the observations:

$$
h = b \cdot  s_{\mathrm{sample}}
$$

SciPy's unweighted univariate Silverman factor:

$$
b = (3\cdot n/4)^{-1/5}
$$

This is not interchangeable with every univariate rule called “Silverman's rule”. Weighted data change effective sample size and covariance conventions. A zero sample variance makes this KDE construction singular; an arbitrary positive bandwidth changes the model.

atoms.title: Gaussian mixtures and kernel-density tail risk / Checks and scope
atoms.text:
## Checks and scope

A one-component mixture reduces to the normal distribution. For continuous integrable losses, $\operatorname{ES}_{c} \ge  q_{c}$. Under a positive rescaling a and shift b0, both risk measures transform as a times the original plus b0. Mixture probabilities, not realized sample frequencies, define theoretical mixture risk. Fitting or sampling a mixture is separate from evaluating its distribution.

atoms.title: Gaussian mixtures and kernel-density tail risk / Source and derivation
atoms.text:
## Source and derivation

[SciPy gaussian_kde documentation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.gaussian_kde.html), Notes and covariance attributes: Gaussian kernels, covariance scaling and Silverman-factor convention. The mixture CDF and tail-moment expressions above are derived directly by conditioning on a Gaussian component and integrating its density; the same distribution defines both the quantile and its tail moment.

atoms.title: Gaussian hidden regimes: filtering, smoothing and estimation
atoms.text: Use this reference when an observed return series is modeled by a latent Markov state with Gaussian emissions. It separates real-time state probabilities from retrospective classifications and from portfolio allocation conditional on those states.

atoms.title: Gaussian hidden regimes: filtering, smoothing and estimation / Shared Foundations
atoms.text:
## Shared Foundations

Map the task's notation, time frequency, emission model and transition orientation explicitly. Initialization, permitted parameter constraints and stopping criteria may be specified separately. A state index has no intrinsic economic meaning.

Let $y_{t}$ be a scalar observation, $s_{t}$ a hidden state in $\{1,\ldots ,K\}, \pi _{j}=\operatorname{P}(s_{1}=j)$, and $\operatorname{P}_{ij}=\operatorname{P}(s_{t+1}=j\vert s_{t}=i)$. Rows of P sum to one. Conditional on the hidden states, observations are independent. State j has mean $\mu _{j}$ and strictly positive variance $v_{j}$.

The Gaussian observation density in state j is:

$$
b_{j}(y) = \exp (-(y-\mu _{j})^{2}/(2\cdot v_{j}))/\sqrt{2\cdot \pi \cdot v_{j}}
$$

These are densities, not probabilities of observing an exact real number. Their values can exceed one.

atoms.title: Gaussian hidden regimes: filtering, smoothing and estimation / Filtered probabilities and likelihood
atoms.text:
## Filtered probabilities and likelihood

Let $f_{t}(j)=\operatorname{P}(s_{t}=j\vert y_{1},\ldots ,y_{t})$. Before the first observation, the predicted probabilities equal $\pi$; at later dates the Markov transition propagates the preceding filtered distribution.

$$
\begin{gathered}
p_{1}(j) = \pi _{j} \\
p_{t}(j) = \sum _{i} f_{t-1}(i)\cdot \operatorname{P}_{ij},  t\ge 2
\end{gathered}
$$

The predictive density $c_{t}$ normalizes the filter.

$$
\begin{gathered}
c_{t} = \sum _{j} p_{t}(j)\cdot b_{j}(y_{t}) \\
f_{t}(j) = p_{t}(j)\cdot b_{j}(y_{t})/c_{t}
\end{gathered}
$$

The log likelihood of T observations is:

$$
\mathrm{logL} = \sum _{t=1}^{T} \ln (c_{t})
$$

For extreme observations, log densities and log-sum-exp express the same identities without multiplying tiny probabilities. With $P_{ij}$ the probability of moving from state i to state j (rows sum to one), the one-step prediction is $p_{t}(j)=\sum_i f_{t-1}(i)P_{ij}$, that is `f_prev @ P`, or in logs `logsumexp(log_f_prev[:, None] + np.log(P), axis=0)`. Using `P.T` or summing over the wrong axis swaps the roles of the states. That error leaves every row sum intact, so check the column sums of ξ against $\gamma_{t+1}$ as well (below). A zero computed normalizer can be numerical underflow; a genuinely zero predictive density is a model-support failure.

atoms.title: Gaussian hidden regimes: filtering, smoothing and estimation / Smoothed probabilities
atoms.text:
## Smoothed probabilities

Smoothing conditions on the entire observed sample, including observations after t. Define a scaled backward quantity $B_{T}(j)=1$. Its recursion uses the same forward normalizers $c_{t}$.

$$
B_{t}(i) = \sum _{j} \operatorname{P}_{ij}\cdot b_{j}(y_{t+1})\cdot B_{t+1}(j)/c_{t+1}
$$

The smoothed state probability is:

$$
\gamma _{t}(j) = f_{t}(j)\cdot B_{t}(j)
$$

The smoothed joint probability for two adjacent states is:

$$
\xi _{t}(i,j) = f_{t}(i)\cdot \operatorname{P}_{ij}\cdot b_{j}(y_{t+1})\cdot B_{t+1}(j)/c_{t+1}
$$

In exact arithmetic $\gamma$ sums to one, $\xi$ sums to one, its row sums equal $\gamma _{t}$, and its column sums equal $\gamma_{t+1}$. These are useful checks on time indexing and transition orientation.

atoms.title: Gaussian hidden regimes: filtering, smoothing and estimation / Financial interpretation and checks
atoms.text:
## Financial interpretation and checks

State labels may be permuted without changing likelihood. If a state is named by a higher fitted mean, the same permutation applies to $\pi$, both axes of P and all state summaries. A per-date maximum smoothed probability is not the Viterbi most likely whole-state sequence. Naming the states (for example by mean) and classifying a date are separate steps: the current regime is the state whose filtered or smoothed probability at the last date is largest, as the task specifies, and the parameters used afterwards (for example a regime covariance) are those of that state.

An emission variance estimated with $\gamma$ weights is not the same statistic as an asset covariance estimated on hard-classified dates. A univariate market-state model does not by itself determine a multivariate asset covariance. Conditional allocations require a separately defined return/covariance estimator and matching annualization conventions.

Filtered probabilities use observations through their date, but parameters estimated on future data still introduce hindsight. Smoothed probabilities are retrospective even with fixed parameters. With $K=1$ the model reduces to one Gaussian distribution. Equal emissions across states remove the observations' information about the latent states, though the Markov prior still evolves.

atoms.title: Gaussian hidden regimes: filtering, smoothing and estimation / References
atoms.text:
## References

[hmmlearn official tutorial](https://hmmlearn.readthedocs.io/en/stable/tutorial.html), model definition, Gaussian emissions, Baum–Welch, decoding and state-label conventions. The normalized forward/backward formulas follow from Bayes' rule; the Gaussian updates follow from maximizing the posterior-weighted complete-data log likelihood. They are independently checked by enumerating finite hidden-state paths, rather than relying on library defaults.

atoms.title: Gaussian hidden regimes: filtering, smoothing and estimation / Gaussian Baum–Welch updates
atoms.text:
## Gaussian Baum–Welch updates

These are unconstrained maximum-likelihood M-step identities for one sequence, using probabilities from the preceding parameter values. Fixed parameters, priors or imposed variance floors define different updates.

The initial-state distribution and transition probabilities update as:

$$
\begin{gathered}\pi_{\mathrm{new}}(j)=\gamma_1(j)\\ P_{\mathrm{new}}(i,j)=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\xi_t(i,j)}{\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\gamma_t(i)}\end{gathered}
$$

The mean uses every observation weighted by state occupancy.

$$
\mu_{\mathrm{new}}(j)=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^T\gamma_t(j)y_t}{\sum_{t=1}^T\gamma_t(j)}
$$

The variance is a weighted maximum-likelihood variance about the new mean, without a sample degrees-of-freedom correction.

$$
v_{\mathrm{new}}(j)=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^T\gamma_t(j)(y_t-\mu_{\mathrm{new}}(j))^2}{\sum_{t=1}^T\gamma_t(j)}
$$

Zero occupancy leaves an update undefined. Gaussian likelihoods can become singular as a state's variance collapses. A specified positive floor regularizes this problem but changes the optimization problem. Exact EM is nondecreasing in likelihood, not a guarantee of a global optimum. When the task states a stopping rule → test exactly the quantity it names (only the means, if it names the means) against its tolerance and nothing more → check that the reported iteration count is the first iteration at which that one test passes; adding variance or transition tests changes that count. Without a stated rule, small mean changes alone do not prove transition or variance convergence. Pass the current start distribution, transition matrix, means and standard deviations explicitly into every forward, backward and E-step function: a helper that reads them from an outer scope keeps stale values after a refit.

When the forward-backward pass is written in log space with transition matrix `P[i, j]` = Pr(next state j | current state i) → sum over the previous state i, and check that the posteriors are normalized at every date (a transposed P breaks this):

```python
from scipy.special import logsumexp
logP = np.log(P)
log_alpha[0] = np.log(pi) + log_b[0]
for t in range(1, T):
    log_alpha[t] = log_b[t] + logsumexp(log_alpha[t - 1][:, None] + logP, axis=0)
log_beta[-1] = 0.0
for t in range(T - 2, -1, -1):
    log_beta[t] = logsumexp(logP + (log_b[t + 1] + log_beta[t + 1])[None, :], axis=1)
log_gamma = log_alpha + log_beta
log_gamma -= logsumexp(log_gamma, axis=1, keepdims=True)
assert np.allclose(logsumexp(log_alpha[-1]), logsumexp(log_alpha[0] + log_beta[0]))   # same likelihood both ways
```

atoms.title: Compound options (Geske 1979) and the simple chooser option (Rubinstein 1991), Black-Scholes-Merton with yield q / Setting and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Setting and assumptions
- Underlying S follows GBM under the risk-neutral measure with constant vol $\sigma$, rate r, continuous dividend yield q
  (cost of carry b = r - q); European exercise; no smile, no jumps.
- Compound option = outer option (strike K1, expiry T1) written on an inner European option (strike K2, expiry $\mathrm{T2} > \mathrm{T1}$).
  At T1 the holder pays K1 (outer call) or receives K1 (outer put) for the inner option. Payoffs at T1:
  outer call $\max (V(S_{\mathrm{T1}}) - \mathrm{K1}, 0)$, outer put $\max (\mathrm{K1} - V(S_{\mathrm{T1}}), 0)$, where V is the BSM value of the inner option
  with remaining life $\tau  = \mathrm{T2} - \mathrm{T1}$.
- Times are measured from today (valuation date): T1 and T2 are times to expiry in years, not dates.

atoms.title: Compound options (Geske 1979) and the simple chooser option (Rubinstein 1991), Black-Scholes-Merton with yield q / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| $S$ | spot today | price |
| K1 | strike of the outer option (premium paid/received at T1 for the inner option) | price (option premium units) |
| K2 | strike of the inner option | price |
| T1, T2 | times from today to the outer and inner expiries, $\mathrm{T1} < \mathrm{T2}$ | years |
| $r, q$ | continuously compounded rate and dividend yield; 5% is 0.05 | $1/\mathrm{year}$ |
| $\sigma$ | annualized lognormal vol; 30% is 0.30 | $1/\sqrt{\mathrm{year}}$ |

atoms.title: Compound options (Geske 1979) and the simple chooser option (Rubinstein 1991), Black-Scholes-Merton with yield q / Step 1: critical price S* (uses tau = T2 - T1, NOT T2)
atoms.text:
## Step 1: critical price S* (uses tau = T2 - T1, NOT T2)
$S^{*}$ solves $\mathrm{BSM}_{\mathrm{inner}}(S^{*}, \mathrm{K2}, \tau , r, q, \sigma ) = \mathrm{K1}$, where $\mathrm{BSM}_{\mathrm{inner}}$ is the call or put price with time $\tau$.
- Inner call: value increases in S from 0 to infinity, so $S^{*}$ always exists for $\mathrm{K1} > 0$. Root-find (Brent/bisection) on
  $f(x) = \;\text{Call}\;(x, \mathrm{K2}, \tau ) - \mathrm{K1}$, bracket [tiny, K2] and double the upper end until $f > 0$.
- Inner put: value decreases in S from $\mathrm{K2} e^{-r \tau}$ (at $S \to  0$) to 0. Root-find $\;\text{Put}\;(x, \mathrm{K2}, \tau ) - \mathrm{K1}$, bracket
  [tiny, K2], double the upper end until $f < 0$. $S^{*}$ exists only if $\mathrm{K1} < \mathrm{K2} e^{-r \tau}$.
  If $\mathrm{K1} \ge  \mathrm{K2} e^{-r \tau}$: call on put = 0 (never exercised) and put on put = $\mathrm{K1} e^{-r \mathrm{T1}} - \;\text{Put}\;(S, \mathrm{K2}, \mathrm{T2})$ (always exercised).
- $\mathrm{K1} \to  0$: for an inner call $S^{*} \to  0$(its value rises in S); for an inner put $S^{*} \to  \infty$(its value falls in S).
  In both cases the outer call tends to the inner option: call on call -> Call(S, K2, T2), call on put -> Put(S, K2, T2).

atoms.title: Compound options (Geske 1979) and the simple chooser option (Rubinstein 1991), Black-Scholes-Merton with yield q / Step 2: d-terms (y pairs S with S* and T1; z pairs S with K2 and T2)
atoms.text:
## Step 2: d-terms (y pairs S with S* and T1; z pairs S with K2 and T2)

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{y1} = [ \ln (S / S^{*}) + (b + \sigma ^{2}/2) \mathrm{T1} ] / (\sigma  \sqrt{\mathrm{T1}}),     \mathrm{y2} = \mathrm{y1} - \sigma  \sqrt{\mathrm{T1}} \\
\mathrm{z1} = [ \ln (S / \mathrm{K2}) + (b + \sigma ^{2}/2) \mathrm{T2} ] / (\sigma  \sqrt{\mathrm{T2}}),     \mathrm{z2} = \mathrm{z1} - \sigma  \sqrt{\mathrm{T2}} \\
\rho  = \sqrt{\mathrm{T1} / \mathrm{T2}}
\end{gathered}
$$

$M(a, c; \rho ) = \operatorname{P}(X \le  a, Y \le  c)$ for standard bivariate normal X, Y with correlation $\rho$; N = univariate normal CDF.
Use an accurate bivariate CDF (e.g. scipy.stats.$\mathrm{multivariate}_{\mathrm{normal}}$.cdf with mean 0, cov [[1, $\rho$], [$\rho$, 1]],
or Drezner-Wesolowsky / Genz). Discounting: $S e^{-q \mathrm{T2}}$, $\mathrm{K2} e^{-r \mathrm{T2}}$, $\mathrm{K1} e^{-r \mathrm{T1}}$.

atoms.title: Compound options (Geske 1979) and the simple chooser option (Rubinstein 1991), Black-Scholes-Merton with yield q / Step 3: the four compound options (Geske 1979; Haug 2007 sign convention)
atoms.text:
## Step 3: the four compound options (Geske 1979; Haug 2007 sign convention)

$$
\begin{gathered}
\text{Call on call} = S e^{-\mathrm{qT2}} M( \mathrm{z1},  \mathrm{y1};  \rho ) - \mathrm{K2} e^{-\mathrm{rT2}} M( \mathrm{z2},  \mathrm{y2};  \rho ) - \mathrm{K1} e^{-\mathrm{rT1}} N( \mathrm{y2}) \\
\text{Put on call}  = \mathrm{K2} e^{-\mathrm{rT2}} M( \mathrm{z2}, -\mathrm{y2}; -\rho ) - S e^{-\mathrm{qT2}} M( \mathrm{z1}, -\mathrm{y1}; -\rho ) + \mathrm{K1} e^{-\mathrm{rT1}} N(-\mathrm{y2}) \\
\text{Call on put}  = \mathrm{K2} e^{-\mathrm{rT2}} M(-\mathrm{z2}, -\mathrm{y2};  \rho ) - S e^{-\mathrm{qT2}} M(-\mathrm{z1}, -\mathrm{y1};  \rho ) - \mathrm{K1} e^{-\mathrm{rT1}} N(-\mathrm{y2}) \\
\text{Put on put}   = S e^{-\mathrm{qT2}} M(-\mathrm{z1},  \mathrm{y1}; -\rho ) - \mathrm{K2} e^{-\mathrm{rT2}} M(-\mathrm{z2},  \mathrm{y2}; -\rho ) + \mathrm{K1} e^{-\mathrm{rT1}} N( \mathrm{y2})
\end{gathered}
$$

$S^{*}$ above is the call-inner root for the first two lines and the put-inner root for the last two.
Outer option exercised at T1 when: call on call $S_{\mathrm{T1}}$ > $S^{*}$; put on call $S_{\mathrm{T1}}$ < $S^{*}$; call on put $S_{\mathrm{T1}}$ < $S^{*}$; put on put $S_{\mathrm{T1}}$ > $S^{*}$.
Correlation argument: +$\rho$ when the outer option is a call, -$\rho$ when the outer option is a put (exactly as written above).

atoms.title: Compound options (Geske 1979) and the simple chooser option (Rubinstein 1991), Black-Scholes-Merton with yield q / Checks (compound put-call parity, exact)
Compound options (Geske 1979) and the simple chooser option (Rubinstein 1991), Black-Scholes-Merton with yield q / Simple chooser option (Rubinstein 1991), with yield q
atoms.text:
## Simple chooser option (Rubinstein 1991), with yield q
At choice time $t (0 < t < T)$ the holder picks a European call or put, both with strike K and expiry T (times from today).
Value at t is $\max (c_{t}, p_{t}) = c_{t} + e^{-q(T-t)} \max (K e^{-(r-q)(T-t)} - S_{t}, 0)$ by put-call parity, so

$$
\mathrm{Chooser} = \;\text{Call}\;(S, K, T) + e^{-q(T-t)} \cdot  \;\text{Put}\;(S, K e^{-(r-q)(T-t)}, t)
$$

where Call(., ., T) and Put(., ., t) are BSM prices with the same r, q, $\sigma$ and the stated time to expiry. Explicitly:

$$
\begin{gathered}
d  = [ \ln (S/K) + (b + \sigma ^{2}/2) T ] / (\sigma  \sqrt{T}) \\
y  = [ \ln (S/K) + b T + \sigma ^{2} t / 2 ] / (\sigma  \sqrt{t}) \\
\mathrm{Chooser} = S e^{-qT} N(d) - K e^{-rT} N(d - \sigma  \sqrt{T}) - S e^{-qT} N(-y) + K e^{-rT} N(-y + \sigma  \sqrt{t})
\end{gathered}
$$

Checks: Chooser >= $\max ( \;\text{Call}\;(S,K,T), \;\text{Put}\;(S,K,T) )$; t -> 0 gives $\max ( \;\text{call}\;, \;\text{put}\; )$; t -> T gives the straddle Call + Put.
Equivalent form: $\;\text{Put}\;(S, K, T) + e^{-q(T-t)} \;\text{Call}\;(S, K e^{-(r-q)(T-t)}, t)$.
Complex choosers (different strikes or expiries for the call and the put) need a critical price and bivariate normals;
the formula above does NOT apply to them.

atoms.title: Compound options (Geske 1979) and the simple chooser option (Rubinstein 1991), Black-Scholes-Merton with yield q / Common mistakes
atoms.text:
## Common mistakes
- Using T2 instead of $\tau  = \mathrm{T2} - \mathrm{T1}$ inside the critical-price equation ($S^{*}$ is a price AT T1 for an option with life $\tau$).
- Pairing $S^{*}$ with T2 or K2 with T1: y-terms use ($S^{*}$, T1), z-terms use (K2, T2).
- Wrong sign of $\rho$ or of an argument for the put variants; check with the two parity relations above.
- Forgetting $e^{-\mathrm{qT2}}$ on S (not $e^{-\mathrm{qT1}}$) and discounting K1 with T2 instead of T1.
- Using the call-inner $S^{*}$ for an option on a put ($S^{*}$ differs per inner type).
- Not handling the no-root case for an inner put; a root-finder with a fixed bracket then fails or returns garbage.
- Chooser: forgetting the $e^{-q(T-t)}$ factor or using strike K $e^{-r(T-t)}$ when $q \ne  0$; putting T instead of t into the put.
- Low-precision bivariate normal approximations can give parity errors far above rounding; prefer a library CDF.

atoms.title: Compound options (Geske 1979) and the simple chooser option (Rubinstein 1991), Black-Scholes-Merton with yield q / Applicability and limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and limits
- Exact only under constant-parameter BSM with European outer and inner options; American features, stochastic or
  term-structure vol and smiles are not covered. Geske's original application is equity as a call on firm value.
- With discrete dividends between T1 and T2, or time-varying r, the formula needs modification.
- Numerical independent check: Monte Carlo of $S_{\mathrm{T1}}$ (exact GBM step), inner option in closed form at T1, outer payoff
  discounted with $e^{-r \mathrm{T1}}$; or 1-D quadrature over $S_{\mathrm{T1}}$ split at $S^{*}$.

atoms.title: Compound options (Geske 1979) and the simple chooser option (Rubinstein 1991), Black-Scholes-Merton with yield q / Sources
Greek VaR components and variance shares
atoms.text:
For n contracts with finite-difference Greeks at the pricing volatility `garch_vol` (annualized) and `z = norm.ppf(c)`:

```python
daily_move = S0 * garch_vol / np.sqrt(252)                       # one-day spot move scale
delta_var = abs(n * delta * z * daily_move)
gamma_var = 0.5 * abs(n * gamma * (z * daily_move) ** 2)
vol_path = np.asarray(res.conditional_volatility) / 100 * np.sqrt(252)   # annualized fitted volatility path over the sample
vov_daily = np.std(np.diff(vol_path), ddof=1)                    # annualized vol-of-vol = this * sqrt(252); its one-day scale is this
vega_var = abs(n * vega * z * vov_daily)
total = delta_var**2 + gamma_var**2 + vega_var**2                # shares of variance: squares, no cross terms
delta_var_pct, gamma_var_pct, vega_var_pct = (100 * v**2 / total for v in (delta_var, gamma_var, vega_var))
```

The three shares sum to 100. Keep the vol-of-vol on the same one-day horizon as the spot move; do not rescale it twice.

atoms.title: HAC observation time and identification: replacement scope
atoms.text: Use this block to clarify the time-axis and rank assumptions of HAC and factor-regression inference. Explicit task definitions govern the observation clock, lag bandwidth and finite-sample correction. This block supplements mathematical definitions, not a strategy or data-cleaning policy.

atoms.title: HAC observation time and identification: replacement scope / Observation time
atoms.text:
## Observation time

A HAC lag refers to a separation in the modeled observation sequence. Consecutive trading sessions need not be consecutive calendar days. Deleting a missing internal month and treating its neighbors as adjacent changes a monthly lag into an observed-row lag. These conventions need not give the same covariance estimate. Neither filling missing returns with zero nor joining arbitrary unequal time intervals is implied by the standard formula.

Overlapping multi-period returns share innovations; this creates serial dependence even when the underlying single-period innovations are independent. Dependence can extend beyond the overlap length because of persistent regressors, estimation windows or underlying serial correlation. A bandwidth based only on overlap is a minimum heuristic in that setting, not a guarantee of valid inference.

atoms.title: HAC observation time and identification: replacement scope / Identification
atoms.text:
## Identification

Let X be the estimation design matrix with T rows and k columns, E the T-by-N residual matrix, and F the T-by-m factor matrix. A prime is transpose. Counting observations is necessary but not sufficient for invertibility; repeated or linearly dependent columns remain unidentified at any sample size.

Full-column-rank condition for the OLS normal matrix:

$$
\operatorname{rank}(X) = k
$$

Nonsingularity of a residual covariance proportional to E'E:

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{E}) = N
$$

Nonsingularity of the centered factor covariance, with $F_{\mathrm{centered}}$ denoting column-demeaned factors:

$$
\operatorname{rank}(F_{\mathrm{centered}}) = m
$$

The degrees-of-freedom inequalities in a joint-$\alpha$ test do not replace these conditions. A generalized inverse defines a different statistic unless the test's theory explicitly allows it. HAC changes estimated uncertainty; it cannot identify coefficients in a rank-deficient design.

atoms.title: HAC observation time and identification: replacement scope / Source and derivation
atoms.text:
## Source and derivation

[Statsmodels HAC documentation](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.stats.sandwich_covariance.cov_hac.html) states the ordered, equally spaced single-series assumption. Calendar interpretation above specifies that spacing's economic meaning. The rank statements follow from v'X'Xv=||Xv||^2 and the same identity for residual and centered-factor matrices. They do not assert a new asymptotic test.

atoms.title: Heston (1993) stochastic volatility: characteristic-function pricing ("little Heston trap" form), Gil-Pelaez P1/P2, Carr-Madan FFT
atoms.text:
Use this reference for Heston European pricing by characteristic-function integration or FFT, with calibration, simulation and implied-volatility checks.

**If the task text defines the formula, inputs or conventions differently, the task text wins.**

atoms.title: Heston (1993) stochastic volatility: characteristic-function pricing ("little Heston trap" form), Gil-Pelaez P1/P2, Carr-Madan FFT / Model (risk-neutral)
atoms.text:
## Model (risk-neutral)
**Risk-neutral stock dynamics**

$$
\mathrm{d}S_{t} = (r - q) S_{t} \mathrm{d}t + \sqrt{v_{t}} S_{t} \mathrm{d}W_{1}
$$

**Variance dynamics and instantaneous correlation**

$$
\mathrm{d}v_{t} = \kappa  (\theta  - v_{t}) \mathrm{d}t + \sigma _{v} \sqrt{v_{t}} \mathrm{d}W_{2},      \mathrm{d}W_{1} \mathrm{d}W_{2} = \rho  \mathrm{d}t
$$

- Constant r, q; European exercise; no jumps. v is a CIR (square-root) variance process.
- For positive CIR parameters and $v_0>0$, the zero boundary is unattainable when $2\kappa\theta\ge\sigma_v^2$, including equality. For $0<2\kappa\theta<\sigma_v^2$, zero is attainable and the standard CIR process is instantaneously reflecting;
  the model and the CF price remain valid, only simulation gets harder. Do not "fix" parameters to satisfy Feller unless told.
- If the task gives Heston's price of volatility risk $\lambda$ (risk premium $\lambda v$), the risk-neutral parameters are
  $\kappa ^{*} = \kappa  + \lambda$, $\theta ^{*} = \kappa  \theta  / (\kappa  + \lambda )$; most tasks give risk-neutral parameters directly.

atoms.title: Heston (1993) stochastic volatility: characteristic-function pricing ("little Heston trap" form), Gil-Pelaez P1/P2, Carr-Madan FFT / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol (aliases) | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| $\kappa$ | speed of mean reversion of the variance | $1/\mathrm{year}$ |
| $\theta  (\eta , \bar{v})$ | long-run VARIANCE (a 20% long-run vol is `0.04`) | $1/\mathrm{year}$ |
| $\sigma_v$ (paper-dependent aliases include $\xi$ or $\nu$) | vol of variance | $1/\mathrm{year}$ |
| $\rho$ | correlation of dW1 and dW2, in (-1, 1); usually negative for equity | none |
| $\mathrm{v0} (\mathrm{V0}, \sigma _{0}^{2})$ | initial VARIANCE (square it if the task gives a vol) | $1/\mathrm{year}$ |
| S0, K, T, r, q | spot, strike, years, continuous rate and dividend yield | |
Papers reuse letters for different roles (Albrecher et al. write $\eta$ for $\theta$ and $\lambda$ for $\sigma _{v}$); map by position in the SDE.

atoms.title: Heston (1993) stochastic volatility: characteristic-function pricing ("little Heston trap" form), Gil-Pelaez P1/P2, Carr-Madan FFT / Characteristic function of ln S_T (little-trap form; use principal complex sqrt and log)
atoms.text:
## Characteristic function of ln S_T (little-trap form; use principal complex sqrt and log)
**Characteristic-function drift coefficient**

$$
b(u) = \kappa  - \rho  \sigma _{v} i u
$$

**Characteristic-function discriminant**

$$
d(u) = \sqrt{b^{2} + \sigma _{v}^{2} (i u + u^{2})}
$$

**Stable characteristic-function ratio**

$$
g(u) = (b - d) / (b + d)
$$

**Constant affine exponent contribution**

$$
C(u) = (\kappa  \theta  / \sigma _{v}^{2}) [ (b - d) T - 2 \ln ( (1 - g e^{-dT}) / (1 - g) ) ]
$$

**Initial-variance affine exponent contribution**

$$
D(u) = (\mathrm{v0} / \sigma _{v}^{2}) (b - d) (1 - e^{-dT}) / (1 - g e^{-dT})
$$

**Log-stock characteristic function**

$$
\phi (u) = \exp ( i u (\ln  \mathrm{S0} + (r - q) T) + C(u) + D(u) )
$$

Checks: $\phi (0) = 1$, $\phi (-i) = F = \mathrm{S0} e^{(r-q)T}$. The original Heston form ($b + d$, $\mathrm{g1} = 1/g$, $e^{+dT}$) is algebraically
equal but with principal branches its log jumps across the branch cut for longer maturities and silently misprices
(Albrecher et al. 2007). Use the form above; do not evaluate the CF at $\sigma _{v} = 0$ (divide by $\sigma _{v}^{2}$).

At the exact moment points, use $\phi(0)=1$ and $\phi(-i)=S_0e^{(r-q)T}$ under the stated martingale model. At $u=-i$, $iu+u^2=0$; if $\kappa-\rho\sigma_v\le0$, the generic $g=(b-d)/(b+d)$ may involve a zero denominator. Evaluate the affine limit or the known first moment there rather than declaring the price model invalid. For nearby complex points use a continuous stable representation; the two exact moment checks alone do not prove integration accuracy.

For a common maturity and quadrature rule, precompute characteristic-function values at that rule's nodes and reuse them across strikes; only the strike-dependent Fourier kernel changes. For a fixed-node rule in numpy (for example `np.polynomial.legendre.leggauss` mapped to [0, U]): with the same parameters and maturity, evaluate the characteristic function once on the node array, build the strike kernel as a (strikes × nodes) array by broadcasting `np.log(K)[:, None]` against the nodes, and sum with the weights along the node axis; this prices every strike of that maturity in one array operation. Compute the nodes and weights once, not inside each price call, and evaluate the integrand on the whole node array rather than node by node in a Python loop or list comprehension. When a large surface grid is priced with such a rule, avoid a Python loop that re-evaluates the characteristic function per (strike, maturity) point. An adaptive routine such as `scipy.integrate.quad` chooses its own nodes per integrand, so its evaluations cannot be shared across strikes; where the task requires it, still run it as specified. Recompute cached values whenever parameters, maturity or the rule change. Keep each required integration rule and assess its truncation and discretization errors separately.

atoms.title: Heston (1993) stochastic volatility: characteristic-function pricing ("little Heston trap" form), Gil-Pelaez P1/P2, Carr-Madan FFT / Variant: Carr-Madan (1999) FFT
atoms.text:
## Variant: Carr-Madan (1999) FFT
**Damped Fourier transform for call pricing**

$$
k = \ln  K,   \psi (v) = e^{-rT} \phi (v - (\alpha  + 1) i) / (\alpha ^{2} + \alpha  - v^{2} + i (2 \alpha  + 1) v)
$$

**Recover the call price by Fourier inversion**

$$
\;\text{Call}\;(k) = (e^{-\alpha  k} / \pi ) \int _{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{Re}[ e^{-i v k} \psi (v) ] \mathrm{d}v
$$

**Fourier and log-strike grids**

Grid: $v_j=j\Delta v$, $j=0,\ldots,N-1$; log strikes $k_m=k_0+m\Delta k$, $m=0,\ldots,N-1$, with $\Delta k\Delta v=2\pi/N$; these grid spacings are separate from model parameters.

Simpson weights $w_j=(\Delta v/3)(3+(-1)^{j+1})$, $w_0=\Delta v/3$. Then

**FFT call-price evaluation**

$\;\text{Call}\;(k_{m}) = (e^{-\alpha  k_{m}}/\pi ) \mathrm{Re}[ \sum _{j} e^{-2 \pi  i j m / N} e^{-i v_{j} k_{0}} \psi (v_{j}) w_{j} ]$ is one FFT; interpolate in k.

Carr-Madan use $k_0=-N\Delta k/2$ (for S0 not near 1 center it: $k_0=\ln S_0-N\Delta k/2$).
- **Damping $\alpha  > 0$ must satisfy $\operatorname{E}[S_{T}^{\alpha +1}] < \infty$.** Under Heston this moment can explode at a finite
  maturity (most easily with positive $\rho$, large $\sigma _{v}$, large $\alpha$, long T); past it the CF at $-(\alpha +1) i$ returns a
  wrong finite (even complex) number and the FFT prices are wrong with no error raised. Check that $\phi (-(\alpha +1) i)$ is real and positive and compare
  a few strikes with the Gil-Pelaez price. Carr-Madan suggest one quarter of the largest admissible $\alpha$; they used
  $\alpha  = 1.5, \eta  = 0.25, N = 4096$ for their example. Smaller $\alpha$ makes $\psi$ peak near $v = 0$: then refine $\eta$ (raise N).

atoms.title: Heston (1993) stochastic volatility: characteristic-function pricing ("little Heston trap" form), Gil-Pelaez P1/P2, Carr-Madan FFT / Common mistakes
atoms.text:
## Common mistakes
- $\theta$ or v0 given as vol but used as variance (or the reverse); $\sigma _{v}$ confused with $\sqrt{\theta}$.
- Using the original-form CF with principal branches (wrong for long T); forgetting `phi(-i)` in P1; dropping $e^{-qT}$.
- Monte Carlo check: full-truncation Euler (Lord et al. 2010) with $v^{+} = \max (v, 0)$:
**Full-truncation simulation step**

  $\ln  S += (r - q - v^{+}/2) \mathrm{d}t + \sqrt{v^{+} \mathrm{d}t} \mathrm{Z1}$,  $v += \kappa  (\theta  - v^{+}) \mathrm{d}t + \sigma _{v} \sqrt{v^{+} \mathrm{d}t} (\rho  \mathrm{Z1} + \sqrt{1 - \rho ^{2}} \mathrm{Z2})$.

  Its bias shrinks with dt but is large when Feller is badly violated; Andersen's (2008) QE scheme is the lower-bias alternative.
- Limit $\sigma _{v} \to  0$: Heston -> Black-Scholes with $\sigma _{\mathrm{eff}}^{2} = \theta  + (\mathrm{v0} - \theta )(1 - e^{-\kappa  T})/(\kappa  T)$; a good unit test.

atoms.title: Heston (1993) stochastic volatility: characteristic-function pricing ("little Heston trap" form), Gil-Pelaez P1/P2, Carr-Madan FFT / Calibration notes
atoms.text:
## Calibration notes
Minimize weighted squared errors in prices (weights ~ 1/vega) or in implied vols over ($\kappa$, $\theta$, $\sigma _{v}$, $\rho$, v0) with
bounds $\kappa , \theta , \sigma _{v}, \mathrm{v0} > 0, -1 < \rho  < 1$(Feller only if the task asks). Roles: v0 sets short-dated ATM level, $\theta$
long-dated level, $\kappa$ the speed between them, $\rho$ the skew, $\sigma _{v}$ the smile curvature; $\kappa$, $\theta$ and $\sigma _{v}$ trade off
(flat objective), so use several starting points and report the fit error.

atoms.title: Heston (1993) stochastic volatility: characteristic-function pricing ("little Heston trap" form), Gil-Pelaez P1/P2, Carr-Madan FFT / Applicability and known limits (own validation)
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits (own validation)
CF price matches Albrecher et al.'s published long-dated ATM table to <= 0.0073% of spot (T up to 15y), where the original form
with principal branches is off by up to 27% of spot. FFT agrees with Gil-Pelaez to < 1e-6 when $\alpha$ is admissible (error 8.0
on a spot of 100 when it is not). Full-truncation MC agrees within noise for Feller-satisfied and mildly violated sets; with
positive $\rho$ and $\sigma _{v}^{2}$ about 11 times $2\kappa\theta$, the MC bias was 3.7 SE at 250 steps/year and vanished by 4000 steps/year.

atoms.title: Heston (1993) stochastic volatility: characteristic-function pricing ("little Heston trap" form), Gil-Pelaez P1/P2, Carr-Madan FFT / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources
Heston (1993) Review of Financial Studies 6(2):327-343; Albrecher, Mayer, Schoutens & Tistaert (2007) "The little Heston trap",
Wilmott Magazine 2007(1):83-92; Gil-Pelaez (1951) Biometrika 38(3-4):481-482; Carr & Madan (1999) J. Computational Finance 2(4):61-73;
Lord, Koekkoek & van Dijk (2010) Quantitative Finance 10(2):177-194; Andersen (2008) J. Computational Finance 11(3).

atoms.title: Heston (1993) stochastic volatility: characteristic-function pricing ("little Heston trap" form), Gil-Pelaez P1/P2, Carr-Madan FFT / Affine-factor conventions and initial variance
atoms.text:
## Affine-factor conventions and initial variance

When a model has several variance factors → compute each factor's affine terms without the spot and carry term, and add that common term once:

```python
log_phi = 1j*u*(np.log(S) + (r - q)*T)          # common term, once
for f in factors:
    C, B = affine_terms(u, T, f)                # excludes the common term; B not yet multiplied by v0
    log_phi = log_phi + C + B*f.v0
phi = np.exp(log_phi)
assert np.isclose(phi_at(0), 1) and np.isclose(phi_at(-1j), S*np.exp((r - q)*T))
```

Multiplying two complete single-factor characteristic functions counts the common term twice. Under the other convention, where the factor term already includes v0, do not multiply by v0 again.

Two common affine-factor conventions are equivalent:

**Affine factors before multiplying initial variance**

$$
\log (\phi ) = i\cdot u\cdot (\log (S)+(r-q)\cdot T) + \sum _{m}(C_{m} + B_{m}\cdot v_{\mathrm{m0}})
$$

or, with $\operatorname{E}_{m}$ defined as $B_mv_{\mathrm{m0}}$,

**Affine factors with initial variance already included**

$$
\log (\phi ) = i\cdot u\cdot (\log (S)+(r-q)\cdot T) + \sum _{m}(C_{m} + \operatorname{E}_{m}).
$$

The initial variance appears once in each factor contribution. $\operatorname{E}_{m}$ already includes $v_{\mathrm{m0}}$ and must not be multiplied by it again. The letter D is used for either convention in different references; match definitions rather than letters. The combined characteristic exponent includes the spot/carry term once, not once per variance factor. Product factorization assumes the model's factor drivers are independent across factors; specified cross-factor dependence requires its own characteristic function.

Before testing Fourier integration, check $\phi (0,T)=1$ and, under the model's risk-neutral martingale assumptions, $\phi (-i,T)=S\cdot \exp ((r-q)\cdot T)$. These two checks alone do not establish the variance dynamics. For independent additive Heston variance factors, a separate short-time check at fixed nonzero real u is:

**Short-maturity variance check**

$$
-2\cdot \log (\mathrm{abs}(\phi (u,T))) / (u^{2}\cdot T) \to  \sum _{m}(v_{\mathrm{m0}}), \mathrm{as} T \to  0.
$$

Use a sequence of decreasing positive maturities while avoiding floating-point cancellation. This tests the initial variance contribution; it does not verify the full characteristic function, long-maturity branch handling, or quadrature accuracy.

atoms.title: Heston (1993) stochastic volatility: characteristic-function pricing ("little Heston trap" form), Gil-Pelaez P1/P2, Carr-Madan FFT / Price-to-implied-volatility consistency
atoms.text:
## Price-to-implied-volatility consistency

Use the same spot, strike, expiry, risk-free discounting and dividend or carry convention for the model price and the Black-Scholes price used to invert it. A zero-rate inversion is not equivalent to inversion at a specified nonzero rate.

For a European call under the standard spot Black-Scholes conventions, check the input price against $\max (S\cdot \exp (-q\cdot T) - K\cdot \exp (-r\cdot T), 0)$ and $S\cdot \exp (-q\cdot T)$, allowing a stated numerical tolerance. A materially negative price or a price below the lower bound is a pricing failure, not zero implied volatility. A failed root solve does not establish zero implied volatility. Reprice each recovered IV with the same inputs and compare it with the input option price. This checks inversion consistency; it does not independently validate the model price.

When model prices are about to be inverted to implied volatilities → check every price against the bounds first and stop if any fails; a price outside them is a pricing error, never an implied volatility of zero (a price exactly at the lower bound may legitimately invert to zero volatility):

```text
lower = np.maximum(S*np.exp(-q*T) - K*np.exp(-r*T), 0.0)
upper = S*np.exp(-q*T)
bad = ~np.isfinite(C) | (C < lower - tol) | (C > upper + tol)     # call prices, broadcast over the K and T grid
assert not bad.any(), "fix the pricer (combined characteristic function, maturity, integration range) before inverting"
```

If Fourier integration produces invalid prices, separate finite-interval quadrature error from truncation error. More nodes on the same interval do not test the omitted tail. Where permitted, vary the interval endpoint separately from the quadrature resolution and inspect price convergence. Retain any explicitly requested methods and settings for the task's comparison; label additional diagnostics separately. Pairwise differences alone do not identify which of two methods is more accurate. At short maturities the characteristic function decays slowly, so a shorter truncation limit leaves a visible error, largest for strikes far from the money. If a selection rule stated in terms of the two methods' common difference cannot separate them, prefer the rule with the longer interval and more nodes, which has the smaller truncation error, and state that reason; this needs no extra computation.

atoms.title: Heston (1993) stochastic volatility: characteristic-function pricing ("little Heston trap" form), Gil-Pelaez P1/P2, Carr-Madan FFT / Pricing in code, with a check after each step
atoms.text:
## Pricing in code, with a check after each step

One or more independent Heston variance factors; each factor m has its own spot shock correlated (rho_m) only with its own
variance shock. The spot/carry term enters the exponent once; each factor adds its affine terms. Run every check: each one
fails on a specific common mistake.

```python
def affine_terms(u, T, kappa, theta, sigma_v, rho):     # one factor, little-trap form, without the spot/carry term
    b = kappa - rho * sigma_v * 1j * u
    d = np.sqrt(b**2 + sigma_v**2 * (1j * u + u**2))
    g = (b - d) / (b + d)
    e = np.exp(-d * T)
    C = kappa * theta / sigma_v**2 * ((b - d) * T - 2 * np.log((1 - g * e) / (1 - g)))
    B = (b - d) / sigma_v**2 * (1 - e) / (1 - g * e)       # not yet multiplied by v0
    return C, B

def phi(u, T, factors):                                  # characteristic function of ln S_T
    log_phi = 1j * u * (np.log(S0) + (r - q) * T)        # spot/carry term, once
    for f in factors:
        C, B = affine_terms(u, T, f["kappa"], f["theta"], f["sigma_v"], f["rho"])
        log_phi = log_phi + C + B * f["v0"]
    return np.exp(log_phi)

fwd = phi(-1j, T, factors)
assert np.isclose(phi(1e-12, T, factors), 1)             # phi(0) = 1
assert np.isclose(fwd, S0 * np.exp((r - q) * T))         # phi(-i) = forward; fails if spot/carry is counted per factor

# Gil-Pelaez: each integral feeds its own probability (P1 stock measure, P2 risk-neutral)
f1 = lambda u: (np.exp(-1j * u * np.log(K)) * phi(u - 1j, T, factors) / (1j * u * fwd)).real
f2 = lambda u: (np.exp(-1j * u * np.log(K)) * phi(u, T, factors) / (1j * u)).real
P1 = 0.5 + integral(f1) / np.pi                           # integral(): the quadrature the task names, on its stated range
P2 = 0.5 + integral(f2) / np.pi
call = S0 * np.exp(-q * T) * P1 - K * np.exp(-r * T) * P2
assert 0 <= P1 <= 1 and 0 <= P2 <= 1
assert max(S0 * np.exp(-q * T) - K * np.exp(-r * T), 0) - 1e-8 <= call <= S0 * np.exp(-q * T)   # no-arbitrage bounds
```

- A price outside the bounds is a bug upstream: do not clip it to 0 or write an empty cell; fix the characteristic function
  or the integration first.
- After inverting implied volatilities, reprice with Black-Scholes at each implied volatility and compare with the model price;
  every surface cell must be finite.
- Check the code with constant variance (sigma_v near 0, v0 = theta): the price must match Black-Scholes with total variance
  equal to the sum of the factor variances.

atoms.title: Heston (1993) stochastic volatility: characteristic-function pricing ("little Heston trap" form), Gil-Pelaez P1/P2, Carr-Madan FFT / Price by Gil-Pelaez / Heston probabilities
atoms.text:
## Price by Gil-Pelaez / Heston probabilities
**Risk-neutral terminal exercise probability**

$$
\mathrm{P2} = 1/2 + (1/\pi ) \int _{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{Re}[ e^{-i u \ln  K} \phi (u) / (i u) ] \mathrm{d}u\quad (\text{risk-neutral} \operatorname{Prob}(S_{T} > K))
$$

**Stock-measure terminal exercise probability**

$$
\mathrm{P1} = 1/2 + (1/\pi ) \int _{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{Re}[ e^{-i u \ln  K} \phi (u - i) / (i u \phi (-i)) ] \mathrm{d}u\quad (\text{stock-measure} \operatorname{Prob}(S_{T} > K))
$$

**European call from the two probabilities**

$$
\;\text{Call}\; = \mathrm{S0} e^{-qT} \mathrm{P1} - K e^{-rT} \mathrm{P2}
$$

**European put from the two probabilities**

$$
\;\text{Put}\;  = K e^{-rT} (1 - \mathrm{P2}) - \mathrm{S0} e^{-qT} (1 - \mathrm{P1})\quad ( = \;\text{Call}\; - \mathrm{S0} e^{-qT} + K e^{-rT}, \;\text{put}\;-\;\text{call}\; \;\text{parity}\;)
$$

- Integration: the integrands have finite limits at $u \to  0$; start just above 0 (or use Gauss-Legendre nodes, which skip 0).
  Truncate at U where the integrand is negligible and verify by doubling U. Decay is slower for short T and low variance:
  for one typical parameter set an error below 1e-6 needed $U = 200$ at T of about a week, $U = 100$ at a quarter, $U = 50$ at
  two years. Adaptive quadrature or a few hundred Gauss-Legendre nodes on [0, U] both work.
  When the task states the range, node count or subinterval limit for an integration method, use exactly those for
  that method; a task that compares two rules wants each rule run on its own stated setting, so do not widen a range
  or raise a limit to make the two agree. The truncation advice above applies only where the task leaves it open.
  A difference between two rules cannot rank them: it is the same number for both. When the task asks to choose
  between two settings, compare each with a reference computed more accurately (a wider range and more nodes, or an
  adaptive rule with tight tolerances) and keep the one closer to the reference. A slightly negative deep
  out-of-the-money price is truncation error of a short range; keep it visible and let the comparison choose, do not
  clip it to zero.

  ```python
  err = {name: np.max(np.abs(price_by(name) - price_ref)) for name in ("rule_a", "rule_b")}   # same strikes and maturity
  chosen = min(err, key=err.get)
  ```

atoms.title: Holdings and proportional-flow workflow
atoms.text:
Use this workflow for selected holdings, common exposure and proportional flow scenarios. Explicit task formulas and output definitions take precedence.

1. Locate each workbook's actual header and retain identifiers as identifiers. Read the required fields together. Resolve numeric display formats and source units before computing exposures; report required values that failed parsing.
2. Before arithmetic, record each required numeric field’s documented source unit, working unit and conversion factor in the computation cell. Preserve raw columns and create normalized working columns once; use them downstream. Verify the conversion relationship in that same cell. This checks execution, not whether the chosen factor is justified: its basis must come from source documentation. Before saving, check working-to-output units. Preserve the distinction between full-fund weights and weights renormalized within a selected subset.
3. Select each fund's requested holdings with the declared tie-break. Every subsequent membership flag and exposure lookup must use these selected tables, not the unfiltered source tables. Build the union with explicit fund-membership flags. Missing selected-fund shares, weights and amounts are zero; an unavailable implied price remains missing.
4. Maintain a canonical exposure table. For asset base A, decimal weight w and positive share quantity q, holding value is A*w and implied price is A*w/q. Combined implied price is combined dollars divided by combined shares. Do not average the individual prices.
5. Form an enriched scenario working table with original exposures, membership, scenario identifiers and per-fund flows. A proportional shock rho gives shares*rho and holding_value*rho. Derive all related aggregates from that table.
6. Write each deliverable by selecting its requested columns from the full working table. Keep the working table intact. A CSV reload contains only exported columns, not earlier in-memory additions. Validate joins and required downstream columns together.
7. Use an explicit denominator for each concentration and cash-flow ratio. Keep original asset totals, redeemed NAV amounts and redeemed market amounts distinct. Compute transfer ratios from their defined amounts rather than rounded display premiums.
8. Compute ranks from each rank's own metric and stated tie policy. Derive summary winners and counts from the completed tables. Read back required files and check schema, units and arithmetic identities. Recompute downstream outputs after an upstream correction.
