## Selection scope check

```python
import pandas as pd
left_all = pd.DataFrame({'id':['a','b'], 'w':[.6,.4]})
right_all = pd.DataFrame({'id':['b','c'], 'w':[.7,.3]})
k = 1  # synthetic selection, use the requested size in a real calculation
left = left_all.sort_values(['w','id'],ascending=[False,True]).head(k).set_index('id')
right = right_all.sort_values(['w','id'],ascending=[False,True]).head(k).set_index('id')
union = left.index.union(right.index)
left_w = left.w.reindex(union,fill_value=0.)
right_w = right.w.reindex(union,fill_value=0.)
assert set(left_w[left_w.ne(0)].index) == set(left.index)
assert left_w.loc['b'] == 0.  # b exists in the raw left source, but was not selected there
assert set(union) == set(left.index)|set(right.index)
```

Before exporting, distinguish source fields from derived fields. A derived ratio is not absent merely because the workbook lacks that column. Keep a calculation for each required derived field; do not export an empty string in its place. Convert all outputs to the declared units, including a maximum selected source percentage: a pct suffix alone is not permission to retain percent units when outputs require decimals.

atoms.title: Holdings and proportional-flow workflow / Measurement bases for proportional holdings
atoms.text:
## Measurement bases for proportional holdings

Use these definitions for a proportional holdings analysis unless an explicit task definition differs. Preserve the original measurement base through a calculation; filtering rows does not change their denominator.

- Full-fund weights stay full-fund weights after selecting holdings. Their contribution to fund concentration is `sum(w**2)`. Only a concentration explicitly conditional on the selected basket uses `sum((w/w.sum())**2)`.
- Holdings valued from reported assets A have modeled total outflow `rho*A`. The selected-flow capture against that asset base is selected flow divided by `rho*A`. Do not substitute market capitalization for assets. A separately requested NAV-based capture instead uses redeemed units times NAV; label which base is being used.
- Redeemed units, NAV value and market value are separate measures. Compute a transfer relative to NAV from the amounts, not a displayed rounded premium. Keep the original displayed premium when the requested field is the source snapshot itself.

```python
import numpy as np
w = np.array([.2, .3])  # decimal full-fund weights for a synthetic subset
A, units, nav, market, rho = 1000., 100., 10.01, 10.02, .04
holding_value = A*w
flow = rho*holding_value
raw_hhi = np.sum(w*w)
conditional_hhi = np.sum((w/w.sum())**2)
redeemed_units = rho*units
nav_amount, market_amount = redeemed_units*nav, redeemed_units*market
asset_capture = flow.sum()/(rho*A)
nav_capture = flow.sum()/nav_amount
transfer_bps = (market_amount/nav_amount-1)*1e4
assert np.isclose(raw_hhi, .13) and np.isclose(conditional_hhi, .52)
assert np.isclose(asset_capture, w.sum())
assert not np.isclose(asset_capture, nav_capture)
assert np.isclose(transfer_bps, (market/nav-1)*1e4)
```


These method examples use synthetic inputs; explicit task definitions take precedence.

atoms.title: Hull-White one-factor short-rate model (extended Vasicek): bonds, bond options, caps, Jamshidian swaptions, trinomial tree / Model and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Model and assumptions
- Risk-neutral short rate: $\mathrm{d}r = (\theta (t) - a r) \mathrm{d}t + \sigma  \mathrm{d}W$, constant $a > 0$(mean-reversion speed) and $\sigma$ (normal vol).
  $\theta$(t) is chosen so the model reprices today's discount curve P(0,T) exactly. r is Gaussian, so negative rates are possible.
- Equivalently $r(t) = x(t) + \phi (t)$, $\mathrm{d}x = -a x \mathrm{d}t + \sigma  \mathrm{d}W$, $x(0) = 0$, $\phi (t) = f(0,t) + \sigma ^{2}/(2a^{2}) (1 - e^{-a t})^{2}$.
- Inputs needed: the initial curve P(0,T) for all T (interpolate zero rates; f needs a smooth curve), a, $\sigma$.

atoms.title: Hull-White one-factor short-rate model (extended Vasicek): bonds, bond options, caps, Jamshidian swaptions, trinomial tree / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| P(0,T) | today's discount factor to time T (from the given zero / swap curve) | none |
| $f(0,t)$ | instantaneous forward rate $-\mathrm{d}\ln  \operatorname{P}(0,t)/\mathrm{d}t$, continuously compounded | $1/\mathrm{year}$ |
| $a$ | mean-reversion speed (not a rate level) | $1/\mathrm{year}$ |
| $\sigma$ | ABSOLUTE (normal, basis-point) vol of the short rate; 1% = `0.01`. Not a Black/lognormal vol | $1/\sqrt{\mathrm{year}}$ in rate units |
| $t, T, S$ | times in years from today (day count of the curve, often ACT/365) | years |
| $\tau$ | accrual fraction of a coupon / caplet period (day count of the instrument, e.g. ACT/360, 30/360) | years |

atoms.title: Hull-White one-factor short-rate model (extended Vasicek): bonds, bond options, caps, Jamshidian swaptions, trinomial tree / Fitting theta(t) to the curve
atoms.text:
## Fitting theta(t) to the curve

$$
\theta (t) = \mathrm{d}f(0,t)/\mathrm{d}t + a f(0,t) + \sigma ^{2}/(2a) (1 - e^{-2 a t})
$$

$r(0) = f(0,0)$(the instantaneous short rate). In practice nobody needs $\theta$ explicitly: the closed forms below and the tree
calibration ($\alpha _{i}$) use P(0,T) directly.

atoms.title: Hull-White one-factor short-rate model (extended Vasicek): bonds, bond options, caps, Jamshidian swaptions, trinomial tree / Zero-coupon bond P(t,T) = A(t,T) exp(-B(t,T) r(t))
atoms.text:
## Zero-coupon bond P(t,T) = A(t,T) exp(-B(t,T) r(t))
The bond loading uses $a$ only, never $\sigma$:

$$
B(t,T) = (1 - e^{-a (T - t)}) / a
$$

$$
\ln  A(t,T) = \ln ( \operatorname{P}(0,T) / \operatorname{P}(0,t) ) + B(t,T) f(0,t) - \sigma ^{2}/(4a) (1 - e^{-2 a t}) B(t,T)^{2}
$$

Here r(t) is the INSTANTANEOUS short rate. If the state is instead the $\Delta t$ period rate R (continuously compounded over
$[t,t+\Delta t]$, which is what the tree node rate is), use $\operatorname{P}(t,T) = \mathrm{Ahat} \exp (-\mathrm{Bhat} R)$ with

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{Bhat} = B(t,T) \Delta  t / B(t,t+\Delta  t) \\
\ln  \mathrm{Ahat} = \ln (\operatorname{P}(0,T)/\operatorname{P}(0,t)) - [B(t,T)/B(t,t+\Delta  t)] \ln (\operatorname{P}(0,t+\Delta  t)/\operatorname{P}(0,t)) - \sigma ^{2}/(4a) (1 - e^{-2 a t}) B(t,T) (B(t,T) - B(t,t+\Delta  t))
\end{gathered}
$$

atoms.title: Hull-White one-factor short-rate model (extended Vasicek): bonds, bond options, caps, Jamshidian swaptions, trinomial tree / European option on a zero-coupon bond (option expiry T, bond maturity S > T, strike K per unit face, face L)
atoms.text:
## European option on a zero-coupon bond (option expiry T, bond maturity S > T, strike K per unit face, face L)
Total standard deviation of $\ln  \operatorname{P}(T,S)$, not annualized:

$$
\sigma _{\operatorname{P}} = (\sigma  / a) (1 - e^{-a (S - T)}) \sqrt{(1 - e^{-2 a T}) / (2a)}
$$

$$
h = (1 / \sigma _{\operatorname{P}}) \ln ( \operatorname{P}(0,S) / (K \operatorname{P}(0,T)) ) + \sigma _{\operatorname{P}} / 2
$$

$$
\;\text{Call}\; = L [\operatorname{P}(0,S) N(h) - K \operatorname{P}(0,T) N(h - \sigma _{\operatorname{P}})]
$$

$$
\;\text{Put}\; = L [K \operatorname{P}(0,T) N(-h + \sigma _{\operatorname{P}}) - \operatorname{P}(0,S) N(-h)]
$$

$K$ is the price per unit face, not a rate; the total strike payment is $LK$. Parity is $\mathrm{Call}-\mathrm{Put}=L[\operatorname{P}(0,S)-K\operatorname{P}(0,T)]$.

atoms.title: Hull-White one-factor short-rate model (extended Vasicek): bonds, bond options, caps, Jamshidian swaptions, trinomial tree / Caplets / floorlets (reset t_k, payment t_{k+1}, accrual tau, cap rate X, notional N, simple forward rate)
atoms.text:
## Caplets / floorlets (reset t_k, payment t_{k+1}, accrual tau, cap rate X, notional N, simple forward rate)
A caplet paying $N \tau  \max (R - X, 0)$ at $t_{k+1}$ equals $N (1 + X \tau )$ European PUTS expiring $t_{k}$ on the zero maturing $t_{k+1}$ (each option has unit face, $L=1$)
with strike $K = 1 / (1 + X \tau )$. A floorlet is the same number of CALLS. A cap (floor) value is the sum over its caplets (floorlets)
(the first period whose rate is already fixed is usually excluded or valued as a known cash flow; follow the task).

atoms.title: Hull-White one-factor short-rate model (extended Vasicek): bonds, bond options, caps, Jamshidian swaptions, trinomial tree / Caplets / Code for the bond option and the caplet
atoms.text:
### Code for the bond option and the caplet

Name arguments by role (option expiry, bond maturity), not by letter. The option formula uses today's discount
factors to both dates; A(t,T) and B(t,T) belong to the bond price at a future date and do not enter h. Put-call parity
holds for any h, so it cannot test h; the at-the-money and zero-volatility limits can.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

def zcb_put(a, sigma, T, S, K, P):                     # option expiry T, bond maturity S, strike K per unit face
    sp = sigma / a * (1 - np.exp(-a * (S - T))) * np.sqrt((1 - np.exp(-2 * a * T)) / (2 * a))
    h = np.log(P(S) / (K * P(T))) / sp + sp / 2          # today's discount factors only, never A(T, S)
    return K * P(T) * norm.cdf(-h + sp) - P(S) * norm.cdf(-h), sp

def caplet(a, sigma, t_reset, t_pay, X, tau, P):       # N = 1; calibrate on (model - market) * 1e4, not raw prices
    K = 1 / (1 + X * tau)
    return (1 + X * tau) * zcb_put(a, sigma, t_reset, t_pay, K, P)[0]

def check_caplet_pricer(a, sigma, t_reset, t_pay, tau, P, price=caplet):
    X_atm = (P(t_reset) / P(t_pay) - 1) / tau          # forward rate: strike bond price = forward bond price
    sp = sigma / a * (1 - np.exp(-a * (t_pay - t_reset))) * np.sqrt((1 - np.exp(-2 * a * t_reset)) / (2 * a))
    approx = P(t_pay) * (2 * norm.cdf(sp / 2) - 1) * (1 + X_atm * tau)   # at the money h = sp/2 exactly
    assert np.isclose(price(a, sigma, t_reset, t_pay, X_atm, tau, P), approx, rtol=1e-8)
    deep = price(a, 1e-6, t_reset, t_pay, X_atm - 0.01, tau, P)         # near-zero vol: intrinsic value
    assert np.isclose(deep, P(t_pay) * tau * 0.01, rtol=1e-3)
```

atoms.title: Hull-White one-factor short-rate model (extended Vasicek): bonds, bond options, caps, Jamshidian swaptions, trinomial tree / European swaption: Jamshidian (1989) decomposition
atoms.text:
## European swaption: Jamshidian (1989) decomposition
Swap starts at option expiry T, fixed payment dates $t_{1}$..$t_{n}$, accruals $\tau _{i}$, fixed rate X, notional N.
Coupons $c_{i} = X \tau _{i}$ for $i < n$ and $c_{n} = 1 + X \tau _{n}$ (per unit notional).
1. Solve for $r^{*}$ (1-D root, monotone in r; use a bracketed solver): $\sum _{i} c_{i} A(T,t_{i}) \exp (-B(T,t_{i}) r^{*}) = 1$.
2. Strikes $K_{i} = A(T,t_{i}) \exp (-B(T,t_{i}) r^{*})$ (bond prices at T when r(T) = $r^{*}$).
3. Receiver swaption (right to receive fixed) = call on the coupon bond with strike 1:
   $N \sum _{i} c_{i} \;\text{Call}\;(T, t_{i}, K_{i})$. Payer swaption (right to pay fixed) = put: $N \sum _{i} c_{i} \;\text{Put}\;(T, t_{i}, K_{i})$.
The standard decomposition requires a common monotone exercise region. Nonnegative coupon weights $c_i$, with at least one positive weight and positive bond loadings, provide this condition. Signed coupons can destroy monotonicity or produce multiple roots; a root alone does not justify decomposition into bond options. These formulas also assume the stated single-curve swap representation, settlement and per-unit-face strikes; a multi-curve or cash-settled swaption can require a different payoff. The one-factor argument does not extend directly to two factors.

atoms.title: Hull-White one-factor short-rate model (extended Vasicek): bonds, bond options, caps, Jamshidian swaptions, trinomial tree / Trinomial tree (Hull-White 1994) for Bermudan / Swap and swaption values on the tree (1)
atoms.text:
### Swap and swaption values on the tree

The value at time T0 of a payer swap (pay fixed X, receive floating) per unit notional is the floating leg, worth 1 at a reset date, minus the coupon bond:

```
payer(T0) = 1 - sum_i c_i P(T0, t_i),   c_i = X tau_i (i < n),   c_n = 1 + X tau_n
          = 1 - P(T0, t_n) - X sum_i tau_i P(T0, t_i)
```

The final principal belongs to the coupon bond; dropping it (writing 1 - X sum tau P) gives values near 1 instead of a few percent. A receiver swap is the negative. At a later exercise date t_k only payments strictly after t_k remain in the sum.

Array skeleton (Hull-White 1994 geometry with textbook M = -a dt; the edge rows use the up- and down-branching probabilities above). Bond prices at a node come from rolling a unit payment back through the tree.

```python
import numpy as np

def hw_tree(a, sigma, dt, n_steps, P0):                 # P0(t): market discount factor at time t
    M = -a * dt; dx = sigma * np.sqrt(3 * dt)
    jmax = max(1, int(np.ceil(0.184 / (a * dt))))
    j = np.arange(-jmax, jmax + 1); m = j * M
    prob = np.stack([1/6 + (m*m + m)/2, 2/3 - m*m, 1/6 + (m*m - m)/2], 1)
    tgt = np.stack([j + 1, j, j - 1], 1) + jmax         # target rows: up, middle, down
    lo, hi = 0, 2 * jmax
    prob[lo] = [1/6 + (m[lo]**2 - m[lo])/2, -1/3 - m[lo]**2 + 2*m[lo], 7/6 + (m[lo]**2 - 3*m[lo])/2]
    tgt[lo] = [lo + 2, lo + 1, lo]                      # up branching at the bottom
    prob[hi] = [7/6 + (m[hi]**2 + 3*m[hi])/2, -1/3 - m[hi]**2 - 2*m[hi], 1/6 + (m[hi]**2 + m[hi])/2]
    tgt[hi] = [hi, hi - 1, hi - 2]                      # down branching at the top
    Q = np.zeros((n_steps + 1, j.size)); Q[0, jmax] = 1.0
    alpha = np.zeros(n_steps + 1)
    for n in range(n_steps + 1):
        alpha[n] = (np.log(np.sum(Q[n] * np.exp(-j * dx * dt))) - np.log(P0((n + 1) * dt))) / dt
        if n < n_steps:
            w = Q[n] * np.exp(-(alpha[n] + j * dx) * dt)
            np.add.at(Q[n + 1], tgt.ravel(), (w[:, None] * prob).ravel())
    return dict(j=j, dx=dx, dt=dt, alpha=alpha, Q=Q, prob=prob, tgt=tgt, jmax=jmax)

def step_back(tr, n, v_next):                           # values at step n from values at step n + 1
    r = tr['alpha'][n] + tr['j'] * tr['dx']
    return np.exp(-r * tr['dt']) * np.sum(tr['prob'] * v_next[tr['tgt']], 1)

def zcb_at(tr, n_from, n_to):                           # P(t_from, t_to) at every node of step n_from
    v = np.ones(tr['j'].size)
    for n in range(n_to - 1, n_from - 1, -1):
        v = step_back(tr, n, v)
    return v

def payer_swaption_tree(tr, n0, n_pay, c, exercise_steps=None):
    ex = [n0] if exercise_steps is None else sorted(exercise_steps)   # European if only n0
    bonds = {(ne, i): zcb_at(tr, ne, ni) for ne in ex for i, ni in enumerate(n_pay) if ni > ne}
    v = np.zeros(tr['j'].size)
    for n in range(max(ex), -1, -1):
        if n < max(ex):
            v = step_back(tr, n, v)
        if n in ex:
            cb = sum(c[i] * bonds[(n, i)] for i, ni in enumerate(n_pay) if ni > n)
            v = np.maximum(v, np.maximum(1.0 - cb, 0.0))
    return v[tr['jmax']]

def bermudan_payer_tree(tr, n_ex, n_pay, c):            # price and exercise boundary, one entry per exercise step
    v = np.zeros(tr['j'].size); boundary = []
    for n in range(max(n_ex), -1, -1):
        if n < max(n_ex):
            v = step_back(tr, n, v)                     # continuation value at step n
        if n in n_ex:
            cb = sum(ci * zcb_at(tr, n, ni) for ci, ni in zip(c, n_pay) if ni > n)   # payments strictly after t_n
            exercise = np.maximum(1.0 - cb, 0.0)
            hit = (exercise > 0) & (exercise >= v)      # both zero deep out of the money: not an exercise node
            j_low = int(tr['j'][hit].min()) if hit.any() else None                  # lowest-rate exercise node
            rate = None if j_low is None else tr['alpha'][n] + j_low * tr['dx']
            boundary.append((n * tr['dt'], j_low, rate))  # time from today (not from expiry), node, short rate
            v = np.maximum(v, exercise)
    return v[tr['jmax']], boundary[::-1]                # boundary in date order
```

atoms.title: Hull-White one-factor short-rate model (extended Vasicek): bonds, bond options, caps, Jamshidian swaptions, trinomial tree / Trinomial tree (Hull-White 1994) for Bermudan / Swap and swaption values on the tree (2)
atoms.text:
Checks, in this order:

```python
tr = hw_tree(a, sigma, dt, n_steps, P0)
assert all(abs(tr['Q'][n].sum() - P0(n * dt)) < 1e-10 for n in range(n_steps + 1))
x = tr['j'] * tr['dx']; xt = x[tr['tgt']]                       # x at the three targets of every row
mean = (tr['prob'] * xt).sum(1); var = (tr['prob'] * xt**2).sum(1) - mean**2
assert tr['tgt'].min() >= 0 and tr['tgt'].max() == 2 * tr['jmax']
assert np.allclose(mean, x * (1 - a * dt), atol=1e-12)          # E[x_next] = x + M x on every row, edges included
assert np.allclose(var, sigma**2 * dt, rtol=1e-9)               # Var[x_next] = dx**2 / 3 = sigma**2 dt
swap0 = tr['Q'][n0] @ (1.0 - sum(ci * zcb_at(tr, n0, ni) for ci, ni in zip(c, n_pay)))
assert abs(swap0 - (P0(n0 * dt) - sum(ci * P0(ni * dt) for ci, ni in zip(c, n_pay)))) < 1e-10
eur = payer_swaption_tree(tr, n0, n_pay, c)
assert abs(eur - jamshidian_payer) * 1e4 < 5                   # a few bp of discretisation error
n_ex = [n0] + list(n_pay[:-1])                                  # expiry first, then every coupon date but the last payment
assert n_ex[0] == n0 and len(n_ex) == len(n_pay)                # one exercise date per coupon period, expiry included
ber, boundary = bermudan_payer_tree(tr, n_ex, n_pay, c)
assert abs(ber - payer_swaption_tree(tr, n0, n_pay, c, exercise_steps=n_ex)) < 1e-12 and ber >= eur - 1e-12
assert len(boundary) == len(n_ex) and all(j is not None and r > 0 for _, j, r in boundary)   # check, then inspect any failure
```

The swap check needs no option: the state-price-weighted swap value at T0 equals the time-zero forward swap value, which is zero at the at-the-money rate. The curve check and the swap check hold for any branch wiring, because alpha is refitted to the curve at every step; only the moment check tests where each row's three branches land. Read the failures in order: a moment-check failure is in the branch targets or probabilities (a target written as j instead of the row index j + jmax sends negative rows to the far end of the array); a swap-check failure is in the bond values or the swap formula; a swaption far from the closed form with all three checks passing is in the payoff or the exercise dates.

Sources: Hull & White (1994), Numerical procedures for implementing term structure models I, J. Derivatives 2(1):7-16 (tree, branching, Arrow-Debreu fitting); Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, 9th ed., ch. 31 (short-rate trees, Bermudan swaptions); Brigo & Mercurio (2006), Interest Rate Models, 2nd ed., sec. 3.3 (Jamshidian swaption in Hull-White) and sec. 1.5 (swap as coupon bond); NumPy reference for numpy.add.at.

atoms.title: Hull-White one-factor short-rate model (extended Vasicek): bonds, bond options, caps, Jamshidian swaptions, trinomial tree / Common mistakes
atoms.text:
## Common mistakes
- $\sigma$ is the normal vol of r; $\sigma _{\operatorname{P}}$ is the vol of the bond price over the option life. Do not plug a Black cap / swaption
  vol in as $\sigma$, and do not annualize $\sigma _{\operatorname{P}}$ again (it already contains the time to expiry).
- B uses a, not $\sigma ; a \to  0$ gives $B = T - t$ and $\sigma _{\operatorname{P}} = \sigma  (S - T) \sqrt{T}$(Ho-Lee limit). Never divide by $a = 0$.
- Using the tree's $\Delta$ t rate R in the instantaneous A/B formula (use Ahat/Bhat), or a zero rate instead of f(0,t) in $\ln  A$.
- In Jamshidian, forgetting the notional in the last coupon, or calling payer = call (payer is a PUT on the coupon bond).
- Caplet: strike is 1/(1+X $\tau$) and the option count is (1+X $\tau$); option expiry is the reset date, bond maturity the payment date.
- Tree: choose $\Delta$ t so every exercise / reset / payment date sits on a node; time 0 is step 0, so n steps span n $\Delta$ t;
  calibrating $\alpha _{i}$ needs P(0,(i+1)$\Delta$ t), i.e. the curve must extend one step past the last node used.
- Mixing day counts: model time uses the curve's year fraction; $\tau$ uses the instrument's accrual convention.

atoms.title: Hull-White one-factor short-rate model (extended Vasicek): bonds, bond options, caps, Jamshidian swaptions, trinomial tree / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- European ZCB options, caps/floors and swaptions have exact closed forms in this model; the tree is for early exercise
  (Bermudan swaptions, callable / putable bonds, American bond options) and converges to the closed forms as $\Delta  t \to  0$.
- One factor: instantaneous diffusion shocks to rates driven by this factor are collinear; this does not imply unit sample correlation of all yield levels; constant a, $\sigma$ cannot fit a whole cap / swaption vol surface or a smile.
  Calibrate a, $\sigma$ to a few instruments the task names; a time-dependent $\sigma$(t) changes the formulas (not covered here).
- Gaussian rates can go negative; that is a model feature, not a bug.

atoms.title: Hull-White one-factor short-rate model (extended Vasicek): bonds, bond options, caps, Jamshidian swaptions, trinomial tree / Sources
Hull-White one-factor short-rate model (extended Vasicek): bonds, bond options, caps, Jamshidian swaptions, trinomial tree / Implementation checks (read before coding)
atoms.text:
## Implementation checks (read before coding)

Curve: add the point (0, 1) to the discount-curve interpolant (internal only) before using the closed forms, and take the instantaneous forward from the same interpolant (log-linear discount factors give piecewise-flat forwards). The model bond price at time zero, with the short rate at the time-zero forward, then reproduces every market discount factor exactly for any mean reversion and volatility. A residual in that check is a curve-construction error, not a parameter effect; a constant relative error at every maturity points at a curve whose value at time zero is not one. The point (0, 1) is not a market quote: a curve table written as an output keeps the input maturities as its rows, in their order, so build that table from the input rows, not from the interpolant's knots.

Jamshidian's critical rate: the coupon-bond value is strictly decreasing in the short rate, so bracket the rate wide (for example from −100 % to +100 %), check that the two ends give opposite signs, and solve with a bracketing routine that has an iteration cap (`scipy.optimize.brentq` with `maxiter`, or a fixed count of about sixty halvings). Never loop until a residual or an interval width falls below a tolerance without a cap: once the width reaches the floating-point spacing of the rate the interval stops shrinking, and a mis-signed update never reaches the tolerance. Bound any per-step drift solve in a tree the same way; the Arrow–Debreu shift has a closed form and needs no iteration.

An exercise boundary marks nodes where the exercise value is positive and at least the continuation value; where both are zero (deep out of the money) the node is not an exercise node, so a test written as `exercise >= continuation` alone marks the whole bottom of the tree.

Value and payoff arrays on the tree hold floats: create them with `np.zeros(n_nodes)`, not `np.zeros_like(j)` when `j` is the integer node-index array, which keeps the integer dtype and truncates every assigned price to 0. For a co-terminal Bermudan swaption the exercise schedule begins at the option expiry (index zero) and ends one coupon period before the final payment.

Trinomial tree as arrays: per node one probability triple and one triple of target indices (edge rows use their up- or down-branching targets). Each forward Arrow–Debreu step adds the origin-discounted mass into the targets with an indexed add (`np.add.at`); each backward step is the discount at the origin node times a probability-weighted gather; at an exercise date value all nodes against all remaining coupon dates in one broadcast. A full set of builds and repricings then takes milliseconds, so a cell that runs for minutes has an unterminated loop, not a large tree.

A DV01 or other bump revaluation holds the contract's fixed strike; re-striking at the bumped at-the-money rate measures a different instrument.

atoms.title: Hull-White one-factor short-rate model (extended Vasicek): bonds, bond options, caps, Jamshidian swaptions, trinomial tree / Tolerance for a tree-versus-analytical consistency flag
atoms.text:
## Tolerance for a tree-versus-analytical consistency flag

When the task asks for a flag saying the tree agrees with the analytical price but gives no tolerance, measure the tree's own discretisation error instead of picking a round number: price the same instrument with N, 2N (and, if cheap, N/2) time steps; the change between successive refinements estimates the remaining error of the finest tree. Set the tolerance to a small multiple of that estimate (state the multiple), compare the analytical-minus-tree gap with it, and record the step counts and the estimate next to the flag. A gap that keeps shrinking as N grows is discretisation, not a bug; a gap that does not shrink points to a mismatch in the payoff, the exercise dates or the discounting.

```python
prices = {n: tree_price(n) for n in (n_steps // 2, n_steps, 2 * n_steps)}
err_est = abs(prices[2 * n_steps] - prices[n_steps])          # remaining error of the finer tree, roughly
tol = 3 * max(err_est, abs(prices[n_steps] - prices[n_steps // 2]) / 2)
ok = abs(analytical - prices[2 * n_steps]) <= tol
print(prices, err_est, tol, ok)
```

atoms.title: Hull-White one-factor short-rate model (extended Vasicek): bonds, bond options, caps, Jamshidian swaptions, trinomial tree / Trinomial tree (Hull-White 1994) for Bermudan / American exercise
atoms.text:
## Trinomial tree (Hull-White 1994) for Bermudan / American exercise
Stage 1, tree for $x (\mathrm{d}x = -a x \mathrm{d}t + \sigma  \mathrm{d}W, x(0)=0)$, time step $\Delta$ t:
- $M = -a \Delta  t$, $V = \sigma ^{2} \Delta  t$ (textbook) or exact $M = e^{-a \Delta  t} - 1$, $V = \sigma ^{2} (1 - e^{-2a \Delta  t})/(2a)$.
- Spacing $\Delta  x = \sqrt{3 V}$; node (i,j) has $x = j \Delta  x$; $j_{\mathrm{max}}$ = smallest integer > $0.184 / (-M)$ (equal to $0.184/(a\Delta t)$ only for the textbook $M=-a\Delta t$).
- With $m = j M$ the probabilities (up, middle, down) are:
  - normal branching (to j+1, j, j-1), |j| < $j_{\mathrm{max}}$: $\mathrm{pu} = 1/6 + (m^{2} + m)/2$, $\mathrm{pm} = 2/3 - m^{2}$, $\mathrm{pd} = 1/6 + (m^{2} - m)/2$
  - up branching at $j = -j_{\mathrm{max}}$(to j+2, j+1, j): $\mathrm{pu} = 1/6 + (m^{2} - m)/2$, $\mathrm{pm} = -1/3 - m^{2} + 2m$, $\mathrm{pd} = 7/6 + (m^{2} - 3m)/2$
  - down branching at $j = +j_{\mathrm{max}}$(to j, j-1, j-2): $\mathrm{pu} = 7/6 + (m^{2} + 3m)/2$, $\mathrm{pm} = -1/3 - m^{2} - 2m$, $\mathrm{pd} = 1/6 + (m^{2} + m)/2$
Stage 2, shift to fit the curve with Arrow-Debreu prices $Q_{i,j} (Q_{0,0} = 1)$; node rate $R_{i,j} = \alpha _{i} + j \Delta  x$:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\alpha _{i}     = [ \ln ( \sum _{j} Q_{i,j} e^{-j \Delta  x \Delta  t} ) - \ln  \operatorname{P}(0, (i+1) \Delta  t) ] / \Delta  t \\
Q_{i+1,k}   = \sum _{j} Q_{i,j} q(j,k) \exp ( -(\alpha _{i} + j \Delta  x) \Delta  t )
\end{gathered}
$$

Check: $\sum _{j} Q_{i,j} = \operatorname{P}(0, i \Delta  t)$ for every i. Value by backward induction, discounting each step with
$\exp ( -R_{i,j} \Delta  t )$; at exercise dates take $\max ( \mathrm{continuation}, \mathrm{exercise} \mathrm{value} )$. An exercise node needs a positive exercise value at least equal to continuation; nodes where both are zero are not exercise nodes, so the boundary is the lowest node of that set, and its short rate sits where exercise first pays. Exercise values of bonds / swaps at a node
can come from rolling bonds back in the tree or from the Ahat/Bhat formula with the node's R.

The environment has NumPy 2.5.3, pandas 3.0.5, SciPy 1.18.1, statsmodels 0.15.0, arch 8.0.0, scikit-learn 1.9.0, Polars 1.44.1, TA-Lib 0.7.1, Backtrader 1.9.78.123, openpyxl 3.1.5, PyArrow 25.0.1, Matplotlib 3.11.1, Seaborn 0.13.2, Plotly 7.0.0, and Python 3.13.15 installed.
Use only APIs verified for these installed versions, following any task-specific construction or function restrictions. The reference entries attached to the first message contain version-specific usage; error hints supply verified replacements when an API fails.
Numba: some task environments may additionally provide it.
Some APIs from older versions have been removed or replaced. Examples (old -> current):
  np.trapz(y, x)                          -> np.trapezoid(y, x)
  from scipy.integrate import trapz       -> from scipy.integrate import trapezoid
  np.math.<function>(...)                 -> math.<function>(...)
  df.resample('M').last()                 -> df.resample('ME').last()   (likewise 'Q' -> 'QE', 'Y' -> 'YE')
  pd.date_range(start, periods=n, freq='H') -> pd.date_range(start, periods=n, freq='h')   ('T' -> 'min', 'S' -> 's')
  df.fillna(method='ffill')               -> df.ffill()
  pd.to_numeric(x, errors='ignore')       -> pd.to_numeric(x, errors='coerce'), then keep the original where the result is NaN
Period operations such as df.to_period('M') still use 'M'.
np.zeros_like, np.ones_like, np.full_like and np.empty_like keep the dtype of their argument: on an integer array
np.full_like(a, 0.01) is all zeros. Pass dtype=float when the values are not integers.
Arithmetic between two DataFrames aligns on column labels: subtracting same-shaped blocks with different column names
gives all-NaN columns. Use .to_numpy() or per-column Series, and keep the input columns the task instructions name.
After resample, sum() and count() give 0 for an empty bin while first/last/min/max give NaN: find empty bins from a
price column or the count, not from a zero-or-NaN sum. In this session sort_values (DataFrame and Series) sorts
stably by default, so rows that tie on the sort key keep their file order.
On trading-day data the first session of each month is dates.groupby(dates.dt.to_period('M')).min(); dt.is_month_start
is true only on calendar day 1 and misses months that begin on a weekend or holiday.
bool is a subclass of int (isinstance(True, int) is True): a converter that tests for int before bool writes 1 for True;
test bool first, or use save_json.
Keep pd and np for pandas and numpy: name a probability of default p_default, never pd.
A boolean mask built from a sorted copy selects from that sorted copy only; apply it to the unsorted array and it picks other rows.
Keep working columns in the working table and write a deliverable table from its own column list: out = work.loc[:, columns].

atoms.title: Implied Volatility: Named Approximations and Black–Scholes Inversion
atoms.text:
Map task quantities to these definitions by meaning and units, not by letter, before the first calculation; recheck when inputs or conventions change.

Use this reference when recovering Black–Scholes or Black-76 volatility from a European option price, comparing named explicit estimators, or checking an implied-volatility solver. It provides price normalization, forward-ATM formulas, the Li quadratic and combined approximations, separate Corrado–Miller and Hallerbach estimators, and numerical inversion checks. It does not price American exercise, identify a local-volatility surface, or supply Minqiang Li's rational approximation. Match the requested formula variant before calculating; a numerical inverse is not a replacement for a named approximation.

atoms.title: Implied Volatility: Named Approximations and Black–Scholes Inversion / 1. Inputs and normalization
atoms.text:
## 1. Inputs and normalization

Use positive spot S, strike K and expiry T. T is in years; r and q are continuously compounded rates in decimals; $\sigma$ is annualized volatility in decimals. C and P are prices per unit of underlying, not position totals. $\Phi$ and $\phi$ denote the standard normal CDF and density; $\Phi _{\mathrm{inv}}$ denotes the inverse CDF.

For constant rates and a continuous yield:

**Discounted stock and strike inputs**

$$
\begin{gathered}
A = S\cdot \exp (-q\cdot T) \\
B = K\cdot \exp (-r\cdot T)
\end{gathered}
$$

**Normalize volatility, strike and option price**

$$
\begin{gathered}
x = \sigma \cdot \sqrt{T} \\
\eta  = B/A \\
c = C/A
\end{gathered}
$$

**Black–Scholes pricing thresholds**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{d1} = \log (A/B)/x + x/2 \\
\mathrm{d2} = \mathrm{d1} - x
\end{gathered}
$$

**Black–Scholes call price**

$$
C_{\mathrm{BS}} = A\cdot \Phi (\mathrm{d1}) - B\cdot \Phi (\mathrm{d2})
$$

**Black–Scholes put price**

$$
\operatorname{P}_{\mathrm{BS}} = B\cdot \Phi (-\mathrm{d2}) - A\cdot \Phi (-\mathrm{d1})
$$

**Vega for numerical inversion**

$$
\mathrm{vega} = A\cdot \phi (\mathrm{d1})\cdot \sqrt{T}
$$

A and B are discounted price quantities; x is total volatility, not annualized volatility and not variance. For Black-76 use A = discount*F and B = discount*K with the appropriate forward F. Deterministic discount/carry curves can likewise be represented by A = discount*F. For FX, q is the foreign rate. Subtracting known cash dividends from spot is an additional model approximation, not an exact treatment of discrete stock-price jumps.

Forward ATM means $A = B$. Spot ATM means $S = K$; these differ when carry is nonzero. If a task explicitly requests evaluation on a spot-ATM subset, preserve that subset but do not call the forward-ATM derivation exact there.

**Convert a put price into its parity-equivalent call price**

$$
C = \operatorname{P} + A - B
$$

For numerical inversion near intrinsic value, directly price the out-of-the-money option when possible; subtraction of large terms can destroy its small time value. Conversion does not change the volatility, but changing a named approximation's normalization or call/put convention can change its approximation error.

atoms.title: Implied Volatility: Named Approximations and Black–Scholes Inversion / 3. Forward-ATM calculations
atoms.text:
## 3. Forward-ATM calculations

Use this block when $A = B$ and the relevant ATM method is requested. When a task applies an ATM method at spot $\mathrm{ATM} (K = S)$, keep the same normalization $c = C/A$ for Brenner–Subrahmanyam and Li ATM: divide by the dividend-discounted underlying A, never by the undiscounted spot. An exact identity provides a separate check:

**Exact forward-ATM volatility inversion**

$$
\begin{gathered}
c = 2\cdot \Phi (x/2) - 1 \\
x_{\mathrm{exact}} = 2\cdot \Phi _{\mathrm{inv}}((1+c)/2) \\
\sigma _{\mathrm{exact}} = x_{\mathrm{exact}}/\sqrt{T}
\end{gathered}
$$

This holds for $0 \le  c < 1$. At $c = 1$ only the infinite-volatility limit exists. For very small c or c near 1, use numerically stable inverse-distribution routines.

Brenner–Subrahmanyam uses the first-order normal expansion:

**Brenner–Subrahmanyam first-order ATM approximation**

The normalizing underlying is dividend-discounted, not the undiscounted spot $S$:

$$
A = S\cdot \exp (-q\cdot T)
$$

$$
c = C/A
$$

$$
\alpha  = \sqrt{2\cdot \pi}\cdot c
$$

$$
x_{\mathrm{BS},\mathrm{approx}} = \alpha
$$

$$
\sigma _{\mathrm{BS},\mathrm{approx}} = \alpha /\sqrt{T}
$$

Li's ATM cubic keeps the next nonzero term. Select the root continuously approaching zero as $\alpha$ approaches zero:

**Li ATM cubic and its selected small-root solution**

$$
\begin{gathered}
x - x^{3}/24 = \alpha \\
u = 3\cdot \alpha /\sqrt{32} \\
z = \cos (\arccos (u)/3) \\
x_{\mathrm{Li},\mathrm{ATM}} = 2\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot z - \sqrt{8\cdot z^{2} - 6\cdot \alpha /(\sqrt{2}\cdot z)} \\
\sigma _{\mathrm{Li},\mathrm{ATM}} = x_{\mathrm{Li},\mathrm{ATM}}/\sqrt{T}
\end{gathered}
$$

Its nonnegative small-root branch requires $0 \le  \alpha  \le  4\cdot \sqrt{2}/3$. The upper endpoint is a repeated root and is poorly conditioned. An algebraically equivalent, less cancellation-prone form is:

**Equivalent sine form of the Li ATM root**

$$
x_{\mathrm{Li},\mathrm{ATM}} = 4\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sin (\arcsin (u)/3)
$$

Preserve the trigonometric form if explicitly prescribed. Check the inverse-trigonometric argument before evaluation; outside its real domain report the approximation as unavailable, not as a zero volatility. This is exact for the displayed cubic, not for Black–Scholes. It is distinct from the inverse-normal identity above.

atoms.title: Implied Volatility: Named Approximations and Black–Scholes Inversion / 4. Li quadratic and combined approximations
atoms.text:
## 4. Li quadratic and combined approximations

The blocks below give the quadratic in Steven Li (2003), equations (13)–(15). It is one branch, not the full combined estimator. Li (2003) uses S for the non-dividend-paying stock and K for the discounted strike; in this entry these correspond to A and B. Thus discounted stock and strike quantities sometimes written $\tilde{S}$ and $\tilde{K}$ mean A and B, respectively; $\eta$ is always B/A. The quadratic expansion is intended for total volatility small relative to $\sqrt{\mathrm{abs}( \eta -1)}$; it is not uniformly accurate across moneyness.

**Li (2003) quadratic coefficients, root and annualization**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\tilde{\alpha} = \sqrt{2\cdot \pi}\cdot (2\cdot c + \eta  - 1)/(1+\eta ) \\
b_{\mathrm{Li}} = (\eta -1)^{2}/(1+\eta ) \\
\mathrm{disc}_{\mathrm{Li}} = \tilde{\alpha}^{2} - 4\cdot b_{\mathrm{Li}} \\
x_{\mathrm{Li},\mathrm{quadratic}} = (\tilde{\alpha} + \sqrt{\mathrm{disc}_{\mathrm{Li}}})/2 \\
\sigma _{\mathrm{Li},\mathrm{quadratic}} = x_{\mathrm{Li},\mathrm{quadratic}}/\sqrt{T}
\end{gathered}
$$

At $\eta  = 1$ it reduces to Brenner–Subrahmanyam, not Li ATM. Require a nonnegative discriminant; a material negative value is outside this approximation's real domain. This failure of the approximation does not imply that the observed price has no Black–Scholes implied volatility. A real result still need not be accurate. Do not replace a failed value with Corrado–Miller or Newton under the Li label.

atoms.title: Implied Volatility: Named Approximations and Black–Scholes Inversion / 4. Li quadratic and combined approximations / Li (2003): original branch diagnostic
atoms.text:
### Li (2003): original branch diagnostic

The working paper's equation (17) gives a rough numerical diagnostic for choosing between its quadratic (13) and near-ATM cubic (16). For $\eta  \ne  1$:

**Li (2003) total-volatility-to-moneyness diagnostic**

$$
\rho _{2003} = x/\sqrt{\mathrm{abs}(\eta -1)}
$$

Use the quadratic when $\rho _{2003} < 2$ and the near-ATM cubic otherwise. Here x is the unknown total volatility: the paper suggests estimating it approximately with either formula before checking the diagnostic. This is not a directly observable statistic or a uniquely specified fixed-point algorithm. State the provisional estimator when implementing this version. At $\eta  = 1$ use the ATM cubic directly. The near-ATM cubic is the Section 3 root with $\alpha$ replaced by $\tilde{\alpha}$, including its real-domain checks.

atoms.title: Implied Volatility: Named Approximations and Black–Scholes Inversion / 4. Li quadratic and combined approximations / Later combined approximation: select the branch first
atoms.text:
### Later combined approximation: select the branch first

Use this block for the later combined rule attributed to Li (2005) (Orlando and Taglialatela, 2017), rather than the standalone quadratic or the 2003 diagnostic. Unlike $\rho _{2003}$, its statistic depends only on observed prices and moneyness. Use the same call normalization throughout. For a strictly positive call price, define:

**Li combined-method branch statistic and normalized coefficient**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\rho  = \mathrm{abs}(\eta -1)/(c^{2}) \\
\tilde{\alpha} = \sqrt{2\cdot \pi}\cdot (2\cdot c + \eta  - 1)/(1+\eta )
\end{gathered}
$$

When $\rho  \le  1.4$, use the near-ATM cubic branch:

**Near-ATM cubic branch of the combined method**

$$
\begin{gathered}
u_{\mathrm{combined}} = 3\cdot \tilde{\alpha}/\sqrt{32} \\
x_{\mathrm{combined}} = 4\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sin (\arcsin (u_{\mathrm{combined}})/3)
\end{gathered}
$$

Require $0 \le  u_{\mathrm{combined}} \le  1$. Equivalently use the cosine-and-radical expression in Section 3 with $\alpha$ replaced by $\tilde{\alpha}$. When $\rho  > 1.4$, use $x_{\mathrm{Li},\mathrm{quadratic}}$ from the preceding block, including its discriminant check. In either branch:

**Annualize the selected combined-method total volatility**

$$
\sigma _{\mathrm{combined}} = x_{\mathrm{combined}}/\sqrt{T}
$$

For the quadratic branch, $x_{\mathrm{combined}}$ means $x_{\mathrm{Li},\mathrm{quadratic}}$. The threshold chooses an approximation, not an exact inverse; a discontinuity at the switch is possible. At $\eta  = 1$ and $c > 0$ this combined method reduces to Li ATM. At $c = 0, \rho$ is undefined: handle the price boundary as in Section 6 and do not evaluate the ratio. An unavailable selected branch is not permission to silently switch methods. The divisor in $u_{\mathrm{combined}}$ is $\sqrt{32}$, not 32; the cubic residual below checks this transcription.

atoms.title: Implied Volatility: Named Approximations and Black–Scholes Inversion / 5. Corrado–Miller and Hallerbach
Implied Volatility: Named Approximations and Black–Scholes Inversion / 6. Numerical inversion
atoms.text:
## 6. Numerical inversion

Use when an accurate Black–Scholes inverse is required, or as a separately labelled benchmark. For positive A, B and T:

**Admissible Black–Scholes price range and inverse-volatility cases**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{intrinsic}_{\mathrm{call}} = \max (A-B, 0) \\
\mathrm{intrinsic}_{\mathrm{call}} < C < A: \text{unique finite positive} \sigma \\
C = \mathrm{intrinsic}_{\mathrm{call}}: \sigma  = 0 \\
C = A: \text{infinite-volatility limit}, \text{no finite solution} \\
C < \mathrm{intrinsic}_{\mathrm{call}} \;\text{or}\; C > A: \text{no nonnegative Black-Scholes solution}
\end{gathered}
$$

At expiry volatility is not identifiable from the payoff. Do not turn a materially invalid price into a valid one by clipping. Distinguish a price genuinely at intrinsic value from one rounded there.

For plain Newton, honor prescribed starting values, iteration limits and stopping rules:

**Newton residual, update and step size**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{residual}_{n} = C_{\mathrm{BS}}(\sigma _{n}) - C_{\mathrm{observed}} \\
\sigma _{\mathrm{next}} = \sigma _{n} - \mathrm{residual}_{n}/\mathrm{vega}(\sigma _{n}) \\
\mathrm{step}_{n} = \sigma _{\mathrm{next}} - \sigma _{n}
\end{gathered}
$$

The generic inflection-point start is $\sqrt{2\cdot \mathrm{abs}(\log (A/B))/T}$; at $A = B$ use a positive ATM estimate. A task-specified start overrides this suggestion. Tiny vega, a nonpositive iterate or a nonfinite step can defeat unsafeguarded Newton. Record failure rather than silently returning a different algorithm's answer.

For a robust inverse when the algorithm is not prescribed, bracket the price monotonically: lo = 0 and increase a finite hi until its price exceeds the target. Use bisection/Brent, or safeguarded Newton accepting only steps inside the updated bracket. Set a bracket-expansion budget and handle numerical saturation. A hybrid is not plain Newton.

Check residual at the final returned iterate. A small step alone may reflect stagnation. Record the actual stopping reason, iterations, last step and price residual. In a vectorized solver keep a per-contract convergence state; an early unconverged step must not permanently mark a later converged contract as failed. Small vega also makes volatility sensitive to rounding even when the price residual is small.

atoms.title: Implied Volatility: Named Approximations and Black–Scholes Inversion / 7. Numerical checks
atoms.text:
## 7. Numerical checks

Evaluate domains before radicals and inverse trigonometric functions. Follow an explicit task rounding tolerance; otherwise clamp only demonstrable floating-point roundoff, scaled to the radicand's terms. Never take an absolute value to make a negative discriminant positive. An unavailable approximation is distinct from a finite estimate.

Verify annualization exactly once. Scaling A, B and C by the same positive factor must leave every reported volatility unchanged. At forward ATM compare the explicit estimators with the inverse-normal result. For the quadratic in Section 4, check its defining polynomial:

**Polynomial residual for the Li quadratic root**

$$
x_{\mathrm{Li},\mathrm{quadratic}}^{2} - \tilde{\alpha}\cdot x_{\mathrm{Li},\mathrm{quadratic}} + b_{\mathrm{Li}} = 0
$$

For the combined near-ATM branch, the independent algebraic check is:

**Polynomial residual for the combined cubic root**

$$
x_{\mathrm{combined}} - x_{\mathrm{combined}}^{3}/24 - \tilde{\alpha} = 0
$$

Polynomial residual checks transcription and root selection, not approximation accuracy. Reprice each finite estimate through Black–Scholes and compare separately with numerical inversion. Do not force approximation errors to zero or claim one estimator is always best. An all-unavailable set is not zero error. Compare method identity, numerical error and solver convergence separately.

atoms.text:
## 8. References

Corrado, C. J., and Miller, T. W. (1996). A note on a simple, accurate formula to compute implied standard deviations. *Journal of Banking & Finance*, 20(3), 595–603.

Hallerbach, W. G. (2004). An improved estimator for Black-Scholes-Merton implied volatility. ERIM Report Series ERS-2004-054-F&A, Erasmus University Rotterdam.
