Li, S. (2005). A new formula for computing implied volatility. *Applied Mathematics and Computation*, 170(1), 611–625.

Orlando, G., and Taglialatela, G. (2017). A review on implied volatility calculation. *Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics*, 320, 202–220.

Płuciennik, P. (2007). A modified Corrado-Miller implied volatility estimator. *Fasciculi Mathematici*, 38.

atoms.title: Implied Volatility: Named Approximations and Black–Scholes Inversion / 2. Select the calculation
atoms.text:
## 2. Select the calculation

| Requested calculation | Use | Required distinction |
|---|---|---|
| Accurate inverse at arbitrary moneyness | Section 6 | Numerical root, not an explicit estimator |
| Forward-ATM quick estimate | Brenner–Subrahmanyam in Section 3 | First-order approximation |
| Forward-ATM cubic/trigonometric estimate | Li ATM in Section 3 | Small root of a cubic approximation |
| Li (2003) quadratic, equation (13) | Section 4, quadratic block | Not the Corrado–Miller discriminant |
| Li combined estimate | Section 4, switching block | Select by $\rho$; do not use the quadratic everywhere |
| Corrado–Miller adjusted estimator | Section 5, CM | Not Hallerbach's tweaked estimator |
| Hallerbach estimator | Section 5, raw or tweaked as specified | Name the chosen variant |

An explicit task formula takes precedence over a generic reference. A compound author label without a formula needs its published variant identified; author names alone do not define an estimator. Li's quadratic branch and his combined approximation are distinct requests.

atoms.title: Implied Volatility: Named Approximations and Black–Scholes Inversion / 4. Li quadratic and combined approximations / Equivalent price-unit form: Li (2003), equation (15)
atoms.text:
### Equivalent price-unit form: Li (2003), equation (15)

Use this equivalent form of the same quadratic when working directly with A, B and C instead of $\eta$ and c. A and B retain the discounted-input definitions in Section $1; T > 0$ is in years.

**Call price minus half the discounted stock–strike difference**

$$
a_{\mathrm{Li}} = C - (A-B)/2
$$

**Radicand in the price-unit form of Li (2003), equation (15)**

$$
\mathrm{rad}_{\mathrm{Li}} = a_{\mathrm{Li}}^{2} - (A-B)^{2}\cdot (1+B/A)/(2\cdot \pi )
$$

**Annualized volatility from Li (2003), equation (15), in this entry's notation**

$$
\sigma _{\mathrm{Li},\mathrm{eq15}} = \sqrt{2\cdot \pi}/((A+B)\cdot \sqrt{T}) \cdot  (a_{\mathrm{Li}} + \sqrt{\mathrm{rad}_{\mathrm{Li}}})
$$

The factor $1/\sqrt{T}$ annualizes the result exactly once; the ratio B/A is discounted strike divided by discounted stock. Apply the same nonnegative-radicand condition as above. This is algebraically identical to $\sigma _{\mathrm{Li},\mathrm{quadratic}}$, not a different approximation. Corrado–Miller in Section 5 instead subtracts $(A-B)^2/\pi$ inside its radicand; the two formulas must not be interchanged. The Li quadratic also equals Hallerbach raw ($\gamma  = 2$) in Section 5, but not Hallerbach tweaked.

atoms.title: Kelly growth, financing and risk scaling / Shared Foundations
atoms.text:
## Shared Foundations

Map returns, cash financing, units and horizon to the explicit definitions in the task. A stated approximation may deliberately differ from exact log optimization. Identify that distinction rather than labeling every inverse-covariance allocation an exact discrete-time Kelly portfolio.

Let R be the vector of risky simple returns over one period, $r_{f}$ the deterministic cash return, and f the risky fractions of current wealth. The remaining fraction $1-\sum (f)$ earns or pays $r_{f}$ under symmetric borrowing/lending. Short sales and leverage require separate feasibility assumptions.

The financed one-period wealth multiplier is:

$$
G(f) = 1 + r_{f} + f'\cdot (R-r_{f}\cdot 1)
$$

The exact discrete-time growth objective requires a positive wealth multiplier almost surely and a well-defined expectation.

$$
g(f) = \operatorname{E}[\ln (G(f))]
$$

Interior optimality, when differentiation under the expectation is justified, is:

$$
\operatorname{E}[(R-r_{f}\cdot 1)/G(f)] = 0
$$

Constraints can replace this condition with boundary optimality. With an unbounded Gaussian simple-return model, any portfolio with nonzero return variance has a positive probability of $G\le 0$. Its exact positive-wealth log objective therefore cannot be justified by ignoring rare simulated ruin.

atoms.title: Kelly growth, financing and risk scaling / Covariance allocation and its scope
atoms.text:
## Covariance allocation and its scope

For continuous diffusion returns with constant excess drift vector $\mu$ and positive-definite instantaneous covariance $\Sigma$, the expected log-growth rate has the following form, by Ito's formula:

$$
\mathrm{growth}_{\mathrm{rate}}(f) = r_{f} + f'\cdot \mu  - (1/2)\cdot f'\cdot \Sigma \cdot f
$$

The unconstrained continuous-time optimum is:

$$
f_{\mathrm{growth}} = \Sigma ^{-1}\cdot \mu
$$

This same expression is often used as a small-return sizing approximation. The mean and covariance must refer to the same time unit. With singular $\Sigma$, a pseudoinverse is not automatically a finite optimum: a zero-variance direction with nonzero excess drift makes the unconstrained objective unbounded.

For comparison, let $x=R-r_{f}\cdot 1$ and $m=\operatorname{E}[x]$. Expanding discrete log wealth around the cash multiplier gives:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{E}[\ln (G(f))] \approx  \ln (1+r_{f}) + f'\cdot m/(1+r_{f}) \\
- f'\cdot \operatorname{E}[x\cdot x']\cdot f/(2\cdot (1+r_{f})^{2})
\end{gathered}
$$

Its second moment is $\Sigma+mm'$, not $\Sigma$ alone. Dropping the mean outer product is an additional approximation. These expressions should not be silently interchanged when a task specifies one of them.

atoms.title: Kelly growth, financing and risk scaling / References
atoms.text:
## References

[Busseti, Ryu and Boyd (2016), Risk-Constrained Kelly Gambling](https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/papers/pdf/kelly.pdf), Sections 2 and 6: log-growth objective and quadratic approximation using the raw second moment. The financing identity, continuous-diffusion first-order condition and positive-homogeneous VaR scaling above are direct derivations under the stated assumptions; the paper's drawdown-constrained optimization is not the VaR scaling rule given here.

atoms.title: Kelly growth, financing and risk scaling
atoms.text:
Use this reference to distinguish log-optimal allocation from a covariance-based approximation, and to scale a fixed portfolio direction to a risk budget. It does not specify a trading signal, simulation ordering or performance aggregation convention.

**Quick checks before writing:** (1) each path's wealth starts at the initial capital, `W = np.hstack([np.full((n_paths, 1), W0), W0 * np.cumprod(1 + R, axis=1)])`, and drawdown is taken on that series; (2) choose the account model for the wealth not held in the risky fractions (see "Account models" below) and use the same period return for wealth, Sharpe ratio and drawdown; (3) a "var" output next to a VaR limit is value-at-risk, not variance; (4) the estimation window is the last N valid rows after removing invalid ones; a count of valid observations is the number of rows that survive cleaning, not the number inside the window.

atoms.title: Kelly growth, financing and risk scaling / Fractional sizing and a one-period risk limit
atoms.text:
## Fractional sizing and a one-period risk limit

Fractional sizing preserves a chosen risky direction, with c between zero and one:

$$
f_{\mathrm{fractional}} = c\cdot f_{\mathrm{growth}}
$$

For Gaussian excess-return loss $L=-f'\cdot x$ at confidence $\alpha$, let $z_{\alpha}$ be the standard normal quantile. The positive-loss convention gives:

$$
\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(f) = -f'\cdot m + z_{\alpha}\cdot \sqrt{f'\cdot \Sigma \cdot f}
$$

If this VaR is positive and the allowed loss fraction is $B\ge 0$, scaling only down along the same direction gives:

$$
c = \min (1, B/\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(f))
$$

This follows from positive homogeneity for $c\ge 0$; it is not the solution of every constrained Kelly problem. Scaling to the budget exactly, $c=B/\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(f)$, can also lever up; wording such as "comply with" or "not exceed" describes the scale-down rule, wording such as "scale to" or "target" the exact one. A zero-mean (relative) VaR drops the $-f'\cdot m$ term; the task's VaR definition decides whether the mean enters. If the unscaled VaR is nonpositive, division is not a valid rule. Including an unscaled cash return in total loss also changes the scaling equation. Currency risk uses wealth times the fractional loss; the budget must use matching units.

In code, keep the variance, the standard deviation and the value-at-risk under separate names, so that an output called "var" next to a VaR limit receives the value-at-risk:

```python
port_variance = f @ Sigma @ f                 # variance of the one-period portfolio return
sigma_p = np.sqrt(port_variance)              # its standard deviation
z = norm.ppf(level)                           # level: confidence level
var_full = z * sigma_p                        # value-at-risk (zero-mean form); add - f @ m for the mean-adjusted form
assert var_full > port_variance               # a daily VaR is far larger than a daily variance; equality of scale means the names were swapped
scale = min(1.0, var_limit / var_full)        # scale down only
f_var = scale * f
```

atoms.title: Kelly growth, financing and risk scaling / Financed risk scaling and simulated paths
atoms.text:
## Financed risk scaling and simulated paths

The earlier VaR formula measures excess-return loss. If total funded return is $r_f+cf'x$, cash is not scaled down with the risky position. Let $v_{\mathrm{ex}}=-f'm+z_\alpha\sqrt{f'\Sigma f}$; for $c\ge0$, total-return VaR is:

$$
\operatorname{VaR}_{\mathrm{funded}}(c)=-r_f+c\,v_{\mathrm{ex}}
$$

If $v_{\mathrm{ex}}>0$ and $B+r_f\ge0$, the largest admissible scale in $[0,1]$ under this particular VaR constraint is:

$$
c_{\max}=\min\left(1,\frac{B+r_f}{v_{\mathrm{ex}}}\right)
$$

For other signs solve the affine inequality over the stated feasible interval; there can be no feasible scale, or an upper-bound rule may be inappropriate. This differs from scaling an excess-return loss directly by $B/v_{\mathrm{ex}}$. A money budget must first be compared to money VaR at the same wealth. Asymmetric borrowing and lending create a different financing equation.

For fixed fractions and a specified financing convention, wealth on simulated path $j$ compounds its own total funded period returns:

$$
W_{j,t+1}=W_{j,t}\left[1+r_{f,t}+f'(R_{j,t+1}-r_{f,t}\mathbf1)\right]
$$

Under this financed account the scheme's period return is that growth factor minus one, $r_{f,t}+f'(R_{j,t+1}-r_{f,t}\mathbf1)$. Drawing total risky returns and then adding the same risky mean again double-counts drift. Drawing excess returns and omitting an intended cash return changes the account model. Multiplying returns by fractions is rebalanced constant-fraction exposure, not fixed-share buy-and-hold. A negative or zero multiplier requires an explicit insolvency convention; normal simple-return shocks do not guarantee positive wealth.

atoms.title: Kelly growth, financing and risk scaling / Financed risk scaling and simulated paths / Account models
atoms.text:
### Account models

Three period returns are in use for risky fractions f and simple returns R. Weighted sum: $f'R$, the remaining $1-\sum(f)$ earns nothing and borrowing costs nothing. Financed: $r_f+f'(R-r_f\mathbf1)$, the remainder is lent or borrowed at the cash rate. Excess only: $f'(R-r_f\mathbf1)$. When the task describes no cash account or financing rate for the remainder, the weighted sum is the literal reading and a cash leg is an added assumption to state. A Sharpe ratio "without subtracting the risk-free rate" keeps whichever of these returns the account model gives. If the simulation draws excess returns, total asset returns are the draws plus $r_f$; drawing total returns and adding the mean again double-counts drift.

Including initial wealth, the path's positive high-water mark and maximum drawdown are:

$$
H_{j,t}=\max_{0\le u\le t}W_{j,u},\qquad
D_j=\max_t\left(1-\frac{W_{j,t}}{H_{j,t}}\right)
$$

When performance statistics are requested for simulated schemes, compute them from each scheme's own simulated period returns, the same returns that compound its wealth under the chosen account model, unless the task names another input. A plug-in ratio $f'm/\sqrt{f'\Sigma f}$ from the input moments is a model value, not a sample statistic of the paths, and subtracting a cash rate from the numerator changes it again; state which one is reported and keep the same definition for every scheme.

Each path's drawdown is measured on the wealth series that starts at the initial capital, so a loss in the first period counts. In numpy: `W = np.hstack([np.full((n_paths, 1), W0), W0 * np.cumprod(1 + R, axis=1)])`, then `dd = 1 - W / np.maximum.accumulate(W, axis=1)` and `dd.max(axis=1)` per path. A median of terminal wealths and a median of pathwise drawdowns are separate distributional summaries. Neither is obtained by taking drawdown of the median wealth path. Similarly, averaging pathwise Sharpe ratios differs from calculating one ratio after pooling all simulated periods. A stated seed alone does not specify random-stream ordering, covariance factorization or how schemes share shocks; those are reproducibility conventions rather than additional financial identities.

atoms.title: Kelly growth, financing and risk scaling / Checks and Scope
atoms.text:
## Checks and Scope

In a task about value-at-risk limits and scaling, an abbreviation such as "var" in an output name means value-at-risk; report a variance only where the text says variance.


Gross exposure is $\sum ( \mathrm{abs}(f) )$; net exposure is $\sum (f)$. A leveraged long-short portfolio can have small net exposure. Leverage without a qualifier measures the size of the positions regardless of direction, that is gross exposure; a net figure is called net exposure or net leverage. Under fixed fractions and the same financing convention, successive wealth multipliers compound; negative wealth requires an explicit insolvency convention rather than continued interpretation as log growth.

A one-period VaR constraint does not bound maximum drawdown over many periods. Expected terminal wealth, median terminal wealth and average log growth are distinct. Fractional Kelly reduces exposure but does not create a universal drawdown guarantee. Performance statistics averaged over paths can differ from statistics computed from pooled observations.

atoms.title: Spread options: Kirk (1995) approximation and Margrabe (1978) exchange option
atoms.text:
Use this reference to choose and evaluate Margrabe exchange pricing or the Kirk approximation for a European spread option.

Map task quantities to these definitions by meaning and units, not by letter, before the first calculation; recheck when inputs or conventions change.

**If the task text defines the formula, inputs or conventions differently, the task text wins.**

atoms.title: Spread options: Kirk (1995) approximation and Margrabe (1978) exchange option / Payoff and model
atoms.text:
## Payoff and model
- Spread call payoff at expiry T: $\max (\mathrm{F1}(T) - \mathrm{F2}(T) - K, 0)$. Leg 1 is the leg you are long. Put payoff: $\max (K + \mathrm{F2}(T) - \mathrm{F1}(T), 0)$.
- Model: F1, F2 are forward/futures prices that follow correlated driftless geometric Brownian motions
  (Black-76 world): constant lognormal vols sigma1, sigma2, constant correlation $\rho$ of the log returns,
  constant rate, European exercise, no jumps, no smile. Then the spread itself is NOT lognormal, so
  for $K \ne  0$ there is no exact closed form. Kirk is an approximation; Margrabe ($K = 0$) is exact in this model.

atoms.title: Spread options: Kirk (1995) approximation and Margrabe (1978) exchange option / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| F1, F2 | forward or futures prices of the two legs for delivery at (or after) T | price units |
| $K$ | fixed strike of the spread, same price units (can be 0 or negative) | price units |
| sigma1, sigma2 | annualized lognormal (percentage) vols of F1, F2; 30% is `0.30` | $1/\sqrt{\mathrm{year}}$ |
| $\rho$ | correlation of the two log returns, in [-1, 1] | none |
| $T$ | time to expiry in years (day count from the task; often days/365) | years |
| $r$ | continuously compounded rate for discounting the payoff; $\mathrm{DF} = \exp (-r T)$ | $1/\mathrm{year}$ |

atoms.title: Spread options: Kirk (1995) approximation and Margrabe (1978) exchange option / Margrabe (K = 0, exact)
atoms.text:
## Margrabe (K = 0, exact)
**Margrabe relative volatility**

$$
\sigma  = \sqrt{\mathrm{sigma1}^{2} - 2 \rho  \mathrm{sigma1} \mathrm{sigma2} + \mathrm{sigma2}^{2}}
$$

**Exchange-option exercise thresholds**

$$
\mathrm{d1} = [\ln (\mathrm{F1}/\mathrm{F2}) + \sigma ^{2} T / 2] / (\sigma  \sqrt{T}),   \mathrm{d2} = \mathrm{d1} - \sigma  \sqrt{T}
$$

**Margrabe exchange-call price**

$$
C  = \mathrm{DF} \cdot  [\mathrm{F1} N(\mathrm{d1}) - \mathrm{F2} N(\mathrm{d2})]
$$

Spot form with continuous yields q1, q2: $C = \mathrm{S1} e^{-\mathrm{q1} T} N(\mathrm{d1}) - \mathrm{S2} e^{-\mathrm{q2} T} N(\mathrm{d2})$ with

$\ln (\mathrm{S1} e^{-\mathrm{q1} T} / (\mathrm{S2} e^{-\mathrm{q2} T}))$ in d1. Without yields the price does not depend on r (Margrabe 1978).

atoms.title: Spread options: Kirk (1995) approximation and Margrabe (1978) exchange option / Kirk (K != 0, approximation; requires F2 + K > 0)
atoms.text:
## Kirk (K != 0, approximation; requires F2 + K > 0)
Treat $\mathrm{F2} + K$ as one lognormal "strike asset" and price a Margrabe/Black-76 call on F1 against it:

**Kirk second-leg weight**

$$
w       = \mathrm{F2} / (\mathrm{F2} + K)
$$

**Kirk effective volatility**

$$
\sigma _{K} = \sqrt{\mathrm{sigma1}^{2} - 2 \rho  \mathrm{sigma1} \mathrm{sigma2} w + \mathrm{sigma2}^{2} w^{2}}
$$

**Kirk exercise thresholds**

$$
\mathrm{d1} = [\ln (\mathrm{F1} / (\mathrm{F2} + K)) + \sigma _{K}^{2} T / 2] / (\sigma _{K} \sqrt{T}),   \mathrm{d2} = \mathrm{d1} - \sigma _{K} \sqrt{T}
$$

**Kirk spread-call approximation**

$$
C  = \mathrm{DF} \cdot  [\mathrm{F1} N(\mathrm{d1}) - (\mathrm{F2} + K) N(\mathrm{d2})]
$$

**Spread-put approximation by parity**

$$
\operatorname{P}  = C - \mathrm{DF} \cdot  (\mathrm{F1} - \mathrm{F2} - K)\quad (\;\text{put}\;-\;\text{call}\; \;\text{parity}\;; \;\text{equals}\; \mathrm{DF}\cdot [(\mathrm{F2}+K)N(-\mathrm{d2}) - \mathrm{F1} N(-\mathrm{d1})])
$$

At $K = 0, w = 1$ and Kirk equals Margrabe exactly.

atoms.title: Spread options: Kirk (1995) approximation and Margrabe (1978) exchange option / Spot inputs (rates, dividend yields, cost of carry)
atoms.text:
## Spot inputs (rates, dividend yields, cost of carry)
- Convert each leg to a forward first: $F_{i} = S_{i} \cdot  \exp ((r - q_{i}) T)$ or, with cost of carry $b_{i}$, $F_{i} = S_{i} \cdot  \exp (b_{i} T)$
  ($q_{i}$ = dividend yield / foreign rate / convenience yield net of storage). Then use the formulas above with $\mathrm{DF} = \exp (-r T)$.
Equivalent spot form: $C = \mathrm{S1} e^{-\mathrm{q1} T} N(\mathrm{d1}) - (\mathrm{S2} e^{-\mathrm{q2} T} + K e^{-r T}) N(\mathrm{d2})$, with

  $w = \mathrm{S2} e^{-\mathrm{q2} T} / (\mathrm{S2} e^{-\mathrm{q2} T} + K e^{-r T})$. Do NOT plug raw spot S2/(S2+K) into w when carry is non-zero.
- Futures inputs: use futures prices as $F_{i}$ directly (no carry adjustment); discount with $\exp (-r T)$ to the payment date.
  If the option itself is futures-style margined (no upfront premium), the task may want $\mathrm{DF} = 1$.

atoms.title: Spread options: Kirk (1995) approximation and Margrabe (1978) exchange option / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources
Margrabe (1978) J. Finance 33(1):177-186; Kirk (1995) in R. Jameson (ed.) Managing Energy Price Risk, Risk Publications & Enron, pp. 71-78
(formula as reproduced in the literature and in QuantLib's KirkEngine); Black (1976) J. Financial Economics 3:167-179;
Carmona & Durrleman (2003) SIAM Review 45(4):627-685.

atoms.title: Spread options: Kirk (1995) approximation and Margrabe (1978) exchange option / Common variants
atoms.text:
## Common variants
- Quantities / heat rates: payoff $a \mathrm{F1} - b \mathrm{F2} - K$ (e.g. spark spread with heat rate b): use `a F1`, `b F2` as the legs; vols and $\rho$ unchanged.
- Leg order: payoff $(F_2-F_1-K)^+$ is a call on the swapped legs with strike $K$. The original spread put $(K+F_2-F_1)^+$ instead requires swapped legs with strike $-K$ (swap sigma1/sigma2 too; $\rho$ stays).
- Negative strike: direct Kirk is defined while $\mathrm{F2} + K > 0 (w > 1)$. If $\mathrm{F2} + K \le  0$ Kirk is undefined
  (log of a non-positive number); price the put $\max (\mathrm{F2}(T) - \mathrm{F1}(T) - (-K), 0)$ as a Kirk call on the swapped legs with strike -K, then
  $C = \operatorname{P} + \mathrm{DF} (\mathrm{F1} - \mathrm{F2} - K)$. This is plain parity, not a published refinement.
- Refinements: modified Kirk of Alos & Leon (2016) adds a skew correction to $\sigma _{K}$ and targets
  $\rho$ near 1; Bjerksund & Stensland (2014) give a closed-form lower bound reported more accurate than Kirk;
  Deng, Li & Zhou (2008) give another closed-form approximation with Greeks. Use one only if the task asks for it.

atoms.title: Spread options: Kirk (1995) approximation and Margrabe (1978) exchange option / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- Literature: Kirk is accurate for small K relative to F2 and degrades when $\rho$ is close to 1
  (Alos & Leon 2016; Harutyunyan & Masip Borras 2018). Bjerksund & Stensland (2014) report their bound is much more precise than Kirk.
- Approximation error depends on both volatilities, maturity, strike and correlation. No universal percentage tolerance follows from the model; relative error is particularly unstable when the true option value is small.
- So when a task asks for Kirk, a gap between Kirk and a Monte Carlo price is expected and is not by itself a bug in the Kirk code.
- Kirk cannot be used with $\mathrm{F2} + K \le  0, \rho$ outside [-1, 1], or a zero ratio vol (then the price is the discounted intrinsic value).
- Assumption failures (smile, jumps, mean reversion, legs with different delivery dates and a term structure of vols, negative prices) are not fixed by Kirk.

atoms.title: Lookback options: floating strike (Goldman-Sosin-Gatto 1979) and fixed strike (Conze-Viswanathan 1991) / Payoffs and model
atoms.text:
## Payoffs and model
- Running extremes over the whole lookback period, including what was already observed: $M_{T} = \max (S_{\mathrm{max}}, \max _{t\le u\le T} S_{u})$, $m_{T} = \min (S_{\mathrm{min}}, \min _{t\le u\le T} S_{u})$.
- Floating-strike call $S_{T} - m_{T}$; floating-strike put $M_{T} - S_{T}$ (always exercised, never negative).
- Fixed-strike call $\max (M_{T} - K, 0)$; fixed-strike put $\max (K - m_{T}, 0)$ (also called hindsight options).
- Model: Black-Scholes GBM, constant r, q, $\sigma$; continuous dividend yield q; European exercise; the extreme is
  monitored **continuously**. Price = $\exp ( -r \tau  )$ $\operatorname{E}_{Q}$[payoff], $\tau$ = time remaining. Cost of carry $b = r - q$.

atoms.title: Lookback options: floating strike (Goldman-Sosin-Gatto 1979) and fixed strike (Conze-Viswanathan 1991) / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| $S$ | spot today (valuation date) | price |
| $S_{\mathrm{min}} / S_{\mathrm{max}}$ | min / max observed so far, today's spot included; at inception $S_{\mathrm{min}} = S_{\mathrm{max}} = S$ | price |
| $K$ | fixed strike (fixed-strike options only) | price |
| $T$ | time remaining to expiry ($\tau$), not the original tenor | years |
| $r$ | continuously compounded risk-free rate | $1/\mathrm{year}$ |
| $q$ | continuous dividend yield (foreign rate for FX); b = r - q | $1/\mathrm{year}$ |
| $\sigma$ | annualized lognormal vol; 30% is `0.30` | $1/\sqrt{\mathrm{year}}$ |

atoms.title: Lookback options: floating strike (Goldman-Sosin-Gatto 1979) and fixed strike (Conze-Viswanathan 1991) / Formulas (b != 0); N = normal CDF, n = normal pdf
atoms.text:
## Formulas (b != 0); N = normal CDF, n = normal pdf

$$
d(X) = [\ln (S/X) + (b + \sigma ^{2}/2) T] / (\sigma  \sqrt{T})
$$

$$
\mathrm{lam} = 2b / \sigma ^{2}
$$

In both expressions, $d = d(X)$:

$$
\mathrm{UP}(X) = (1/\mathrm{lam}) [ e^{bT} N(d) - (S/X)^{-\mathrm{lam}} N(d - 2b \sqrt{T}/\sigma ) ]
$$

$$
\mathrm{DOWN}(X) = (1/\mathrm{lam}) [ (S/X)^{-\mathrm{lam}} N(-d + 2b \sqrt{T}/\sigma ) - e^{bT} N(-d) ]
$$

Floating call ($\mathrm{a1} = d(S_{\mathrm{min}}), \mathrm{a2} = \mathrm{a1} - \sigma  \sqrt{T}$):

$$
C_{\mathrm{fl}} = S e^{-qT} N(\mathrm{a1}) - S_{\mathrm{min}} e^{-rT} N(\mathrm{a2}) + S e^{-rT} \mathrm{DOWN}(S_{\mathrm{min}})
$$

Floating put ($\mathrm{b1} = d(S_{\mathrm{max}}), \mathrm{b2} = \mathrm{b1} - \sigma  \sqrt{T}$):

$$
\operatorname{P}_{\mathrm{fl}} = S_{\mathrm{max}} e^{-rT} N(-\mathrm{b2}) - S e^{-qT} N(-\mathrm{b1}) + S e^{-rT} \mathrm{UP}(S_{\mathrm{max}})
$$

Fixed call, two branches ($\mathrm{d1} = d(K), \mathrm{d2} = \mathrm{d1} - \sigma  \sqrt{T}; \mathrm{e1} = d(S_{\mathrm{max}}), \mathrm{e2} = \mathrm{e1} - \sigma  \sqrt{T}$):

$$
\begin{gathered}
K >  S_{\mathrm{max}}:  C_{\mathrm{fx}} = S e^{-qT} N(\mathrm{d1}) - K e^{-rT} N(\mathrm{d2}) + S e^{-rT} \mathrm{UP}(K) \\
K \le  S_{\mathrm{max}}:  C_{\mathrm{fx}} = e^{-rT}(S_{\mathrm{max}} - K) + S e^{-qT} N(\mathrm{e1}) - S_{\mathrm{max}} e^{-rT} N(\mathrm{e2}) + S e^{-rT} \mathrm{UP}(S_{\mathrm{max}})
\end{gathered}
$$

Fixed put, two branches ($\mathrm{d1} = d(K); \mathrm{f1} = d(S_{\mathrm{min}}), \mathrm{f2} = \mathrm{f1} - \sigma  \sqrt{T}$):

$$
\begin{gathered}
K <  S_{\mathrm{min}}:  \operatorname{P}_{\mathrm{fx}} = K e^{-rT} N(-\mathrm{d2}) - S e^{-qT} N(-\mathrm{d1}) + S e^{-rT} \mathrm{DOWN}(K) \\
K \ge  S_{\mathrm{min}}:  \operatorname{P}_{\mathrm{fx}} = e^{-rT}(K - S_{\mathrm{min}}) - S e^{-qT} N(-\mathrm{f1}) + S_{\mathrm{min}} e^{-rT} N(-\mathrm{f2}) + S e^{-rT} \mathrm{DOWN}(S_{\mathrm{min}})
\end{gathered}
$$

The branches meet continuously at K = extreme. Both hold for $b > 0$ and $b < 0 (q > r)$.

atoms.title: Lookback options: floating strike (Goldman-Sosin-Gatto 1979) and fixed strike (Conze-Viswanathan 1991) / r = q (b = 0): the formulas above divide by zero; use the limits
atoms.text:
## r = q (b = 0): the formulas above divide by zero; use the limits

$$
\mathrm{UP}(X)   \to  \sigma  \sqrt{T} [ d N(d) + n(d) ],      \mathrm{DOWN}(X) \to  \sigma  \sqrt{T} [ -d N(-d) + n(d) ],   d = d(X) \;\text{at}\; b = 0
$$

Do not plug $b = 0$ into $\sigma ^{2}/(2b)$; a tiny nonzero b (e.g. 1e-8) also works but loses digits.

atoms.title: Lookback options: floating strike (Goldman-Sosin-Gatto 1979) and fixed strike (Conze-Viswanathan 1991) / Identities (exact, model-free from the payoffs; useful as self-checks)
Lookback options: floating strike (Goldman-Sosin-Gatto 1979) and fixed strike (Conze-Viswanathan 1991) / Variants
atoms.text:
## Variants
- Inception vs seasoned: at inception set $S_{\mathrm{min}} = S_{\mathrm{max}} = S$. Later, pass the observed extreme and the REMAINING time;
  the fixed-strike branch is chosen by comparing K with the observed extreme, not with spot.
- Discrete monitoring (daily/weekly fixings, interval $\mathrm{d}t = T/m$): the continuous formula OVERPRICES all four
  (a discrete max is lower, a discrete min is higher). Variant only, use if the task asks: Broadie-Glasserman-Kou
  (1999) first-order shift with $\beta  = 0.5826 \cdot  \sigma  \cdot  \sqrt{\mathrm{d}t} (0.5826 = -\zeta (1/2)/\sqrt{2 \pi})$:
  fixed call $e^{-\beta} C_{\mathrm{fx}}(S, S_{\mathrm{max}} e^{\beta}, K e^{\beta})$; fixed put $e^{\beta} \operatorname{P}_{\mathrm{fx}}(S, S_{\mathrm{min}} e^{-\beta}, K e^{-\beta})$;
  floating put $e^{-\beta} \operatorname{P}_{\mathrm{fl}}(S, S_{\mathrm{max}} e^{\beta}) + (e^{-\beta} - 1) S e^{-qT}$;
  floating call $e^{\beta} C_{\mathrm{fl}}(S, S_{\mathrm{min}} e^{-\beta}) - (e^{\beta} - 1) S e^{-qT}$. Error $o(1/\sqrt{m})$.
  BGK state these for $q = 0$ with S in place of S $e^{-qT}$; the $q \ne  0$ form is our extension (checked by MC).
- Not covered here: partial-time / percentage (partial) lookbacks, American lookbacks, double lookbacks, extreme-spread options.

atoms.title: Lookback options: floating strike (Goldman-Sosin-Gatto 1979) and fixed strike (Conze-Viswanathan 1991) / Sources
Lookback options: floating strike (Goldman-Sosin-Gatto 1979) and fixed strike (Conze-Viswanathan 1991) / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- Valid only under continuous monitoring and constant r, q, $\sigma$. Smile, jumps, stochastic vol and discrete
  dividends are not captured; the extreme is very sensitive to vol, so vol-model error is larger than for vanillas.
- The continuous-vs-discrete gap is first order in $\sigma  \sqrt{\mathrm{d}t}$ and is often the largest "error" seen against a
  discretely sampled Monte Carlo: it is a monitoring bias, not a formula bug. Compare with a Brownian-bridge MC
  or apply the BGK shift before concluding a formula is wrong.
- When the simulation is specified with a fixed number of steps (for example one step per trading day) and the closed form is the continuous one, the two prices measure different contracts. With many paths the Monte Carlo standard error is small and the monitoring bias is not, so the difference is typically several standard errors: a check of the form |cf - mc| < k * se then fails as an honest result. Report the closed-form and simulated prices as the task defines them and write the check's value as computed (False), together with the other outputs; do not replace the closed form by a corrected one, change the stated step count, or keep the outputs back while trying to make the check pass. A BGK-shifted closed form or a Brownian-bridge extreme is a separate quantity to report only where the task asks for it.
- Requires $S > 0, \sigma  > 0, T > 0, S_{\mathrm{min}} \le  S \le  S_{\mathrm{max}}, K > 0$. At $T = 0$ the price is the intrinsic payoff.
- Common errors: using r instead of b inside d; forgetting $e^{-qT}$ on the S terms; using S instead of $S_{\mathrm{min}}$ or $S_{\mathrm{max}}$
  when the option is seasoned; using total tenor instead of remaining time; swapping the K-vs-extreme branch.

atoms.title: Merton lognormal jump diffusion
atoms.text:
Use this reference for European pricing, simulation and parameter interpretation under Merton lognormal jump diffusion.

Explicit task definitions and contract conventions take precedence. If they conflict or are incomplete, identify the ambiguity and state the convention used.

atoms.title: Merton lognormal jump diffusion / 1. Shared foundations
atoms.text:
## 1. Shared foundations
Symbols are local. Under a specified pricing measure, use
**Compensated jump-diffusion stock dynamics**

$$
\mathrm{d}S/S_{\mathrm{left}}=(r-q-\lambda \cdot \kappa )\cdot \mathrm{d}t+\sigma \cdot \mathrm{d}W+(J-1)\cdot \mathrm{dN}_{\mathrm{jump}},
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{jump}}$ is a Poisson counting process with intensity $\lambda$. At each jump draw a fresh IID multiplier J with $\ln (J)$ normal of mean $\mu _{J}$ and variance $\delta _{J}^{2}$; jump marks, counting process and Brownian motion are independent. Define $\Phi$ as the standard normal CDF and $\kappa =\exp (\mu _{J}+\delta _{J}^{2}/2)-1$. Require $S>0, K>0, T>0, \lambda \ge 0, \sigma \ge 0$ and $\delta _{J}\ge 0; r$ and q are constant continuous rates. At $T=0$ return the payoff directly. Rates and $\lambda$ are annualized, T in years, $\sigma$ annualized decimal diffusion volatility. J is a price multiplier, not a log-return. The compensator ensures $\operatorname{E}[S_{T}]=S\cdot \exp ((r-q)\cdot T)$.

atoms.title: Merton lognormal jump diffusion / 2. European pricing by conditioning
atoms.text:
## 2. European pricing by conditioning
Conditional on $N_{\mathrm{jump}}(T)=n$:
$\log (S_{T})$ is normal with mean $m_{n}=\ln (S)+(r-q-\lambda \cdot \kappa -\sigma ^{2}/2)\cdot T+n\cdot \mu _{J}$,

and variance $v_{n}=\sigma ^{2}\cdot T+n\cdot \delta _{J}^{2}$.

For $v_{n}>0$ set $\mathrm{d2}_{n}=(m_{n}-\ln (K))/\sqrt{v_{n}}, \mathrm{d1}_{n}=\mathrm{d2}_{n}+\sqrt{v_{n}}$.

**Call value conditional on jump count**

$$
C_{n}=\exp (-r\cdot T)\cdot (\exp (m_{n}+v_{n}/2)\cdot \Phi (\mathrm{d1}_{n})-K\cdot \Phi (\mathrm{d2}_{n})).
$$

**Put value conditional on jump count**

$$
\operatorname{P}_{n}=\exp (-r\cdot T)\cdot (K\cdot \Phi (-\mathrm{d2}_{n})-\exp (m_{n}+v_{n}/2)\cdot \Phi (-\mathrm{d1}_{n})).
$$

**Poisson mixture of conditional option values**

$$
C=\sum _{n} p_{n}\cdot C_{n}
$$

$$
\operatorname{P}=\sum _{n} p_{n}\cdot \operatorname{P}_{n}
$$

where

$$
p_{n}=\exp (-\lambda \cdot T)\cdot (\lambda \cdot T)^{n}/n!
$$

At $v_{n}=0$ use the discounted deterministic payoff instead. This representation uses the original Poisson intensity; do not mix its weights with a transformed-intensity formula from another convention.

Choose the truncation from BOTH probability and asset-weighted tails. A call tail is at most $\exp (-r\cdot T)\cdot \sum _{\mathrm{tail}} p_{n}\cdot \exp (m_{n}+v_{n}/2)$; a put tail is at most $\exp (-r\cdot T)\cdot K\cdot \sum _{\mathrm{tail}} p_{n}$. For a sum retaining $n=0,\ldots ,n_{\mathrm{max}}$, these upper bounds (not the actual omitted option prices) equal $S\cdot \exp (-q\cdot T)$ times the Poisson survival probability with $\operatorname{mean} \lambda \cdot T\cdot \exp (\mu _{J}+\delta _{J}^{2}/2)$, and $K\cdot \exp (-r\cdot T)$ times that with mean $\lambda T$, respectively; survival probability means $\Pr[\operatorname{Poisson}(\mathrm{mean})>n_{\mathrm{max}}]$. For large intensities use log weights or stable Poisson functions, not underflowing recursion from $p_{0}$.

atoms.title: Merton lognormal jump diffusion / 3. Historical estimation and simulation
atoms.text:
## 3. Historical estimation and simulation
Historical and pricing parameters need not agree.
If the physical expected price drift is $b_{\operatorname{P}}$ and jump parameters carry subscript P, an interval dt has log-return mixture means $(b_{\mathrm P}-\lambda_{\mathrm P}\kappa_{\mathrm P}-\sigma_{\mathrm P}^2/2)\mathrm{d}t+n\mu_{\mathrm{JP}}$ and variances $\sigma_{\mathrm P}^2\mathrm{d}t+n\delta_{\mathrm{JP}}^2$. Fit the actual mixture likelihood using log-sum-exp, valid bounds and a controlled tail. If drift is instead defined as the log drift, do not subtract $\sigma^2/2$ again. Identify parameters by definitions. Multiple starts and parameter sensitivity matter: sparse jumps can make calibration weakly identified.

Historical estimation alone does not determine a risk-neutral jump premium. Setting physical jump parameters equal to pricing parameters is an additional assumption, usable when explicitly specified. Simulate an increment by drawing the Poisson count, a diffusion normal, and a jump sum with conditional mean $n\mu_J$ and variance $n\delta_J^2$. Include the compensator once. Terminal simulation suffices only for terminal payoffs; path-dependent contracts need their monitoring schedule.

atoms.title: Merton lognormal jump diffusion / 4. Checks and limits
atoms.text:
## 4. Checks and limits
$\lambda =0$ reduces to Black-Scholes; zero jump size reduces to pure diffusion even with nonzero intensity. Call-put parity remains $S\cdot \exp (-q\cdot T)-K\cdot \exp (-r\cdot T)$. Verify the forward moment and compare the mixture with direct payoff integration or independent simulation. Check tails after changing parameters. Implied volatility is a separate inversion of the final option price. A Gaussian approximation to aggregate jumps is not the Poisson mixture model.

## 5. References
Merton (1976), Option Pricing When Underlying Stock Returns Are Discontinuous, Journal of Financial Economics 3, 125-144. Formulas above are derived by conditioning on the Poisson count; they state the parameter convention explicitly.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes: terms, estimators, checks and library calls
atoms.text:
This reference covers European and arithmetic-average (Asian) options under constant-parameter geometric Brownian
motion (GBM): Monte Carlo prices, Greeks by finite differences (FD), pathwise differentiation (PW) and likelihood
ratios (LR), their standard errors, Black–Scholes (BS) benchmarks, consistency checks, Greek surfaces and the library
calls used to build them. Every formula below was checked numerically against the BS closed form. Formulas the task
states are part of its contract: use them as written and map them to the definitions here.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes: terms, estimators, checks and library calls / 1. Terms
atoms.text:
## 1. Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Spot S, strike K | Current underlying price; fixed exercise price |
| r, q | Annual continuously compounded risk-free rate and dividend yield (decimals) |
| sigma | Annual volatility as a decimal (0.20 means 20%) |
| T | Time to maturity in years |
| Delta, Gamma | dV/dS and d2V/dS2 |
| Vega | dV/dsigma, per unit of decimal volatility |
| Rho | dV/dr, per unit of decimal rate |
| Maturity sensitivity V_T | dV/dT, the change in value when time to maturity grows; positive for ordinary European calls |
| Calendar Theta | dV/dt as calendar time passes with maturity date fixed; for European options Theta = -V_T (usually negative) |
| Bump | The small change h applied to one input in a finite difference |
| Finite difference (FD) | Reprice with the input bumped and take a difference quotient |
| Common random numbers (CRN) | Reuse the same normal draws for every bumped repricing so the noise cancels in the difference |
| Pathwise (PW, IPA) | Differentiate the discounted payoff along each simulated path, then average |
| Likelihood ratio (LR, score function) | Multiply the payoff by the derivative of the log density of the simulated variable, then average |
| Per-path contribution G_i | The value one path adds to an estimator; the estimate is the mean of G_i |
| Standard error (SE) | Sample standard deviation of the G_i divided by sqrt(number of paths) |
| Estimator variance | Sample variance of the G_i; comparing two methods needs the same level (per-path variance with variance, SE with SE) |
| BS benchmark | Closed-form European price or Greek used as the reference value |
| Put–call parity | C - P = S exp(-qT) - K exp(-rT); differentiating it gives exact relations between call and put Greeks |
| Arithmetic Asian option | Payoff on the arithmetic mean of prices at monitoring dates t_1 < ... < t_m |
| Convergence study | The same estimator at increasing path counts N, with value and SE at each N |
| Greek surface | A Greek evaluated on a grid of (spot, volatility) pairs |
| Unavailable estimate | A Greek a method does not produce; written as JSON null, never 0 or NaN |
| Check flag | Boolean result of one stated check; an overall flag is the AND of the required checks |

Units and labels. A difference quotient divided by its bump is per unit of the bumped input: dividing by a volatility
bump gives per unit of decimal volatility; dividing by a time bump measured in years gives per year. A text label may
describe another unit (per one volatility point, per day). The stated formula fixes the number: compute what the formula
says, note any label that differs in a comment, and express every method, SE and benchmark of that Greek in the same
units so that they are comparable. Convert all of them together only when a conversion is stated explicitly.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes: terms, estimators, checks and library calls / 2. Paths and random draws
atoms.text:
## 2. Paths and random draws

Purpose: simulate risk-neutral GBM at the monitoring dates. b is the log drift.

```text
b = r - q - sigma^2 / 2
dt_j = t_j - t_(j-1),  t_0 = 0
W_j = sum over k <= j of sqrt(dt_k) * Z_k        (Z_k independent standard normal)
S_j = S * exp(b * t_j + sigma * W_j)
```

Purpose: a European payoff needs only the terminal price; with the same draws it is the last monitoring date.

```text
S_T = S * exp(b * T + sigma * sqrt(T) * Z)        (Z = W_T / sqrt(T))
```

Draw the normal array once and reuse it in every estimator, every bump and every check. A seeded generator gives a
stream whose split into arrays depends on the shapes requested; a different request order or shape gives different
numbers, so fix the order once and keep it.

```python
rs = np.random.RandomState(seed)                   # legacy seeded generator; not interchangeable with default_rng
Z = rs.standard_normal((N, m))                     # one row per path, one column per monitoring date
W = np.cumsum(np.sqrt(dt) * Z, axis=1)
S_path = S0 * np.exp(b * t + sigma * W)
assert np.allclose((np.log(S_path / S0) - b * t) / sigma, W)   # ln(S_j/S) - b t_j is sigma*W_j, not W_j
```

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes: terms, estimators, checks and library calls / 3. Estimate and standard error from per-path contributions
atoms.text:
## 3. Estimate and standard error from per-path contributions

Purpose: every estimator (price, FD, PW, LR) is a mean of per-path contributions G_i.

```text
estimate = mean(G_i)
SE = std(G_i, ddof=1) / sqrt(N)
```

Compute the price SE from the discounted payoffs. For an FD Greek, form the per-path difference quotient first and take
its SE; the SE of a bumped price alone is not the SE of the Greek. Bias from the bump size is not part of the SE.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes: terms, estimators, checks and library calls / 4. Finite differences with common random numbers
atoms.text:
## 4. Finite differences with common random numbers

Purpose: central first derivative in an input a with bump h, same draws in both repricings.

```text
G_i = (H_i(a + h) - H_i(a - h)) / (2 h)
```

Purpose: central second derivative (Gamma from spot bumps).

```text
G_i = (H_i(a + h) - 2 H_i(a) + H_i(a - h)) / h^2
```

Purpose: backward maturity difference; it estimates V_T = dV/dT (not calendar Theta). With the same Z, the shorter
maturity path is S * exp(b (T - h) + sigma sqrt(T - h) Z) and is discounted with exp(-r (T - h)).

```text
G_i = -(H_i(T - h) - H_i(T)) / h  =  (H_i(T) - H_i(T - h)) / h   ->   V_T
```

Recompute everything that depends on the bumped input (drift b, diffusion, discount factor, monitoring dates when they
scale with T). With CRN the SE of a one-day maturity difference is of the same order as the PW SE; an SE thousands of
times larger means the two repricings used different draws.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes: terms, estimators, checks and library calls / 5. Time sensitivity: one quantity across all methods
atoms.text:
## 5. Time sensitivity: one quantity across all methods

Use one definition of the time Greek for every method, chosen by the formula the task gives. This table maps each
form; values were checked against BS (call: FD 6.892, PW 6.884, -Theta_BS 6.891 in per-year units).

| Form | Estimates | Pathwise contribution of the same quantity | BS reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| -(V(T-h) - V(T))/h | V_T = dV/dT | D (g'(S_T) U_T - r g(S_T)) | -Theta_BS |
| -(V(T+h) - V(T-h))/(2h) | Theta = -V_T | D (r g(S_T) - g'(S_T) U_T) | Theta_BS |

Purpose: maturity derivative of the terminal price with Z fixed, used by the PW contribution above (payment at T).

```text
U_T = S_T * (b + sigma * Z / (2 sqrt(T)))
```

If FD and PW of the time Greek have opposite signs, one of them estimates the other quantity in this table: keep the
task's formula and change the other estimator or the reference to the same row. Do not drop a sign from the stated
formula.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes: terms, estimators, checks and library calls / 6. Pathwise estimators
atoms.text:
## 6. Pathwise estimators

Purpose: payoff derivatives. g' is 1 above the strike for a call and -1 below the strike for a put.

```text
call: g(U) = max(U - K, 0),  g'(U) = 1{U > K}
put:  g(U) = max(K - U, 0),  g'(U) = -1{U < K}
D = exp(-r T)
```

Purpose: European Delta, Vega and Rho per path (Rho includes the discount factor's derivative).

```text
G_Delta = D * g'(S_T) * S_T / S
G_Vega  = D * g'(S_T) * S_T * (sqrt(T) Z - sigma T)
G_Rho   = D * (g'(S_T) * T * S_T - T * g(S_T))
```

Purpose: arithmetic Asian with average A = mean_j S_j; Delta and Vega per path.

```text
G_Delta = D * g'(A) * A / S
G_Vega  = D * g'(A) * mean_j( S_j * (W_j - sigma t_j) )
```

Gamma: the payoff derivative jumps at the strike, so differentiating PW Delta again misses that jump and does not give
Gamma; use FD or LR for Gamma. Whether other PW Greeks of an Asian (time, rate) are requested is set by the task.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes: terms, estimators, checks and library calls / 7. Likelihood-ratio estimators (European, terminal density)
atoms.text:
## 7. Likelihood-ratio estimators (European, terminal density)

Purpose: recover the standard normal that generated S_T; it must be the same draw, with mean about 0 and SD about 1.

```text
Z = (ln(S_T / S) - b T) / (sigma sqrt(T))
```

Purpose: per-path LR contributions; weights are derivatives of the lognormal log density in S, sigma and r.

```text
G_Delta = D * g(S_T) * Z / (S sigma sqrt(T))
G_Gamma = D * g(S_T) * (Z^2 - 1 - sigma sqrt(T) Z) / (S sigma sqrt(T))^2
G_Vega  = D * g(S_T) * ((Z^2 - 1) / sigma - Z sqrt(T))
G_Rho   = D * g(S_T) * (Z sqrt(T) / sigma - T)
```

For an Asian payoff the score uses the joint density of all monitoring prices: spot enters only the first transition,
so the Delta weight is Z_1 / (S sigma sqrt(dt_1)) with Z_1 recovered from the first observed price of the same path.
LR Delta is usually noisier than PW Delta for the same paths; compare their SEs (or per-path variances) at the same N.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes: terms, estimators, checks and library calls / 8. Black–Scholes benchmarks and parity
atoms.text:
## 8. Black–Scholes benchmarks and parity

```text
d1 = (ln(S/K) + (r - q + sigma^2/2) T) / (sigma sqrt(T)),   d2 = d1 - sigma sqrt(T)
C = S e^(-qT) N(d1) - K e^(-rT) N(d2)
P = K e^(-rT) N(-d2) - S e^(-qT) N(-d1)
Delta_C = e^(-qT) N(d1),   Delta_P = e^(-qT) (N(d1) - 1)
Gamma = e^(-qT) n(d1) / (S sigma sqrt(T))
Vega = S e^(-qT) n(d1) sqrt(T)
Rho_C = K T e^(-rT) N(d2),   Rho_P = -K T e^(-rT) N(-d2)
Theta_C = -S e^(-qT) n(d1) sigma / (2 sqrt(T)) + q S e^(-qT) N(d1) - r K e^(-rT) N(d2)
Theta_P = -S e^(-qT) n(d1) sigma / (2 sqrt(T)) - q S e^(-qT) N(-d1) + r K e^(-rT) N(-d2)
```

N is the standard normal CDF and n its density. Theta here is calendar Theta, per year.

Purpose: Greek relations from differentiating parity (exact for BS; MC estimates on the same paths satisfy them to
within a few paired SEs).

```text
Delta_C - Delta_P = e^(-qT)
Gamma_C - Gamma_P = 0
Rho_C - Rho_P = K T e^(-rT)
V_T,C - V_T,P = -q S e^(-qT) + r K e^(-rT)
```

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes: terms, estimators, checks and library calls / 9. Asian versus European
atoms.text:
## 9. Asian versus European

An arithmetic average varies less than the terminal price, so for the same strike, maturity and parameters an
at-the-money arithmetic Asian call or put usually has a lower price than the European one, and the Asian call a lower
Delta. These orderings are typical, not laws: confirm them with the computed numbers and their SEs before writing a
flag.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes: terms, estimators, checks and library calls / 10. Check flags
atoms.text:
## 10. Check flags

Each flag compares two values that measure the same quantity in the same units and sign (Sections 1 and 5).

```text
relative error = |estimate - reference| / |reference|
```

Use the tolerance the task states. Where it gives none, choose one from the SEs and the bump bias, write it in a comment,
and use it for every flag of that kind. When the reference is near zero (a parity difference), use an absolute
tolerance scaled by the SEs. A flag computed from the files as written is the value to report: read the files back,
then compute the flags. If a flag is False, look for a mismatch in quantity, sign, units, draws or bump; if none is
found the flag stays False.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes: terms, estimators, checks and library calls / 11. Library calls (NumPy 2.5, SciPy 1.18, Matplotlib 3.11, pandas 3.0)
atoms.text:
## 11. Library calls (NumPy 2.5, SciPy 1.18, Matplotlib 3.11, pandas 3.0)

```python
import numpy as np, json, pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import norm
N_cdf, n_pdf = norm.cdf(d1), norm.pdf(d1)            # standard normal CDF and density, vectorised
put_slope = -1.0 * (S_T < K)                          # unary minus on a boolean array raises TypeError; multiply instead
json.dump({"value": None, "se": None}, f)            # None is written as JSON null
json.dumps(float("nan"))                              # writes NaN, which is not valid JSON; use None for unavailable
json.dumps(x, allow_nan=False)                        # raises ValueError if any NaN or inf is left
float(np.float64(1.5))                                # convert NumPy scalars before json.dump
pd.DataFrame(rows).to_csv(path, index=False)          # column order follows the dict keys or columns=
```

Purpose: a surface over a (spot, volatility) grid and its 3D plot.

```python
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")                                  # file output without a display
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
Sg, Vg = np.meshgrid(spots, vols)                      # shapes (len(vols), len(spots)); default indexing="xy"
fig = plt.figure()
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")                  # 3D axes; no separate import needed in Matplotlib 3.11
ax.plot_surface(Sg, Vg, delta_grid)                    # delta_grid has the same shape as Sg
ax.set_xlabel("S0"); ax.set_ylabel("sigma"); ax.set_zlabel("delta")
fig.savefig(path, dpi=120); plt.close(fig)
```

On a surface, each grid point reuses the same draws (CRN across the grid) so that the surface is smooth; check
monotonicity along the axes where the closed form is monotone (European call Delta increases in spot).

atoms.text:

- Glasserman (2004), *Monte Carlo Methods in Financial Engineering*, Chapter 7.

atoms.title: Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows
atoms.text: This reference explains the valuation of deposits, fixed and floating swap legs, and curve sensitivities when discounting and rate projection use different curves. It also covers the single-curve limit and the dependence of bootstrapping on interpolation. It does not specify market calendars, quote corrections or a universal currency convention.

atoms.title: Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows / 1. Shared Foundations
atoms.text:
## 1. Shared Foundations

Map the task's notation to economic quantities and units. Explicit definitions of accrual, curve time, settlement and shocks take precedence. If requirements conflict, state the ambiguity and interpretation; do not infer conventions from a currency or field name alone.

Let v be the valuation date and $\operatorname{P}_{d}$(v,t) the discount factor for a payment at t, under the chosen collateral/funding convention. $Q_{x}$(v,t) is a positive projection-curve parameter for index tenor x; it need not be a tradable zero-coupon bond price. N denotes notional, k a fixed coupon rate, and b a spread, all rates in decimals. A basis point of rate is 0.0001. The curve coordinate u(t) is a year fraction measured from v; coupon accrual fractions are separate quantities.

For a positive discount factor and $u(t)>0$, the continuously compounded zero rate is:

$$
\begin{gathered}
z_{d}(t) = -\ln (\operatorname{P}_{d}(v,t))/u(t) \\
\operatorname{P}_{d}(v,v) = 1
\end{gathered}
$$

Positive discount factors need not decrease with maturity when forward rates can be negative. At $u=0$ a quoted zero rate requires a limiting or short-end convention; the logarithmic quotient is undefined.

atoms.title: Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows / 2. Rate projection and known fixings
atoms.text:
## 2. Rate projection and known fixings

For a simple rate accruing from a to c with index accrual $\delta _{x}$(a,c), the projection-curve definition is:

$$
F_{x}(v;a,c) = (Q_{x}(v,a)/Q_{x}(v,c)-1)/\delta _{x}(a,c)
$$

The reverse relation recovers an end-date projection factor from a forward quote and a known start-date factor.

$$
Q_{x}(v,c) = Q_{x}(v,a)/(1+\delta _{x}(a,c)\cdot F_{x}(v;a,c))
$$

The denominator must be positive. A simple deposit discount identity uses the same algebra only when the quoted instrument's start/end values and relevant curve justify it. At $a=v$, the start factor is one. A spot-starting instrument has a later start date, so setting its start factor to one is a distinct assumption.

For an already fixed coupon, its rate is the contractual fixing, not the forward currently implied by the curve. If fixing is still ahead, $F_{x}$ denotes the model's projected rate appropriate to that payment. In a full stochastic multiple-curve model, measure changes may require adjustments; the curve-ratio formula alone is not a universal expectation under every measure. The conventional cash-flow framework separates projection from discounting [1].

atoms.title: Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows / 3. Fixed and floating leg values
atoms.text:
## 3. Fixed and floating leg values

For fixed payments on dates $t_{i}$ with fixed-leg accrual fractions $\alpha _{i}$, the discounted annuity per unit notional is:

$$
A_{d} = \sum _{i} \alpha _{i}\cdot \operatorname{P}_{d}(v,t_{i})
$$

For a constant fixed coupon k, the fixed-leg value before assigning the holder's receive/pay sign is:

$$
\mathrm{PV}_{\mathrm{fixed}} = N\cdot k\cdot A_{d}
$$

For floating accrual intervals ($a_{j}$,$c_{j}$), payment dates $p_{j}$, accrual fractions $\delta _{j}$ and rates $H_{j}$ (known fixings or projected rates), the floating-leg value before assigning the holder's receive/pay sign is:

$$
\mathrm{PV}_{\mathrm{float}} = N\cdot \sum _{j} \delta _{j}\cdot (H_{j}+b)\cdot \operatorname{P}_{d}(v,p_{j})
$$

The two legs may use different accrual bases, frequencies and dates. Payment lag changes the discount date, not the accrual interval. Principal exchanges, amortization and accrued-interest treatment are contractual additions; an ordinary fixed-for-floating swap does not acquire principal exchanges merely because a bond representation is useful.

From the holder's perspective, paying fixed and receiving floating gives:

$$
\begin{gathered}
V_{\mathrm{pay},\mathrm{fixed}} = \mathrm{PV}_{\mathrm{float}}-\mathrm{PV}_{\mathrm{fixed}} \\
V_{\mathrm{receive},\mathrm{fixed}} = -V_{\mathrm{pay},\mathrm{fixed}}
\end{gathered}
$$

The par fixed rate sets this value to zero, assuming a nonzero annuity and the floating-leg spread already included.

$$
k_{\mathrm{par}} = \mathrm{PV}_{\mathrm{float}}/(N\cdot A_{d})
$$

In the single-curve case only, with $Q_{x}=\operatorname{P}_{d}$, consecutive accrual intervals, payment at each interval end and no floating spread, algebra makes the floating coupons telescope:

$$
\mathrm{PV}_{\mathrm{float}} = N\cdot (\operatorname{P}_{d}(v,a_{1})-\operatorname{P}_{d}(v,c_{\mathrm{last}}))
$$

Using this expression with distinct curves, historical off-market fixings, payment lag or nonconcatenating intervals generally changes the valuation.

atoms.title: Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows / 4. Overnight coupons and product definitions
atoms.text:
## 4. Overnight coupons and product definitions

An overnight compounded coupon over observations l, with annualized overnight fixings $r_l$ published daily and accrual fractions $d_l$ (for example, elapsed days divided by 360), has a realized accumulation factor [2]. Nonbusiness days may enter through a multi-day $d_{l}$; observation shifts and lookbacks are contract-specific.

$$
\begin{gathered}
G_{\mathrm{ON}} = \prod _{l} (1+r_{l}\cdot d_{l}) \\
\mathrm{coupon}_{\mathrm{ON}} = N\cdot (G_{\mathrm{ON}}-1)
\end{gathered}
$$

The equivalent simple coupon rate over an accrual $\delta$ is:

$$
R_{\mathrm{ON}} = (G_{\mathrm{ON}}-1)/\delta
$$

An arithmetic overnight average is another payoff. A simple single-payment instrument can be defined instead of a compounded OIS; its stated payoff determines its pricing equation. The word OIS by itself does not make every quoted pillar a deposit or impose one fixed accrual schedule. Adding a contractual spread outside compounding differs from compounding the spread with each daily rate.

atoms.title: Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows / 5. Interpolation and calibration equations
atoms.text:
## 5. Interpolation and calibration equations

A curve fitted to quotes must value every instrument with its contractual cash flows and the same interpolant. Let $\theta$ contain curve parameters, $q_{j}$ a market quote and $\mathrm{model}_{\mathrm{quote},j}$ the corresponding par rate or price. Exact calibration requires:

$$
\mathrm{model}_{\mathrm{quote},j}(\theta ) = q_{j}
$$

For a par coupon bond with unit redemption at $T_{n}$, coupons $c\alpha_j$, and payment dates on already determined knots except for the final date, the last factor solves:

$$
\operatorname{P}_{d}(v,T_{n}) = (1-c\cdot \sum _{j<n} \alpha _{j}\cdot \operatorname{P}_{d}(v,t_{j}))/(1+c\cdot \alpha _{n})
$$

If earlier coupon dates lie between the previous and new knots, their interpolated factors may depend on the new unknown. The equation is then implicit. A nonlocal interpolant can also change earlier intervals when later knots are added; fitting one knot at a time does not by itself establish final repricing.

For two knots $u_{a}<u_{b}$ and weight $w=(u-u_{a})/(u_{b}-u_{a})$, interpolation linear in log discount factors gives:

$$
\ln (\operatorname{P}_{d}(u)) = (1-w)\cdot \ln (\operatorname{P}_{d}(u_{a}))+w\cdot \ln (\operatorname{P}_{d}(u_{b}))
$$

Interpolation linear in continuous zero rates gives a different curve:

$$
\begin{gathered}
z_{d}(u) = (1-w)\cdot z_{d}(u_{a})+w\cdot z_{d}(u_{b}) \\
\operatorname{P}_{d}(u) = \exp (-u\cdot z_{d}(u))
\end{gathered}
$$

The first has a constant instantaneous forward on each interval. A spline applied to the exponent $g(u)=u\cdot z_{d}(u)$ is yet another choice. Positivity of factors, calibration and local shape are separate properties; a smooth interpolant does not guarantee nonnegative forwards.

The continuously compounded average forward over a curve-coordinate interval is:

$$
f_{\mathrm{average}}(a,c) = \ln (\operatorname{P}_{d}(v,a)/\operatorname{P}_{d}(v,c))/(u(c)-u(a))
$$

This is not the instantaneous forward except in a constant-forward interval. The instantaneous forward, where differentiable, is:

$$
f_{\mathrm{instant}}(u) = -d \ln (\operatorname{P}_{d}(u))/\mathrm{d}u
$$

atoms.title: Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows / References
atoms.text:
## References

[1] Ametrano and Bianchetti (2009), Bootstrapping the Illiquidity: Multiple Yield Curves Construction for Market Coherent Forward Rates Estimation, Sections 2–5. [Author manuscript](https://www.bianchetti.org/finance/bootstrappingtheilliquidity-v1.0.pdf). Bianchetti (2009), Two Curves, One Price, distinguishes forwarding/discounting measures and possible quanto adjustments. [Author paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.2770).

[2] Alternative Reference Rates Committee (2019), A User's Guide to SOFR, discussion of simple versus compound averaging. [Official guide hosted by the New York Fed](https://www.newyorkfed.org/medialibrary/Microsites/arrc/files/2019/Users_Guide_to_SOFR.pdf). Actual contractual calendars and accrual conventions govern a trade.

atoms.title: Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows / 6. Risk definitions and checks
atoms.text:
## 6. Risk definitions and checks

Let $V(\theta)$ be value and e specify the shocked curve/risk factor. The central sensitivity to an absolute rate change h is:

$$
\mathrm{d}V_{\mathrm{dtheta},e} \approx  (V(\theta +h\cdot e)-V(\theta -h\cdot e))/(2\cdot h)
$$

The signed change for a positive one-basis-point bump is distinct from a derivative or its absolute value:

$$
\mathrm{change}_{\mathrm{up},1\mathrm{bp}} = V(\theta +0.0001\cdot e)-V(\theta )
$$

A projection-zero shock at coordinate u changes $Q_{x}$ by a factor $\exp (-h\cdot u)$ while an unshocked discount curve stays fixed. A market-quote shock instead changes an input quote and recalibrates affected curves. These are different risks, and recalibration may change multiple parameters. Risk terminology alone does not identify the shock definition.

Useful identities are zero PV at the par fixed rate, opposite signs for opposite swap positions, single-curve telescoping under its conditions, and recovery of the original forward after converting to factor ratios and back. Repricing checks must include earlier quotes when a nonlocal interpolant changes. Small residuals do not validate a wrong day-count or cash-flow model.

This reference does not cover stochastic basis calibration, caplet volatility stripping, FX-reset notionals, or historical short-rate estimation. LIBOR is an index label in historical models here, not a recommendation for a present-day trading convention.

When a task defines a swap's NPV from the perspective of the fixed payer or receiver → compute it from the two leg values by that direction and check its sign:

```python
value = (pv_float - pv_fixed) if payer else (pv_fixed - pv_float)      # payer: pays fixed, receives floating
assert (value > 0) == ((pv_float > pv_fixed) == payer)
```

A provided script that computes the NPV another way is checked against this before its output is used.

When curves are bootstrapped from quotes (by your code or a provided script) → reprice every input instrument on the finished curves and stop on any residual above the task's stated tolerance (without one, report the residuals and fix only clear errors); a nonzero residual means a remaining error in the bootstrap (pillar dates, day count, which curve discounts, the order the curves are built in):

```python
worst = max(abs(model_rate(q) - q.rate) for q in quotes) * 1e4      # in basis points, the unit of the check
assert worst < tolerance_bp, f"input quotes do not reprice: {worst:.3g} bp"   # the tolerance the task states
```

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Model and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Model and assumptions
- A smooth parametric curve for the zero-coupon (spot) rate z(m) and the instantaneous forward rate f(m) at time to maturity m,
  for ONE trade date. Nelson-Siegel (NS) has 3 betas + 1 decay; Svensson (NSS) adds a second hump: 4 betas + 2 decays.
- In both papers the rates are CONTINUOUSLY compounded: discount factor $\mathrm{DF}(m) = \exp (-z(m) \cdot  m)$, and
  $z(m) = (1/m) \cdot  \int _{0}^{m} f(u) \mathrm{d}u$, i.e. $f(m) = d[m z(m)]/\mathrm{d}m$. Not arbitrage-free; a fitting device, not a dynamic model.

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Formulas (x1 = m/tau1, x2 = m/tau2)
atoms.text:
## Formulas (x1 = m/tau1, x2 = m/tau2)
Loadings (write them once and reuse):

$$
\begin{gathered}
S(x) = (1 - \exp (-x)) / x\quad (\mathrm{slope} \mathrm{loading}; S(0) = 1) \\
C(x) = S(x) - \exp (-x)\quad (\mathrm{curvature}/\mathrm{hump} \mathrm{loading}; C(0) = 0, C(\infty ) = 0)
\end{gathered}
$$

Svensson zero rate and forward rate:

$$
\begin{gathered}
z(m) = \mathrm{beta0} + \mathrm{beta1} \cdot  S(\mathrm{x1}) + \mathrm{beta2} \cdot  C(\mathrm{x1}) + \mathrm{beta3} \cdot  C(\mathrm{x2}) \\
f(m) = \mathrm{beta0} + \mathrm{beta1} \cdot  \exp (-\mathrm{x1}) + \mathrm{beta2} \cdot  \mathrm{x1} \cdot  \exp (-\mathrm{x1}) + \mathrm{beta3} \cdot  \mathrm{x2} \cdot  \exp (-\mathrm{x2})
\end{gathered}
$$

- beta1 AND beta2 both use tau1; ONLY beta3 uses tau2. Nelson-Siegel = the same formulas with $\mathrm{beta3} = 0$(no tau2).
- Limits: $m \to  0$: $z = f = \mathrm{beta0} + \mathrm{beta1}$(the "instantaneous short rate"); m -> infinity: $z = f = \mathrm{beta0}$.
  z approaches beta0 slowly (like 1/m); f approaches it exponentially. At $m = 0$ use $S = 1, C = 0$(no 0/0).
- Discount factor $\mathrm{DF}(m) = \exp (-z(m) m)$; $\mathrm{bond\ price}=\sum_j\mathrm{CF}_j\mathrm{DF}(t_j)$; forward between $\mathrm{m1} < \mathrm{m2}$:
  $F(\mathrm{m1}, \mathrm{m2}) = [z(\mathrm{m2}) \mathrm{m2} - z(\mathrm{m1}) \mathrm{m1}] / (\mathrm{m2} - \mathrm{m1})$ (continuous).
- Original NS (1987) zero form: $z = \mathrm{beta0} + (\mathrm{beta1} + \mathrm{beta2}) \cdot  S(x) - \mathrm{beta2} \cdot  \exp (-x)$ is algebraically identical to the above.
- Diebold-Li (2006) form: $y(m) = \mathrm{L1} + \mathrm{L2} \cdot  S(\lambda  m) + \mathrm{L3} \cdot  C(\lambda  m)$ = NS with $\tau  = 1/\lambda$,
  L1 = level, L2 = slope, L3 = curvature. DL measure m in MONTHS and fix $\lambda$ for all dates at the value they say puts the
  peak of C at 30 months. Use the $\lambda$ value the task gives: solving dC/dm = 0 at exactly 30 months gives a value slightly
  below the one DL print. A $\lambda$ per month becomes per year by multiplying by 12. With $\lambda$ fixed the model is linear in
  L1..L3, so fit by ordinary least squares on each date.

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Which parameterization the task uses
atoms.text:
## Which parameterization the task uses
- The same curve can be written with decay times ($x = m / \tau$) or decay rates ($x = \lambda  m, \lambda  = 1/\tau$). The name of a
  parameter does not decide which: some texts and tasks write the decay TIME as $\lambda$.
- Decide from the task's formula for the loadings, or from units the task states explicitly. If the task gives neither, report
  the parameter in the form you fitted and say which form it is; do not take a reciprocal only because an output field is named $\lambda$.
- Before writing the outputs, plug the parameters you will report into the formula you used and check that they reproduce your
  fitted curve and the fit error you report.

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Compounding conversions (apply to OUTPUTS only if the task asks)
atoms.text:
## Compounding conversions (apply to OUTPUTS only if the task asks)
- Annual: $R_{a} = \exp (z) - 1$, $z = \ln (1 + R_{a})$. Periodic k per year: $R_{k} = k (\exp (z/k) - 1)$, $z = k \ln (1 + R_{k}/k)$.
- If the observed yields are annual / semi-annual (e.g. bond-equivalent) convert them to continuous BEFORE fitting, or fit in
  their convention and say so; never mix. Percent vs decimal: keep one unit throughout.

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Common mistakes
atoms.text:
## Common mistakes
- Pairing beta3 with tau1, or giving beta2 its own tau2: wrong curve (the error can be hundreds of basis points).
- Using forward loadings ($\exp (-x), x \exp (-x)$) in the zero-rate formula or vice versa.
- Switching between decay time and decay rate (taking 1/x) when the task's parameter is already in the form you fitted;
  reporting parameters that do not reproduce your own fitted curve; using a $\lambda$ calibrated for months with maturities in years.
- Evaluating S(0) as 0/0 (NaN) at $m = 0$.
- Reporting fitted parameters from one local optimum without checking the fit residuals.

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Applicability and limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and limits
- Good for smoothing and interpolation inside the observed maturity range; extrapolation is governed by beta0.
- Does not reprice every bond exactly (a least-squares fit); if exact repricing is required, bootstrap instead.
- Parameters are unstable when the problem is ill-conditioned (Gilli et al. 2010); compare fitted curves, not parameters.

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Sources
Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| $m$ | time to maturity (years unless the task says months) | years |
| beta0 | long-run level: z and f tend to beta0 as $m \to  \infty$(must be > 0) | rate, decimal (5% = 0.05) |
| beta1 | $\mathrm{slope}: z(0) = f(0) = \mathrm{beta0} + \mathrm{beta1}$ | rate |
| beta2 | first hump/trough, decay tau1 | rate |
| beta3 | second hump/trough, decay tau2 (Svensson only) | rate |
| tau1, tau2 | decay times (> 0), same time unit as m | years |
| $\lambda$ | an ambiguous name: Diebold-Li use it for the decay RATE $1/\tau$ (loadings in $\lambda m$); other texts and tasks use it for the decay TIME $\tau$ itself (loadings in $m/\lambda$). See "Which parameterization" below | depends |

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Fitting (estimate the betas and taus)
atoms.text:
## Fitting (estimate the betas and taus)
- Yield errors: minimize $\sum _{i} (z_{\mathrm{model}}(m_{i}) - z_{\mathrm{obs}}(m_{i}))^{2}$ over zero yields, or over model-implied vs observed YTMs of coupon bonds.
- Price errors: model price $\operatorname{P}_{i} = \sum _{j} \mathrm{CF}_{ij} \exp (-z(t_{ij}) t_{ij})$, minimize $\sum _{i} w_{i} (\operatorname{P}_{i} - \operatorname{P}_{\mathrm{obs},i})^{2}$. Unweighted price errors
  underweight short bonds; weights $w_{i} = 1/D_{i}^{2}$($D_{i}$ = modified duration) make price errors approximate yield errors.
  Use full (dirty) prices for cash flows; if clean prices are given add accrued interest.
- Nonlinear least squares (e.g. bounded trust-region). Bounds: $\mathrm{beta0} > 0, \mathrm{beta0} + \mathrm{beta1} > 0$ if rates must be positive,
  $\mathrm{tau1}, \mathrm{tau2} > 0$ within the observed maturity range. The objective is non-convex with local minima (Gilli et al. 2010):
  use several starting points (e.g. beta0 from the longest yield, beta1 from shortest minus longest, $\mathrm{betas2}/3 = 0$, a few $\tau$ pairs)
  and keep the lowest objective; or profile: grid over (tau1, tau2), OLS for the betas at each grid point, keep the best.
- If tau1 ~ tau2 the beta2 and beta3 loadings are nearly collinear and the betas explode in opposite directions: impose
  $\mathrm{tau1} < \mathrm{tau2}$(or a minimum gap) and report the curve, not individual betas, as the stable output.

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Setting and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Setting and assumptions
- Linear regression $y_{t} = x_{t}' b + u_{t}$, $t = 1\ldots T, k$ regressors (constant included in k). The errors may be heteroskedastic and
  serially correlated; correlation is assumed to die out with the lag. OLS point estimates are unchanged; only the covariance changes.
- A sample mean is the special case $x_{t} = 1$ ($k = 1$): use it for the mean of a return series, of Fama-MacBeth slopes, of a strategy P&L.
- Time order matters: rows must be sorted by time with no gaps; HAC is not for a pure cross-section.

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning |
|---|---|
| $T, k$ | number of time observations; number of regressors including the constant |
| $L$ | maximum lag ("maxlags", "truncation lag"); integer >= 0; L = 0 means White (no autocorrelation) |
| $w_{l}$ | Bartlett weight of lag l |
| $\hat{u}_{t}$ | OLS residual; for a mean, $y_{t} - \bar{y}$ |
The covariance is in squared units of the coefficient per the data frequency; do not annualize unless the task says so.

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Formulas (OLS)
atoms.text:
## Formulas (OLS)

$$
\hat{b} = (X'X)^{-1} X'y
$$

The score vector has $k$ components:

$$
g_{t} = x_{t} \cdot  \hat{u}_{t}
$$

A $k$ by $k$ SUM, not divided by $T - l$:

$$
\Gamma _{l} = \sum _{t=l+1}^{T} g_{t} g_{t-l}'
$$

$$
w_{l} = 1 - l / (L + 1)
$$

For $l = 0\ldots L$.

$$
S = \Gamma _{0} + \sum _{l=1}^{L} w_{l} (\Gamma _{l} + \Gamma _{l}')
$$

Sandwich covariance:

$$
V_{\mathrm{NW}} = (X'X)^{-1} S (X'X)^{-1}
$$

$$
\mathrm{se}_{j} = \sqrt{V_{\mathrm{NW}}[j,j]}
$$

$$
t_{j} = (\hat{b}_{j} - \mathrm{b0}_{j}) / \mathrm{se}_{j}
$$

With the small-sample scaling, $V_{\mathrm{NW},\mathrm{adj}} = T/(T-k) \cdot  V_{\mathrm{NW}}$ (Stata `newey` applies this factor; see below for statsmodels).

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Formulas (sample mean)
atoms.text:
## Formulas (sample mean)
Divisor $T$ for every $l$:

$$
\gamma _{l} = (1/T) \sum _{t=l+1}^{T} (y_{t} - \bar{y})(y_{t-l} - \bar{y})
$$

Long-run variance:

$$
\Omega  = \gamma _{0} + 2 \sum _{l=1}^{L} (1 - l/(L+1)) \gamma _{l}
$$

$$
\mathrm{se}(\bar{y}) = \sqrt{\Omega  / T}
$$

Optionally multiply by $\sqrt{T/(T-1)}$.

$$
t = (\bar{y} - \mathrm{mu0}) / \mathrm{se}(\bar{y})
$$

Note $\gamma _{0}$ uses divisor T, so with $L = 0$ this is $\operatorname{sd}_{\mathrm{pop}} / \sqrt{T}$, not the usual `sd(ddof=1) / sqrt(T)`.

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Choosing L
atoms.text:
## Choosing L
- If the task gives L, use it. For overlapping h-period returns ($h > 1$ periods summed each observation) use at least $L = h - 1$.
- Rule of thumb: $L = \operatorname{floor}(4 (T/100)^{2/9})$ (statsmodels' default when no lag is given to $\mathrm{cov}_{\mathrm{hac}}$).
- Newey-West (1994) automatic lag (Bartlett): with a scalar series $v_{t}$ (the demeaned series for a mean) and
  $n = 4 (T/100)^{2/9}$ rounded to an integer (implementations differ: floor or ceil),
  $\sigma _{j} = (1/T) \sum _{t=j+1}^{T} v_{t} v_{t-j}$, $\mathrm{s0} = \sigma _{0} + 2 \sum _{j=1}^{n} \sigma _{j}$, $\mathrm{s1} = 2 \sum _{j=1}^{n} j \sigma _{j}$,
  $\gamma  = 1.1447 (\mathrm{s1}/\mathrm{s0})^{2/3}$, bandwidth $m = \gamma  T^{1/3}$, then $L = \operatorname{floor}(m)$(R sandwich) or ceil(m) (arch); weights 1 - l/(L+1).
  For a vector $g_{t}$ the series is a weighted sum of its components; the weighting is implementation-specific.

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / statsmodels mapping (checked on statsmodels 0.15)
atoms.text:
## statsmodels mapping (checked on statsmodels 0.15)
- `sm.OLS(y, X).fit(cov_type='HAC', cov_kwds={'maxlags': L})` = $V_{\mathrm{NW}}$ above with Bartlett weights, **no** T/(T-k) factor
  (`use_correction` defaults to False in `fit`), p-values from the **normal** distribution (`use_t=False` by default).
- `cov_kwds={'maxlags': L, 'use_correction': True}` multiplies by T/(T-k). `kernel='uniform'` gives equal weights (not Newey-West).
- `statsmodels.stats.sandwich_covariance.cov_hac(results, nlags=None)` defaults differ: **`use_correction=True`** and
  nlags = floor(4(T/100)^(2/9)).
- HAC standard error of a mean = `sm.OLS(y, np.ones(T)).fit(cov_type='HAC', cov_kwds={'maxlags': L}).bse[0]`.

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Common variants and mistakes
atoms.text:
## Common variants and mistakes
- Divisor of $\gamma _{l}$: T (Newey-West, PSD) vs T - l (not guaranteed PSD); weights 1 - l/(L+1), not 1 - l/L.
- Lag definition: L counts lags beyond 0; "L lags" includes lags 1..L. Some software instead takes a bandwidth b with weights 1 - l/b; then $b = L + 1$.
- Not demeaning the series for a mean, or forgetting the factor 2 on the autocovariances.
- Reporting statsmodels HAC p-values (normal) when the task asks for t(T - k) p-values, or vice versa.
- Asymptotic Wald alternative to GRS: $T \alpha ' \Sigma _{\mathrm{mle}}^{-1} \alpha  / (1 + \mu ' \hat{\Omega}^{-1} \mu ) \sim \mathrm{chi2}(N)$; use only if the task asks.

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- NW is consistent as T grows with L growing slowly; in small samples with persistent series it understates the variance
  (our AR(1) simulations: coverage of nominal 95% intervals well below 95% when autocorrelation is strong and L is small).
- GRS is exact only under iid normal errors and traded factors; with non-normal or autocorrelated errors use a GMM/HAC Wald test.

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Sources
Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test of joint zero alphas
atoms.text:
## Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test of joint zero alphas
Time-series regressions $R_{it} = \alpha _{i} + \beta _{i}' f_{t} + e_{it}$ for N test assets (excess returns) on L' traded factors (excess returns),
$t = 1\ldots T$, errors iid normal over time with covariance $\Sigma$. H0: all $\alpha _{i} = 0$.

Unbiased residual covariance, $N$ by $N$:

$$
\hat{\Sigma} = (1/(T - L' - 1)) \sum _{t} e_{t} e_{t}'
$$

$\hat{\mu}$ denotes the factor sample means. Divisor $T$:

$$
\hat{\Omega} = (1/T) \sum _{t} (f_{t} - \hat{\mu})(f_{t} - \hat{\mu})'
$$

$$
\mathrm{GRS} = (T/N) \cdot  ((T - N - L')/(T - L' - 1)) \cdot  \hat{\alpha}' \hat{\Sigma}^{-1} \hat{\alpha} / (1 + \hat{\mu}' \hat{\Omega}^{-1} \hat{\mu})
$$

Under $\mathrm{H0}$:

$$
\mathrm{GRS} \sim F(N, T - N - L')
$$

The p-value is $1 - F_{\mathrm{cdf}}(\mathrm{GRS}; N, T - N - L')$.Equivalent form: $((T - N - L')/N) \cdot  \alpha ' \Sigma _{\mathrm{mle}}^{-1} \alpha  / (1 + \mu ' \hat{\Omega}^{-1} \mu )$ with $\Sigma _{\mathrm{mle}}$ = residual
cross-products / T. Do not mix the two ($\Sigma _{\mathrm{mle}}$ with the T/(T-L'-1) factor over-rejects). One factor: the denominator is
1 + (factor Sharpe ratio)^2, with mean and sd at the data frequency. Requires $T > N + L'$ so $\hat{\Sigma}$ is invertible.
