[1] Israel, Rosenthal and Wei (2001), Finding Generators for Markov Chains via Empirical Transition Matrices, with Applications to Credit Ratings, Sections 2–3. [Author manuscript](https://www.probability.ca/jeff/ftpdir/wei.pdf).

[2] Lencastre, Raischel, Lind and Rogers (2014), Are credit ratings time-homogeneous and Markov?, Section 3, including the exposure-time estimator and distinction between assumptions. [Author manuscript](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.8018).

Cohort pooling, conditional normalization, path-likelihood maximization and count-test formulas above are statistical definitions/derivations. State mappings, censoring decisions and issuer populations remain data-specific. This reference does not prescribe an agency's current taxonomy or reconcile incompatible event datasets.

atoms.title: Estimating rating transitions and continuous-time generators / Reconciling reported counts
atoms.text:
## Reconciling reported counts

Build the reported cohort sizes and their total from one explicitly selected origin population. Choose `origin_rows` from the task's definition; a total for non-default origins excludes default-to-default observations, while an explicitly all-origin total includes them. Apply observation corrections once to counts before selecting and normalizing.

```python
# adjusted_counts: cohort x origin x destination; counts, not probabilities. Keep it unchanged.
population_counts = adjusted_counts[:, origin_rows, :]   # origin_rows chosen from the task's definition
cohort_sizes = population_counts.sum(axis=2)
reported_total = int(cohort_sizes.sum())                   # the summary total: this value, not a sum over adjusted_counts
assert reported_total == int(population_counts.sum())
```

Generate the cohort table and summary from these same objects. An identity fallback for an empty probability row does not add an observed issuer: keep its count and cohort size zero. Recompute both after changing records. Do not pool normalized probability matrices as though they were counts.

atoms.title: Estimating rating transitions and continuous-time generators / 2. Withdrawal and censoring
atoms.text:
## 2. Withdrawal and censoring

A missing rating or withdrawn issuer is not intrinsically a default or a surviving credit. Dropping an unknown destination and renormalizing estimates a distribution conditional on retained observations; it is not automatically an unbiased unconditional transition estimate. A survival analysis can retain observed time before independent right censoring. Informative withdrawal may require a richer observation model.

Removing an excluded destination set W from an already normalized row gives a conditional retained-state distribution, when its denominator is positive:

$$
\operatorname{P}_{\mathrm{conditional},ij} = \operatorname{P}_{ij} / (1-\sum _{k \in  W} \operatorname{P}_{ik}),  j \;\text{not}\; \in  W
$$

Independent event records can resolve previously unobserved outcomes only when the population, origin, event definition and window agree. A revised count must not count the same issuer twice. A supplied reconciliation rule is a data convention, not a universal identity between withdrawals and defaults.

When several source grades are merged into one bucket, apply such a correction at the bucket level: add up the event counts of every source grade mapped to the bucket, then compare that sum with the bucket's row of the merged count matrix. Looking up `event_counts[bucket_name]` reads only the source grade whose name equals the bucket's and drops the others merged into it.

```python
true_by_bucket = {}
for grade, n in event_counts.items():          # every source grade in the event table
    b = bucket_of(grade)                       # the same mapping used to merge the matrix
    if b is not None:
        true_by_bucket[b] = true_by_bucket.get(b, 0) + n
for b, i in bucket_index.items():              # non-absorbing origin buckets only
    hidden = max(true_by_bucket.get(b, 0) - counts[i, absorbing], 0)
    counts[i, absorbing] += hidden
```

atoms.title: Estimating rating transitions and continuous-time generators / Aligning and normalizing a labelled matrix
atoms.text:
## Aligning and normalizing a labelled matrix

When the task asks for a supplied matrix to be renormalized over its retained columns → put the labels on the index before any arithmetic, so the numbers and their row sums share one index; dividing a frame on a position index by sums on a label index gives NaN. Treat a zero row as the task says.

```python
numeric = raw.set_index(label_column).loc[:, retained_columns].astype(float)
row_sums = numeric.sum(axis=1)
assert row_sums.gt(0).all()
normalized = numeric.div(row_sums, axis=0)
assert np.isfinite(normalized.to_numpy()).all()
assert np.allclose(normalized.sum(axis=1), 1)
```

After correcting such a matrix, recompute the deviations and their summary statistics and rewrite every file they appear in.

atoms.title: Realized variance with microstructure noise: Bandi-Russell noise variance and optimal sampling, bipower variation, two-scales RV / Model and setting
atoms.text:
## Model and setting
- Observed log price = efficient log price + noise: $y_{t} = x_{t} + \eta _{t}$. x is a continuous semimartingale with integrated variance
  

$$
\mathrm{IV} = \int  \sigma _{s}^{2} \mathrm{d}s
$$

 over the period (usually one trading day). $\eta$ is iid, mean 0, variance $\sigma _{\eta}^{2}$, independent of x.
- Intraday return j of day i: $r_{j} = y_{t_{j}} - y_{t_{j-1}} = (x_{t_{j}} - x_{t_{j-1}}) + \mathrm{eps}_{j}$, $\mathrm{eps}_{j} = \eta _{j} - \eta _{j-1}$.
  So $\operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}) = 2 \sigma _{\eta}^{2}$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(\mathrm{eps}_{j}, \mathrm{eps}_{j-1}) = -\sigma _{\eta}^{2}$: noise makes high-frequency returns negatively autocorrelated (MA(1)).
- Use LOG returns of consecutive prices inside one day. Do not include the overnight return or the jump from day i's last price to
  day i+1's first price. M = number of returns in the day = number of prices in the day minus 1 (zero returns count).

atoms.title: Realized variance with microstructure noise: Bandi-Russell noise variance and optimal sampling, bipower variation, two-scales RV / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| $r_{j}, j = 1\ldots M$ | intraday log returns of one day at the chosen sampling frequency | log units |
| $M$ | returns per day; $M^{*}$ = optimal count; interval = (trading-day length) / M | count |
| IV, Q | integrated variance and integrated quarticity $\int  \sigma ^{4} \mathrm{d}s$ of one day | per day, per day^2 |
| $\sigma _{\eta}^{2}$ | variance of the noise in the $\log  \mathrm{PRICE}$ | log units^2 |
| $\operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}), \operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{4})$ | 2nd / 4th moment of the noise in RETURNS; $\operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}) = 2 \sigma _{\eta}^{2}$ | log units^2, ^4 |
| $N_{d}$ | number of days pooled | count |

atoms.title: Realized variance with microstructure noise: Bandi-Russell noise variance and optimal sampling, bipower variation, two-scales RV / Variants and common mistakes
atoms.text:
## Variants and common mistakes
- Price noise vs return noise: "noise variance" usually means $\sigma _{\eta}^{2} = \mathrm{RV}/(2M); \operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}) = \mathrm{RV}/M$ is twice that. The rule of thumb
  uses E(eps^2); plugging $\sigma _{\eta}^{2}$ instead makes $M^{*}$ too large by a factor 4^(1/3).
- n / M counts RETURNS, not prices. Pooled estimates divide the pooled sum by the total number of returns, not by days times a nominal M.
- Per-day vs pooled: per-day RV/(2M) gives one noise estimate per day; pooled (Prop. 1b) assumes the noise is iid across days. Use what the task asks.
- Q^ from the highest frequency is dominated by noise; compute it from sparse returns. Do not use $Q = \mathrm{RV}^{2}$ unless the task says so.
- BV constant is $\pi/2$, not $2/\pi$. Some papers multiply BV by M/(M-1) (finite-sample variant). BV is robust to jumps, NOT to noise: compute it at a sparse frequency.
- Sparse RV at M returns: sample every (day length / M) using the last price at or before each grid time (previous tick), starting at the open.
- Simple returns, percentage returns, or including the overnight return all change the number.

atoms.title: Realized variance with microstructure noise: Bandi-Russell noise variance and optimal sampling, bipower variation, two-scales RV / Sources
Realized variance with microstructure noise: Bandi-Russell noise variance and optimal sampling, bipower variation, two-scales RV / Formulas
atoms.text:
## Formulas
Realized variance of one day: $\mathrm{RV} = \sum _{j=1}^{M} r_{j}^{2}$. On a fixed efficient-price grid define $\mathrm{RV}_x=\sum_{j=1}^M(x_j-x_{j-1})^2$. Conditional on that path and independent price noise, the exact expectation is $\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{RV}\mid x]=\mathrm{RV}_x+2M\sigma_\eta^2$. For a continuous Ito process, $\mathrm{RV}_x$ converges to IV as the mesh vanishes, but need not equal it on a finite grid. Accordingly $\mathrm{E}[\widehat\sigma_\eta^2\mid x]=\sigma_\eta^2+\mathrm{RV}_x/(2M)$ for the estimator below. Adjacent return-noise covariance is $-\sigma_\eta^2$; non-iid or endogenous price noise changes these identities.

Bandi-Russell noise moments, from returns at the HIGHEST available frequency (every price change / tick):
Per day:

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{E}}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}) = \mathrm{RV} / M
$$

$$
\hat{\sigma}_{\eta}^{2} = \mathrm{RV} / (2 M)
$$

Pooled:

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{E}}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}) = \sum _{i} \sum _{j} r_{ij}^{2} / \sum _{i} M_{i}
$$

The denominator equals $N_{d} M$ when every day has $M$ returns.

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{E}}(\mathrm{eps}^{4}) = \sum _{i} \sum _{j} r_{ij}^{4} / \sum _{i} M_{i}
$$

$$
\hat{\sigma}_{\eta}^{2} = \widehat{\mathrm{E}}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}) / 2
$$

Conditional on the efficient path, $\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{RV}/(2M)\mid x]-\sigma_\eta^2=\mathrm{RV}_x/(2M)$. This is an upward conditional-mean bias, not an inequality for every random estimate. For a continuous efficient price, $\mathrm{RV}_x$ approaches $\mathrm{IV}$ as sampling becomes fine, so this bias vanishes.

Quarticity (Barndorff-Nielsen & Shephard), per day, from LOWER-frequency returns (Bandi & Russell 2006 use 15-minute returns), $M_{q}$ returns:

$$
\widehat Q= (M_{q} / 3) \cdot  \sum _{j=1}^{M_{q}} r_{j}^{4}
$$

MSE-optimal number of returns per day (Bandi & Russell 2006 Prop. 3; 2008):

$$
\mathrm{MSE}(M) \approx 2 Q / M + M \beta  + M^{2} \alpha
$$

$$
\alpha  = (\operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}))^{2}
$$

$$
\beta  = 2 \operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{4}) - 3 (\operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}))^{2}
$$

$M^{*}$ solves the exact first-order condition:

$$
2 M^{3} \alpha  + M^{2} \beta  - 2 Q = 0
$$

Rule of thumb (Prop. 4; good when $M^{*}$ is large):

$$
M^{*} \approx ( Q / (\operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}))^{2} )^{1/3}
$$

For one $M^{*}$ over many days, use the average of the daily Q^ (or compute M*_i per day with Q^_i). Optimal interval = day length / $M^{*}$.

Bipower variation (Barndorff-Nielsen & Shephard 2004), per day:

$$
\mathrm{BV} = \mathrm{mu1}^{-2} \cdot  \sum _{j=2}^{M} \vert r_{j}\vert  \vert r_{j-1}\vert ,   \mathrm{mu1} = \operatorname{E}\vert Z\vert  = \sqrt{2/\pi},  \mathrm{so} \mathrm{mu1}^{-2} = \pi /2
$$

Jump part of quadratic variation: $\mathrm{RV} - \mathrm{BV}$ (often floored at 0). Without noise and jumps, BV and RV both estimate IV.

Two-scales realized variance (Zhang, Mykland & Ait-Sahalia 2005), one day with log prices $y_{0}$..$y_{n}$ (n returns):

$$
\mathrm{RV}_{\mathrm{all}} = \sum _{j=1}^{n} (y_{j} - y_{j-1})^{2}
$$

$\mathrm{RV}^{(k)}$ sums squared differences over consecutive points of subgrid $k$.

$$
\mathrm{subgrid}_{k} = \{y_{k-1}, y_{k-1+K}, y_{k-1+2K}, \ldots \}
$$

For $k = 1\ldots K$.

$$
\mathrm{RV}_{\mathrm{avg}} = (1/K) \sum _{k} \mathrm{RV}^{(k)}
$$

$$
\bar{n} = (n - K + 1) / K
$$

$$
\mathrm{TSRV} = \mathrm{RV}_{\mathrm{avg}} - (\bar{n} / n) \mathrm{RV}_{\mathrm{all}}
$$

Small-sample adjusted:

$$
\mathrm{TSRV}_{\mathrm{adj}} = \mathrm{TSRV} / (1 - \bar{n} / n)
$$

Noise variance (ZMA), same as Bandi–Russell per day:

$$
\hat{\sigma}_{\eta}^{2} = \mathrm{RV}_{\mathrm{all}} / (2 n)
$$

$K$ grows like $c n^{2/3}$.
Annualization: annual variance = (periods per year from the task, commonly 252 trading days) * mean of daily estimates;
volatility = sqrt of that. Average VARIANCES across days, then take the square root. Daily vol = $\sqrt{\text{daily RV}}$.

atoms.title: Realized variance with microstructure noise: Bandi-Russell noise variance and optimal sampling, bipower variation, two-scales RV / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- iid noise independent of the price is assumed. Serially dependent noise or noise correlated with x breaks RV/(2M) and the $M^{*}$ formula.
- With finite M a jump J still inflates BV by about $\vert J\vert  \sqrt{2 \pi  \mathrm{IV} / M}; \mathrm{RV} - \mathrm{BV}$ is then a noisy jump estimate.
- TSRV subgrids lose up to $K-1$ edge intervals. With driftless constant intraday volatility and an equidistant grid,

$$
\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{TSRV}]
=\mathrm{IV}\frac{(n-K+1)(K-1)}{nK}.
$$

  The unadjusted relative downward bias is about $K/n+1/K$, not just $K/n$. For the adjusted estimator,

$$
\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{TSRV}_{\mathrm{adj}}]
=\mathrm{IV}\frac{n-K+1}{n+1},
$$

  whose relative downward bias is $K/(n+1)$. These finite-grid expectations use the stated constant-volatility setup; changing endpoint handling changes the edge terms.
- In a simulation, separate the realized efficient-grid quantity from its continuous target: conditional on $x$, $\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{RV}\mid x]-\mathrm{RV}_x=M\mathrm{E}(\mathrm{eps}^2)$. Comparing against $\mathrm{IV}$ adds efficient-price discretization error; it is not an exact pathwise identity.

atoms.title: Backtest of a portfolio rebalanced from rolling estimates (regimes, inverse volatility, risk metrics): workflow (1)
atoms.text:
Use this when weights are set on scheduled dates from rolling-window estimates (correlation eigenvalues, a regime label, volatilities) and the realised strategy is then evaluated. Read the scenario table in section 16 of the VaR and ES conventions note first: it says which rebalance dates, initial holdings and earning day fit the task's wording. This workflow is the code for the first row of that table (estimates on a fixed calendar, no stated start); the other rows change only the `before_first` argument. Every step ends with a check; fix a failed check before moving on.

Each step below shows one common setting. Tasks vary; before coding, settle each row of this table from the task text and change the code accordingly.

| Step | Choice | Options and the wording that selects them |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | Matrix for the eigenvalues | correlation (denominator n, unit-free) or covariance (denominator = trace, keeps scale); "correlation" / "covariance" in the text decides |
| 2 | Estimate window | equal-weighted rolling window of W rows, or exponentially weighted with a stated half-life; expanding window when the text says "all data to date" |
| 2 | Which rows an estimate for day t uses | rows before t when it sets day t's regime or weights; rows through t when it is dated at the close of t and used from t + 1 |
| 2 | Regime rule | fixed thresholds with the stated comparison signs; thresholds that move with the indicator's own moving average and dispersion; a standardized shift (short minus long average over a long standard deviation); the text names which |
| 2 | Weights | inverse volatility (1/sigma), inverse variance (1/sigma^2), equal risk contribution (solve for equal contributions), or equal weight; then scaled by a regime budget, by a volatility target, or not scaled. A budget below 1 leaves cash that earns nothing unless the text gives a cash rate |
| 3 | Rebalance calendar | month-end rows, month-start rows, weekly, every N rows, or on regime changes; dates are rows present in the data |
| 3 | Last data row | excluded when weights set at a close earn from the next day; included when the text rebalances at the open of the same day |
| 4 | Holdings before the first rebalance | equal, cash, first_estimate, start_at_first: see section 16 of the VaR and ES conventions note |
| 4 | When new weights earn | from the next day (set at a close), or the same day (set at the open); never both a loop delay and an extra shift |
| 4 | Costs | none unless stated; a proportional cost charges turnover sum(abs(w_new - w_old)) at each rebalance |
| 5 | Annualised return | arithmetic mean times periods per year, or geometric (1 + total)^(periods/n) - 1; the text says "mean daily return x 252" or "CAGR" |
| 5 | Sharpe ratio | zero risk-free rate unless given; ddof as stated |
| 5 | Drawdown | on the wealth path, as a positive magnitude unless the text reports it negative |
| 5 | VaR / CVaR of the strategy | one trailing window, the full evaluated sample, or a rolling series (then the text says which statistic of it); quantile rule and tail mean per conventions sections 2 and 3 |
| 5 | Average weight of an asset | over all evaluated days (held weights) or over rebalance dates (target weights); the text's "average weight" without a qualifier is the time average of the held weights |

1. Clean, count, cut the window.
```python
clean, counts = clean_return_table(raw, "date", value_cols, "last", "drop_row")   # conventions section 9
n_valid = len(clean)                                   # count of valid observations: rows after cleaning
r = clean.iloc[-window_n:] if window_n else clean      # estimation window, cut from the cleaned table
n, W = r.shape[1], rolling_window
```
Check: `n_valid >= len(r)`; print both; a reported count of valid observations is `n_valid`, not `len(r)`.

atoms.title: Backtest of a portfolio rebalanced from rolling estimates (regimes, inverse volatility, risk metrics): workflow (2)
atoms.text:
2. Rolling estimates known before each day.
```python
est = {}
for t in range(W, len(r)):
    win = r.iloc[t - W:t]                              # rows t-W .. t-1: known before day t
    ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh(win.corr().values)[::-1]   # symmetric decomposition, largest first
    ar = ev[:k].sum() / ev.sum()                       # share of the top-k eigenvalues
    regime = classify(ar)                              # thresholds and comparison signs exactly as the task states
    iv = 1.0 / win.std(ddof=1)                         # ddof as the task states
    est[r.index[t]] = dict(ar=ar, lam1=ev[0], regime=regime, w=iv / iv.sum() * budget[regime])
days = list(est)                                       # the evaluated sample
mp_threshold = (1 + np.sqrt(n / W)) ** 2               # Marchenko-Pastur upper edge for a W x n correlation matrix
```
Check: `len(days) == len(r) - W`; the trace of each correlation matrix is n; `mp_threshold > 1`. Summary statistics of these series (mean, standard deviation) use the ddof the task states elsewhere, consistently.

3. Rebalance dates.
```python
d = pd.Series(days, index=days)
month_end = d[d.groupby(d.dt.to_period("M")).transform("max") == d].index   # from days that have an estimate
rebalance = [x for x in month_end if x != r.index[-1]]                      # a weight set at a close needs a later day
n_rebalances = len(rebalance)
```
Check: `all(x in est for x in rebalance)`; `n_rebalances` is at most the number of calendar months in `days`.

4. Holdings before the first rebalance, then the daily loop.
```python
if before_first == "equal":                            # fixed calendar, no stated start, no cash account (table row 1)
    w = pd.Series(1.0 / n, index=r.columns)
elif before_first == "cash":                           # the task says flat or in cash until the first rebalance
    w = pd.Series(0.0, index=r.columns)
elif before_first == "first_estimate":                 # the task allows an allocation at the start
    w = est[days[0]]["w"]
elif before_first == "start_at_first":                 # the evaluation starts after the first rebalance
    days = [x for x in days if x > rebalance[0]]
    w = est[rebalance[0]]["w"]
port = []
held = []
for x in days:
    held.append(w)
    port.append(float((w * r.loc[x]).sum()))           # day x earns with the weights held at its start
    if x in rebalance:
        w = est[x]["w"]                                # the new weights earn from the next day
port = pd.Series(port, index=days)
```
Check: `len(port) == len(days)`; no other shift or forward-fill is applied on top of this loop (that would delay the weights twice); write in a comment which `before_first` reading the task text supports.

5. Performance and risk.
```python
ann_ret = port.mean() * periods_per_year
ann_vol = port.std(ddof=1) * np.sqrt(periods_per_year)
sharpe = ann_ret / ann_vol                             # zero risk-free rate unless the task gives one
wealth = (1 + port).cumprod()
max_dd = (1 - wealth / wealth.cummax()).max()          # positive magnitude
tail = port.iloc[-cvar_window:].to_numpy()             # one trailing window of realised returns
var_t, cvar_t = empirical_var_es(tail, level, q_method, es_rule)   # conventions sections 2 and 3, on the window only
win_rate = (port > 0).mean()
mean_w = pd.DataFrame(held).mean()                                 # time average of held weights; see the table for other readings
```
Check: `len(tail) == cvar_window`; `cvar_t >= var_t > 0` as losses; with a short window and a high level the tail may hold one observation, so state the quantile rule used.

6. Write the deliverables and read them back: every requested key present, counts are integers, magnitudes reported as the task states (positive losses and drawdowns).

atoms.title: Security events, earnings comparisons and contingent claims
atoms.text: Use this note to interpret financial quantities before applying a prescribed data recipe. Explicit contract and data definitions determine adjustment, classification and settlement. These concepts do not replace a supplied algorithm or invent an undefined business metric.

atoms.title: Security events, earnings comparisons and contingent claims / Splits, dividends and share units
atoms.text:
## Splits, dividends and share units

For a split with ratio $R>0$ new shares per old share, economic ownership is unchanged by the split itself. The share-count and theoretical ex-split price transformations are:

$$
n_{\mathrm{new}}=Rn_{\mathrm{old}},\qquad
P_{\mathrm{new}}=P_{\mathrm{old}}/R
$$

Historical volume expressed in new-share units changes by the inverse price factor. A dividend per old share and a dividend per new share cannot be added without a common share basis. A cash dividend moves value from the company to the shareholder; its ex-date, record date and payment date are distinct. A backward-adjusted price is a constructed series, not the historical transaction price. Vendor formulas can use different reference prices and reinvestment assumptions.

For one share held across an interval with no split, initial price $P_0$, final price $P_1$ and cash dividend $D$, the simple holding-period return before costs is:

$$
R=\frac{P_1+D-P_0}{P_0}
$$

With splits, first express the final holding and all distributions in consistent units. Summing raw dividend labels is not automatically the cash received per original share.

atoms.title: Security events, earnings comparisons and contingent claims / Earnings surprise
atoms.text:
## Earnings surprise

Let $A$ be reported EPS and $E$ a comparable consensus estimate. Their unscaled surprise is:

$$
U=A-E
$$

The EPS definition, share basis, currency, fiscal period and information date must agree. Dividing by analyst-estimate dispersion and dividing by the historical variability of seasonal earnings changes produce different standardized surprises. Neither denominator is automatically the standard error of the consensus mean. A zero denominator does not mathematically define a finite standardized score; a stipulated fallback remains a reporting convention. Percentage surprise with a near-zero benchmark is unstable, even when a deterministic classification rule is provided.

atoms.title: Security events, earnings comparisons and contingent claims / Complementary event claims
atoms.text:
## Complementary event claims

Let $I$ indicate a defined event. A unit YES claim pays $I$ and its truly complementary NO claim pays $1-I$ at the same settlement date. Their combined payoff is:

$$
I+(1-I)=1
$$

With discount factor $D(t,T)$, matched settlement and no costs or counterparty friction, combined value is $D(t,T)$. Different event definitions, cancellation terms, settlement currencies or payment dates can break the apparent complementarity. Quote dislocation is not automatically executable arbitrage: fees, liquidity, funding, outcome disputes and venue credit risk can matter. Trading close time, event resolution time and cash settlement time are different clocks. A settled receivable is not necessarily immediately reusable cash.

atoms.title: Security events, earnings comparisons and contingent claims / Debt and equity offering sizes
atoms.text:
## Debt and equity offering sizes

An offering announced with an underwriters' or initial purchasers' option (over-allotment, greenshoe) has a base size and a final size. When a filing says the total issued "includes" an amount sold under the full or partial exercise of that option, the base size is the total minus the exercised amount. Report the size the task asks for (base, before over-allotment, or total, including it) and quote the sentence that splits them.

atoms.title: Security events, earnings comparisons and contingent claims / Availability and measurement
atoms.text:
## Availability and measurement

A filing's fiscal period identifies what it measures; publication time identifies when it can first enter a contemporaneous information set. An amendment changes available knowledge from its own availability date, unless the analysis explicitly uses a revised-history dataset. Same-period facts with different units, consolidation scope or duration do not become comparable merely by sharing a label. Signal dates, active positions and realized return periods must refer to the same economic timeline.

atoms.title: Security events, earnings comparisons and contingent claims / References
atoms.text:
## References

[Investor.gov, Stock Split](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary/stock-split), unchanged proportional ownership. [SEC, EDGAR APIs](https://www.sec.gov/search-filings/edgar-application-programming-interfaces), submissions and structured fact context. The holding-return and complementary-payoff identities are direct cashflow accounting.

atoms.title: Cleaning time series: sort, de-duplicate, fill, in a defined order
atoms.text: Use this when input rows must be sorted by time and duplicates removed before returns or signals are computed.

atoms.title: Cleaning time series: sort, de-duplicate, fill, in a defined order / Duplicates and "keep the last record"
atoms.text:
## Duplicates and "keep the last record"

- "Keep the last occurrence" refers to the order in which the records appear in the input. A sort only preserves that order among equal keys when it is stable: `df.sort_values("date", kind="stable")` (or `"mergesort"`). The pandas default (`kind="quicksort"`) may reorder rows with the same date, and `drop_duplicates("date", keep="last")` then keeps an arbitrary one of them.
- Equivalent alternatives: keep the original row number (`df.reset_index(names="row")`) and sort by `["date", "row"]`, or de-duplicate first (`df.drop_duplicates("date", keep="last")` on the input order) and sort afterwards. Use whichever matches the task's stated order of operations.
- With several keys (date and ticker), apply the same rule to the full key.

## Order of operations

Follow the task's stated sequence (for example sort, de-duplicate, forward-fill, drop remaining gaps). Forward-filling before removing duplicates, or dropping rows before filling, gives different prices on the affected dates and changes every return computed from them.

## Check

Count the rows removed as duplicates and compare with the number of repeated keys in the input. For a repeated key, print the input rows and the kept row, and confirm that the kept row is the last one in input order.

atoms.title: Cleaning time series: sort, de-duplicate, fill, in a defined order / Timestamps
atoms.text:
## Timestamps

- Keep the time of day. Parse timestamps with their time and zone (`pd.to_datetime(col, utc=True)`); flooring to dates (`.dt.date`, `.dt.normalize()`, `.dt.floor("D")`) or reading only the date part merges rows from the same day and moves an endpoint such as 16:00 to 00:00.
- Date-only bounds on timestamped data: an inclusive range `[start, end]` given as dates covers the whole end day. Comparing timestamps with `ts <= pd.Timestamp(end)` stops at 00:00 of the end day and drops its later records; use `ts < pd.Timestamp(end) + pd.Timedelta(days=1)` (and `ts >= pd.Timestamp(start)`), with both sides in the same time zone.
- Durations come from the full timestamps: `(t_end - t_start).total_seconds() / 86400` days, then the day-count basis the task states. Counting whole calendar days drops the hours.
- Writing a UTC timestamp as text: `ts.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")` after converting to UTC. `ts.isoformat()` already ends in `+00:00`; appending `"Z"` to it gives an invalid `+00:00Z`. Copy timestamps that the task passes through unchanged (input values echoed in an output) as the original strings.
- Check after cleaning: the row count equals the input count minus the rows the task says to remove (print each removal reason with its count), and the first and last timestamps match the input's, including the time of day.

A window of the last N usable observations is built by removing invalid rows (missing or non-finite values in the columns used) first, then keeping the last N. Slicing the last N rows first and dropping invalid ones afterwards leaves fewer than N and shifts the window start. Check the count after selection.

A month's final trading date is the latest date observed in that month in the data (for example `df.groupby(df.index.to_period('M')).tail(1)` or the index maximum per month). Calendar month-end labels from `resample('ME')` fall on weekends or holidays, and matching them against the data's dates drops those months.

atoms.title: VaR backtest coverage tests
atoms.text:
`viol` is the 0/1 violation series over T forecast days, x violations, alpha the expected violation rate (1 - level).
Use `xlx(k, p) = 0 if k == 0 else k * log(p)` so that 0 * log 0 = 0.

```python
viol = np.asarray(viol)[-T:]                        # only the T forecast days, not the estimation window before them
assert len(viol) == T
x = int(viol.sum())
pi = x / T
lr_uc = -2 * (xlx(x, alpha) + xlx(T - x, 1 - alpha) - xlx(x, pi) - xlx(T - x, 1 - pi))
n00 = n01 = n10 = n11 = 0
for a, b in zip(viol[:-1], viol[1:]):               # transitions between consecutive days
    n00 += a == 0 and b == 0; n01 += a == 0 and b == 1; n10 += a == 1 and b == 0; n11 += a == 1 and b == 1
p01 = n01 / (n00 + n01) if n00 + n01 else 0.0
p11 = n11 / (n10 + n11) if n10 + n11 else 0.0
p = (n01 + n11) / (n00 + n01 + n10 + n11)
l0 = xlx(n00 + n10, 1 - p) + xlx(n01 + n11, p)
l1 = xlx(n00, 1 - p01) + xlx(n01, p01) + xlx(n10, 1 - p11) + xlx(n11, p11)
lr_ind = -2 * (l0 - l1); lr_cc = lr_uc + lr_ind
p_uc, p_ind, p_cc = chi2.sf(lr_uc, 1), chi2.sf(lr_ind, 1), chi2.sf(lr_cc, 2)
```

With a single violation that is not followed by another, n11 = 0 and lr_ind is small but not zero.

atoms.title: Variance swaps and option-strip replication
atoms.text:
Use this reference to calculate a variance strike from an option strip and interpret realized-variance settlement and notional units.

Map task quantities to these definitions by meaning and units, not by letter, before the first calculation; recheck when inputs or conventions change.

Explicit task definitions and contract conventions take precedence. If they conflict or are incomplete, identify the ambiguity and state the convention used.

atoms.title: Variance swaps and option-strip replication / 1. Shared foundations
atoms.text:
## 1. Shared foundations
Symbols are local. $T>0$ is years, $D>0$ is the deterministic discount factor to expiry, $F>0$ the forward at that expiry, C(K)/P(K) discounted European call/put prices, and $K_{\mathrm{var}}$ the annualized variance strike in decimal-squared units. $K_{\mathrm{var}}$ is not volatility. A standard ideal replication assumes a positive continuous price process, deterministic carry and a sufficiently rich strike continuum. Discrete monitoring, jumps and finite strike coverage require qualifications.

atoms.title: Variance swaps and option-strip replication / 2. Continuous-strike replication
atoms.text:
## 2. Continuous-strike replication
For the ideal continuous-monitoring variance claim:
**Continuous-strike replication of the fair variance strike**

$$
K_{\mathrm{var}} = 2/(T\cdot D) \cdot  (\int _{0}^{F} \operatorname{P}(K)/K^{2} \mathrm{d}K + \int _{F}^{\infty} C(K)/K^{2} \mathrm{d}K).
$$

For the normalized log payoff $f(x)=-2\cdot \ln (x/F), f''(x)=2/x^{2}$. Its static option-strip representation, combined with dynamic trading and Ito's formula, gives this identity when the relevant expectations are finite and the trading stochastic integral has zero expectation. Under constant-volatility Black-Scholes it returns $\sigma^{2}$. With jumps, the log-contract jump term is not the squared-log-return jump term: do not call the strip an exact replication of an arbitrary realized-variance definition.

**Extract the forward from matched options**

Use puts below F and calls above F at the SAME maturity and consistent discount/carry. From matched call/put quotes, $F=K+(C-\operatorname{P})/D$. Cleaning rules, duplicate handling and quote selection come from the data contract. The model does not impose one universal cleaning policy.

atoms.title: Variance swaps and option-strip replication / 4. Settlement and units
atoms.text:
## 4. Settlement and units
Use the contract's realized-variance definition.
**Realized-variance convention**

For equally spaced adjacent log returns $x_{j}$, one common convention is $\mathrm{RV}=(A/N)\cdot \sum _{j} x_{j}^{2}$, where N is the number of included returns and A is observations per year. Demeaned sample variance with denominator N-1 is a different statistic. Missing observations, irregular intervals and annualization must follow the contract.

**Variance-swap settlement**

For a long variance notional $N_{\mathrm{var}}$ defined per unit decimal variance, payoff $=N_{\mathrm{var}}(\mathrm{RV}-K_{\mathrm{var}})$. Its present value at inception is zero at the fair strike under the stated model; a deterministic terminal scenario payoff is not automatically a present value. Multiply by the appropriate discount factor only if present value is requested.

**Variance and vega notional conversion**

If variance is quoted in percentage-squared units, decimal variance is multiplied by 10000 and the notional must change consistently. If vega notional $N_{\mathrm{vega}}$ is defined as derivative of payoff with respect to decimal realized volatility at strike $\sigma _{K}=\sqrt{K_{\mathrm{var}}}$, then $N_{\mathrm{vega}}=2\cdot \sigma _{K}\cdot N_{\mathrm{var}}$. Other unit conventions change the numerical conversion. A volatility swap has a square-root payoff and is not a variance swap.

atoms.title: Variance swaps and option-strip replication / 5. Checks and references
atoms.text:
## 5. Checks and references
Reproduce $\sigma^{2}$ from a synthetic flat Black-Scholes surface with converged integration; then vary strike density and endpoints separately. Check forward extraction with independent parity, nonnegative option weights, and notional units. Equality to ATM implied variance is not a general identity under a smile.
Cboe Volatility Index Mathematics Methodology, Section 3(a), documents the discrete convention in Section 3; it is not a universal variance-swap contract specification. The continuous representation and ledger conventions above are stated separately.
https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/indices/Cboe_Volatility_Index_Mathematics_Methodology.pdf

atoms.title: Variance swaps and option-strip replication / 3. Discrete strike conventions
atoms.text:
## 3. Discrete strike conventions
One approach numerically integrates the OTM price divided by K^2, inserting a split at F and stating the quadrature and tail treatment. Finite coverage omits nonnegative tails and need not reproduce the continuum integral.
A different, Cboe-style convention uses K0, the largest available strike not exceeding F:
**Discrete option-strip variance convention**

$$
K_{\mathrm{var}} \approx  2/(T\cdot D)\cdot \sum _{i} (\mathrm{DeltaK}_{i}/K_{i}^{2})\cdot Q_{i} - (F/\mathrm{K0}-1)^{2}/T.
$$

**Strike widths and option selection**

This discrete rule needs positive, distinct sorted strikes spanning the forward and enough strikes to define widths. Interior $\mathrm{DeltaK}_{i}=(K_{i+1}-K_{i-1})/2$; endpoint widths are the full adjacent gaps, $K_2-K_1$ and $K_n-K_{n-1}$. $Q_{i}$ is a put below K0, call above K0, and the average call/put at K0. Apply the required quote-selection rules. Do not add this correction to an unrelated quadrature formula without deriving the convention. Nonuniform strike spacing requires actual widths.

atoms.title: Degree-day indices and temperature-option valuation
atoms.text: Use this note for temperature-index contracts, historical burn valuation and seasonal Gaussian temperature models. Match the observation calendar, temperature scale, index unit and cash multiplier to the contract. Its explicit definitions govern; a convention from another city or exchange is not interchangeable.

atoms.title: Degree-day indices and temperature-option valuation / Index and payoff
atoms.text:
## Index and payoff

Let $T_{j}$ be the specified daily temperature statistic, b the reference temperature, and J the set of covered days. Heating degree-days measure temperatures below b.

$$
H_{j} = \max (b-T_{j}, 0)
$$

Cooling degree-days measure temperatures above b.

$$
C_{j} = \max (T_{j}-b, 0)
$$

The heating index accumulates the daily contributions, rather than taking the positive part of a monthly temperature difference.

$$
H = \sum _{j \in  J} H_{j}
$$

A call on the index, with strike K in degree-days and multiplier m in currency per degree-day, pays at its settlement date.

$$
\;\text{payoff}\; = m\cdot \max (H-K, 0)
$$

Temperature conversion changes the index unit as well as the base. Celsius conversion for a temperature level is affine.

$$
T_{C} = (5/9)\cdot (T_{F}-32)
$$

When both temperature and base are converted consistently, degree-day differences scale linearly.

$$
H_{C} = (5/9)\cdot H_{F}
$$

The same monetary contract then requires $K_{C}=(5/9)\cdot K_{F}$ and $m_{C}=(9/5)\cdot m_{F}$. A contract explicitly denominated in Celsius degree-days already has its own strike and multiplier; it is not a Fahrenheit contract merely because the base was supplied in Fahrenheit. Convert the strike only together with the index: when the index is computed in Fahrenheit degree-days (base in °F, temperatures converted to °F), the contract's Fahrenheit strike and multiplier are used unchanged → check that each year's payoff equals max(index − strike, 0) · multiplier with all three in the same unit. Summary fields named after the monthly index (a mean or standard deviation of monthly HDD, say) are statistics of the per-year monthly totals, the same numbers as the yearly table, not of the daily contributions; check that such a mean lies within the range of the yearly totals. Rounded regional base conventions are not exact unit conversion.

When the task asks for the target month's data to be cleaned and the temperature model fitted on that month's sample → the cleaned daily data, seasonal means, the fit, the simulation and the daily output file are restricted to that month's days in each year, and adjacent-day pairs are formed within the same month and year → check that the daily row count is about the number of years times the month's length. A task that calibrates on the whole year keeps the whole year.

atoms.title: Degree-day indices and temperature-option valuation / Historical and model valuations
atoms.text:
## Historical and model valuations

For Y comparable historical seasons, $H_{y}$ denotes each complete index. Discounted burn value averages each season's option payoff; D is the discount factor to payment.

$$
V_{\mathrm{burn}} = D\cdot m\cdot \sum _{y=1}^{Y} \max (H_{y}-K, 0)/Y
$$

This is generally different from an option payoff on the average index. Missing observations and climate trends change comparability; a partial season is not automatically a complete low-index season. Weather itself is not a traded replicating asset, so a physical historical expectation is a valuation convention, not a uniquely forced no-arbitrage price. State the probability measure or premium assumption when one is specified.

Write temperature as a deterministic seasonal curve s(t) plus a residual $x_{t}$. For a Gaussian OU residual with reversion level $\theta$, speed $\kappa >0$ and diffusion scale $\sigma$, a gap h has the following conditional mean.

$$
\operatorname{E}[x_{t+h} \vert  x_{t}] = \theta  + (x_{t}-\theta )\cdot \exp (-\kappa \cdot h)
$$

Its conditional variance uses the same time unit as $\kappa$ and $\sigma$.

$$
\operatorname{Var}[x_{t+h} \vert  x_{t}] = \sigma ^{2}\cdot (1-\exp (-2\cdot \kappa \cdot h))/(2\cdot \kappa )
$$

Observations of the same residual path are dependent. The first observation date may coincide with the known initial state or occur later; that distinction changes the index distribution. Exact OU transitions do not make Euler-based calibration an exact maximum-likelihood fit.

For independent simulated season payoffs $\operatorname{P}_{i}$, the Monte Carlo standard error is sampling uncertainty, not weather-model uncertainty.

$$
\mathrm{SE} = D\cdot \;\text{sample}\;_{\mathrm{std}}(\operatorname{P}_{i})/\sqrt{\mathrm{number}_{\mathrm{of},\mathrm{paths}}}
$$

A sensitivity is a derivative with respect to the bumped quantity. For a relative parameter bump e, the denominator in a central difference with respect to parameter a is 2*e*a, not 2*e. A zero parameter needs an absolute bump convention. Paired scenarios using common innovations reduce noise in the difference.

atoms.title: Degree-day indices and temperature-option valuation / Checks and sources
atoms.text:
## Checks and sources

Heating-call payoff is nonincreasing when all temperatures rise and nonincreasing in strike. Calendar and unit conversion should preserve the same economic contract. Historical and model prices need not coincide when their distributions differ.

[CME, Temperature Based Indexes](https://www.cmegroup.com/trading/weather/temperature-based-indexes.html) describes HDD/CDD/CAT and regional conventions. Index unit scaling, payoff aggregation and OU moments above follow directly from their definitions and the linear SDE solution; this is not a claim that all exchange contracts share one base or multiplier.

atoms.title: Age-weighted empirical loss distributions
atoms.text: Use this reference when past scenarios receive unequal probabilities, particularly exponentially decaying age weights. Probability weighting changes the empirical distribution; it is different from scaling each observation's return.

atoms.title: Age-weighted empirical loss distributions / Shared Foundations
atoms.text:
## Shared Foundations

$L_{i}$ is the loss in scenario i, with larger values representing worse outcomes. Map the task's return/loss sign, horizon, weighting clock, quantile interpolation and ES convention explicitly. Observation age and calendar age are not interchangeable.

For nonnegative ages $a_{i}$, newest age zero, and decay $0<\lambda \le 1$, normalized scenario probabilities are:

$$
p_i=\frac{\lambda^{a_i}}{\sum_j\lambda^{a_j}}
$$

At $\lambda =1$ all observations are equally weighted. Weights remain attached to their scenarios when losses are sorted. They are not reassigned according to loss severity.

atoms.title: Age-weighted empirical loss distributions / Quantile and tail mean
atoms.text:
## Quantile and tail mean

The weighted empirical cumulative distribution is:

$$
F(x) = \sum _{i} p_{i}\cdot \operatorname{indicator}(L_{i}\le x)
$$

The lower generalized-inverse loss quantile at confidence $0<\alpha <1$ is:

$$
q_{\alpha} = \inf \{x: F(x)\ge \alpha \}
$$

Round-off in cumulative normalized weights can move an exact atom boundary. Use a tolerance tied to floating-point summation error when testing that boundary, and check it against the exact count for equal weights; do not change the confidence level or merge genuinely different small probability masses. This step quantile differs from an interpolated sample quantile. An implementation's unweighted default does not define a universal weighted interpolation rule.

For integrated-quantile expected shortfall, include all probability above the threshold and only the needed part of the atom at the threshold:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha} = [\sum _{L_{i}>q_{\alpha}} p_{i}\cdot L_{i} \\
+ q_{\alpha}\cdot (1-\alpha -\sum _{L_{i}>q_{\alpha}} p_{i})]/(1-\alpha )
\end{gathered}
$$

The fraction of the atom used is nonnegative and no larger than its probability. This ES is generally not $\operatorname{E}[L\vert L\ge q_{\alpha}]$; the latter includes the entire threshold atom. If a task explicitly requests that conditional mean, it defines a different statistic.

An equivalent characterization, useful for an independent mathematical check, is:

$$
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha} = \min _{c} [c + \sum _{i} p_{i}\cdot \max (L_{i}-c,0)/(1-\alpha )]
$$

atoms.title: Age-weighted empirical loss distributions / Horizon and scope
atoms.text:
## Horizon and scope

For log returns $x_{t}$, a cumulative H-period log return is the sum of H consecutive values. For simple returns, cumulative return is $\prod (1+r_{t})-1$. These are different scenarios. Overlapping scenarios are statistically dependent; empirical quantiles still exist, but an iid uncertainty calculation need not apply. The age assigned to a multi-period scenario must correspond to a stated observation endpoint or other explicit convention.

If losses become $L_{\mathrm{new}}=a+bL$ with $b>0$, quantile and integrated ES transform affinely: $q_{\mathrm{new}}=a+b\cdot q_{\mathrm{old}}$ and $\operatorname{ES}_{\mathrm{new}}=a+b\cdot \operatorname{ES}_{\mathrm{old}}$. Equal weights recover the discrete empirical distribution, including its atoms. Greater emphasis on recent observations does not imply that risk must increase.

atoms.title: Age-weighted empirical loss distributions / References
atoms.text:
## References

[NumPy quantile documentation, weighted quantiles](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.quantile.html), for empirical probability and generalized-inverse conventions. Tail-atom and minimization identities follow directly by integrating the discrete loss quantile; no continuity assumption is needed.

atoms.text:

Work in the Python session one stage per cell, reusing what earlier cells left in memory. For example, for a task that
prices options from a curve file and a quote file and writes two result files (your stages will differ):
  cell 1: curve = pd.read_csv(...); quotes = pd.read_csv(...); params = json.load(...); print shapes and missing values
  cell 2: def build_curve(curve, params): ...      then  zc = build_curve(curve, params); print(zc.head())
  cell 3: def price(quotes, zc, params): ...       then  prices = price(quotes, zc, params); print a few checks

If cell 3 shows a mistake, the next cell is only the corrected def price(...), prices = price(...) and the checks;

atoms.title: arch 8.0.0: conventions and calls, as code / r
atoms.text: - `r`: daily decimal returns (Series).

atoms.title: arch 8.0.0: conventions and calls, as code / res
atoms.text: - `res`: an arch fit on `100 * r`.

atoms.title: arch 8.0.0: conventions and calls, as code / B = 252
atoms.text:
- `B = 252` trading days unless the task instructions name another count.
- The official description of each function is attached separately.

## 1. Fit a GARCH(1,1)

There are two cases, set by whether the task instructions fix the fitting units.

### Case 1 (default): the task instructions do not fix the fitting units

Fit percentage returns, `100 * r`, for numerical stability; then divide every output back to the units of `r`.

```python
res = arch_model(100 * r, vol="GARCH", p=1, o=0, q=1, mean="Zero", dist="normal", rescale=False).fit(disp="off")
omega = res.params["omega"] / 100**2                        # every variance and omega: / 100**2 (decimal units)
alpha, beta = res.params["alpha[1]"], res.params["beta[1]"] # unchanged by the scaling
cond_vol = res.conditional_volatility / 100                 # every volatility and mean: / 100
assert omega < 1e-3 and float(cond_vol.mean()) < 0.1, "still in percent units"
```

### Case 2: the task instructions fix the fitting units

For example "fit the raw returns, do not rescale": fit `r` as stated. Every output is already in the units of `r`;
no conversion.

```python
res = arch_model(r, vol="GARCH", p=1, o=0, q=1, mean="Zero", dist="normal", rescale=False).fit(disp="off")
omega = res.params["omega"]
alpha, beta = res.params["alpha[1]"], res.params["beta[1]"]
cond_vol = res.conditional_volatility
```

### Check either fit: did the optimizer move?

A fit can report `convergence_flag == 0` and still return the starting values unchanged; a case 2 fit on raw decimal
returns often does.

```python
start = res.model.volatility.starting_values(np.asarray(res.resid))   # where the optimizer began
assert not np.allclose(res.params.values[-len(start):], start), "fit did not move from the starting values"
```

Sections 2 and 3 write the case 1 conversions (`/ 100`, `/ 100**2`); in case 2 leave out the `/ 100` and `/ 100**2` conversions.

## 2. Pick the volatility the task instructions mean

There are two use cases. Match the task instructions to use case 1 or use case 2, then use the call listed under the matching use case.

### Use case 1: the volatility of a day inside the sample: `res.conditional_volatility`

Task instructions that ask for the "conditional volatility" of an in-sample day, or of the final in-sample day.
The value on day t is the volatility of day t's return, forecast on day t-1, so the value on day t does not use day t's return.

```python
sigma_for_t = res.conditional_volatility / 100              # day t: volatility of r[t], forecast on day t-1
sigma_last_fit = res.conditional_volatility.iloc[-1] / 100  # the final in-sample day
```

### Use case 2: a volatility forecast from a chosen day forward: `res.forecast(...)`

Task instructions that ask for a one-step-ahead forecast, the volatility of the next day, a volatility known at a
day's close, or a variance over the next H days. A forecast made on an origin day uses every return up to and
including that day.

```python
sigma_next = np.sqrt(res.forecast(horizon=1).variance.iloc[-1, 0]) / 100   # first day after the sample
sigma_close = np.sqrt(res.forecast(horizon=1, start=0, align="origin").variance["h.1"]) / 100   # day t: known once day t has closed
var_h_days = res.forecast(horizon=H).variance.iloc[-1].sum() / 100**2      # variance of the next H days, from the last day
```

Notes:

atoms.title: arch 8.0.0: conventions and calls, as code / sigma_close
atoms.text:
- `sigma_close` on day t equals `sigma_for_t` on day t+1: the same number, labeled one day apart.
- When the task instructions mention both the final observation and a one-step-ahead forecast, the words
  "one-step-ahead forecast" decide: use case 2, `sigma_next`.
- A rolling estimate refits on each window `r.iloc[end - W:end]` for `end in range(W, len(r) + 1)` and uses the
  `sigma_next` of each window's fit.

## 3. Long-run variance and annualized values

Turns the daily parameters and volatilities into the long-run and annual figures that task instructions usually ask for.

```python
assert alpha + beta < 1
long_run_var = omega / (1 - alpha - beta)                   # decimal daily variance
long_run_vol_ann = np.sqrt(B * long_run_var)                # an "unconditional / long-run volatility, annualized"
vol_ann = vol_daily * np.sqrt(B); var_ann = var_daily * B; mean_ann = mean_daily_log_return * B
assert 0.03 < long_run_vol_ann < 1.5 and 0.03 < float(np.nanmean(vol_ann)) < 1.5
```
- "Annualized" applies to every quantity labeled annualized: composite, portfolio and long-run volatilities alike.

## 4. Standardised residuals

The unit-free shocks used by EVT on GARCH residuals, filtered simulation and correlation models.

```python
z = res.std_resid                                           # residual / conditional volatility of the same day; the percent scaling cancels
assert abs(float(z.std()) - 1) < 0.2
```

## 5. VaR and ES as positive losses

Parametric normal VaR and ES at a tail probability, reported as positive numbers.

```python
tail = 0.01                                                 # tail probability = 1 - level (confidence level); "1% VaR" and "99% VaR" both mean tail = 0.01
z_q = norm.ppf(tail)                                        # -2.326
var_t = -(mu + sigma * z_q)                                 # keep mu unless the task instructions state a zero mean
es_t = -mu + sigma * norm.pdf(z_q) / tail                   # divide by the tail probability, not by the confidence level
assert es_t > var_t > 0
```
- If the task instructions, or the entry for the product, define an ES formula (for example ES scaled from VaR) or a VaR
  formula, the ES formula or VaR formula from the task instructions or the product entry replaces the `var_t` and `es_t` lines.

## 6. Warm-up of indicator signals

Rows where an indicator does not exist yet must carry no position.

```python
valid = fast.notna() & slow.notna()                         # np.where on NaN would return the else value (a full short)
signal = pd.DataFrame(np.where(fast > slow, 1.0, -1.0), index=fast.index, columns=fast.columns).where(valid)
```

## 7. Two consistency rules

- Every later step uses the return series the task instructions defined first (log or simple); do not rebuild returns from prices with
  the other definition, backtests included.

NumPy 2.5.3; statsmodels 0.15.0 are installed. Use only APIs that exist in this version: not older removed forms, and not newer or unverified ones.

When the task text specifies how to build something or forbids a function, follow the task text.

# LibraryReference: Regressions, coefficient indexing and robust errors

Build the intercept as specified. fit(cov_type='HAC',cov_kwds={'maxlags':L,'use_correction':False}) nests keywords; get_robustcov_results(cov_type='HAC',maxlags=L,use_correction=False) takes them directly. Bartlett is default; False omits T/(T-k). Set use_t explicitly. Robust-result params/tvalues are arrays: map model.exog_names. A sample-mean long-run variance with 1/T autocovariances is a different estimator, not an OLS shortcut.

```python
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm
x=np.arange(8.); X=np.column_stack([np.ones(8),x]); y=x+np.sin(x)
r=sm.OLS(y,X).fit(); h=r.get_robustcov_results(cov_type='HAC',maxlags=1,use_correction=False,use_t=False)
assert h.params.shape==(2,)
```

# LibraryReference: Manage random streams and paired simulation draws

RandomState/seed and default_rng do not produce interchangeable sequences. Keep the specified interface and draw order. For finite-difference simulation sensitivities, reuse the same base random variates for both bumps instead of advancing a shared stream independently. Preserve distribution parameter units and array shape. Pair antithetic draws deliberately; estimate uncertainty for the actual dependent sampling scheme.

```python
import numpy as np
z=np.random.default_rng(53).normal(size=12)
up=np.exp(.03+.2*z); down=np.exp(-.03+.2*z)
assert np.allclose(up/down,np.exp(.06))
```

# LibraryReference: Read typed local spreadsheet and columnar tables

read_excel(sheet_name=None) returns a sheet/DataFrame dict. openpyxl data_only reads cached formula values, not recalculation; missing caches can be None. Close workbooks. PyArrow read_table returns Table, then to_pandas; preserve_index=False avoids implicit index columns. For read_parquet inspect schema, timezones, nullable types and original row count before filtering. CSV date and numeric types require explicit parsing.

```python
import pandas as pd, pyarrow as pa, openpyxl
f=pd.DataFrame({'value':[2.,4.]}); t=pa.Table.from_pandas(f,preserve_index=False)
assert t.to_pandas().equals(f)
w=openpyxl.Workbook(); w.close()
```

atoms.title: LibraryReference: Pair lags before slicing rolling windows
atoms.text:
pandas 3.0.5 is installed. Use only APIs that exist in this version: not older removed forms, and not newer or unverified ones.

When the task text specifies how to build something or forbids a function, follow the task text.

# LibraryReference: Pair lags before slicing rolling windows

Create (lag,response) on the full timeline before slicing by response date; then jointly drop missing pairs. Slicing first loses the window's valid outside predecessor. rolling includes the current row; shift(1) moves values, freq moves labels. ewm(adjust=False) is recursive; adjust=True differs. Do not double-shift an engine's already lagged signal.

```python
import pandas as pd
s=pd.Series([3.,6.,2.,8.,4.])
pairs=pd.concat({'lag':s.shift(1),'response':s},axis=1).iloc[2:4].dropna()
assert pairs['lag'].tolist()==[6.,2.]
```

atoms.title: LibraryReference: Propagate a transition matrix over multiple periods
atoms.text:
NumPy 2.5.3; SciPy 1.18.1 are installed. Use only APIs that exist in this version: not older removed forms, and not newer or unverified ones.

When the task text specifies how to build something or forbids a function, follow the task text.

# LibraryReference: Propagate a transition matrix over multiple periods

Use matrix_power(P,h) for integer horizons, not elementwise P**h. A continuous-time generator uses expm(Q*t). Rows/columns must follow the stated convention. logm(P)/t may be complex or fail generator constraints; inspect imaginary parts, row sums and off-diagonal signs.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import expm
P=np.array([[.8,.2],[0.,1.]])
assert np.allclose(np.linalg.matrix_power(P,3),P@P@P)
Q=np.array([[-.3,.3],[0.,0.]]); assert np.allclose(expm(Q).sum(axis=1),1)
```

# LibraryReference: Fit and forecast conditional variance

arch_model(...,rescale=False).fit(disp='off') needs convergence_flag==0. Choose the specified mean/innovation model. If inputs are multiplied by 100, undo means/volatility by 100 and variance/omega by 10000; alpha/beta stay unchanged. forecast(...,align='origin',reindex=False) labels origins; residual_variance differs from total variance with mean dynamics. Analytical multistep support depends on model; preserve named fitted parameters.

```python
import numpy as np
from arch import arch_model
v=np.random.default_rng(47).normal(size=250)
r=arch_model(v,mean='Zero',rescale=False).fit(disp='off')
assert r.convergence_flag==0 and r.forecast(horizon=1,reindex=False).variance.shape[1]==1
```

# LibraryReference: Parse structured text and enumerate ordered pairs

ElementTree handles local XML structure; namespaces need a mapping or {URI}tag. find returns None for missing nodes: use is None, not element truthiness. Do not treat missing amounts as zero or replace XML structure with regex. itertools.combinations preserves input positions/order and avoids reversed pairs; do not reorder a specified universe with set. Standard json/csv/math/os remain available under standard-library-only constraints.

```python
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
from itertools import combinations
r=ET.fromstring('<r><v>2</v></r>'); assert r.findtext('v')=='2' and r.find('absent') is None
assert list(combinations(['a','b','c'],2))[0]==('a','b')
```

atoms.title: LibraryReference: NumPy: arrays, grouped accumulation and numerical linear algebra / mean(a, axis=None)
atoms.text:
- `mean(a, axis=None)` and `std(a, axis=None, ddof=0)` return a scalar or ndarray. The default population standard deviation uses ddof=0; request ddof=1 for a sample standard deviation. NaNs are not ignored automatically; use nanmean/nanstd explicitly when appropriate.
```python
assert np.asarray(x).shape == (4,); assert np.isclose(np.std(x,ddof=1)**2,np.var(x,ddof=1)); assert np.isnan(np.mean([1.,np.nan])); assert np.nanmean([1.,np.nan])==1.
```

atoms.title: LibraryReference: NumPy: arrays, grouped accumulation and numerical linear algebra / add.at(a, indices, b)
atoms.text:
- `add.at(a, indices, b)` returns None and accumulates repeated indices in place, one occurrence at a time. Advanced indexing `a[idx] += b` does not reliably accumulate repeated locations. `bincount(x,weights=None,minlength=0)` returns a one-dimensional ndarray; group keys must be nonnegative integers.
```python
z=np.zeros(3); np.add.at(z,[0,0,2],[2.,3.,7.]); assert np.array_equal(z,np.bincount([0,0,2],weights=[2.,3.,7.],minlength=3))
```

atoms.title: LibraryReference: NumPy: arrays, grouped accumulation and numerical linear algebra / linalg.solve(a,b)
atoms.text:
- `linalg.solve(a,b)` returns an ndarray solving a square system; prefer it to an explicit inverse. `linalg.lstsq(a,b,rcond=None)` returns (coefficients, residual sum of squares, rank, singular values); the residual array can be empty. `linalg.pinv(a,rcond=...)` returns a pseudoinverse ndarray.
```python
b=np.array([1.,4.]); assert np.allclose(A@np.linalg.solve(A,b),b); coef,ss,rank,sv=np.linalg.lstsq(A,b,rcond=None); assert rank==2; assert np.allclose(np.linalg.pinv(A,rcond=1e-12)@b,coef)
```

atoms.title: LibraryReference: NumPy: arrays, grouped accumulation and numerical linear algebra / linalg.matrix_power(a,n)
atoms.text:
- `linalg.matrix_power(a,n)` returns the integer matrix power as an ndarray; `a**n` is elementwise. `linalg.eigh(a)` returns ascending eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors in columns for a real symmetric matrix. Reverse the order when selecting the largest PCA components.
```python
assert np.allclose(np.linalg.matrix_power(A,3),A@A@A); val,vec=np.linalg.eigh(A); assert np.allclose(A@vec,vec*val); assert np.linalg.matrix_rank(A)==2
```

atoms.title: LibraryReference: NumPy: arrays, grouped accumulation and numerical linear algebra / random.default_rng(seed)
atoms.text:
- `random.default_rng(seed)` returns a Generator. Keep the generator and draw order fixed; use `.normal(size=...)` or `.choice(...)` without relying on global random state.
```python
assert np.array_equal(np.random.default_rng(17).normal(size=4),np.random.default_rng(17).normal(size=4)); assert np.random.default_rng(17).choice([-1,1],size=(3,4)).shape==(3,4)
```
Do not mix simple and log returns. Near zero, `log1p` and `expm1` are more stable than adding/subtracting separately around log/exp.
```python
assert np.allclose(np.expm1(np.log1p(x/100)),x/100)
```

atoms.title: LibraryReference: NumPy: arrays, grouped accumulation and numerical linear algebra / np.linspace(start,stop,num=50,endpoint=True)
atoms.text:
- `np.linspace(start,stop,num=50,endpoint=True)` returns equally spaced points as an ndarray; num counts points, not step size. `np.ones(shape,dtype=float)` creates the requested shape. `np.column_stack(tup)` stacks one-dimensional inputs as columns; `np.vstack(tup)` stacks along the first axis. `np.append(arr,values,axis=None)` returns a new array and flattens by default; it is not an in-place list append.
```python
assert np.linspace(-2.,2.,5).tolist()==[-2.,-1.,0.,1.,2.]; assert np.ones((2,3)).shape==(2,3); assert np.column_stack([np.ones(4),np.arange(4)]).shape==(4,2); assert np.vstack([np.ones((1,3)),np.zeros((1,3))]).shape==(2,3); assert np.append([2,3],[5]).tolist()==[2,3,5]
```

atoms.title: LibraryReference: NumPy: arrays, grouped accumulation and numerical linear algebra / np.gradient(f,*varargs,axis=None,edge_order=1)
atoms.text:
- `np.gradient(f,*varargs,axis=None,edge_order=1)` returns an ndarray for one-dimensional input, or a sequence of gradient arrays for multiple axes. Pass nonuniform coordinates through varargs. edge_order=2 uses a second-order boundary formula and requires at least three points on the axis. When two successive gradient calls are specified for a second derivative, use the same coordinates both times rather than substituting another stencil.
```python
coord=np.array([-2.,-.5,1.,3.]); values=coord**2; first=np.gradient(values,coord,edge_order=2); second=np.gradient(first,coord,edge_order=2); assert np.allclose(first,2*coord) and np.allclose(second,2.)
```

atoms.title: LibraryReference: NumPy: arrays, grouped accumulation and numerical linear algebra / np.corrcoef(x,y=None,rowvar=True)
atoms.text:
- `np.corrcoef(x,y=None,rowvar=True)` returns a correlation matrix. Variables occupy rows by default; use rowvar=False when samples occupy rows. Constant columns have undefined correlations. Dates and lagged observations are not aligned automatically. `np.dot(a,b)` contracts axes according to dimensionality; two-dimensional products can use @. `np.outer(a,b)` flattens inputs into an outer product, not an elementwise product.
```python
mat=np.column_stack([np.arange(6.),2*np.arange(6.)+3]); assert np.allclose(np.corrcoef(mat,rowvar=False),np.ones((2,2))); assert np.dot([1.,2.],[3.,4.])==11.; assert np.outer([2.,3.],[4.,5.]).shape==(2,2)
```

atoms.text:


atoms.title: LibraryReference: NumPy: arrays, grouped accumulation and numerical linear algebra / np.random.seed(seed)
atoms.text:
- `np.random.seed(seed)` returns None and resets legacy global state. `np.random.RandomState(seed)` creates a separate legacy generator; `np.random.default_rng(seed)` creates a new Generator. Equal seeds do not make all three produce the same sequence. Preserve a specified legacy interface rather than replacing it with default_rng, and do not reset the seed before each draw.
```python
np.random.seed(29); legacy=np.random.normal(size=5); state=np.random.RandomState(29); assert np.array_equal(legacy,state.normal(size=5)); assert not np.array_equal(legacy,np.random.default_rng(29).normal(size=5))
```

atoms.title: LibraryReference: NumPy: arrays, grouped accumulation and numerical linear algebra / np.cumsum(a,axis=None)
atoms.text:
- `np.cumsum(a,axis=None)` / `np.cumprod(a,axis=None)` return cumulative arrays. Simple-return wealth is cumprod(1+r); log-return wealth is exp(cumsum(r)). `np.prod` reduces the input; `np.maximum.accumulate` tracks the running maximum. `np.diag(v,k=0)` constructs a diagonal matrix from a vector or extracts a diagonal from a two-dimensional array.
```python
simple=np.array([.03,-.01,.02]); assert np.allclose(np.cumprod(1+simple),np.exp(np.cumsum(np.log1p(simple)))); assert np.isclose(np.prod(1+simple),np.cumprod(1+simple)[-1]); assert np.maximum.accumulate([2.,1.,4.]).tolist()==[2.,2.,4.]; assert np.diag(np.diag([2.,3.])).tolist()==[2.,3.]
```

## Version check: forms that fail in this version

### Removed or renamed forms
- fillna(method=...) -> ffill()/bfill().
- to_numeric(errors='ignore') -> errors='raise' or 'coerce'; handle invalid values explicitly.
- np.math -> Python math.
- groupby(axis=1) -> df.T.groupby(...).agg(...).T; check dtypes.
- resample('M') -> resample('ME'); to_period('M') still uses M.
- resample('Q') -> resample('QE').
- resample('Y') -> resample('YE').
- DataFrame.applymap -> DataFrame.map.
- np.trapz -> np.trapezoid.

### Unavailable or wrong-object forms
- np.clip(axis=...) -> np.clip(...); pandas DataFrame.clip still supports axis.
- pd.random -> the specified NumPy RNG interface.
- s.get_loc(label) -> s.index.get_loc(label).
- Series.to_series() -> omit it, or copy(); Index.to_series is valid.
- expanding().shift(...) -> aggregate before shift; ordering follows the definition.
- string Series.dt -> to_datetime(series).dt.
- ndarray.values -> the array itself.
- DatetimeIndex.dt.year -> index.year.
- datetime64.strftime -> pd.Timestamp(value).strftime(...).
- PeriodIndex.dt.year -> index.year.

Wrong/current executions are recorded in LibraryReference API compatibility evidence; absence is not inferred from API memory.

atoms.title: LibraryReference: SciPy: matrix functions, integration and interpolation / linalg.expm(A)
atoms.text:
- `linalg.expm(A)` returns a matrix exponential ndarray, for example from a generator to a transition matrix; it is neither elementwise exp nor an integer matrix power. `linalg.cholesky(a,lower=False)` returns a triangular ndarray, upper triangular by default. For simulation, use lower=True so L@L.T equals covariance.
```python
Q=np.array([[-.2,.2],[.1,-.1]]); P=linalg.expm(Q*2); assert np.allclose(P.sum(axis=1),1) and np.all(P>=0); L=linalg.cholesky(A,lower=True); assert np.allclose(L@L.T,A)
```

atoms.text:
- `scipy.linalg.logm(A)` returns a matrix logarithm ndarray, locally inverse to expm rather than elementwise log. - `pct_change(periods=1,fill_method=None)` returns fractional changes, not percentages. `std(ddof=1)` is sample standard deviation; pandas defaults to ddof=1, whereas NumPy defaults to 0.
```python
assert np.isclose(s.pct_change(fill_method=None).iloc[1],1.5); assert np.isclose(s.std(ddof=1),np.std(s.to_numpy(),ddof=1))
```
For AR pairing, first construct response=s and lag=s.shift(1) on the complete timeline, then restrict by response date and jointly drop missing pairs. Slicing before shifting loses the first response's valid predecessor outside the window. Preserve calendar gaps; do not independently drop missing values and splice the two sides by position.
```python
pairs=pd.concat({'response':s,'lag':s.shift(1)},axis=1); win=pairs.loc[s.index[2]:s.index[4]].dropna(); assert len(win)==3; assert win.iloc[0]['lag']==s.iloc[1]
```

atoms.title: LibraryReference: Time series: rolling windows, lag pairing and trading dates / DatetimeIndex.searchsorted(value,side='left')
atoms.text:
- `DatetimeIndex.searchsorted(value,side='left')` returns an insertion position and requires ascending dates. left selects the first date not earlier than the target; right selects strictly later. A position equal to the length means no next trading day exists and cannot be passed to iloc. Timezones must agree.
```python
calendar=pd.DatetimeIndex(['2021-03-05','2021-03-08','2021-03-09']); pos=calendar.searchsorted(pd.Timestamp('2021-03-06'),side='left'); assert pos<len(calendar) and calendar[pos]==pd.Timestamp('2021-03-08'); assert calendar.searchsorted(calendar[-1],side='right')==len(calendar)
```

atoms.title: LibraryReference: Time series: rolling windows, lag pairing and trading dates / Series.ewm(span=...,adjust=True,min_periods=0,ignore_na=False).mean()
atoms.text:
- `Series.ewm(span=...,adjust=True,min_periods=0,ignore_na=False).mean()` returns a Series on the same index. adjust=False uses a recursion with alpha=2/(span+1), initialized at the first valid observation. adjust=True normalizes finite-history weights, producing different short-sample results. ignore_na controls whether missing positions affect weighting; do not interchange EMA defaults.
```python
recursive=s.ewm(span=3,adjust=False).mean(); assert recursive.iloc[0]==s.iloc[0]; assert np.isclose(recursive.iloc[1],.5*s.iloc[1]+.5*s.iloc[0]); assert not np.isclose(recursive.iloc[1],s.ewm(span=3,adjust=True).mean().iloc[1])
```

## Version check: forms that fail in this version

### Removed or renamed forms
- fillna(method=...) -> ffill()/bfill().
- to_numeric(errors='ignore') -> errors='raise' or 'coerce'; handle invalid values explicitly.
- np.math -> Python math.
- groupby(axis=1) -> df.T.groupby(...).agg(...).T; check dtypes.
- resample('M') -> resample('ME'); to_period('M') still uses M.
- resample('Q') -> resample('QE').
- resample('Y') -> resample('YE').
- DataFrame.applymap -> DataFrame.map.
- np.trapz -> np.trapezoid.

### Unavailable or wrong-object forms
- np.clip(axis=...) -> np.clip(...); pandas DataFrame.clip still supports axis.
- pd.random -> the specified NumPy RNG interface.
- s.get_loc(label) -> s.index.get_loc(label).
- Series.to_series() -> omit it, or copy(); Index.to_series is valid.
- expanding().shift(...) -> aggregate before shift; ordering follows the definition.
- string Series.dt -> to_datetime(series).dt.
- ndarray.values -> the array itself.
- DatetimeIndex.dt.year -> index.year.
- datetime64.strftime -> pd.Timestamp(value).strftime(...).
- PeriodIndex.dt.year -> index.year.

atoms.title: LibraryReference: pandas: types, labels, joins and grouped sums / .loc[label]
atoms.text:
- `.loc[label]` selects labels and `.iloc[position]` selects positions. Series `s[0]` does not mean the first item. Filtering preserves original labels; NumPy delete/take accept positions only.
```python
sub=df.loc[df['value']>2]; assert sub.iloc[0].name==14; assert sub.loc[14,'value']==3.; assert np.delete(sub['value'].to_numpy(),0).tolist()==[7.]
```
- A `.loc` label slice includes both end labels: `.loc[:d]` and `.loc[a:b]` contain the rows labelled `d` and `b`. To stop before a label, use a boolean mask `index < d` or positions `.iloc[:i]`; choose the rule from the definition of the window, then check the first and last kept dates.
```python
w=pd.Series(1.,index=pd.to_datetime(['2024-01-02','2024-01-03','2024-01-04'])); d=pd.Timestamp('2024-01-03')
a=w.copy(); a.loc[:d]=0.; assert a.tolist()==[0.,0.,1.]; b=w.copy(); b.loc[b.index<d]=0.; assert b.tolist()==[0.,1.,1.]; assert len(w.loc['2024-01-02':'2024-01-03'])==2
```

atoms.title: LibraryReference: pandas: types, labels, joins and grouped sums / reindex(index=None,columns=None)
atoms.text:
- `reindex(index=None,columns=None)` aligns labels. Arithmetic also aligns labels; do not silently convert mismatches into NaNs and fill them with zero. `sort_values(by,kind='stable')` preserves the original order of ties; explicitly list every tie-breaking key for multi-column sorts.
```python
assert df['value'].reindex([19,11]).tolist()==[7.,2.]; assert df.sort_values('key',kind='stable').index.tolist()==[11,14,19]
```
pandas 3 uses Copy-on-Write: chained assignment cannot reliably modify the original table. Use one `.loc[mask,col]=value` assignment. `.to_numpy()` may return a read-only view; request copy=True if modifying it. Missing-return treatment follows the definition; do not forward-fill by default.
```python
cp=df.copy(); cp.loc[cp['key']=='a','value']=0.; assert cp['value'].tolist()==[0.,0.,7.]; arr=df['value'].to_numpy(copy=True); arr[0]=99.; assert df.iloc[0]['value']==2.
```

atoms.title: LibraryReference: pandas: types, labels, joins and grouped sums / DataFrame.drop_duplicates(subset=None,keep='first',ignore_index=False)
atoms.text:
- `DataFrame.drop_duplicates(subset=None,keep='first',ignore_index=False)` returns a new table by default. keep='last' retains the last occurrence in the current order, so define sorting and ties first. `Series/DataFrame.ffill(axis=None,limit=None)` returns a new object, propagating past observations along sorted time. Do not backfill future information or fill across different securities.

```python
dup=pd.DataFrame({'date':['2022-02-01','2022-02-01','2022-02-02'],'price':[3.,4.,np.nan]}); kept=dup.drop_duplicates(subset=['date'],keep='last'); assert kept['price'].ffill().tolist()==[4.,4.]
```

atoms.text:
- `add_constant(data,has_constant='skip')` returns a DataFrame/ndarray and does not normally add a duplicate constant. Align indices and drop missing rows jointly; do not filter y and X separately.


atoms.title: LibraryReference: statsmodels: regression, HAC and diagnostics / fit(cov_type='HAC',cov_kwds={'maxlags':L,'use_correction':False},use_t=False)
atoms.text:
- `fit(cov_type='HAC',cov_kwds={'maxlags':L,'use_correction':False},use_t=False)` preserves labeled results. Bartlett is the default kernel; maxlags is the largest included lag. False omits the T/(T-k) correction. use_t=False uses normal reference tails; True uses a t reference distribution. Covariance correction and reference distribution are distinct choices.

Predicting at one new point. add_constant treats its input as a column-ordered design matrix, so a 1-D list is a column of observations, not one row. sm.add_constant([1, x_new]) therefore builds two rows, [[1, 1], [1, x_new]], and predict(...)[0] returns the fit at x = 1 without raising an error. A single row has zero variance in every column, so with the default has_constant='skip', sm.add_constant(np.array([[x_new]])) returns it unchanged and adds no constant. Build the row explicitly instead:

```python
x_row = np.column_stack([np.ones(1), [x_new]])                      # shape (1, 2): [const, x]
# or: x_row = sm.add_constant(np.array([[x_new]]), has_constant='add')
y_hat = res.predict(x_row)[0]
assert np.isclose(y_hat, res.params[0] + res.params[1] * x_new)    # same as the hand-written line
```

For several regressors, pass one row in the same column order as the fitted exog, or compute params @ [1, x1, x2, ...] directly.
